case_summary.text: INCOME TAX : Where assessee was a works contractor and had income from various sources and Assessing Officer rejected assessee's account books and estimated net profit at 6 per cent on gross receipts, since sundry creditors of assessee was not examined by Assessing Officer, estimation of profit on contract receipts alone would be an erroneous exercise and it caused prejudice to interest of revenue

IT : Where a civil contractor did not produce salary and wage register and other evidences in support of expenses incurred, Assessing Officer was justified in estimating profit at 8 per cent of gross contract receipts

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, a civil contractor, who worked for State government departments furnished income at 3 per cent turnover based on estimates and contended that volume of work was higher and there was heavy competition which resulted in his inability to get more profits, since in previous assessment years AO estimated its net profit at 3.5 per cent, AO could not estimate net profit at 8 per cent under section 44AD in relevant assessment year on ground that assessee should have kept accounting records

IT : Where assessee, a civil contractor, did not maintain proper books of account and, thus, Commissioner (Appeals) having regard to profit margin of earlier years, adopted profit rate of 5 per cent of contractual receipts, in absence of any discussion on merits, Tribunal could not enhance said profit rate to 8 per cent of gross turnover by invoking provisions of section 44AD

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, a civil contractor with receipts exceeding Rs. 2 crores, did not maintain books of account and filed his return in ITR-2 estimating profit at 6 per cent of contract receipts, since assessee was not entitled to pay tax under section 44AD and Assessing Officer accepted said estimate after thorough analysis, Principal Commissioner could not invoke revisionary proceedings only on premise that income should be estimated at 8 per cent without citing any supporting

INCOME TAX : Where assessee was engaged in construction work and Assessing Officer rejected book results and estimated net profit at rate of 4 per cent of total contractual receipts as against 1 per cent declared by assessee and Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed appeal ex parte, matter was to be remanded back to Commissioner (Appeals) to decide issue on merit

INCOME TAX : Where explanation of assessee-contractor regarding decline in net profit was evasive and there were various defects in books of account of assessee, rejection of books of account was proper; however, in absence of any comparative instances of similar assessees in same line of business, it was appropriate to estimate profit at a percentage worked out on basis of preceding three years profit of assessee herself

IT: Where assessee, a civil contractor, declared net profit ratio of 5.64 per cent of gross contract receipts and Assessing Officer after rejecting book results determined total income by estimating net profit ratio of 15 per cent of gross receipts, income from contracting business be estimated by applying net profit ratio of 8 per cent of gross receipts

INCOME TAX : Where assessee engaged in civil construction business failed to produce necessary bills and vouchers and Assessing Officer after rejecting books of account under section 145(3), adopted 5 per cent net profit on gross receipts but failed to bring on record any comparable case of similar nature, since assessee agreed for estimation of 3 per cent profit on gross receipts, reasonable profit of 3 per cent on total receipts would meet ends of justice

INCOME TAX: Where assessee, a civil contractor executing works for Government departments/PWD, had all contractual receipts through banking channels and declared net profit rate of 6.06% on turnover, which was higher than presumptive rate of 6% prescribed under section 44AD, estimation of net profit at 15% without proper basis was unjustified, and AO was to be directed to recompute income by applying net profit rate of 7%

IT: Where in case of government contractor engaged in construction of roads books of account was rejected, Tribunal, relying upon profit rates of preceding three years, was justified in estimating profits earned by assessee during relevant years at 5 percent of gross receipts

INCOME TAX : Where during scrutiny assessment, Assessing Officer rejected books of account of assessee, a civil contractor and estimated income by applying rate of 8 per cent of contract receipt, no separate claim of depreciation is allowable as same was deemed to have been allowed in computing assessee's profit as per proviso to section 44AD

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in business of civil construction on contractual basis, followed project completion method in respect of contract receipts from one, GTEC, since said method of accounting was well recognized and was in consonance with standard accounting practice, Assessing Officer was not justified in estimating income of assessee at rate of 8 per cent on basis of contract receipts from GTEC

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, a civil contractor, who worked for State Government departments furnished income at 3 per cent turnover based on estimates and contended that volume of work was higher and there was heavy competition which resulted in his inability to get more profits, Tribunal was justified in upholding order of Commissioner (Appeals) in adopting net profit at 4 per cent from civil contracts in view of order passed in previous assessment years
IT: Where work carried out by assessee was not as a civil contractor but as a builder, provision of section 44AD could not be warranted to estimate gross profit at 8 per cent

INCOME TAX: Where assessee engaged in road construction disclosed audited net profit in returns and, in absence of any incriminating or distinguishing material, Assessing Officer estimated higher net profit mechanically, no interference was warranted with relief granted by Commissioner (Appeals) in restricting or deleting additions based on net profit estimation
INCOME TAX: AO not justified in applying 8% NP u/s 44AD in "no accounts, no audit" case of PWD contractor with Rs. 74 crores turnover; CIT(A)'s 4% NP estimate upheld

INCOME TAX : Assessee following percentage of completion method was required to produce a proper certification whether by in-house department of assessee or by an independent chartered engineer certifying percentage of work completed under contract, before Assessing Officer at time of assessment; mere qualification in Annual Report of company containing balance sheet and profit and loss account by itself was not sufficient to conclude that assessee had disclosed percentage of work completed during previous year relevant for assessment year; assessee having failed to produce relevant documents at time of assessment, reopening of assessment was justified

IT : Where there was difference in civil contract receipts shown by assessee in books of account and by contractee in form 26AS, net profit rate at rate of 8 per cent was to be applied to determine income embedded in said receipts
IT: Profit of contractor depend upon various factors like place of execution of contract, accessibility of labour, raw material, etc. and would, therefore, vary from contractor to contractor

IT: On rejection of books of account under section 145, profit margin of assessee, a sub-contractor, is to be estimated at rate much less than average profit margin worked out by Assessing Officer of its principal (i.e., contractor)

INCOME-TAX : Where assessee engaged in civil construction business failed to produce necessary bills and vouchers and the AO has rejected books of accounts u/s.145(3) and resorted to best judgement assessment as per provisions of section 144 and he adopted 5 % net profit on gross receipts but failed to bring on record any comparable case of similar nature and reason for adopting such rate of profit,

INCOME TAX : Where assessee was involved in execution of civil works and it had shown purchases from twelve parties even if assessee failed to produce said parties for verification, Assessing Officer could not have treated entire purchases as non-genuine purchases but only profit element on such purchases and thus, Appellate Authorities were justified in restricting addition by estimating profit of 12.5 per cent on total purchases

INCOME TAX : Where assessee had produced all books of account with bills, vouchers, confirmations etc. and AO rejected books of account of assessee relying upon proceedings before Settlement Commission for preceding assessment years and had not brought on record any irregularity or defects in books, bills and vouchers etc., addition made by Assessing Officer estimating net profit rate at rate of 10 per cent of gross contract receipts was rightly deleted by Commissioner (Appeals)
Net profit rate to be fixed on basis of past tax history of assessee, value of contract and price of raw materials

INCOME TAX : Where assessee carried on civil construction business and Assessing Officer rejected books of account as some of assessee's purchases were not verifiable, working of income at rate of 8 per cent of contract receipts was justified

INCOME TAX : Where assessee carried on civil construction business and Assessing Officer rejected books of account as some of assessee’s purchases were not verifiable, working of income at rate of 8 per cent of contract receipts was justified

INCOME TAX : Where during course of assessment proceedings, assessee-builder did not produce books of account and other documents as sought by Assessing Officer, Assessing Officer had rightly rejected books of account of assessee under section 145(3) and estimated income at rate of 10 per cent
Revision u/s 263 quashed as AO rightly accepted civil contractor’s voluntary 6% profit estimate, no error found: ITAT

IT : Where assessee-construction contractor explained that he did not accumulate construction materials to avoid pilferage and, hence, no stock register was required to be maintained, Assessing Officer could not reject books of account on this ground and apply net profit rate of 8 per cent

INCOME TAX : where assessee, engaged in construction of flats, was consistently following completed contract method of accounting and said method had been accepted by revenue authorities in past, there was no justification on part of Assessing Officer to change same and to determine income of assessee on estimate basis in assessment year in question

IT: Under circumstances of rejection of books of account in case of assessee being a civil contractor, presumptive statutory rate as prescribed under section 44AD provide a good guideline for purpose of estimation of income

IT: Where contract receipts and costs were accounted by assessee and were measurable, profit was to be computed based on actual revenue recognised (of which recovery was certain) and actual expenses incurred during financial year relevant to assessment year and not on basis of estimated costs

IT: Where assessee was fully engaged in labour oriented contract work and it had taken contracts from a construction company, which in turn had taken main contract from Government, Assessing Officer was directed to apply 5 per cent net profit on gross receipts of assessee
IT : Where assessee builder could not prove expenditure incurred with relevant books and vouchers, estimation of income at rate of 11 per cent was reasonable

INCOME TAX: Assessing Officer could not have rejected books of account of assessee and estimated gross profit at rate of 12 per cent of total sales turnover as against rate of 8.36 per cent without providing assessee an opportunity to present his claim

INCOME TAX : Where Assessing Officer rejected books of account of assessee under section 145(3) and applied 8 per cent net profit rate on total turnover and accordingly made addition as assessee failed to furnish relevant details, since even during appellate proceedings before CIT (Appeals) also assessee did not submit any submissions and CIT (Appeals) had decided appeal on basis of material available on record and merely upheld orders of Assessing Officer matter was to be set aside

INCOME TAX : Where assessee was a construction contractor, Assessing Officer was required to examine both revenues whether duly accounted for as per ICDS standard and secondly, examination of corresponding contract costs and other expenses in profit/loss account, and since Assessing Officer had failed to examine same, Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in setting aside assessment order for denovo framing

INCOME TAX : Where Assessing Officer rejected books of account of assessee under section 145(3) and applied 8 per cent net profit rate on total turnover and accordingly made addition as assessee failed to furnish relevant details, since even during appellate proceedings before CIT (Appeals) also assessee did not submit any submissions and CIT (Appeals) had decided appeal on basis of material available on record and merely upheld orders of Assessing Officer, matter was to be set aside to file of CIT (Appeals) to decide issue afresh

INCOME TAX : Where Assessing Officer completed assessment ex parte and brought gross professional receipts to tax without allowing deduction for expenses, since books of account maintained by assessee had not been rejected, there was no basis to disturb profits so declared as per books of account and, thus, net profit was to be determined at 68.19 per cent of gross professional receipts
7% net profit rate held reasonable for civil contractor as against AO's 15% estimate:ITAT

IT : Merely because, assessee's income from civil construction work had been accepted at six per cent of contract receipt in earlier year, it could not be ground to claim that for relevant year also, assessee's income was to be assessed at six per cent of contract receipt

INCOME TAX: Where dispute was only with regard to rate of gross profit on income which was not disclosed by assessee, it could not be said that Assessing Officer erred in adopting gross profit at rate of 2 per cent on undisclosed income declared by assessee

INCOME TAX : Where Assessing Officer rejected books of account of assessee, a wholesale trader, as parties to whom assessee made sales were untraceable and estimated gross profit at rate of 2 per cent on basis of invoices of sales and purchases filed by assessee,
Estimation of income by AO without disclosing to assessee materials relied upon by him wasn't justified
Profit rightly estimated on gross receipt as assessee failed to produce evidence in support of expenditures

INCOME TAX : Assessee following percentage of completion method was required to produce a proper certification whether by in-house department of assessee or by an independent chartered engineer certifying percentage of work completed under contract, before Assessing Officer at time of assessment;

IT : Discretion to determine net profit rate vested in authorities must be exercised on basis of relevant factors which are past tax history of assessee, an appraisal of value of contract, price of raw material, labour etc.

INCOME TAX : Where after rejection of books of account, impugned contract receipt had been included in total turnover/trading receipts for estimation of net profit then further addition of same amount was not permissible and allowable for making further addition

IT: Estimation of income made by Assessing Officer without disclosing materials relied on and also denying assessee an opportunity to rebut said material was not only in violation of statutory provisions, but also in violation of principles of natural justice

HEADNOTE: Section 143, read with section 256, of Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 33, read with section 66, of Indian Income tax Act, 1922] - Assessment - General - Assessment year 1924-25 - In respect of contracts spread over a number of years, assessee produced accounts but accounts for relevant accounting year could not be separated - ITO assessed profit at a standard rate without informing assessee of information or evidence on which rate was based and without giving him any opportunity to produce evidence in rebuttal - Whether question of law arose out of order of ITO - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, a contractor, was assessed to income-tax for the relevant assessment year in respect of certain contracts which commenced in 1922 and were finished some time in 1924. The assessee produced his accounts, but the accounts for the relevant accounting year could not be separated. The ITO considered the accounts to be unreliable. He, therefore, assumed profit at the standard rate of 10 per cent for the purposes of his assessment. On appeal, the Assistant Commissioner concluded that in any case it was impossible to ascertain from the assessee’s accounts what the income had been for one year and, therefore, the only way of ascertaining it was to apply the usual rate of 10 per cent on the total payments received. On application under section 66(2) of the 1922 Act, the Commissioner declined to make any reference.

On application under section 66 (3) of the 1922 Act.

HELD: In the instant case the assessee did not allege that he derived no income at all from any contracts, nor did the assessment proceed definitely on the ground that the accounts were unreliable. The Assistant Commissioner adopted a standard rate for the assessment merely because no separate accounts were available for the accounting year. This was apparently due to the manner in which the accounting were kept. As the assessee failed to produce correct and complete accounts for the accounting year, it was open to the Income-tax Officer to make an assessment to the best of his judgment: vide section 23, read with section 11, of the 1922 Act. The Assistant Commissioner, however, gave no reasons for adopting what he called the usual rate of 10 per cent for the purposes of the assessment, and it was not known how that rate was arrived at. In the circumstances of the case, the point of law emerged for decision was whether in the case of a contract spread over a number of years when accounts for the year under assessment could not be separated, the ITO was legally justified in assessing profits at a flat rate without informing the assessee of the information or evidence on which the rate was based and without giving him any opportunity to produce evidence in rebuttal.

Accordingly, the petition was accepted and the Commissioner was directed to state the case and refer the point of law to the High Court for decision.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

Sardha Ram for the Assessee .

Jagan Nath Aggarwal for the Crown.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment years 1957-58 to 1962-63 - Assessee was a contractor and undertaking jobs of various Govt. departments - Books of account of assessee were rejected by ITO and he determined assessee's income on estimate - Terms and conditions as to supply of materials by contractee was not known - Element of profit on such supply if any was to be ascertained and it was also not known whether assessee had submitted its tenders for said contracts anticipating on being assured of supply of such materials - Whether case was to be remanded back to Tribunal to ascertain terms and conditions of contract - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a contractor and undertook jobs under various Government departments. The books of account were maintained by the assessee. The were not accepted by the ITO at the time of assessment and the assessee's income was determined on estimate. For the assessment years 1957-58 to 1959-60, estimated amounts were added to the net receipts of the assessee. For 1959-60, this figure was 10 per cent on account of the materials supplied by the Government departments. For the assessment years 1957-58 and 1958-59, lump sum additions were made on this account. For the assessment year 1962-63, the ITO went into the matter in detail. The assessee was called upon to produce certificates from various authorities under which he had carried on the work. Independent enquiries were also made from such authorities. On the basis of the aforesaid the ITO came to the conclusion that the total gross receipts during the said year would be Rs. 7,76,000 as against the amount of Rs. 5,25,000 as shown by the assessee. On such material, the ITO also reopened the proceedings for the earlier assessment years including the assessment years 1954-55, 1955-56 and 1956-57. On appeal, the AAC held that in all the years the assessee's income should be determined by applying a flat rate of 12.5 per cent on the net receipts of the assessee and that the value of materials supplied to the assessee by the departments concerned should not be included in such net receipts for the purpose of application of this flat rate. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that, on the facts and circumstances, the original assessment orders made for the assessment years 1957-58 to 1959-60 were correct and thus set aside the reassessments made under section 147. The Tribunal further held that in respect of the assessment year 1962-63, the assessment made by the ITO was correct and the total receipts for the purpose of estimation of the assessee's profits should include the cost of materials supplied by the contractees.

On reference :

HELD: In the facts and circumstances of the instant case, it appeared that it was not possible to answer the questions referred without further findings on fact. It was not clear whether the lower authorities had seen or considered the terms and conditions of the contracts under which the assessee had carried on the work of construction. The terms and conditions as to supply of materials by the contractee were also not known.

Such terms were of some importance. It would be necessary to determine whether the materials to be supplied would be free of cost or price on the basis of market value or otherwise would be charged. On such facts it may be found that an element of profit was there on such supply (sic ). Whether the assessee submitted its tenders for the said contracts anticipating on being assured of supply of such materials were also not known. In this view, the matter was remanded back to the Tribunal. The Tribunal was directed to ascertain the terms and conditions of the contracts in question, if any, in respect of supply of materials and determine whether the assessee bid for such contracts taking into account such materials which were in fact supplied. If it was found on such facts that there was an element of profit involved in the materials supplied then the profits of the assessee will be estimated on the gross receipts of the assessee computed by including the value of the materials supplied to the net receipts. The Tribunal will be at liberty to take further evidence in the matter and will afford opportunity to the parties to adduce further evidence and to make further representations in the matter.

Note: Case remanded back.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 13 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Method of accounting - Valuation of stock - Assessment year 1959-60 - While completing assessment ITO did not accept assessee's reasons for low profits at rate of 9% in respect of a contract undertaken by him and applied flat rate of 12Â½% profit - On appeal assessee had not derived before AAC that full quantitative details were not available in respect of stores of value of Rs. 1,30,000 - For subsequent assessment year assessee declared a profit of 9.9% - Whether on facts provisions of section 13 were applicable to assessee's case and therefore, Tribunal was justified in upholding addition in assessee's income - Held, yes

FACT: The business of the assessee was execution of construction contracts. The assessee commenced its business from 25-1-1958, and the accounts were closed for the first time on 25-1-1959. During the accounting year the assessee undertook three contracts with respect to which it submitted separate profit and loss statements.

The accounts in respect of the first two contracts were accepted by the authorities under the Act in toto but with regard to the accounts relating to the third contract the ITO declined to accept the assessee's reasons for low profits at the rate of 9% in respect of that contract. He, therefore, applied a flat rate of 12Â½% profit and made certain addition to the assessee's income.

On appeal, the AAC had accepted the assessee's reasons for the low profit of 9% but had sustained an addition of Rs. 10,000 on the ground that the assessee's representative had not denied before him that full quantitative details might not be available in respect of the stores of the value of over Rs. 1,30,000 consumed in the execution of the contract. When the case came up before the Tribunal the addition of Rs. 10,000 was found to be excessive and was reduced to Rs. 6,000.

On reference :

HELD: In the instant case there was material before the Tribunal on which its finding could be based: the assessee's representative had admitted before the AAC that full quantitative details in respect of the stores of the value of Rs. 1,30,000 consumed in the execution of that contract might not be available. In the circumstances, recourse to estimating the profits on the contract was inevitable. He, therefore, made an addition of Rs. 10,000 as against Rs. 26,434 added by the ITO. If the assessee wished to displace the AAC's estimate it was open to him to adduce evidence in support of its claim that the consumption of stores of the value of Rs. 1,30,000 was fully justified. This the assessee apparently did not do. For the subsequent year 1960-61 the assessee itself declared a net profit rate of 9.9% as against 9% declared in the assessment year in question. It could not be disputed that this was additional material which the Tribunal could take into consideration as it did. There was thus material before the Tribunal on which its estimate was based. The Tribunal's decision was, therefore, in conformity with the decision in the case of CIT v. Maharajadhiraj of Darbhanga [1933] 1 ITR 94 (P.C.).

The Tribunal was therefore justified in holding that the proviso to section 13 was applicable and there was material before it to sustain the aforesaid addition.

In the case of a contractor, it cannot be said that merely because of incompleteness of the contract in the relevant accounting year profits of the assessee for that accounting year cannot be ascertained. It also cannot be said that merely because a contract was completed after the accounting year, no profit arose or accrued to the assessee in the accounting year. In the case of an incomplete contract there is a well-established method of calculating profits accruing in the accounting year. In the instant case, the Tribunal had found that for the assessment years 1939-40 and 1940-41 no accounts were kept for the contract the assessee had executed. For the assessment year 1943-44 he wrote a letter to the Income-tax Officer and admitted that he had no accounts to produce. For the assessment year 1944-45 he produced two sets of accounts. One was maintained for the two contracts he had taken from PWD but the profits of each contact was not separately worked out and there was one consolidated receipts and payments account for both the contracts. For the military contract he kept a separate set of accounts. These accounts were maintained from 14-4-1943 to 3-12-1944. The total value of contract was Rs. 3,78,766 and out of this the assessee received of Rs. 3,00,000 before 31-3-1944. He did not close the accounts on 31-3-1944, or prepare balance sheet but the accounts were kept open till 3-12-1944, when the execution of the contract was completed. It was argued on behalf of the assessee that the account are maintained on completed contract basis and the assessee had no objection if the income of the Hospital contract was taxed for the assessment year 1945-46 and that there was a single and indivisible contract for the Hospital and the work upon the entire contract was completed on 3-12-1944, and that was the proper date on which the profits should be ascertained. This argument was not acceptable if accounts are maintained and completed on contract basis the profits or gains of the previous year cannot properly be extracted from these accounts. For a contract may take several years for being completed. The payments in regard to the contract may also be received by the assessee in several years. It may be convenient for the assessee that profit should be ascertained on the completion of the contract and assessment of the profit should take place on the date of the completion of the contract. But section 3 imposes a charge of income-tax upon the profits and gains accruing to the assessee for the accounting year and it is the duty of the Income-tax authorities to make ascertainment of such profits and gains accruing to the assessee in respect of the payment received during the accounting year. Since the accounts maintained by the assessee did not correctly reflected the profits of the assessee for the accounting year the Tribunal was right in holding that the proviso to section 13 applied and that the ITO was entitled to discard the accounting method of the assessee and instead to make computation of the profits on such basis as he thought fit.

As regards the objection that the estimate of income on this formula would still be an estimate and would not be mathematically accurate, mathematical certainty is not demanded in a matter of this description.

The proviso to section 13 had been rightly applied by the Tribunal in regard to the accounts maintained for the contract business, which were not closed to profit at the end of each previous year but were closed to profit only after the completion of a contract.

PER AHMAD, J. (CONCURRENT VIEW ):

In the instant case the finding given by the Tribunal was that "the assessee never produced any account till the assessment in the present case and that no account was maintained by the assessee and therefore he had no method of accounting till 1943-44." On this finding of fact alone, therefore, the case attracted at once the operation of the rule of law laid down in the proviso, that is, it was the duty of the Income-tax Officer in such a state of facts to compute the income, profits and gains of the assessee upon such basis and in such manner as he thought best.

Even, however, if it be assumed in favour of the assessee, for which there was no evidence, that the account presented before the Income-tax Officer in the next year was one in accordance with a method regularly employed by the assessee, finding of fact given by the Tribunal that the method employed by the assessee in that account was such that the income, profits and gains could not properly be deduced there from. On that finding also the proviso to section 13 at once came into play and the duty was cast on the Income-tax Officer to compute the income, profit and gains of the assessee upon such basis and upon such manner as the income-tax Officer might determine.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

It is a dangerous proposition to recognise that the profit accrues only after the completion of a contract, Such a proposition is liable to be abused by dishonest taxpayers. It is a judicially recognised proposition that in the case of a contract in order to ascertain the income one need not wait till the contract is completed and that it is open to the revenue to estimate the profit on the basis of receipts in each year of construction, although the contract is not complete. Section 3 makes each previous year a distinct unit of time for the purpose of assessment and the profits made before or after that unit of time are entirely immaterial in assessing the profits of that year. In the case of contracts, if accounts are maintained and completed on contract basis, the profits or gains of the previous year can not properly be extracted from the accounts, for a contract may take several years for being completed and payment in regard to it may also be received by the assessee in several years. It may be convenient from the point of view of the assessee that profit should be ascertained on the completion of the contract and assessment of the profit should take place after the completion of the contract. But section 3 imposes a charge of income-tax upon the profits and gains of the assessee for the accounting year and it is the duty of the ITO to ascertain the profits and gains accruing to the assessee in respect of the payment received during the accounting year. It cannot be said that merely because a contract is completed after the accounting year, no profit arises or accrues to the assessee in the accounting year. In the case of an incomplete contract, there is a well-established method of calculating profits accruing in the accounting year. In such a contract, the long-term contract method is adopted in respect of contracts which have to be completed by stages over a course of years, such as, building contracts or building schemes by co- operative or private enterprise, or contracts entered into with public authorities such as public works, military, etc. The ascertainment of the profit in the execution of such contracts cannot be deferred till the completion of the entire constructions which may take several years. Each year’s profit shall have to be, in the nature of things, computed on an estimate, having regard to the work completed during the year. There are recognised methods of estimating with reasonable accuracy the profits accrued from time to time on uncompleted contracts. The fact that the contracts have not been completed or the accounts thereof have not been closed, is not sufficient reason for not estimating the profit of each year though absolute accuracy may not be reached. Thus, in a contract running over several years, the entire profits cannot be attributed to a single last year in which the contract was completed. The fact that it is not convenient or easy to allocate receipts or expendi- ture as against various items of trading assets is no reason for uphold- ing that profits emerge only after the entire expenditure on the assets has been recouped; the allocation of expenditure and receipts must somehow be made on a reasonable basis and the debts and trading assets valued on the closing date. In such cases, a workable method is for the revenue to assess on the basis of gross receipts of each year at a flat rate of profit on such receipts. The assessment in the case of a building

contractor, therefore, need not be postponed till the completion of the contract.

If the profits could reasonably be arrived at from year to year, such profit should be assessed from year to year only. In the instant case, the assessee had not correctly valued the closing work-in-progress and, therefore, it was the duty of the Assessing Officer to correctly value the closing work-in-progress: and arrive at the true picture of the profit. Thus, in the case of a building contractor, the revenue need not wait till the completion of the contract and the reasonable profit can be estimated from year to year and brought to tax.

Regarding the estimate of profits at 8 per cent there was no material on record to show that the estimate of profit at 8 per cent was excessive and unreasonable having regard to the facts of the case. However, the profit at 8 per cent estimated for these three years was only a mere estimate and the true profit of the entire project would be arrived at when the contract was complete. The assessee was, therefore, entitled to the adjustment of profit or loss in the year of completion of the contract. Hence, the estimate of profit at 8 per cent was reasonable.

HELD: Per Ramaswami, J.

The scheme and structure of the Income-tax Act, read with the Finance Act is to make the tax an annual tax for the purpose of assessment. Section 3 makes each "previous year" a distinct unit of time for the purpose of assessment and the profits made before or after that unit of time are entirely immaterial in assessing the profits of that year. If section 3 is read in the context of section 13, it is clear that the accounts maintained by the assessee must correctly show or reflect the profits of the preceding year. If the method of accounting adopted by the assessee does not reflect the true profits of the preceding year the proviso to section 13 will apply and the ITO would be entitled to compute the profits upon such basis and in such manner as he may determine.

In the case of a contractor, it cannot be said that merely because of incompleteness of the contract in the relevant accounting year profits of the assessee for that accounting year cannot be ascertained. It also cannot be said that merely because a contract was completed after the accounting year, no profit arose or accrued to the assessee in the accounting year. In the case of an incomplete contract there is a well-established method of calculating profits accruing in the accounting year.

FACT: On a search of the assessee’s premises under section 132 certain investments hitherto not disclosed were found. The Assessing Officer called for year-wise statements of receipts and outgoings for all the assessment years from 1980-81 and on the basis of such statements, he determined the assessee’s income. The assessee did not maintain regular books of account for his business in contract work and the income was admitted from year to year on the basis of estimates and assessed also on the basis of estimates. The assessee furnished statements of funds flow referred to as cash flow statements for various years. The total income determined for the assessment year 1985-86 was Rs. 6,10,070. On appeal, the assessee contended that the tax deducted at source by the Government could not be considered as an outgoing for the year. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, dismissed the assessee’s plea.

On second appeal :

HELD: The revenue would certainly be right in its submission if only the assessee had taken the gross receipts and set them off against all the outgoings including the tax deducted at source and the expenditure incurred or laid out on the contract work in earning the gross receipts before arriving at the profit in contract business. This method was not adopted by the assessee. The assessee had only estimated the ‘cash profits’ with reference to the gross receipts and thus the quantum of gross receipts was only intended to serve as a basis to measure the cash profit retained. HELD: It is true that there is no res judicata in the income-tax law and that the ITO has authority to take a different view from what has been taken in an earlier year. But neither he can exercise this authority in caprice, nor has he an unrestricted, unlimited, unconditional or absolute right in this matter. It was undisputed that the ITO had completed the assessments of the assessee’s income for the assessment years 1978-79 to 1981-82 on a flate rate basis observing, inter alia, that in the absence of maintenance of vouchers and receipts for the expenditure incurred by the assessee, the books of account were not acceptable. Now to examine whether the books of account kept in all the years inclusive of the year under appeal were maintained in the same manner or not, the trading and profit and loss accounts were the best available guide on which one should rely. There was no difference in the manner in which they had been kept in any of the assessment years inclusive of the assessment year under appeal. However, it was strange that though the assessee was a big contractor and executions of many of the contracts were spread in these years, no work-in-progress or closing stock had been recorded in the trading account. In view of the circumstances, it was not possible for the ITO to presume that the true profit could be computed on the basis of the books of account. He had overlooked the orders for the assessment years 1978-79 to 1981-82 framed by his predecessors. As a matter of fact, his finding was not very much different. He had also overlooked his own letter dated 16-2-1985 addressed to the assessee. Again, there was no whisper in his order as to what were the defects in the earlier years, which were not present in the relevant assessment year. He failed to prove his finding. Accordingly, the reasoning of the ITO to change the mode of assessment could not be accepted and the estimate of profit at a flat rate method as adopted in earlier years in the same circumstances should also apply in the assessment year under appeal, except that, in view of the finding that a large amount of expenses claimed was unestablished, the profit rate to be applied should be 12½ per cent instead of 10 per cent adopted for the earlier years.

from facts or even as a guess work it has not been arrived at by an honest exercise of judgment, it may be disturbed by the appellate authority or Tribunal. In the instant case, the ITO arrived at the figure on the basis of the receipts extending over three accounting year. He took the sum total of these receipts to be the base for the net income that had accrued to the assessee during the accounting year 1943-44 as the entire contract work had been completed during that year. Mere execution of the contract work will not necessarily entitle the contractor to make a demand for payment until it is ascertained that the works are up to the standard agreed upon between the parties. Some parts of such work may be wholly rejected and like bad debts in every earning may be ignored in computing the gains or profits. It might have been open to the ITO, in exercise of his discretion, to make an enquiry into whether and when the bills for payment became due to the assessee. Much depended upon the terms in the contract, and the manner of its performance. Even as a basis of guess work, which the Income-tax Officer was entitled to do, the basis could not be said to be in consonance with honest guess work. The ITO did not seem to have taken into consideration why the payments which, according to him, were due to the assessee in the accounting year were not fully paid till three years after. Sometimes the payments to the contractors are withheld on account of unsatisfactory execution and they are held entitled to payments only if and when they replace the rejected work by acceptable and accepted ones. The bare possibility of such contingency could not be wholly eliminated in the instant case. If the ITO, in arriving at the figure for assessment, left out these considerations, he certainly could not be said to have exercised his judgment which he was none the less called upon to do in making the assessment in cases of assessee's default under sections 23(4) and 13 proviso of the 1922 Act. Any method of accounting adopted by the ITO acting under the proviso of section 13 of 1922 Act can be rejected if the method in fact does not show the true income, profits and gains. In this view of the matter, the Appellate Tribunal was right in asking the ITO to assess the assessee on receipt basis with regard to contracts carried out and completed during the year of accounting, there being every presumption that the incomes were paid as soon as they became due. At any rate, the Tribunal's decision might be upheld on the ground that when two methods of guess work are available for the purpose of assessment, the one which is more just to the assessee and which involves a much less margin of chance of uncertainty should be taken as the basis.

In the result, the Tribunal was right in asking the ITO to assess the assessee on receipts basis with regard to contracts carried on and completed during the year of account.

As regards the reduction of flat rate, the Appellate Tribunal had arrived at the lesser flat rate on the basis of their decisions in similar cases in the district. Their opinions were not receivable evidence in the instant case. The decisions in different cases must have been based upon different facts and different inferences deducible from such facts. In this connection, it might be observed that the ITO had been very fair to the assessee bearing in mind the difference between the gross value and net value of the bills. The Appellate Tribunal, therefore, did commit a mistake of law in arriving at a finding for which there was no relevant evidence to support.

Therefore, the reduction of the estimated profit rate from 40 per cent adopted by the ITO to 30 per cent by the Tribunal on the ground that 30 per cent was the general rate adopted by it in the cases of other assessees doing the same kind of contract works during the same assessment year was not legal.

Note : The case was partially decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 3 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 2(11) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Previous year - Assessment year 1959-60 - In respect of a contract work for which no accounts were maintained till completion is for a period of 2 years and 8 months, ITO adopted 30th September as accounting year, for assessment year 1958-59, as was done by assessee in respect of other sources of income - Succeeding ITO however relying on section 2(11)(i) of 1922 Act, took year ending 31st March as previous year and apportioned profits between assessment years 1958-59 and 1959-60 - Whether words “previous year" ordinarily means a period from 1st April to 31st March but if assessee wants to adopt any other period, then his accounts must be made up for that period and if, those accounts are not made up for that period, he cannot ask for that period - Held, yes - Whether since accounts had not been made up for over a period of 2 years and 8 months, assessee could not adopt any other period than 1st April to 31st March - Held, yes - Whether, therefore adoption by ITO of accounting period from October to September for year of assessment 1958-59, could not be conclusive, nor could next ITO be barred from adopting correct accounting period in terms of section 2(11)(i)(a) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether questions about estimation of profit on gross amount instead of on net amount received by assessee after deduction of costs of material supplied by Government or about apportionment of profit to be made over a period of 4 years instead of 2 years, not having been raised at any stage of assessment proceedings, could not be gone into - Held, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 1959-60, the assessee, an individual contractor, having other sources of income also, had undertaken to complete the building contract work, the contract having been undertaken much earlier. The contract started on 1-1-1957 and was completed on 30-8-1959. Accounts maintained for this business were, however, closed only once i.e., when the contracts were completed; so much so, the profit from the contracts was ascertained for the entire period from 1-1-1957, to 30-8-1959, when the accounts were so closed and not periodically with reference to any previous year. For the assessment year 1-1-1957 to 30-8-1959, the ITO had adopted the previous year as the year ending with 30th September, because the assessee was maintaining accounts from October to September in respect of his other businesses, such as film exhibition business, medical stores, etc., and this was also the accounting period which he preferred for the earlier assessment year in respect of the contract business.

For the assessment year 1959-60, the succeeding ITO, however, adopted the accounting period ending on 31st March as the previous year, and apportioned the profits as between the two assessment years 1958-59 and 1959-60. He further estimated the profit on the gross amount and not on the net amount received by the assessee after deduction of costs of material supplied by the Government. On second appeal, the Tribunal upheld the ITO’s assessments.

On reference :

HELD: The adoption by the ITO of the previous year, October to September, for the assessment year 1958-59, was wrongly adopted, because it did not satisfy the requirements of section 2(11)(i)(a ). It was only in cases where the assessee could adopt a different period to the financial year, 1st April to 31st March, that any other period could be adopted, which would invariably mean a period of twelve months. This was also subject to the requirement of the section.

"Previous year" ordinarily means a period from 1st April to 31st March. But if the assessee wanted to adopt any other period, then his accounts must be made up for that period. If, however, those accounts were not made up for that period, he could not ask for that period. In the instant case, admittedly the accounts had not been made up for over a period of 2 years and 8 months, so that the assessee could not adopt any other period than 1st April to 31st March. In these circumstances, the adoption by the ITO of the accounting period from October to September for year of assessment 1958-59, could not be conclusive, nor could the next ITO be barred from adopting the correct accounting period in terms of section 2(11)(i )(a).

Section 145, read with section 263, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (Revision) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee was a works contractor, who in addition to said income had income from a firm, house property and other sources - Assessing Officer rejected account books of assessee on premise that it had failed to produce bills and vouchers of materials purchased and estimated net profit at 6 per cent on gross receipts of assessee to which other incomes were added - Commissioner took revisional proceedings against assessee and having found that sundry creditors of assessee having not been examined by Assessing Officer held assessment order to be erroneous - It was noted that whether unexplained sundry credits are added to contract receipts or as income from other sources definitely tax payable by assessee would be higher than that paid by a mere estimation of net profit - Whether since sundry creditors having been not examined by Assessing Officer, estimation of profit on contract receipts alone would be an erroneous exercise and it caused prejudice to interests of revenue - Held, yes [Para 13] [In favour of revenue]

FACT: The assessee was a works contractor, who in addition to the said income had income from a firm, house property and other sources.

The Assessing Officer looked at the account books and directed the assessee to produce the bills and vouchers of the materials purchased.

The assessee having failed to produce the same, the Assessing Officer rejected the account books and estimated the net profit at 6 per cent on the gross receipts of the assessee to which the other incomes were added.

On appeal to the High Court by revenue:

HELD: The Assessing Officer had estimated the gross profit at 6 per cent of the total receipts and had completed the assessment after adding the income from other sources also. The sundry creditors, as is seen from the explanation offered by the assessee before the Commissioner, came to Rs. 3.44 crores out of which the liability in the previous year was Rs. 1.92 crores. Obviously this was not noticed by the Assessing Officer and presumably the same was not accounted in the total receipts as undisclosed income. If the sundry credits are not explained properly, then disclosing that in the account books would amount to a device employed to suppress the income received, as a credit taken by a third party, with whom the assessee had a transaction. The assessee explained the reasons for low profit as to that the company has been in the construction industry for more than two decades. The company for quite some years focused its core activity in civil works consisting of mostly industrial/housing structures. Besides such civil contracts, the company diversified its activities into cement industry, wind power, manufacture of cylinders and other incidental jobs. Heavy losses resulted in closure of its cement division during financial year 1999-2000. The company also started focusing on infrastructure projects because of its line of business in construction and contracts. Hence, in the initial years, the company had undertaken some of the smaller projects especially the road works outside the State of Andhra Pradesh. To intrude into the competitive section like this, and to withstand the obvious competition from the established giants and multinationals, obviously the company had to quote the price in tenders either without a profit or with nominal profit. the contrary, as against the standard norm of 25 per cent labour charges amounting to Rs. 91.13 lakhs, the assessee had actually incurred only Rs. 75.37 lakhs, which worked out to be at 20.67 per cent. Income-tax provisions nowhere either authorize the Assessing Officer or cast an obligation on the assessee to prove the negative result, i.e., to prove as to why he had failed to make a profit at a particular rate. The accounts may be rejected as unreliable if important entries and transactions are omitted therefrom or if proper particulars and vouchers, bills, etc., are not forthcoming or if they do not include entries relating to particular class of business transaction. Reasons for rejecting wages record as commented by the Assessing Officer related to full address of the labour, which was not given on the muster roll register. The wages record had been kept by the assessee as per regulation known as 'Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970. The addresses of the labourers to whom wages had been paid were not mentioned, since the labourers stayed in the Jhugi Jhoperies at a work site itself and to that effect the assessee had already replied to the Assessing Officer vide its letter dated 23-3-2001, through which site of construction where labourers resided was given which was, however, not taken notice of by the Assessing Officer and the same was sent to him by courier and was found to be duly received by the Assessing Officer. The Assessing Officer had also alleged that the actual date of payment was not mentioned by the payee receiving the wages. The date on which the entry had been made in the wages register was the actual date of payment. As per the nature of the contract work executed by the assessee, he had got a contract to carry out a particular job or a contract for which the material was supplied by the CPWD/DOT and the labour was provided by the assessee-contractor. The assessee used to make payments to the labourers on the basis of mandays put in by the labourers and not on the basis of work performed by them on each day. Therefore, there was no merit in the allegations of the Assessing Officer that work performed by the labour was not mentioned on the payment vouchers and in making them as basis for rejection of books of account. The payment to the assessee-contractor was also made on the basis of work completed which was measured by the department itself and not on the basis of what the labourer had done. The bills for such a contract were prepared, which were not verified by the engineers of contractee before making payments. On the basis of those bills which were finally approved by the Government engineers/contractee, the payment was given to the assessee-contractor after deducting TDS. Thus, it was humanly not possible to provide the details as to what work a particular labourer had done at the site. Further, the Assessing Officer had also not indicated any defect in the system of accounting regularly followed by the assessee, or its correctness, nor was there any change in the method of accounting during the year under consideration as compared to the earlier years to indicate any intention of the assessee to show low profit.

While examining the books of the assessee, the Assessing Officer has to consider the following aspects : (i) whether the assessee has regularly employed a method of accounting; (ii) even if regular adoption of a method of accounting is there, whether the annual profits can properly be deduced from the method employed; (iii ) whether the accounts have been correctly maintained; (iv) whether the accounts maintained are complete in the sense that there is no significant omission therein. If the answers to above four questions would be in the affirmative, then the assessee's profits would be computed on the basis of his accounts. In such cases, proviso to section 145(1) or section 145(2) cannot be invoked. On the perusal of the materials placed on record in the instant case, it was found that the answers to all the above four questions were in the affirmative. No finding had been recorded by either of the lower authorities as to the unacceptability of the method and to the irregularity of the accounts kept by the assessee. It is well-settled that in the absence of such a finding recorded by the authorities, the book results cannot be ignored or brushed aside.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits Assessment year 1964-65 - Assessee was a military contractor - Finding some irregularities in accounts, ITO assessed profits of assessee from military contracts by applying flat rate of 10 per cent on total receipts - Tribunal held that price of stores supplied by Government was to be excluded while applying flat rate to assessee's contract receipts - Whether order passed by Tribunal was justified - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a military contractor. During the relevant accounting period, the assessee took three military engineering service contracts. On reference, the Division Bench noticed the divergent views taken by the various High Courts and particularly because of the challenge laid to the correctness of the judgment in Brij Bhushan Lal v. CIT [1971] 81 ITR 497 (Punj.) and, thus, referred the matter for decision of the Full Bench.

HELD: The Supreme Court in Brij Bhushan Lal Parduman Kumar v. Section 5 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income - Accrual of - Assessment years 1981-82 to 1983-84 - Whether profit in a building contract accrues from year to year - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company had undertaken a project of construction of a multi-storeyed building. For the assessment years 1981-82 to 1983-84, it had realised certain amounts as the sale proceeds of a few flats. However, the assessee had filed ‘nil’ return for all the three years on the plea that in the case of a building contractor the profits should not be assessed on year-to-year basis and the ascertainment of the profit could be done only after the contract work was completed. The Assessing Officer, however, was of the view that the method of accounting followed by the assessee being defective and incomplete, did not lead to the correct computation of income. According to him, the assessee would put on credit side any amount in order to bring the profit to ‘nil’. The Assessing Officer accordingly applied the provisions of section 145 and computed the business income of the assessee at 8 per cent of the receipts. In addition, he disallowed the interest payment under the provisions of section 40A(8). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the determination of business income at 8 per cent, being reasonable. He,

however, deleted the addition in respect of interest payments on the ground that the business profit of the assessee had been estimated under section 145, and, therefore, such estimate should be deemed to include the disallowable interest under section 40A(8).

On cross-appeals:

HELD: The profit in a long-term contract should be taxed on year-to-year basis. It is a dangerous proposition to recognise that the profit accrues only after the completion of a contract, Such a proposition is liable to be abused by dishonest taxpayers. It is a judicially recognised proposition that in the case of a contract in order to ascertain the income one need not wait till the contract is completed and that it is open to the revenue to estimate the profit on the basis of receipts in each year of construction, although the contract is not complete.

For the relevant assessments year, it received certain amount on account of work done from the authorities concerned. Apart from the payments on account of work done, the assessee had also received cement, steel and bricks from the concerned department. The assessee’s case before the ITO was that since it had not earned any profit on the value of the materials received by it from the Government, no profit should be charged from it. That contention was not accepted by the ITO and he estimated the gross profit at five per cent on value of materials also. The assessee's appeals before the AAC on this question having failed, it took up the matter in further appeal before the Tribunal. The Tribunal referred the matter back to the ITO with a view to examine the tenders and find out as to whether the assessee had calculated its profit on the value of the materials while submitting the tenders and, if that was so, then estimate the reasonable profit on such value. If, on the other hand, it was found that the assessee was under an understanding that the department concerned would supply the required materials to it for the execution of those contracts and the assessee adjusted its rates on that basis, then there would not arise any occasion for estimating any profit on the value of the materials supplied. For that reason, the Tribunal remanded the case to the ITO.

On reference :

HELD: The view taken by the Tribunal was correct.

the observations, it was to be held that when the Assessing Officer offered to apply a net profit rate of more than 11 per cent, the assessee had only alternatively given a counter-proposal which, in fact, was not acted upon by the Department and as such, such an offer made thereof by the appellant was of no consequence and the same did not bind the assessee in any manner and, accordingly, it could not be validly held that the instant assessment was an agreed assessment. Having come to the conclusion that the proposal made by the assessee was not a binding proposal and as such not an agreed assessment, the next question for consideration was as to what could be the reasonable profit that could have been applied on the basis of material on record and the submissions of the parties. On that issue, the observations of the Accountant Member as well as the findings for arriving at the conclusion for application of profit rate of 8 per cent were contained in his order. The Bench fully agreed with the findings as well as the observations contained in the orders of the Accountant Member. As pointed out by the Accountant Member, the Assessing Officer himself had analysed each and every transaction with reference to the reply furnished by the assessee and he was of the firm opinion that the assessee could justify only a few transactions and the Assessing Officer, however, did not bring any material with respect to any remaining transactions with which he was not satisfied though admittedly the reply thereto was duly furnished by the assessee; that merely because some of the sub-contractors could not be produced at the relevant time could not lead to the conclusion of application of exorbitant rate of 11 per cent, that too without giving a finding that the expenditure so claimed was not for business necessity or that it did not relate wholly and exclusively for the purpose of business or the carrying on of business as required under section 37; and that, in fact, the Assessing Officer did ask the assessee through various queries to give explanation but he had not stated basis of its estimate nor given chance to the assessee to rebut basis for or the application of arriving at the precision rate of 11 per cent.

As observed by the Accountant Member, assessment is a quasi-judicial proceeding in which the personal will or rough estimation does not have any place, that the Assessing Officer is bound to disclose the mental process through which he arrived at a particular figure of income as his orders are being subjected to appeal and, therefore, should be speaking one. The Accountant Member observed that it was evident from the past history of the appellant that never a profit rate of more than 7 per cent was applied in the case of the appellant, more particularly when two of the past assessments had already been completed as a consequence of the search and incriminating documents as alleged in the year under appeal were also available with the Assessing Officer in those assessments; that keeping in view the peculiar circumstances like nature of business, expenses on public issue, etc., in the year under appeal, the assessee’s own history for the earlier years, over all facts, findings and circumstances of the case, suppression of profits having not been established, allegations having not been proved, explanation rendered by the appellant and the legislative history, that there was no justification in applying or confirming net profit rate of 11 per cent and that the ad-hoc application of 8 per cent net profit rate subject to allowability of depreciation and interest thereon in the case of the assessee was justified.

The department referred to the statement of ‘S’, in reply to a query as to what was the income of the company from the contract work usually. He replied that it was 10 per cent to 15 per cent to the total receipts. That statement was taken at the time of search without confronting ‘S’ with the books of account or any contract work specifically. The question posed to him was not in respect of the specific income of the year under consideration nor do the income from total contract work of the assessee. There was no clarification sought by the authorized officer or by the Assessing Officer as to the fact whether the said ‘S’ was stating so in respect of any of a single venture forming part of the one and individual business of the appellant comprised of several contract works secured by it, for which the assessee had maintained a combined profit and loss account or it was only a hypothetical calculation. The affidavit filed before the Assessing Officer of the same person was also not found false. The statement so given before the authorized officer was, thus, not a conclusive statement as the same was not based on any material on record but was only on approximation basis and not relevant to the facts of the case. The statement also did not quantify any correct rate as to whether it should be 10 per cent or 11 per cent or any higher rate. Thus, the statement so given by ‘S’ was of no credence and the same could not be used against the assessee for applying a profit rate of 11 per cent, which was not supported by any material or basis and was contrary to the facts of the case.
