HEADNOTE: Section 143 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Assessment - Addition to income - Assessment year 1993-94 - Assessing Officer disallowed 1 per cent of labour payments and material purchase expenses on ground that in respect of internal vouchers genuineness could not be ascertained for want of details - Assessee contended that complete details with bills, vouchers, labour registers, etc., were produced but no comments were made by Assessing Officer and that percentage of gross profit on sales had actually gone up as compared to previous year - Assessing Officer had not made any averment that books of account were not correct or defective - Whether since additions made were not based on any cogent material nor any basis given for arriving at figure of one per cent, first appellate authority had rightly deleted addition - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a contractor. The Assessing Officer noticed that for the assessment year 1993-94, the net profit from contract came to less than 1 per cent of the net receipt which was more than rupees one crore. The Assessing Officer was of the view that in respect of materials purchased and labour payments, which were based on several internal vouchers, the genuineness could not be ascertained in the absence of complete details. He, therefore, disallowed 1 per cent of the expenses relating to the above as inflated expenses and added the same to the total income of the assessee. The assessee contended that the disallowance was arbitrary and based on assumptions, conjectures and surmises; that complete details of all purchases along with bills, vouchers, etc., and full details of labour payments with labour registers were being maintained and the same were also produced before the Assessing Officer but no comments were made by the Assessing Officer; that the percentage of the gross profit on sales in the assessment year under appeal had actually gone up as compared to the earlier year. The first appellate authority deleted the addition.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: The revenue had not brought any material on record to controvert the submission of the assessee. The additions made by the Assessing Officer were not based on cogent material. The Assessing Officer had not given any basis for arriving at the figure of 1 per cent of the expenses shown by the assessee on account of material purchases and labour payments. There was no averment by the Assessing Officer that the books of account maintained by the assessee were not correct or contained any defect. The Assessing Officer did not adopt any basis for increase made by him. As held by the Supreme Court in the case of State of Orissa v. Maharaja Sri B.P. Singh Deo [1970] 76 ITR 690 that the mere fact that the material placed by the assessee before the assessing authorities was unreliable did not empower the authorities to make an arbitrary order. In view of the above facts and for the reasons stated hereinabove, the assessee’s contention was to be upheld.

Sampat Kr. Jain and K.K. Jain for the Appellant. S.K. Malakar for the Respondent.

headnotes.text: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment years 1957-58 to 1962-63 - Assessee was a contractor and undertaking jobs of various Govt. departments - Books of account of assessee were rejected by ITO and he determined assessee's income on estimate - Terms and conditions as to supply of materials by contractee was not known - Element of profit on such supply if any was to be ascertained and it was also not known whether assessee had submitted its tenders for said contracts anticipating on being assured of supply of such materials - Whether case was to be remanded back to Tribunal to ascertain terms and conditions of contract - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment years 1964-65 and 1965-66 - Assessee was carried on business of executing contracts for Government - He received gross amounts of bills for assessment years 1964-65 and 1965-66 from Government - As assessee did not maintain any books of account, ITO applied net profit rate of 12.6 per cent on gross bill amounts and computed total income for two years - Assessee contended that cost of materials supplied by Government should have been deducted before applying net profit rate - Tribunal held that assessee though tendered contract as a whole, it must have included cost of material which were supplied by Government as an element of profit in respect of cost of material also - Whether since there was no evidence on record to show that assessee did not know about supply of material by Government to be made or at what price and furthermore gross profit had been computed on total gross bill of assessee, it could not be said that Tribunal was indulging in any surmise, or acting without any proper evidence - Held, yes

Section 143, read with section 256, of Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 33, read with section 66, of Indian Income tax Act, 1922] - Assessment - General - Assessment year 1924-25 - In respect of contracts spread over a number of years, assessee produced accounts but accounts for relevant accounting year could not be separated - ITO assessed profit at a standard rate without informing assessee of information or evidence on which rate was based and without giving him any opportunity to produce evidence in rebuttal - Whether question of law arose out of order of ITO - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 13, Proviso to the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Method of accounting - Works contract - Assessment year 1944-45 - Whether merely because a contract was completed after relevant accounting year, it could not be said that no profits arose or accrued to assessee in that accounting year - Held, yes - Assessee was a contractor - As contracts entered into by assessee were not completed during accounting year in question, no income therefrom was declared on ground that no profits accrued on incomplete contracts - Assessee maintained no accounts till accounting year relevant to assessment year 1943-44 and accounts maintained for accounting year relevant to assessment year 1944-45 were not closed on 31-3-1944 but were kept open till execution of contract was completed - These accounts did not reflect profits of assessee for accounting year in question - Whether in instant case proviso to section 13 was applicable and ITO was entitled to discard accounting method of assessee and estimate profits on such basis as he thought fit - Held, yes - Whether objection of assessee that estimate of income on his formula would still be an estimate and would not be mathematically accurate had no substance as mathematical certainty is not demanded in a matter of this description - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits - Assessment years 1970-71 and 1971-72 - Assessee carried on business of undertaking public works contracts - It received cement, steel, bricks etc. from public works department - Its case before ITO was that since it had not earned any profits on value of materials received, no profit should be charged from it - ITO, however, estimated gross profit at five per cent on value of materials - On appeal Tribunal however, referred matter back to ITO with a view to examine tenders and find out as to whether assessee had calculated its profits on value of materials while submitting tenders - If that was so, ITO could estimate reasonable profit on such value - If, on other hand, it was seen that assessee had understanding with department that it would supply materials for execution of contracts and assessee adjusted its rate on that basis, profit on value of material supplied could not be estimated - Whether, on facts, order passed by Tribunal was correct - Held, yes

Section 145, read with section 144, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Rejection of accounts - Assessment years 1993-94 to 1997-98 - Assessee-firm was engaged in work of civil construction in Public Works Department (PWD) - Assessing Officer, after rejecting books of account, made assessment determining 8 per cent profit at flat rate - Commissioner (Appeals) reduced rate of profit from 8 per cent to 5 per cent on ground that since turnover of assessee exceeded Rs. 40 lakhs, it was bound to incur more expenses and rate of profit would be less - Further, Tribunal reduced profit rate to 4 per cent on ground that assessee was doing work for PWD and normally, profit rate was much less for work of PWD, as contract work had to be done under certain specifications and under supervision of PWD authorities - Whether rate of profit cannot be assumed, merely on assumptions or surmises and conjectures - Held, yes - Whether since Assessing Officer as well as Commissioner (Appeals) as also Tribunal had not recorded any finding based on any material and findings recorded were merely based on surmises and conjectures, findings of rate of profit could not be sustained and 
 matter deserved to be remanded to assessing authority for re-determination thereof - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income- Assessment year 2010-11 - Where despite various opportunities given, assessee, civil contractor failed to produce books of account and relevant vouchers and there had been a lot of variation in profit rate of assessee during different years, Assessing Officer was justified in rejecting audited balance-sheet filed by assessee and making assessment by applying net profit rate of 12 per cent [In favour of revenue]

Section 144, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Best judgment assessment - Assessment year 1974-75 - Whether while making a best judgment assessment, though there must necessarily be guess work in matter, it must not be arbitrary - Held, yes - Assessee-contractor did not main books of account - He filed his return of income on estimate basis by computing profit at flat rate of 10 per cent on gross receipts - ITO, however, computed net profit at rate of 15 per cent - Revision petition filed by assessee was dismissed by Commissioner - Whether since neither ITO nor Commissioner had referred to any material for applying flat rate of 
15 percent while estimating net profits, impugned orders passed by them deserved to be set aside - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment year 2001-02 - Assessee, a labour contractor, failed to produce books of account and vouchers to justify expenses made against gross receipts - Therefore, Assessing Officer estimated net profit rate at 8 per cent against 1.52 per cent shown by assessee - On appeal, Tribunal reduced net profit rate to 6.5 per cent - Whether there was any justification to interfere with order passed by Tribunal - Held, no

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment year 1966-67 - ITO rejected books produced by assessee, a liquor contractor and estimated sales - Thereafter, taking into consideration case of another liquor contractor of very same area for an earlier year, profit was estimated at 7½ per cent on estimated sale - Whether in absence of better material revenue was well justified in taking into consideration case relating to another liquor contractor of very area in respect of earlier year - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, rate of profit at 7½ per cent was justifiably applied on turn over of assessee - Held, yes

Section 145, read with section 263, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (Revision) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee was a works contractor, who in addition to said income had income from a firm, house property and other sources - Assessing Officer rejected account books of assessee on premise that it had failed to produce bills and vouchers of materials purchased and estimated net profit at 6 per cent on gross receipts of assessee to which other incomes were added - Commissioner took revisional proceedings against assessee and having found that sundry creditors of assessee having not been examined by Assessing Officer held assessment order to be erroneous - It was noted that whether unexplained sundry credits are added to contract receipts or as income from other sources definitely tax payable by assessee would be higher than that paid by a mere estimation of net profit - Whether since sundry creditors having been not examined by Assessing Officer, estimation of profit on contract receipts alone would be an erroneous exercise and it caused prejudice to interests of revenue - Held, yes [Para 13] [In favour of revenue]

Section 145, read with section 263, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (Revision) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee was a works contractor, who in addition to said income had income from a firm, house property and other sources - Assessing Officer rejected account books of assessee on premise that it had failed to produce bills and vouchers of materials purchased and estimated net profit at 6 per cent on gross receipts of assessee to which other incomes were added - Commissioner took revisional proceedings against assessee and having found that sundry creditors of assessee having not been examined by Assessing Officer held assessment order to be erroneous - It was noted that whether unexplained sundry credits are added to contract receipts or as income from other sources definitely tax payable by assessee would be higher than that paid by a mere estimation of net profit - Whether since sundry creditors having been not examined by Assessing Officer, estimation of profit on contract receipts alone would be an erroneous exercise and it caused prejudice to interests of revenue - Held, yes [Para 13] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where assessee was a works contractor and had income from various sources and Assessing Officer rejected assessee's account books and estimated net profit at 6 per cent on gross receipts, since sundry creditors of assessee was not examined by Assessing Officer, estimation of profit on contract receipts alone would be an erroneous exercise and it caused prejudice to interest of revenue

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Rejection of accounts - Assessment years 1981-82 to 1983-84 - Assessee was engaged in construction of flats and since project was not complete, it claimed that no profit accrued during the construction period and that in case of a building contractor profits should not be assessed on year-to-year basis but at end of contract work - Assessing Officer held that method of accounting followed by assessee was defective and, consequently, by applying provisions of section 145 computed assessee’s business income at 8 per cent of receipts - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) upheld computation of business income - Whether in case of building contractor, profits should be assessed on year-to-year basis, and, thus, in absence of material to the contrary, profit at 8 per cent estimated by Assessing Officer was neither excessive nor unreasonable - Held, yes

Section 145, read with section 144 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income - Civil contract work - Assessment year 2007-08 - In view of non-maintenance of proper books of account by assessee-contractor, revenue authorities estimated its net income at 8 per cent of gross receipts - It was found that assessee made purchases more than 80 per cent which were billed and were forming part of gross receipts from contractees - Whether remaining amount could not fetch 8 per cent as per provisions of section 44AD when assessee rendered civil contract work without material - Held yes - Whether it was also not case of assessee to make profit of 8 per cent on material cost and in this view of matter, it would be reasonable to estimate income on gross receipts at rate of 6 per cent - Held, yes [Para 8] [In favour of assessee]

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income - Civil contract work - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessing Officer estimated assessee's income at 8 per cent of gross receipts - He made additions on account of disallowance of sundry creditors which had increased not in proportion to increase in material cost thereby indicating that assessee had raised bills on contractees when material cost was still to be borne by assessee - Whether, estimation of 8 per cent after deleting additions and disallowance was not proper and 7 per cent profit on gross receipts would be reasonable - Held, yes [Para 8] [In favour of assessee]

Section 28 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Assessee, carrying contract work under government departments, did not maintain proper account books - Whether net profit could be estimated at a flat rate on gross receipts including value of material supplied by government - Held, on facts, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Rejection of accounts (Illustrations) - Assessment year 2010-11 - Assessee was a contractor - Assessing Officer rejected books of account of assessee on ground that assessee failed to verify genuineness of opening and closing balance of labour charges payable and, accordingly, assessed net profit at 12 per cent - Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed rejection of books of account but reduced net profit rate from 12 per cent to 5 per cent - It was found that assessee failed to verify genuineness of opening and closing balance of labour payable or furnish details called for by Assessing Officer or justify quantitative and qualitative details of closing stock - Further, queries raised by Assessing Officer were not properly addressed and assessee was not able to rebut findings given by Assessing Officer - Whether, therefore, rejection of books of account was justified - Held, yes - Whether since true picture of profits earned by assessee could not be found out due to substantial defects in maintenance of books of account, it was reasonable to estimate profit of assessee by applying net profit rate of 8 per cent - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 12] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where assessee failed to verify genuineness of opening and closing balance of labour charges payable or furnish details called for by Assessing Officer, rejection of books of account was justified

u Section 145 of Income-tax Act, 1961
Where assessee, a construction company, did not maintain any books of account and it was also an undisputed fact that the assessee did not produce before the Assessing Officer the vouchers or any other documentary evidence to support the correctness of various expenses shown in the profit and loss account submitted long with the returns of income, Assessing Officer was justified in estimating assessee’s profits by applying net profit rate
Eastern Construction Co. v. ITO [1997] 59 TTJ (Delhi) 723
It is true that the assessing Officer, while making the best judgment, has to make a fair, just and reasonable estimate of income. Such estimation of profit in a fair and just manner could be done by the Assessing Officer either by applying a net profit rate on the contract receipts or he could also estimate the profit in any other manner which can be regarded as fair and reasonable. 
Where assessee, a construction company, did not maintain any books of account and it was also an undisputed fact that the assessee did not produce before the Assessing Officer the vouchers or any other documentary evidence to support the correctness of various expenses shown in the profit and loss account submitted long with the returns of income, and the Assessing Officer completed assessment by resorting to section 145 and he estimated profits by applying net profit rate of 12.5 per cent : 
Held that, on the facts of the case, it was incumbent upon by the Assessing Officer to have resorted to estimation of profit from the contract business. It could not, therefore, be said that the method of computing the taxable income adopted by the Assessing Officer while making the best judgment was patently erroneous or invalid. The year under consideration was the first accounting year of the firm. The contention that the income ought to have been assessed on the basis of past assessed history was, therefore, not relevant and justified on the facts of the present case.

Section 3 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 2(11) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Previous year - Assessment year 1959-60 - In respect of a contract work for which no accounts were maintained till completion is for a period of 2 years and 8 months, ITO adopted 30th September as accounting year, for assessment year 1958-59, as was done by assessee in respect of other sources of income - Succeeding ITO however relying on section 2(11)(i) of 1922 Act, took year ending 31st March as previous year and apportioned profits between assessment years 1958-59 and 1959-60 - Whether words “previous year" ordinarily means a period from 1st April to 31st March but if assessee wants to adopt any other period, then his accounts must be made up for that period and if, those accounts are not made up for that period, he cannot ask for that period - Held, yes - Whether since accounts had not been made up for over a period of 2 years and 8 months, assessee could not adopt any other period than 1st April to 31st March - Held, yes - Whether, therefore adoption by ITO of accounting period from October to September for year of assessment 1958-59, could not be conclusive, nor could next ITO be barred from adopting correct accounting period in terms of section 2(11)(i)(a) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether questions about estimation of profit on gross amount instead of on net amount received by assessee after deduction of costs of material supplied by Government or about apportionment of profit to be made over a period of 4 years instead of 2 years, not having been raised at any stage of assessment proceedings, could not be gone into - Held, yes

Section 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Rejection of accounts (Estimation of profit) - Assessment year 2014-15 - Assessee was engaged as civil contractor - Assessing Officer being not satisfied with explanation of assessee regarding decline in net profit rejected account books and estimated net profit at rate of 10 per cent of turnover - Whether in light of various defects/deficiencies/irregularities along with assessee’s evasive approach towards explanation sought by Assessing Officer, allegation that rejection of books was done in arbitrary manner did not hold any ground and, thus, rejection of books of account was justified - Held, yes - Whether however, in absence of any comparative instances of similar assessees in same line of business, it was appropriate to estimate profit at a percentage worked out on basis of preceding three years profit of assessee herself - Held, yes [Paras 10 and 12] [Partly in favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where explanation of assessee-contractor regarding decline in net profit was evasive and there were various defects in books of account of assessee, rejection of books of account was proper; however, in absence of any comparative instances of similar assessees in same line of business, it was appropriate to estimate profit at a percentage worked out on basis of preceding three years profit of assessee herself

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimate of profits - Assessment year 1985-86 - Assessee, a contractor, did not maintain regular books of account - Assessee had only estimated cash profit with reference to gross receipts and, thus, quantum of gross receipt was only intended to serve as a basis to measure cash profit retained - Assessee contended that tax deducted at source by Government could not be considered as an outgoing for year - Whether there was substance in plea of assessee that tax deducted at source could not be considered as having to come out of profits thus estimated - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits - Assessment year 1992-93 - Assessee-contractor declared profit rate of 9.3 per cent - Assessing Officer in view of higher profit rate in earlier two years enhanced it to 11.5 per cent - However, no comparable case was cited - Assessee explained that fall in profit rate was due to execution of huge pending works of earlier year and price hike of materials as a result of gulf war - Whether having regard to specific reasons given by assessee for fall of gross profit rate in assessment year in question together with fact that in assessee’s own case for assessment year 1986-87, Tribunal held profit rate 9 per cent to be reasonable, conclusion/finding of Commissioner (Appeals) in treating profit rate of 9.3 per cent in current year was reasonable, proper and justified - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (Rate of income) - Assessment year 2007-08 - Assessee was a contractor and undertook works for municipal corporation - Assessee declared a net taxable income which represented his share of profit from a firm, in addition to his own income from proprietary concern - During course of assessment proceedings, Assessing Officer made enquiries into loans taken, purchases made, genuineness of some sub-contracts awarded by assessee and penalty paid by him - Assessing Officer treated said sums as income of assessee - Commissioner (Appeals) took cognizance of several irregularities in accounts of assessee and estimated income of assessee at 8 per cent of turnover - On cross-appeals, assessee contended that rate of estimated income was to be 6.5 per cent whereas revenue contended that estimated rate of income by Commissioner (Appeals) was on lower side - Tribunal concluded that in comparable cases net profit rate had varied from 2.93 per cent to 9.96 per cent; but these were big concerns, which maintained proper accounts and also maintained quality standards and in instant case accounts were not reliable and, hence, estimation of net profit at 8 per cent was justified - Whether since estimation of net profit by Assessing Officer was on higher side, Tribunal's order was to be upheld - Held, yes [Paras 7 and 8] [Partly in favour of assessee]IT : Where Tribunal after referring to comparable cases applied net profit at 8 per cent, since estimation of net profit by Assessing Officer was on higher side, order passed by Tribunal was justified

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income (In case of estimation of profit) - Assessment year 1995-96 - Assessee was a contractor and assessee declared its income at an estimated 3 per cent of contract receipts - Search took place in assessee's premises and in view of seized materials Assessing Officer gave due opportunity to assessee to justify disclosed income and explain discrepancies noticed by special auditor - Assessee was also permitted to inspect seized documents - Despite that assessee could not explain said discrepancies - Accordingly Assessing Officer resorted to estimation of profits by adopting 11 per cent on gross contract receipts and initiated penalty proceedings - Whether there was gross or wilful negligence on part of assessee in failing to return correct income, penalty would be levied under section 271(1)(c) - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of revenue]IT: Where assessee could not explain discrepancies noticed by special auditor and disclosed a lesser income than what it actually earned, penalty under section 271(1)(c) was to be levied

Section 145(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Assessment year 1989-90 - Assessee was in business of construction of ownership flats - He got part of work done through sub-contractors and claimed deduction of payment made to them but failed to produce them for examination - Details of payment of salary, etc., to staff were also not furnished - Basis of valuing work-in-progress was also not given -Whether on facts ITO was justified in invoking provisions of section 145(1) and making an estimated addition of Rs. 30,000 to be returned net profit - Held, yes.

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 13 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Method of accounting - Rejection of accounts - Assessment year 1943-44 - Whether while making assessment under section 23(3), it is open to ITO to take into account other materials that may come to his knowledge apart from accounts submitted by assessee but principles of natural justice require that assessee should be given opportunity to rebut any inference that may be drawn against him from such other material and though for that purpose he is not bound to disclose actual source of information he should indicate to assessee that he intended to use additional material against him and give him opportunity to have his say regarding it - Held, yes - In his books of account, assessee had disclosed a profit of 7½ per cent - ITO, however, notived that neighbournig shopkeepers who were also dealing with same kind of goods showed a profit of 15 percent for period in question - He thus, rejected assessee’s accounts and assessed him at a profit of 12½ per cent - Whether since assessee was given an opportunity  to rebut inference arising against him from high profits shown by neighbouring shop-keepers and he did put forward an explanation which was rejected by lower authorities, there was no illegality in assessment under section 23(3) of 1922 Act on basis of profits of neighbouring shop-keepers - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 13 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Method of accounting - Valuation of stock - Assessment year 1959-60 - While completing assessment ITO did not accept assessee's reasons for low profits at rate of 9% in respect of a contract undertaken by him and applied flat rate of 12Â½% profit - On appeal assessee had not derived before AAC that full quantitative details were not available in respect of stores of value of Rs. 1,30,000 - For subsequent assessment year assessee declared a profit of 9.9% - Whether on facts provisions of section 13 were applicable to assessee's case and therefore, Tribunal was justified in upholding addition in assessee's income - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment year 1995-96 - Assessing Officer made lump sum addition to trading accounts of assessee civil contractor on ground that it was not possible to verify value of work done at each site, material consumed and labour expenses incurred - Whether considering fact that assessee had done work only for Government and payments were made by cheques, Commissioner’s view that addition made by Assessing Officer was on higher side was acceptable - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income [Gross profit rate] - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee was engaged in business of contract work of military engineering services - Assessing Officer having found that assessee disclosed lower gross profit rate 7.20 per cent in relevant year, in comparison to 10.25 per cent in immediately preceding year despite three fold increase in gross receipt and assessee had not maintained salary register, payment register etc., rejected books of account of assessee and estimated income of assessee by applying net profit rate of 12.5 per cent - Whether since explanations of assessee that gross receipts had substantially increased by three times for which assessee had to reduce margin, and that contract works were executed in military and air force areas where working hours were lesser in comparison to normal civil work and that cost of various expenses and material had also been increased, was not rebutted by revenue, gross profit rate applied by Assessing Officer could not be sustained - Held, yes - Whether on facts, it would be fair and reasonable if net profit rate of 7.50 per cent was applied subject to interest to third parties, depreciation, interest to partners and salary to partners - Held, yes [Para 2.12] [Partly in favour of assessee]IT : Explanations of assessee which were not rebutted by revenue, were to be considered in estimation of his income

Section 44AD, read with sections 44AB and 144, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Presumptive taxation (Illustrations) - Assessment year 2016-17 - Assessee executed works contract for State Public Works Department relating to road construction - Assessee received payments from various Government departments from which TDS had been deducted by payer departments - However, assessee did not get his accounts audited and furnished income at 3 per cent turnover based on estimates - Assessee had justified for adopting net profit at 3 per cent from civil contracts by stating that his volume of work was higher and due to heavy competitions, he was unable to get more profits - Assessing Officer being of view that since assessee had not maintained accounts, determined income at 8 per cent as per section 44AB, resulting in enhancement of income liable to tax - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) scaled it down to 4 per cent without depreciation - It was noted that in previous assessment years assessee had estimated 3 per cent as estimated net profit which was accepted by Assessing Officer - Tribunal upheld estimation of profit at 4 per cent by Commissioner (Appeals) in view of earlier assessment orders - Whether there was no infirmity in order passed by Tribunal - Held, yes [Paras 3 and 5] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee, a civil contractor, who worked for State Government departments furnished income at 3 per cent turnover based on estimates and contended that volume of work was higher and there was heavy competition which resulted in his inability to get more profits, Tribunal was justified in upholding order of Commissioner (Appeals) in adopting net profit at 4 per cent from civil contracts in view of order passed in previous assessment years

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 13 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment year 1959-60 - Assessee was a contractor who had undertaken construction of houses under a project for relevant assessment year - Assessee showed expenditure incurred on jobs during year at 
Rs 4,45,904 which was treated by assessee as work-in-progress and showed a sum of Rs 3,21,358 as received against contracts from executive engineer - Assessee did not show any profit or loss from jobs and claiming overhead expenses at Rs 12,764 a net loss was returned - ITO considered that a profit had to be calculated on basis of receipts from authorities and he accordingly computed gross profit of Rs. 40,169 at 12½ per cent of receipts - Before AAC, assessee claimed that since accounts were maintained on completed job basis which was recognised system of accounting, proviso to section 13 of 1922 Act could not be invoked - AAC did not accept assessee’s contention and upheld order of ITO in invoking provisions of section 13 of 1922 Act for computing assessee’s income - However, he computed gross profit by applying rate of 12½ per cent on gross value of work done and not on net payments received by assessee - Tribunal upheld order of AAC - Whether order of Tribunal was justified - Held, yes

Section 145, read with  section 144 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 13, read with  section 23(4) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits - Assessee firm engaged in business of dyeing, printing and selling cloth disclosed gross profit at rate of 18 per cent of total turnover - ITO rejected accounts submitted by assessee and relying upon certain private enquiries in similar cases enhanced rate of profit to 50 per cent of turnover - Tribunal upheld ITO's order - Whether since authorities below had not drawn attention of assessee to material collected by them on private enquiry, impugned order passed by them was to be set aside and case was to be remanded back to Tribunal with direction to disclose material gathered from private enquiries to assessee and give him full opportunity to place any relevant material to meet substance of private enquiry - Held, yes

Section 143 of the Income-tax, Act, 1961 - Assessment - Additions to - Assessment years 1993-84 and 1984-85 -Whether profit disclosed by assessee- contractor in succeeding year can be taken to be a sure guide for determining profit for preceding year - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, where assessee-contractor had disclosed net profit at 8.4 per cent in assessment year in question, it would be incorrect to raise it to 12 per cent merely on ground that in succeeding year net profit returned was at 12.8 per cent - Held, yes - Whether lower authorities were unjustified in not allowing separate deduction for depreciation after estimating profits on gross receipts - Held yes - Whether, on consideration of facts, it would be appropriate to estimate net profits in instant case at 11.5 per cent with separate deduction for depreciation - Held, yes

Section 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Rejection of accounts (Estimation of profit) - Assessment year 2014-15 - Assessee was engaged as civil contractor - Assessing Officer being not satisfied with explanation of assessee regarding decline in net profit rejected account books and estimated net profit at rate of 10 per cent of turnover - Whether in light of various defects/deficiencies/irregularities along with assessee’s evasive approach towards explanation sought by Assessing Officer, allegation that rejection of books was done in arbitrary manner did not hold any ground and, thus, rejection of books of account was justified - Held, yes - Whether however, in absence of any comparative instances of similar assessees in same line of business, it was appropriate to estimate profit at a percentage worked out on basis of preceding three years profit of assessee herself - Held, yes [Paras 10 and 12] [Partly in favour of assessee]

Section 254, read with section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 33(4), read with section 13 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Appellate Tribunal - Order of - Assessment years 1943-44 to 1945-46 - Assessee-firm carried on business of aerodrome work, katcha building constructions etc. - On firm's failure to produce books of account for relevant assessment years, ITO took sum total of receipts of assessee for three accounting years and, thereupon adopted profit rate of 40 per cent in exercise of his power under section 13, read with section 23(4) of 1922 Act - Tribunal, however, opined that ITO should have applied rate of profit to annual receipts instead of total receipts and that by amalgamating receipts under one assessment ITO raised tax liability of assessee which was not fair - Besides, Tribunal also reduced profit rate from 40 per cent to 30 per cent - Whether Tribunal was right in asking ITO to assess assessee on receipt basis with regard to contracts carried out and completed during year of accounting, there being every presumption that incomes were paid as soon as they became due - Held, yes - Whether, however, as regards reduction of flat rate of profit, Tribunal did commit a mistake of law in arriving at said finding for which there was no relevant evidence to support - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Works contract - Assessee was maintaining no accounts and its gross receipts included cost of materials supplied by Government - No profit was allowed on such cost of materials -Whether cost of materials could be included while applying a flat rate to the assessee's gross receipts - Held, no

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment years 1965-66 to 1967-68 - Assessee was executing constructional contract works under military authorities - He was not maintaining any account books - Military authorities had supplied certain materials to assessee - Tribunal found that there was no element of profit on cost of materials supplied by authorities - Whether having regard to Tribunal is finding, cost of materials supplied by military authorities was not liable to be included in total receipts of assessee for calculating his net profit - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits - Assessment year 2005-06 - Assessee, engaged in business of execution of contracts, was not able to submit all relevant details called for by Assessing Officer - Assessing Officer rejected assessee's books of account and estimated profit of assessee at 15 per cent of gross receipts without allowing any depreciation allowance, etc. - Commissioner (Appeals) following order of Tribunal in assessee's own case for preceding assessment year directed Assessing Officer to adopt net profit at 8 per cent on gross receipts and determine assessable income without granting any further allowance therefrom - Whether since no case was made out to suggest that facts of earlier year were not comparable to year under consideration, impugned order passed by Commissioner (Appeals) was to be upheld - Held, yes [In favour of assessee]

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits - Assessment year 1984-85 - Assessee-firm was carrying on construction business - During period relevant to assessment year under consideration, it had taken a contract for construction of hotel building - Assessee contended that it was only on completion of project that profitability 
 or otherwise of contract could be judged - Assessing authority, however, found that there was no day-to-day maintenance of accounts and, therefore, concluded that profit from return could not be ascertained and, accordingly, estimated profit at 8 per cent of gross receipts which was reduced to 5 per cent by Commissioner (Appeals) - Whether in absence of properly maintained accounts, authorities were bound to follow accepted method of calculating profits on yearly basis and ‘project-completion-method’ was inapplicable - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961- Method of accounting - Estimation of profits - Assessment years 1985-86 to 1988-89. Assessee was engaged in construction work - It took a huge project in 1980 which had to take several years to complete . It adopted ‘Project Completion Method’ as its method of accounting and contended that it should be treated to have earned no profits till assessment year 1985-86. During a search on 11-5-1987 department found some incriminating materials - Assessee declared unaccounted profit of Rs. 66 lakhs as ‘on money’ and wanted that Rs. 26 lakhs should be assessed in assessment year 1987-88 and Rs. 40 lakhs in assessment year 1988-89 - Two employees of assessee deposed that it was charging 30 to 40 per cent ‘on money’ and one of directors stated that it was charging 15 to 20 per cent ‘on money’- Because of unaccounted ‘on money’ Assessing Officer concluded that accounts were not properly kept so that income could be properly deduced therefrom and, therefore, rejected method of account followed by assessee. He worked out ‘on money’ receipts on basis of statements of employees and version of director - He also applied rate of profit at 25 per cent on total receipts and allocated profits in different years - Whether Assessing Officer had rightly rejected method followed by assessee and assessed income in each assessment year by application of provisions of section 145(2) - Held, yes Whether rate of profit at 25 per cent was correctly applied on total receipts and not on receipts after deducting profits - Held, yes - Whether Assessing Officer was justified in rejecting assessee’s version that ‘on money’ was received only in last two assessment years and, therefore, was justified in spreading it in all assessment years under consideration and preceding years - Held, yes

Section 44AD, read with sections 44AB and 144, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Presumptive taxation (Illustrations) - Assessment year 2016-17 - Assessee executed works contract for State Public Works Department relating to road construction - Assessee received payments from various Government departments from which TDS had been deducted by payer departments - However, assessee did not get his accounts audited and furnished income at 3 per cent turnover based on estimates - Assessee had justified for adopting net profit at 3 per cent from civil contracts by stating that his volume of work was higher and due to heavy competitions, he was unable to get more profits - Assessing Officer being of view that since assessee had not maintained accounts, determined income at 8 per cent as per section 44AB, resulting in enhancement of income liable to tax - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) scaled it down to 4 per cent without depreciation - It was noted that in previous assessment years assessee had estimated 3 per cent as estimated net profit which was accepted by Assessing Officer - Tribunal upheld estimation of profit at 4 per cent by Commissioner (Appeals) in view of earlier assessment orders - Whether there was no infirmity in order passed by Tribunal - Held, yes [Paras 3 and 5] [In favour of assessee]

Section 145, read with section 36(1)(iia) and section 32, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits - Assessment year 1992-93 - Assessee carried on contract business of construction of roads by obtaining contracts from Government departments - Books maintained by assessee were not verifiable - Assessee filed his return of income along with tax audit report under section 44AB - During assessment proceedings, assessee was asked to prove genuineness of transactions with various parties from whom raw material had been purchased - Assessee filed confirmation letters from parties but failed to produce them in person before Assessing Officer for verification - Assessing Officer rejected books of assessee and estimated profits - Assessing Officer also made disallowance on account of labour payments holding that payments were excessive and inflated - Further, Assessing Officer disallowed depreciation - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) held that assessee had not maintained verifiable accounts and he applied net profit rate of 10 per cent on receipt - He also granted depreciation after applying net profit rate - Whether in absence of verifiable accounts maintained by assessee, Assessing Officer should have examined past history of assessee and should have adopted net profit rate instead of making additions on account of purchases in raw materials - Held, yes - Whether since department itself had accepted net profit rate in case of same assessee in different years at 8 per cent to 8.25 per cent on receipt after deducting material and sales tax in past, looking to past history and comparable cases, it would be reasonable and appropriate if net profit rate of 8 per cent on receipts after deducting cost of material supplied by Government department was applied in instant case - Held, yes - Whether keeping in view past history of assessee in which depreciation was allowed, Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in allowing depreciation after applying net profit rate - Held, yes - Whether assessee was entitled to deduction of interest paid to third parties after applying net profit rate - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of net profits - Assessment year 1989-90 - Assessee, and individual contractor, received certain payments and declared net profit rate which worked out to 6.54 per cent if claims for interest and depreciation were ignored - Assessing Officer in absence of proper record about labour and Hazri expenses as also on consumption of material, applied net profit rate of 10 per cent on total receipts subject to interest and depreciation - whether engaging of employees to carry out work was not a very special feature which should weigh heavily while determining income on basis adopted by department, and thus, Commissioner (Appeals)’s order reducing it to 9 per cent subject to interest and depreciation was to be upheld - Held, yes

Section 145, read with  section 263, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (Rate of profit of civil sub-contractor) - Assessment year 2005-06 - Assessee was working under main civil contractor IVRCL - Assessee showed 0.12 per cent profit - Whether while in case of civil contractor profit rate is 8 per cent, for civil sub-contractor it is normally 5 per cent - Held, yes - Whether where as against profit rate of 0.12 per cent declared by assessee sub-contractor, Assessing Officer worked out same to be 6.4 per cent, in absence of any material, Commissioner could not interfere with same in revision under section 263 - Held, yes [Para 8] [In favour of assessee]IT: In case of civil sub-contract normal profit rate was about 5 per cent; where Assessing Officer worked out same to be 6.4 per cent in assessee's case, after scrutiny, said order could not be regarded as erroneous

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment year 2001-02 - Whether applying net profit rate on basis of best judgment assessment in a given situation will be a question of fact unless, such an assessment is shown to be arbitrary or perverse - Held, yes - Assessee was a contractor engaged in work of civil construction and filed its return for assessment year in question - Assessing Officer made addition to returned income mainly on account of claim for wages being found to be not verifiable - On appeal, Tribunal while considering issue of addition on account of unverifiable wages, considered it appropriate to apply reasonable rate of profit, which was assessed at rate of 12 per cent on contract receipts, excluding material supplied by department - Whether since assessment of 12% of net profit rate of contract receipt was not shown to be arbitrary or perverse, no question of law arose from Tribunal's order - Held, yes

Section 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (GP/NP Rate) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee, a joint venture, was formed for purpose to bid and execute construction work - It declared net profit at rate of 1 per cent of contractual receipts - Assessing Officer having noticed that assessee had failed to establish its claim of 1 per cent net profit by producing any evidence to that effect rejected book results and estimated net profit at rate of 4 per cent of total contractual receipts - Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed appeal on ground that assessee did not pursue its appeal before him - Whether matter required to be remanded back to Commissioner (Appeals) to decide issue on merit after affording reasonable opportunities of being heard to assessee - Held, yes [Para 11] [Matter remanded]INCOME TAX : Where assessee was engaged in construction work and Assessing Officer rejected book results and estimated net profit at rate of 4 per cent of total contractual receipts as against 1 per cent declared by assessee and Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed appeal ex parte, matter was to be remanded back to Commissioner (Appeals) to decide issue on merit

Section 145,  read with section 44AD, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (Gross profit rate) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Assessee was engaged in business of execution of civil works contract - He filed his return of income for relevant assessment year declaring certain taxable income - In course of assessment, Assessing Officer noted that assessee had kept self-made vouchers in support of major expenditure and, accordingly, opined that books of account maintained by assessee were not amenable for verification - He thus rejected books of account under provisions of section 145(3) and estimated net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts net of all deductions - Whether since assessee failed to controvert findings of Assessing Officer with any positive evidence to come to conclusion that books of account maintained by him gave a true and correct profit from business, Assessing Officer was right in rejecting books of account - Held, yes - Whether as regards rate of profit, since assessee had disclosed 6.73 per cent to 7.44 per cent net profit in earlier period, impugned estimation made by Assessing Officer was justified - Held, yes - Whether even otherwise, since nature of business carried on by assessee was squarely fit into specified business referred to in provisions of section 44AD, estimation of net profit at rate of 8 per cent of gross receipts specified in said section was rightly adopted - Held, yes [Paras 8, 9 and 10] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where assessee had kept self-made vouchers in support of major expenditure and books of account maintained by him did not give true and correct profit from business, Assessing Officer was justified in rejecting said books of account and estimating net profit of 8 per cent of gross receipts  IT : Where Assessing Officer had adopted reasonable rate of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts, further deduction towards depreciation could not be allowed as it would result into determination of total income below income returned by assessee   IT : Where there was no nexus between interest receipts and works contracts executed by assessee, interest on fixed deposits was separately assessable under head 'Income from other sources'

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (GP rate) - Assessment years 2004-05 and 2005-06 - Assessee-company was carrying out contract of construction of roads awarded by Government - Due to various discrepancies in books of account, Assessing Officer rejected same and estimated profit at 10 per cent of gross receipts - Tribunal relying upon profit rates of preceding three years, reduced profit earned during relevant year to 5 per cent of gross receipts - Where since assessee had not done any private construction work during assessment years in question, impugned order passed by Tribunal did not require any interference - Held, yes. [Paras 5 and 6] [In favour of assessee]IT: Where in case of government contractor engaged in construction of roads books of account was rejected, Tribunal, relying upon profit rates of preceding three years, was justified in estimating profits earned by assessee during relevant years at 5 percent of gross receipts

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment year 2001-02 - Where while considering issue of addition on account of unverifiable wages, Tribunal considered it appropriate to apply reasonable rate of profit, which was assessed at rate of 12 per cent on contract receipts, excluding material supplied by department, 12 per cent of net profit rate of contract receipt was not shown to be arbitrary or perverse and, hence, no question of law arose [In favour of assessee]

Section 44AD, read with sections 44AB and 144, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Presumptive taxation (Audit) - Assessment year 2016-17 - Assessee was a civil contractor who worked for State PWD departments - Assessee received payments from various government departments from which TDS had been deducted by payer departments - However, assessee did not get his accounts audited and furnished income at 3 per cent turnover based on estimates - Assessing Officer determined income at 8 per cent under section 44AD on ground that assessee should have kept accounting records - Commissioner (Appeals) restricted net profit margin to 4 per cent - It was noted that assessee was justified in adopting net profit at 3 per cent from civil contracts by stating that his volume of work was higher and due to heavy competitions, he was unable to get more profits - Also in previous assessment years assessee had estimated 3 per cent as estimated net profit which was accepted by Assessing Officer - Whether, thus, there was no infirmity in order passed by Commissioner (Appeals) in reducing net profit to 4 per cent - Held, yes [Para 8] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee, a civil contractor, who worked for State government departments furnished income at 3 per cent turnover based on estimates and contended that volume of work was higher and there was heavy competition which resulted in his inability to get more profits, since in previous assessment years AO estimated its net profit at 3.5 per cent, AO could not estimate net profit at 8 per cent under section 44AD in relevant assessment year on ground that assessee should have kept accounting records

facts.text:
The assessee, a contractor, was assessed to income-tax for the relevant assessment year in respect of certain contracts which commenced in 1922 and were finished some time in 1924. The assessee produced his accounts, but the accounts for the relevant accounting year could not be separated. The ITO considered the accounts to be unreliable. He, therefore, assumed profit at the standard rate of 10 per cent for the purposes of his assessment. On appeal, the Assistant Commissioner concluded that in any case it was impossible to ascertain from the assessee’s accounts what the income had been for one year and, therefore, the only way of ascertaining it was to apply the usual rate of 10 per cent on the total payments received. On application under section 66(2) of the 1922 Act, the Commissioner declined to make any reference.

On application under section 66 (3) of the 1922 Act.

The business of the assessee was execution of construction contracts. The assessee commenced its business from 25-1-1958, and the accounts were closed for the first time on 25-1-1959. During the accounting year the assessee undertook three contracts with respect to which it submitted separate profit and loss statements.

The accounts in respect of the first two contracts were accepted by the authorities under the Act in toto but with regard to the accounts relating to the third contract the ITO declined to accept the assessee's reasons for low profits at the rate of 9% in respect of that contract. He, therefore, applied a flat rate of 12Â½% profit and made certain addition to the assessee's income.

On appeal, the AAC had accepted the assessee's reasons for the low profit of 9% but had sustained an addition of Rs. 10,000 on the ground that the assessee's representative had not denied before him that full quantitative details might not be available in respect of the stores of the value of over Rs. 1,30,000 consumed in the execution of the contract. When the case came up before the Tribunal the addition of Rs. 10,000 was found to be excessive and was reduced to Rs. 6,000.

On reference :

The assessee, a contractor undertaking projects of Indian Railways on turnkey basis, filed its return of income.

On the basis of the materials gathered by the income-tax authorities in the course of a search carried out in the assessee's premises as well as in the premises of the directors and trusted persons, the Assessing Officer referred the matter to a special audit in terms of section 142(2A). The special audit report, inter alia, reported that there were large number of transactions in which several discrepancies were noticed.

In response to the queries raised by the Assessing Officer on the basis of the special audit report the assessee could not give any proper explanation and wherever an explanation was sought to be given, it was found to be evasive. The assessee was also allowed inspection of the seized documents and was supplied photocopies of the seized records. Despite such opportunity, no convincing reason was given by the assessee.

The Assessing Officer proceeded to estimate the net profit of the assessee at 11 per cent of the gross receipts from the contracts. The Assessing Officer also found that some income from business activities was not included in the aforesaid receipts and the profit from such activity was taken at Rs.13.34 lakhs. Demands were accordingly raised.

Penalty proceedings were initiated by the Assessing Officer for concealment of income and after rejecting the assessee's explanation, a penalty was imposed for concealment of income under section 271(1)(c).

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) cancelled the penalty order on the ground that the Assessing Officer has not stated the basis of this estimate nor did he give an opportunity to the assessee to rebut the proposal to estimate the profits at 11 per cent of the gross receipts. He held that the assessee made a counter proposal which was a conditional offer as to the taxability of the profits and even if it is assumed that there was an agreement on the part of the assessee for being taxed at the rate of 11 per cent of the gross receipts, it does not follow automatically that the assessee concealed its income.

On second appeal by Revenue, the Tribunal dismissed it.

On appeal to the High Court:

The assessee was a private limited company carrying on business of execution of contracts. The company commenced its business in 1956 and closed its accounts on June 30 every year. The work undertaken by the assessee took a period of nearly 5 years to complete but it had not worked out its profits every year. No separate job work account had been prepared and the value of work-in-progress had not been taken into account. The annual expenses were shown on the balance sheet and the overhead expenses were charged to the profit and loss account. At the end of the contract period a consolidated revenue account was struck on the total receipt of Rs. 42.23 lakhs for all the contracts, a gross profit of 10.1 per cent and a net profit of 2.8 percent were shown by the assessee in its books. The ITO required the assessee to furnish the evidence regarding the total receipts of each year and the details of the relevant expenses in respect of each contract. The expenses, however, were neither fully verifiable nor allowable properly against the receipts from any individual contracts. The ITO had, therefore, to resort to estimate under the proviso to section 13 and applied a flat rate of 15 per cent on the receipts of each year and allowed some expenses there against. Per Ramaswami, J.

The scheme and structure of the Income-tax Act, read with the Finance Act is to make the tax an annual tax for the purpose of assessment. Section 3 makes each "previous year" a distinct unit of time for the purpose of assessment and the profits made before or after that unit of time are entirely immaterial in assessing the profits of that year. If section 3 is read in the context of section 13, it is clear that the accounts maintained by the assessee must correctly show or reflect the profits of the preceding year. If the method of accounting adopted by the assessee does not reflect the true profits of the preceding year the proviso to section 13 will apply and the ITO would be entitled to compute the profits upon such basis and in such manner as he may determine.

In the case of a contractor, it cannot be said that merely because of incompleteness of the contract in the relevant accounting year profits of the assessee for that accounting year cannot be ascertained. It also cannot be said that merely because a contract was completed after the accounting year, no profit arose or accrued to the assessee in the accounting year. In the case of an incomplete contract there is a well-established method of calculating profits accruing in the accounting year.

In the instant case, the Tribunal had found that for the assessment years 1939-40 and 1940-41 no accounts were kept for the contract the assessee had executed. For the assessment year 1943-44 he wrote a letter to the Income-tax Officer and admitted that he had no accounts to produce. For the assessment year 1944-45 he produced two sets of accounts. One was maintained for the two contracts he had taken from PWD but the profits of each contact was not separately worked out and there was one consolidated receipts and payments account for both the contracts. For the military contract he kept a separate set of accounts. These accounts were maintained from 14-4-1943 to 3-12-1944. The total value of contract was Rs. 3,78,766 and out of this the assessee received of Rs. 3,00,000 before 31-3-1944. He did not close the accounts on 31-3-1944, or prepare balance sheet but the accounts were kept open till 3-12-1944, when the execution of the contract was completed. It was argued on behalf of the assessee that the account are maintained on completed contract basis and the assessee had no objection if the income of the Hospital contract was taxed for the assessment year 1945-46 and that there was a single and indivisible contract for the Hospital and the work upon the entire contract was completed on 3-12-1944, and that was the proper date on which the profits should be ascertained. This argument was not acceptable if accounts are maintained and completed on contract basis the profits or gains of the previous year cannot properly be extracted from these accounts. For a contract may take several years for being completed. The payments in regard to the contract may also be received by the assessee in several years. It may be convenient for the assessee that profit should be ascertained on the completion of the contract and assessment of the profit should take place on the date of the completion of the contract. But section 3 imposes a charge of income-tax upon the profits and gains accruing to the assessee for the accounting year and it is the duty of the Income-tax authorities to make ascertainment of such profits and gains accruing to the assessee in respect of the payment received during the accounting year. Since the accounts maintained by the assessee did not correctly reflected the profits of the assessee for the accounting year the Tribunal was right in holding that the proviso to section 13 applied and that the ITO was entitled to discard the accounting method of the assessee and instead to make computation of the profits on such basis as he thought fit.

As regards the objection that the estimate of income on this formula would still be an estimate and would not be mathematically accurate, mathematical certainty is not demanded in a matter of this description.

The proviso to section 13 had been rightly applied by the Tribunal in regard to the accounts maintained for the contract business, which were not closed to profit at the end of each previous year but were closed to profit only after the completion of a contract.

PER AHMAD, J. (CONCURRENT VIEW ):

It is true that there is no res judicata in the income-tax law and that the ITO has authority to take a different view from what has been taken in an earlier year. But neither he can exercise this authority in caprice, nor has he an unrestricted, unlimited, unconditional or absolute right in this matter. It was undisputed that the ITO had completed the assessments of the assessee’s income for the assessment years 1978-79 to 1981-82 on a flate rate basis observing, inter alia, that in the absence of maintenance of vouchers and receipts for the expenditure incurred by the assessee, the books of account were not acceptable. Now to examine whether the books of account kept in all the years inclusive of the year under appeal were maintained in the same manner or not, the trading and profit and loss accounts were the best available guide on which one should rely. There was no difference in the manner in which they had been kept in any of the assessment years inclusive of the assessment year under appeal. However, it was strange that though the assessee was a big contractor and executions of many of the contracts were spread in these years, no work-in-progress or closing stock had been recorded in the trading account. In view of the circumstances, it was not possible for the ITO to presume that the true profit could be computed on the basis of the books of account. He had overlooked the orders for the assessment years 1978-79 to 1981-82 framed by his predecessors. As a matter of fact, his finding was not very much different. He had also overlooked his own letter dated 16-2-1985 addressed to the assessee. Again, there was no whisper in his order as to what were the defects in the earlier years, which were not present in the relevant assessment year. He failed to prove his finding. Accordingly, the reasoning of the ITO to change the mode of assessment could not be accepted and the estimate of profit at a flat rate method as adopted in earlier years in the same circumstances should also apply in the assessment year under appeal, except that, in view of the finding that a large amount of expenses claimed was unestablished, the profit rate to be applied should be 12½ per cent instead of 10 per cent adopted for the earlier years.

PER AHMAD, J. (CONCURRENT VIEW ): In the instant case the finding given by the Tribunal was that "the assessee never produced any account till the assessment in the present case and that no account was maintained by the assessee and therefore he had no method of accounting till 1943-44." On this finding of fact alone, therefore, the case attracted at once the operation of the rule of law laid down in the proviso, that is, it was the duty of the Income-tax Officer in such a state of facts to compute the income, profits and gains of the assessee upon such basis and in such manner as he thought best.

Even, however, if it be assumed in favour of the assessee, for which there was no evidence, that the account presented before the Income-tax Officer in the next year was one in accordance with a method regularly employed by the assessee, finding of fact given by the Tribunal that the method employed by the assessee in that account was such that the income, profits and gains could not properly be deduced there from. On that finding also the proviso to section 13 at once came into play and the duty was cast on the Income-tax Officer to compute the income, profit and gains of the assessee upon such basis and upon such manner as the income-tax Officer might determine.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

The profit in a long-term contract should be taxed on year-to-year basis. It is a dangerous proposition to recognise that the profit accrues only after the completion of a contract, Such a proposition is liable to be abused by dishonest taxpayers. It is a judicially recognised proposition that in the case of a contract in order to ascertain the income one need not wait till the contract is completed and that it is open to the revenue to estimate the profit on the basis of receipts in each year of construction, although the contract is not complete.

Section 3 makes each previous year a distinct unit of time for the purpose of assessment and the profits made before or after that unit of time are entirely immaterial in assessing the profits of that year. In the case of contracts, if accounts are maintained and completed on contract basis, the profits or gains of the previous year can not properly be extracted from the accounts, for a contract may take several years for being completed and payment in regard to it may also be received by the assessee in several years. It may be convenient from the point of view of the assessee that profit should be ascertained on the completion of the contract and assessment of the profit should take place after the completion of the contract. But section 3 imposes a charge of income-tax upon the profits and gains of the assessee for the accounting year and it is the duty of the ITO to ascertain the profits and gains accruing to the assessee in respect of the payment received during the accounting year. It cannot be said that merely because a contract is completed after the accounting year, no profit arises or accrues to the assessee in the accounting year. In the case of an incomplete contract, there is a well-established method of calculating profits accruing in the accounting year. In such a contract, the long-term contract method is adopted in respect of contracts which have to be completed by stages over a course of years, such as, building contracts or building schemes by co- operative or private enterprise, or contracts entered into with public authorities such as public works, military, etc. The ascertainment of the profit in the execution of such contracts cannot be deferred till the completion of the entire constructions which may take several years. Each year’s profit shall have to be, in the nature of things, computed on an estimate, having regard to the work completed during the year. There are recognised methods of estimating with reasonable accuracy the profits accrued from time to time on uncompleted contracts. The fact that the contracts have not been completed or the accounts thereof have not been closed, is not sufficient reason for not estimating the profit of each year though absolute accuracy may not be reached. Thus, in a contract running over several years, the entire profits cannot be attributed to a single last year in which the contract was completed. The fact that it is not convenient or easy to allocate receipts or expendi- ture as against various items of trading assets is no reason for uphold- ing that profits emerge only after the entire expenditure on the assets has been recouped; the allocation of expenditure and receipts must somehow be made on a reasonable basis and the debts and trading assets valued on the closing date. In such cases, a workable method is for the revenue to assess on the basis of gross receipts of each year at a flat rate of profit on such receipts. The assessment in the case of a building

contractor, therefore, need not be postponed till the completion of the contract.

If the profits could reasonably be arrived at from year to year, such profit should be assessed from year to year only. In the instant case, the assessee had not correctly valued the closing work-in-progress and, therefore, it was the duty of the Assessing Officer to correctly value the closing work-in-progress: and arrive at the true picture of the profit. Thus, in the case of a building contractor, the revenue need not wait till the completion of the contract and the reasonable profit can be estimated from year to year and brought to tax.

Regarding the estimate of profits at 8 per cent there was no material on record to show that the estimate of profit at 8 per cent was excessive and unreasonable having regard to the facts of the case. However, the profit at 8 per cent estimated for these three years was only a mere estimate and the true profit of the entire project would be arrived at when the contract was complete. The assessee was, therefore, entitled to the adjustment of profit or loss in the year of completion of the contract. Hence, the estimate of profit at 8 per cent was reasonable.

It is no doubt true that in the case of a contractor, work-in-progress has to be brought into accounts in order to show the profits earned in respect of the work turned out and the profit embedded in the receipts received during the year. The concept of bringing to accounts the work-in-progress is no different from the concept of bringing into accounts the closing in the case of a trader or a manufacturer. But unlike the case of a trader or a manufacturer, in the case of a contractor the workin-progress cannot be exactly arrived at with reference to any particular books because there are so many components which go to make up the work-in-progress and which have to be estimated. Therefore, estimate in arriving at the work-in progress was necessary and there was bound to be certain amount of approximation and guess work. Merely on the ground that the work-in-progress is estimated, it cannot be said that the book results were not to be accepted and that proviso to section 145 is applicable unless it is shown that the work-in-progress was arrived in such a way as to be too far from reality. In the instant case, the ITO attempted to prove the unreliability of the amount of work-in-progress arrived at by pointing out that the closing stock ought to have been Rs. 3,82,000 as against Rs. 1 lakh shown by the assessee. The basis for this was the assumption that normally the advance was given at 75 per cent of the material lying at site. There was no basis for this assumption nor any figure were given to show that this hypothesis could be accepted as correct. It was mere ipsi dixit of the ITO, without any basis to support it. The advance could be given at 75 per cent. It could be more, it could be less. This was, therefore, a surmise and conjecture.

As regards the receipts, following the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Brij Bhushan Lal Parduman Kumar v. CIT [1978] 115 ITR 524 , in the instant case, the value of the material supplied by the Government must be excluded. So the balance of receipts should come to only Rs. 14.63 lakhs shown by the assessee. The estimate of the income at Rs. 1,50,000 on those receipts of Rs. 14.63 lakhs would work out to about 10.4 per cent. In none of the previous years, the assessee had shown such a high rate of profit nor had the department estimated the profit at such a rate nor the books of account were ever rejected. The previous results are only the points of reference, in relation to which the results of subsequent years are to be judged and reasons for variations are investigated. The range of profit would be discernible from the previous records. The lowest rate of net profit rate shown and accepted by the department was 2.8 per cent. In the immediately preceding assessment year rate of net profit shown and accepted was 2.75 per cent and the gross profit was 11.75 per cent. The estimate made by the ITO in the year in question of the profit at 10.5 per cent was very excessive and unreasonable. The ITO had not shown the basis for determining the income of Rs. 1,50,000. It is now the settled law that whenever estimates of income are resorted to in order that they are not arbitrary, unreasonable and unjustified, the ITO must show the basis on which and the method by which and the manner in which the estimate was made. These are the safeguards provided to act as an insurance against arbitrary estimates. None of these guidelines settled by the law of the land was disclosed by the ITO except leaving one to infer that because of the variations in the closing stock, he determined to fix the income at Rs. 1,50,000. Therefore, the estimate made by the ITO was not justified.

A fair estimate of the income has to be made. Further, the Jurisdictional High Court held that Guesswork is inevitable; but, it cannot be wild guess; the guesswork should have a reasonable nexus to the available material and the circumstances of each case.
