■ Now coming to the present facts of the case, it is found that the assessee is a civil contractor and the entire contract receipts were from government departments/PWD as can be verified from form 26AS and all the proceeds were received through proper banking channels on which the tax had been deducted at source. On perusal of the assessment order, we also noticed that in absence of any details/evidences filed by the assessee, the AO estimated the income @ 15% by holding that once the profit is determined on estimated basis, the assessee is not entitled to any further deduction as per provisions of section 30 to 43D and by holding that when the net profit rate to gross receipts is determined on estimation basis, no further deduction is to be allowed. The AO while applying the net profit @15% was guided by the provisions of section 44AD only & held that once the profit is determined on estimated basis, the assessee is not entitled to any further deduction as per provisions of section 30 to 43D as contained in section 44AD. It is the considered opinion that the AO estimated the profit of the assessee @15% without reference to any material gathered. The AO should not make his best judgment assessment on mere suspicion, impulsively or arbitrarily. The best judgment assessment must be based on the material on record which could be gathered by the AO on proper investigation. In the present case, the assessee's entire contractual receipts were from Government department & all proceeds were received through banking channel & thus the assessee's estimation of the net profit @ 6.06% of the turnover is higher than the rate of 6% prescribed u/s 44AD. It is viewed that flat 15% income on turnover is highly unjustified. However, it is the considered opinion that net profit rate of 7% in civil contract business especially when all the contract receipts were received through proper banking channel on which the tax has been deducted at source is a reasonable one and accordingly the AO is directed to recompute the net profit of the assessee @7% of the total turnover declared by the assessee i.e. Rs.17.40 crores. Accordingly, this ground of Appeal of the assessee is partly allowed. [Para 10.4]

In the instant case, the ITO arrived at the figure on the basis of the receipts extending over three accounting year. He took the sum total of these receipts to be the base for the net income that had accrued to the assessee during the accounting year 1943-44 as the entire contract work had been completed during that year. Mere execution of the contract work will not necessarily entitle the contractor to make a demand for payment until it is ascertained that the works are up to the standard agreed upon between the parties. Some parts of such work may be wholly rejected and like bad debts in every earning may be ignored in computing the gains or profits. It might have been open to the ITO, in exercise of his discretion, to make an enquiry into whether and when the bills for payment became due to the assessee. Much depended upon the terms in the contract, and the manner of its performance. Even as a basis of guess work, which the Income-tax Officer was entitled to do, the basis could not be said to be in consonance with honest guess work. The ITO did not seem to have taken into consideration why the payments which, according to him, were due to the assessee in the accounting year were not fully paid till three years after. Sometimes the payments to the contractors are withheld on account of unsatisfactory execution and they are held entitled to payments only if and when they replace the rejected work by acceptable and accepted ones. The bare possibility of such contingency could not be wholly eliminated in the instant case. If the ITO, in arriving at the figure for assessment, left out these considerations, he certainly could not be said to have exercised his judgment which he was none the less called upon to do in making the assessment in cases of assessee's default under sections 23(4) and 13 proviso of the 1922 Act. Any method of accounting adopted by the ITO acting under the proviso of section 13 of 1922 Act can be rejected if the method in fact does not show the true income, profits and gains. In this view of the matter, the Appellate Tribunal was right in asking the ITO to assess the assessee on receipt basis with regard to contracts carried out and completed during the year of accounting, there being every presumption that the incomes were paid as soon as they became due. At any rate, the Tribunal's decision might be upheld on the ground that when two methods of guess work are available for the purpose of assessment, the one which is more just to the assessee and which involves a much less margin of chance of uncertainty should be taken as the basis.

In the result, the Tribunal was right in asking the ITO to assess the assessee on receipts basis with regard to contracts carried on and completed during the year of account.

As regards the reduction of flat rate, the Appellate Tribunal had arrived at the lesser flat rate on the basis of their decisions in similar cases in the district. Their opinions were not receivable evidence in the instant case. The decisions in different cases must have been based upon different facts and different inferences deducible from such facts. In this connection, it might be observed that the ITO had been very fair to the assessee bearing in mind the difference between the gross value and net value of the bills. The Appellate Tribunal, therefore, did commit a mistake of law in arriving at a finding for which there was no relevant evidence to support.

Therefore, the reduction of the estimated profit rate from 40 per cent adopted by the ITO to 30 per cent by the Tribunal on the ground that 30 per cent was the general rate adopted by it in the cases of other assessees doing the same kind of contract works during the same assessment year was not legal.

Note : The case was partially decided in favour of the assessee.

As per provisions of section 158BB, the block assessment is to be made based on evidence before the Assessing Officer. The word 'Evidence' has to be construed in a comprehensive manner and it includes all circumstantial evidence also. The material or evidence with the Assessing Officer on which assessment may be based is not confined to direct testimony by witnesses. Such evidence need not only be evidence found during the course of search but also material gathered by him. The Assessing Officer was not fettered by the Technical rules of evidence and the like and he may act on material which may not strictly speaking, be accepted as an evidence in the Court of law. It may be circumstantial evidence or assessment based on the preponderance of probabilities judged by human conduct. For this purpose, the past history of the case, and general market conditions will constitute relevant material for the purpose of assessment. For the purpose of block assessment under Chapter XIV-B, in view of amendment by Finance Act, 2002 to section 158BC(b) of the Income-tax Act which is effective retrospectively from 1-7-1995 wherein there is insertion of section 145 for the purpose of determining the undisclosed income. As per amendment to section 158BC(b ), the section 145 could also be invoked by Assessing officer for determining the undisclosed income. [Para 37]

However, it is to be made clear that if no material was found during the search which could show suppression of income, no estimation of undisclosed income of block period by resorting to section 145 could be made. In other words, where there is a material, such an estimation of income can be made. It is not necessary that addition should be limited to what is found during the search. [Para 38]

Adverting to the facts of the instant case, assessment was made by applying the flat rate of net profit at the rate of 10 per cent for the Assessment years 1998-99 and 1999-2000 for which no reasons has been given except stating that considering the nature of contract works executed by the assessee-company and the percentage of income admitted for the assessment years 1996-97, 1997-98 and 2000-01 and also for the percentage of income admitted by other contractors viz., M/s Prasad & Co. (PW) and M/s SEW Construction Ltd., income was estimated before depreciation at the rate of 10 per cent for the assessment years 1998-99, 1999-2000, 2001-02 and for the period 1-4-2001 to 20-12-2001 and treated the difference of income estimated and the income admitted as undisclosed income of the assessee-company for such assessment year. The Commissioner (Appeals) though held that for the assessment year 1998-99, income declared at the rate of 9.08 per cent before depreciation and 8.5 per cent for the assessment year 1999-2000 as reasonable. However, he has given different finding for the assessment year 2001-02 and for the period from 1-4-2001 to 20-12-2001. The assessee explained the reasons for low profit as to that the company has been in the construction industry for more than two decades. The company for quite some years focused its core activity in civil works consisting of mostly industrial/housing structures. Besides such civil contracts, the company diversified its activities into cement industry, wind power, manufacture of cylinders and other incidental jobs. Heavy losses resulted in closure of its cement division during financial year 1999-2000. The company also started focusing on infrastructure projects because of its line of business in construction and contracts. Hence, in the initial years, the company had undertaken some of the smaller projects especially the road works outside the State of Andhra Pradesh. To intrude into the competitive section like this, and to withstand the obvious competition from the established giants and multinationals, obviously the company had to quote the price in tenders either without a profit or with nominal profit. During the financial years 2000-01 and 2001-02 (up to 31-12-2001) the company has incurred losses in certain major projects. [Para 39]

It was clear from the narration of the facts hereinabove set out that the books of account were not found reliable and correct by the ITO. Under section 145(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, since the ITO was not satisfied about the correctness or the completeness of the accounts of the assessee, he could make an assessment in the manner provided in section 144. Section 144 provides for best judgment assessment and it enables the ITO, after taking into account all relevant material which he has gathered, to make the assessment of the total income or loss to the best of his judgment and determine the sum payable by the assessee or refundable to the assessee on the basis of such assessment. Thus, section 144 provides for best judgment assessment and if the conditions mentioned in section 145(2) are satisfied, as they were satisfied in the instant case, the best judgment assessment could be made by the ITO.

It must be pointed out that the best judgment assessment referred to in section 144 is regarding the figure of income, which, in the opinion of the ITO, is the proper figure of income and he makes the assessment of the total income to the best of his judgment after taking into account all relevant material which he has gathered.

It might be mentioned at the outset that, in the instant case, as shown by the material papers filed, it was obligatory on the part of the assessee to obtain the cement required for the work from the railway authorities on the conditions laid down in the contract and that bazaar cement was not allowed to be used.

Certificates issued by railway engineers did indicate exactly how the contract was entered into and on what basis the railway authorities and the assessee dealt with each other. It was clear that, if the ITO had to assess the income of the assessee to the best of his judgment and since, in the instant case, he had to arrive at the figure of profits or gains from the business of the assessee to the best of his judgment he must arrive at the figure of profits which the assessee was said to have earned from his contract with the railway authorities. The very fact that some materials, viz., cement, iron and steel, were to be supplied by the railway authorities and it was not open to the assessee-contractor, to purchase cement, iron and steel from outside or to use cement, iron and steel other than those supplied by the railway authorities, clearly showed that these items could never have entered into the making of profit by the assessee. It could not be said that the cement, iron and steel supplied by the railway authorities contributed to the profit made by the assessee. The question, therefore, arose as to whether, it could be said that the cost of materials in cases like the instant one must be excluded before the profits were ascertained on the best judgment assessment.

The facts and circumstances of each case would determine as to whether the cost of materials can or cannot be taken into consideration in determining the profits of a particular contractor on the best judgment assessment basis. It must be borne in mind that what the ITO has to determine is the profit of the assessee and the question whether the assessee was not maintaining his accounts properly. The question was of determining the profits which the assessee could be said to have earned and if the cost of materials supplied by the department concerned was never intended to contribute to the profits earned or to be earned by the contractor, and, in fact, had not resulted in any profit for the assessee, it was difficult to understand how the cost of materials supplied by the other party to the contract could be taken into consideration for estimating the profit earned by the contractor.

Therefore, on the facts and in the circumstances of this case, it was held that the value of the materials supplied by the railway authorities could not be taken into consideration for estimating the net income for the assessment years 1964-65 to 1967-68. Hence, the Tribunal was justified in law in giving directions to the AAC that the value of the materials supplied by the railway authorities should not be taken into consideration for estimating the net income for the assessment years 1964-65 to 1967-68.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

Assessee's books of account stand rightly rejected by Assessing officer

The assessee is admittedly not maintaining any stock register, so that there is no basis to verify the material consumption, which constitutes a very significant part of its operating cost. Not only that, it is admittedly following the 'method' of writing off its purchases for the year to the operating statement, treating the same as consumed. Now there is no basis to state that the material is actually consumed as soon as it is purchased, or that the assessee maintains no inventory thereof. The accounts as maintained are thus admittedly inconsistent with the actual, obtaining state of affairs, which the books of account of any entity or enterprise are supposed to reflect. There is no basis whatsoever, either in law or in accountancy; the law only upholding the accepted principles of commercial accounting, for the said concocted and/or arbitrary method of accounting being followed by the assessee. That the method has been followed from year to year, does not in any manner mitigate the defect, or justify its adoption. The assessee's books of account, as maintained, are thus not amenable to yielding correct operating results, so that the same stand rightly not accepted by Assessing Officer, applying section 145(3). [Para 3.1]

Continuing further, there is no basis in the Assessing Officer's estimation of material consumption at 36 per cent. Equally unjustifiable is his separate addition toward closing stock, which arises as a by-product to the finding of an actual lower material consumption. In fact, neither any separate addition can be sustained nor there is any warrant for allowing the assessee, as claimed by it, credit for the closing stock. The assessee would also have, similarly, opening stock, which has to be necessarily taken into account in determining the profit of the year. In fact, the opening stock being taken at nil, i.e., the value of the closing stock as reflected and accepted for the immediately preceding year, no opening stock for the year could be taken without first sustaining an addition toward the same under section 69/69A. [Para 3.2]

Presumptive statutory rate under section 44AD provides a good guideline for estimation of income

Section 145(3) mandates for making the assessment in the manner as provided in section 144, i.e., according to the best judgment of the assessing authority, taking all the relevant material into account. The assessee has relied on case law, i.e., Kesharbhai Ghamarbhai Chaudhary v. ITO [2012] 23 taxmann.com 273 (Ahd.), to the effect that under the circumstance of rejection of books of account, the prescription of section 44AE; the assessee in that case being a transport operator, is a good guideline for the purpose of estimation of income. The presumptive provision in the case of civil contractors is section 44AD, which provides for a net profit rate of 8 per cent. The matter is purely factual, though the prescribed presumptive statutory rate, applicable for assessees with a turnover of up to Rs. 40 lakh, without doubt provides a good guideline. The Apex Court in Brij Bushan Lal Parduman Kumar v. CIT [1978] 115 ITR 524 approved a profit rate of 10 per cent. The Tribunal has in such cases upheld profit rates varying from 8 per cent upwards to as much as 20 per cent, or even higher. A net profit rate of 10 per cent on the assessee's contract receipt of Rs. 360.86 lakh, i.e., involving material consumption, would be a reasonable estimate. Qua its labour receipt of Rs. 82.95 lakh, a net profit rate of 20 per cent, in view of a much lower base, as appropriate under the given facts and circumstances of the case. The Assessing Officer is directed to work out the assessee's income for the year by applying the said percentages. No other addition is sustainable. [Para 3.3]

In the instant case, the assessee contractor had not been able to satisfy the lower authorities as to what were the terms of the contract with the contractee and in what terms and consideration the materials were supplied by the contractee to the contractor. Furthermore, in the instant case the total amount of profit had to be computed by applying the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act. The rate of profit had also to be determined by applying the proviso to section 13 of the 1922, Act. As the Tribunal had pointed out that if the normal experience and expectation of a contractor as to how the profit would vary, were taken into consideration and in the circumstances where the contractor had not been actually able to satisfy the terms of the contract and where the estimates were to be based by applying the provisions to section 13 of the 1922 Act, it could not be said that the Tribunal was not justified in upholding the decision of the AAC in the manner as it did. In cases where there was clear and unambiguous evidence that there was contract which provided sufficient limit, beyond which the tender could not be quoted and there was a stipulation that the contract was to be quoted at a particular rate, excluding the cost of materials, to be supplied by the contractee, other considerations might apply.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

In the instant case there was material before the Tribunal on which its finding could be based: the assessee's representative had admitted before the AAC that full quantitative details in respect of the stores of the value of Rs. 1,30,000 consumed in the execution of that contract might not be available. In the circumstances, recourse to estimating the profits on the contract was inevitable. He, therefore, made an addition of Rs. 10,000 as against Rs. 26,434 added by the ITO. If the assessee wished to displace the AAC's estimate it was open to him to adduce evidence in support of its claim that the consumption of stores of the value of Rs. 1,30,000 was fully justified. This the assessee apparently did not do. For the subsequent year 1960-61 the assessee itself declared a net profit rate of 9.9% as against 9% declared in the assessment year in question. It could not be disputed that this was additional material which the Tribunal could take into consideration as it did. There was thus material before the Tribunal on which its estimate was based. The Tribunal's decision was, therefore, in conformity with the decision in the case of CIT v. Maharajadhiraj of Darbhanga [1933] 1 ITR 94 (P.C.).

The Tribunal was therefore justified in holding that the proviso to section 13 was applicable and there was material before it to sustain the aforesaid addition.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of revenue.

The Tribunal on various dates directed the assessee to file details of the length of road, quantity of store and grit and basis of evidence for consumption of the raw material and the details of the sales-tax and TDS certificate issued on that account. The assessee submitted that 5 per cent sales tax was deducted and, therefore, on that basis, tried to argue that if the figure of the raw material was calculated in respect of sales tax at 5 per cent, then the same amount of the sales-tax as deducted by the Government would come to approximately the same figure. The road was constructed by the assessee as per contract otherwise, the Government would not have released the payments to the assessee. It was also established from the explanation and more particularly from the deduction of the sales tax on the amount that the assessee had used considerable dalla grits (purchased material) in the construction of the road. The assessee could not give evidence regarding the consumption of the dalla grit in the construction of the road, but applying the test of human probabilities to the explanation and the material on record and that the books account had not been rejected and that the assessee had also filed audit report showed that considerable purchases of raw material were used in the construction of the road, but it was difficult to arrive at definite conclusion about exact consumption of raw material in the absence of specific evidence. It was also established fact from the past history of the assessee that in the preceding years and subsequent years, income of the assessee was computed and assessed by the department on the basis of estimation by applying the net profit rate of 8 per cent to 8.25 per cent and the matters had become final. The authorities below had pointed out the defects in the bills and purchases and therefore, possible leakage was not ruled out. Even if the value of the dalla grit was calculated on the basis of sales tax deduction, the figure would come in approximation. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly held that the assessee had not maintained verifiable accounts and the assessee also did not dispute the handwriting expert’s report. The Commissioner (Appeals) also rightly held that the road was constructed by the assessee as per the specification of the principal as the payment was made to the assessee. It was also noted that the payment of wages as compared to last year was very low and as such, no separate addition could have been made on that account. It appeared that the Assessing Officer had not considered the case of the assessee by adopting the test of human probabilities. The Assessing Officer had also not looked into the case of the assessee from the angle as to whether the consumption of grit was made in the construction of the road. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in adopting the net profit rate in view of the facts and circumstances of the case and more particularly looking to the past history of the assessee. The Assessing Officer should have examined the past history of the assessee and should have himself adopted the net profit rate instead of making the additions on account of purchases in the raw material. The department had accepted the orders of the Commissioner (Appeals) in the preceding assessment years, i.e. , 1989-90, 1990-91 and 1991-92, in which 8 per cent to 8.2 per cent minus depreciation adopted by the first appellate authority was not challenged in the second appeal. In the subsequent years also, the same position was there. [Para 18]

Before applying the net profit, the past record and the comparable cases should be used. The department itself had accepted the net profit rate in the case of the same assessee in different years at 8 per cent to 8.25 per cent on the receipts after deducting the material and sales tax as in the past and allowed the depreciation. Therefore, looking to the past history and comparable cases, it would be reasonable and appropriate if the net profit rate of 8 per cent on the receipts after deducting the cost of the material supplied by the Government department was applied in the instant case. The Assessing Officer was directed that he should calculate the net profit of 8 per cent on the net receipt. The findings of the CIT(A) were accordingly modified to the extent stated above. The appeal of the assessee on that issue was partly allowed and the appeal of the revenue was dismissed. [Para 20]

In the instant case the assessee as sub-contractor to execute the civil construction works awarded by the principals, which was a small part of the projects executed by the principals. On the contract receipts, the principals had also deducted the tax under section 194C. Besides, the assessee was also engaged in the business of trading of sarees. It was also a fact that the assessee filed duly audited profit and loss account and balance sheet along with its annexure. It also produced the audited books of account, bills/vouchers and bank statements before the Assessing Officer as admitted by him in the assessment order. Besides, it further produced all the details and explanations called for by the Assessing Officer from time to time. It also produced labour registers before the Assessing Officer. However, he was of the opinion that the said registers had not been maintained in a conventional manner and according to him, there were no signatures or thumb impressions of all the recipients. Because of the aforesaid observations, the Assessing Officer rejected the audited books of account of the assessee and estimated the net profit. The Assessing Officer gave the examples of net profit earned by three companies and, thereafter, he relied on the provisions of section 11AD and estimated the net profit at the rate of 8 per cent of gross receipts. Now the assessee argued that the estimation of net profit at the rate of 8 per cent by relying on provisions of section 44AD was totally incorrect and without any basis for the reason that the assessee was sub-contractor and its profit margin was low in comparison to the contractors. Further, the Assessing officer had compared the profit of the assessee with the companies whose turnover and business paraphernalia was huge in comparison to the assessee. Further, the assessee had executed the part of work of civil construction for these companies and, therefore, it was not correct to compare the profit of those companies with the profit margin of the assessee. In fact the profit margin of those companies was also less than the margin which had been estimated by the Assessing Officer in the case of assessee. In the case of assessee as per audited books of account, the net profit margin for assessment years 2007-08, 2008-09, 2009-10 and 2010-11 was 1.94 per cent, 0.67 per cent, 0.20 per cent and 0.09 per cent respectively. Now, the assessee argued that the Assessing Officer had failed to appreciate that the profit margins of contractors and sub-contractors could not be same. In the assessment order he had worked out the average profit margins in the case of those three companies at 5.93 per cent, 6.15 per cent and 5.19 per cent respectively and in the case of assessee he had estimated the profit at the rate of 8 per cent, whereas, in the case of assessee the profit margin would be much less than in these companies being a sub-contractor of these companies. [Para 5]

In view of the above factual position and comparative figures given by assessee of its principal, wherein the net profit was ranging from 5.19 per cent to 6.15 per cent, it was held that definitely there would be lower profit in the case of sub-contractor, i.e., the assessee and, hence, the Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly estimated the net profit rate at 4 per cent. Accordingly, the order of Commissioner (Appeals) and this issue of revenue's appeal was dismissed. [Para 6]

The department referred to the statement of ‘S’, in reply to a query as to what was the income of the company from the contract work usually. He replied that it was 10 per cent to 15 per cent to the total receipts. That statement was taken at the time of search without confronting ‘S’ with the books of account or any contract work specifically. The question posed to him was not in respect of the specific income of the year under consideration nor do the income from total contract work of the assessee. There was no clarification sought by the authorized officer or by the Assessing Officer as to the fact whether the said ‘S’ was stating so in respect of any of a single venture forming part of the one and individual business of the appellant comprised of several contract works secured by it, for which the assessee had maintained a combined profit and loss account or it was only a hypothetical calculation. The affidavit filed before the Assessing Officer of the same person was also not found false. The statement so given before the authorized officer was, thus, not a conclusive statement as the same was not based on any material on record but was only on approximation basis and not relevant to the facts of the case. The statement also did not quantify any correct rate as to whether it should be 10 per cent or 11 per cent or any higher rate. Thus, the statement so given by ‘S’ was of no credence and the same could not be used against the assessee for applying a profit rate of 11 per cent, which was not supported by any material or basis and was contrary to the facts of the case.

The proviso to section 13 empowers the ITO to assess the profits on such basis and in such manner as he thinks proper where he comes to the conclusion that the income and profits could not be properly deduced from the accounts of the assessee. But it has to be observed that the power of the ITO under this proviso is not an arbitrary power. He must exercise his discretion and judgment judicially and reasonably. Further, if the ITO proposes to use against the assessee the result of any private enquiry made by him, he should put him in possession of the full particulars and gave him an opportunity to meet the same. Although the assessing authority, having had no other means of arriving at the correct amount of profit by reason for the accounts, of the assessee being unsatisfactory, could have recourse to the method of independent enquiries about profits made by like concerns doing similar business, he cannot come to his own conclusions without affording an opportunity to the assessee to be able to satisfy the income-tax authorities that the cases relied upon by him were not comparable cases and were distinguishable on various grounds. The ITO cannot be said to make an assessment to the best of his judgment if he is not guided by the dictates of justice and fair-play. Natural justice demands that he should draw the attention of the assessee to the particular cases the authority had in view. The income-tax authority is not competent to make a random assessment based on his private enquiries which may not be revealed to the assessee. Local enquiry and the placing on record a note of the results of such enquiry are essential to sustain an ex-parte assessment. If the ITO proposes to act upon information collected by him independently on private enquiries, he should disclose to the assessee the nature of that information to rebut it. There ought to be an opportunity to the assessee to displace the Taxing Officer's estimate by adducing evidence. In the instant case, it was not shown that any attempt was made by the ITO to draw the attention of the assessee to the material collected by him on private enquiry and which formed the basis for his conclusions. He merely felt content on the circumstance that in the year of account the manufactures of dyed and printed cloth like the assessee made bumber profits shooting up to 50 per cent and over. It was all the more necessary in a business of the kind that the assessee firm was doing that the information gathered with regard to other manufacturers should have been placed before the assessee, because in a business of this kind there could be no two truly comparable cases. The assessee's business consisted of (a) buying mill cloth and selling it in the market as cloth, (b) buying handloom cloth, getting it dyed and printed in his own karkhana and selling them same, and (c) buying mill cloth and handloom cloth and getting it dyed and printed elsewhere and selling final dyed and printed cloth in the market.

The profit in business (a) was bound to be different from the profit made in business (b), likewise the percentage of the profit in business (c) could not be the same in business (d). These factors had necessarily to be taken into consideration in arriving at the amount of profit. There could not be a rule of thumb in these matters. The Tribunal seemed to have taken it for granted that the assessee would have made as such profit as the others, because of the boom period, without going into the matter as to whether such profit could be made in the particular variety of business undertaken by the assessee.

The result was that the order of the Tribunal was set aside and the case was remanded to it with the direction to disclose the material gathered from private enquiries to the assessee and give full opportunity to the assessee to place any relevant material to meet the substance of the private enquiry.

In the instant case the assessee had not maintained any books of account and the revenue applied a rate of profit of 12.6 per cent on the gross amounts of bills received by the assessee. The assessee had tendered for the contract as a whole including the cost of materials which were subsequently supplied by the Government. Furthermore, the gross profit had been computed on the total gross bill of the assessee. In the aforesaid background the Tribunal had come to the conclusion that the assessee, though tendered the contract as a whole, it must have included the cost of materials which were supplied by the Government as an element of profit in respect of cost of materials also. In the aforesaid background, it could not be said that the Tribunal was indulging in any surmise or acting without any proper evidence. The adoption by the ITO of the previous year, October to September, for the assessment year 1958-59, was wrongly adopted, because it did not satisfy the requirements of section 2(11)(i)(a ). It was only in cases where the assessee could adopt a different period to the financial year, 1st April to 31st March, that any other period could be adopted, which would invariably mean a period of twelve months. This was also subject to the requirement of the section.

"Previous year" ordinarily means a period from 1st April to 31st March. But if the assessee wanted to adopt any other period, then his accounts must be made up for that period. If, however, those accounts were not made up for that period, he could not ask for that period. In the instant case, admittedly the accounts had not been made up for over a period of 2 years and 8 months, so that the assessee could not adopt any other period than 1st April to 31st March. In these circumstances, the adoption by the ITO of the accounting period from October to September for year of assessment 1958-59, could not be conclusive, nor could the next ITO be barred from adopting the correct accounting period in terms of section 2(11)(i )(a).

Therefore, the ‘previous year’ for the assessment year 1959-60 in respect of the contract business was correctly taken as the year ending on 31-3-1959.

The second question whether estimation of profit on the gross amount instead of estimating on the net amount received by the assessee after deduction of costs of material supplied by the Govt. was justified, must be answered in favour of the department inasmuch as the contentions now urged had not been raised before the Tribunal nor had the assessee adduced any evidence in this respect. Therefore, this question could not be gone into.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of revenue.

The proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act does not entitle the Income-tax Officer to have a leap in the dark but requires him to compute the income ‘upon such basis and in such manner as the Income-tax Officer may determine.’ He has therefore to find out ‘the basis and the manner of computation’. The assessment is under section 23(3) of the 1922 Act after hearing such evidence as the assessee may produce and such other evidence as the Income-tax Officer may require on specified points. The Income-tax Officer may use material not placed before him by the assessee; but in such a case natural justice demands that he should give the assessee an opportunity of showing, if he can, that the material is incorrect, though the officer is not bound to disclose the source of his information. It may be that there is an adequate explanation against the information sought to be used against the assessee or that the Income-tax Officer might be misinformed. Although there is no express provision in the Act to require the Income-tax Officer to make such disclosure, it is necessary on the principles of natural justice.

The order is appealable and must stand scrutiny by an appellate court. It must, therefore, be a speaking order. If the basis and manner of computation are not disclosed in the order, the assessee’s right of appeal may be illusory unless the appellate authority refers the matter back to the Income-tax Officer to disclose the basis and manner of his computation. If the profits are computed under this proviso upon a basis determined by the Income-tax Officer, profits included in such computation cannot be included again in the assessment for any subsequent year. The burden is on the assessee to prove that the profits sought to be assessed were included in the assessment for any preceding year. This burden cannot be adequately discharged unless the assessment orders disclose the basis and manner of computation. If after rejecting the method of accounting employed by the assessee, the Income-tax Officer were simply to add a particular amount to the income returned or to disallow a part of the business expenses properly incurred by the assessee and allowable under section 10 of the 1922 Act, he would not be acting under the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act. The Income-tax Officer would be acting contrary to law if he were to disallow such business expenses or make an addition of a lump sum simply on the ground that the trading profits cannot be properly determined from the books of account. The Income-tax Officer is not entitled to discard the evidence of the books of account altogether merely because the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act is attracted.

It is certainly not a "leap in the dark". The Income-tax Officer is not entitled to make a guess without evidence.

The Tribunal did not make a distinction between an assessment under section 23(3) of the 1922 Act where the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act is invoked, and an assessment "to the best of judgment" under section 23(4) of the 1922. If the Income-tax Officer has made "best judgment assessment" under section 23(3) of the 1922 Act in the instant case, they were bad in law. Under section 23(3) of the 1922 Act the Income-tax Officer has to determine the income on the evidence before him produced by the assessee or collected by him, while under sub-section (4) he acts in the absence of such evidence because the assessee is in default in supplying information.

It was, therefore, held that in a case to which the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 applies, the ITO is bound to disclose in his order the basis and the manner of computation of the income, gains or profits and to disclose the date on which he arrives at the result.

As regards the question whether there was any material on record to warrant the estimate of the profits at the several rates adopted in this case unfortunately the statement of the case was not satisfactory. This was evidently due to the view of the Tribunal that the assessment was a leap in the dark. Instead of referring the case back under section 66(4) of the 1922 Act and wasting considerable time, the Court proposed to examine the orders of the Income-tax Officer to see if there was any material on record to warrant the estimate of profits at the several rates adopted by the Income-tax Officer.

The profit and loss account of a trading concern is usually divided into two sections. The first section is termed the trading account which is so framed as to show the gross profit. The gross profit as shown by the trading account is transferred to the second section which is the profit and loss account proper.

The excess of the credit total over the debit is called the gross profit, i.e., the excess realised on the sales over the purchase price of the goods sold, and is transferred to the profit and loss account. These principles appear to exclude from the computation of gross profit any items which do not affect the cost of the goods sold. It was, perhaps, for this reason that the AAC deleted certain items from the items which the ITO computed for deduction from the gross profit, such as the lease amount and certain establishment charges as claimed by the assessee. But it appeared from the order of the AAC that the items which the assessee claimed had been allowed. The department contended that the assessee did not take any objection before the Appellate Tribunal that the other items ought to have also been deleted from the gross profit. But the assessee contended that his grounds of appeal covered this aspect of the matter also, and that the amounts in respect of the items which had been deleted from the gross profit returned by him were also shown in the profit and loss account, from which they had been computed. It was also contended that the computation of the gross profit must be in accordance with law and on the material on record. It was not permissible for the income-tax authorities to allow a part and disallow the rest, if, in law, he was entitled not to take any of these items into consideration in arriving at the gross profits.

For the aforesaid reason there was no basis or material for the department to compute the income.

The Assessing Officer has rejected books of account for the reason that the assessee has failed to produce necessary bills and vouchers in respect of expenditure. Having said, one has to examine, on facts and circumstances of the case whether the Assessing Officer was right in adopting net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts. There is no dispute with regard to the facts that the assessee is in the business of execution of works contracts. It is also an admitted fact that the assessee had disclosed 6.73 per cent to 7.44 per cent net profit, in the earlier period. For the assessment year 2007-08 in the scrutiny assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer has estimated net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts for which the assessee has not preferred any appeal. Estimation of net profit from the business is one of the accepted method of determination of income from business. But, there is no hard and fast rule for estimation of income.

The department is following estimation of net profit on various rates depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case. But, while estimating net profit from the business, there should be a basis for adopting a particular rate of net profit, either based on comparable cases of similar nature of business or assessee's own book results for earlier years. When there is no possibility of getting a comparable cases, and there is no possibility of reference to assessee's own book results for earlier periods, a reference to the provisions of section 44AD can be made, wherein the Act provides for estimation of net profit from the specified businesses subject to certain conditions. [Para 9]

The provisions of section 44AD provide for estimation of net profit of 8 per cent on gross receipts, in case where the assessees are involved in specified businesses and turnover from the business does not exceed specified limit. Although, the assessee's case does not fall within the ambit of the provisions of section 44AD of the Act, as its contract receipts exceed the specified limit, the analogy provided in the provisions of section 44AD can be adopted for estimation of net profit because of nature of business carried out by the assessee. The nature of business carried on by the assessee was squarely fit into the specified businesses referred to in the provisions of section 44AD of the Act. The presumptive rate of net profit of 8 per cent incorporated in section 44AD, reflects the legislative approved rate of net profit, which can be considered as fair and reasonable to estimate income from civil contract business, where the books of account are not found reliable by the Assessing Officer.

In this case, admittedly, the Assessing Officer had rejected books of account for the reason that the assessee has failed to produce supporting bills and vouchers in respect of expenditure. It is also an admitted fact that the assessee himself has admitted about 8 per cent net profit in the earlier period net of all deductions including depreciation. Therefore, considering the overall facts and circumstances of the case, the rate of net profit adopted by the Assessing Officer appears to be fair and reasonable. Hence, estimation of net profit of 8 per cent on total receipts net of all deductions including depreciation is upheld. [Para 10]

In so far as separate deductions towards depreciation is concerned, the assessee submitted that when estimation of net profit is made, separate deductions towards depreciation should be allowed, as depreciation is a notional deduction for normal wear and tear of the assets.

In this case, the assessee is involved in the business of execution of main works which carries more profit than sub-contract works and hence, the Assessing Officer has rightly adopted reasonable net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts and accordingly, further deductions towards depreciation is not allowed. Whether separate deductions can be allowed towards depreciation or not is a fact which is to be decided based on the facts and circumstances of each case and also based on the rate of net profit adopted for estimation of profit.

On the language of the proviso to section 13 of 1922 Act, it is plain that if no method of accounting has been regularly employed, or, if the method employed is such that, in the opinion of the ITO, income, profits and gains cannot properly be deduced therefrom, then the ITO is empowered to make the computation upon such basis, and in such manner, as he may determine.

In the instant case, the ITO had found that the assessee did not maintain any account books, as none were produced at the time of the visit of the then ITO, at least in respect of three shops which he visited, and, therefore, he was justified in concluding that the account books now produced for these shops also had been written up at a later stage. He had further given reasons, for holding that the account books produced by the assessee did not reflect the true profits of the previous years. In such circumstances, the ITO was perfectly justified in applying the proviso to section 13 of 1922 Act to the present case, and in making his own estimate of the profit upon such basis and in such manner as he thought proper.

Further fact that the Tribunal upheld the ITO’s went to show that it found no reason to differ from the decision arrived at by it in the preceding year 1945-46. This also clearly went to show that the Tribunal in the year under assessment also found the account books to be unreliable, as they were found to be so in the previous year by it, for the reasons given by it in the preceding year, and by the ITO in the present year.

There is no rule of law as to the proper way of making an estimate. The only rule of law is that the true gains are to be ascertained as nearly as it can be done. There is no way of estimating, which is right or wrong in itself. It is a question of fact and figure whether the way of making the estimate, in any case, is the best way for that case. In making the estimate, the Income-tax Officer acts under section 23(4) of the 1922 Act, and he is required under it to make an estimate to the best of his judgment against a person, who is in default as regards supplying information. He must make what he honestly believes to be a fair estimate of the proper figure of assessment, and for this purpose he must be able to take into consideration local knowledge and repute in regard to the assessee's circumstances, and his own knowledge of previous returns by, and assessments of, the assessee, and all other matters which he thinks will assist him in arriving at a fair and proper estimate: and though there must necessarily be guess-work in the matter, it must be honest guess-work. It was open to the Income-tax Officer, therefore, to maintain the same percentage in respect of the year of assessment when the assessment at a flat rate of profit at a certain percentage in the preceding year or years had been adopted, and the objection of the assessee to such an assessment taken by him had been rejected in the preceding years. The Income-tax Officer, therefore, was well warranted in maintaining the same percentage in the year of assessment, and, in taking into consideration the past records of an assessee, provided there was some evidence or material before the income-tax authorities for making the best judgment assessment, and it was not absolutely arbitrary, although in that sense too assessment must be to some extent arbitrary.

In view of aforesaid, impugned order of the Tribunal was to be affirmed.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

The Assessing Officer had estimated the gross profit at 6 per cent of the total receipts and had completed the assessment after adding the income from other sources also. The sundry creditors, as is seen from the explanation offered by the assessee before the Commissioner, came to Rs. 3.44 crores out of which the liability in the previous year was Rs. 1.92 crores. Hence the sundry credit claimed by the assessee came to Rs. 1.51 crores. Obviously this was not noticed by the Assessing Officer and presumably the same was not accounted in the total receipts as undisclosed income. If the sundry credits are not explained properly, then disclosing that in the account books would amount to a device employed to suppress the income received, as a credit taken by a third party, with whom the assessee had a transaction. [Para 9]

The assessee was a works contractor, who had executed contracts awarded by various State Government departments. There is no question of the credit being attributed to any of the awarders which even if existing, there was no difficulty in establishing the same. [Para 10]

In the assessment order the assessee has income from a firm, house property and other sources. Hence the income declared by the assessee is not solely from the contract work. When the assessment made is of income from one single source, if the total contract receipts are taken to estimate the gross profit, necessarily there cannot be any further addition made. If the gross receipts are taken, on which the net profit is assessed, the entire receipts are not reflected, then definitely there is scope for addition to the receipts. The sundry creditors if not explained will have to be added to the contract receipts before the net profit is assessed or otherwise added in the income from other sources, bringing in that quantum, as unexplained income. [Para 11]

Hence either way whether the unexplained sundry credits are added to the contract receipts or as income from other sources definitely the tax payable by the assessee would be higher than that paid by a mere estimation of net profit looking at the quantum returned on which no explanation was sought. The Commissioner in order under section 263 had also reckoned non payment of tax deducted at source. [Para 12]

Essentially the Commissioner has found the order to be erroneous for reason of non payment into the treasury of the tax deducted at source having not been verified and also the sundry creditors having not been examined. The latter of which ground results in the finding that the estimation of profit on the contract receipts alone would be an erroneous exercise and it causes prejudice to the interest of the revenue. There is absolutely no reason to interfere with the order of the Commissioner. The order of Tribunal is set aside. [Para 13]

at the several rates adopted in this case unfortunately the statement of the case was not satisfactory. This was evidently due to the view of the Tribunal that the assessment was a leap in the dark. Instead of referring the case back under section 66(4) of the 1922 Act and wasting considerable time, the Court proposed to examine the orders of the Income-tax Officer to see if there was any material on record to warrant the estimate of profits at the several rates adopted by the Income-tax Officer. The assessee had returned profits by estimate. This was obviously unwarranted. As the trading profits could not be properly deduced from the account books for want of opening and closing stocks, the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 was attracted; but that did not entitle the Income-tax Officer to reject the books. In fact, the Income-tax Officer had not rejected the books as unreliable. He rejected the method of deducing the gross profits. Under such circumstances, the Income-tax Officer could have ascertained the rate of profits from the books of account and from outside information of returns and examination of books of local merchants in similar circumstances. If the assessee failed to satisfy the Income-tax Officer as to the correctness of the percentage of profits returned by him, it was open to the officer to take a higher percentage consistent with the state of trade in the locality or with any special circumstances of the assessee which warrant a higher rate of profits. The Income-tax Officer must disclose the basis and manner of computation and make his order a speaking order.

Under these circumstances it was held that there was material on record to warrant an estimate of the profits at the several rates adopted in this case.

Note: The case was decided partly against the assessee and partly against the revenue.

In the instant case, the Assessing Officer rejected the books of account on the reason that the assessee had not maintained proper books of account and also had failed to produce vouchers for verification and the expenditure claimed by the assessee was not substantiated. The assessee in the earlier years also had not maintained the proper books of account. The assessee’s past track record showed that it neglected presenting of the books of account in accordance with law. When the assessee claimed any expenditure, it was mandatory on its part to produce the books of account supported by proper bills and vouchers. Since the assessee had not produced books of account, true profits or loss could not be deduced from its books of account. The Assessing Officer having no other option rejected the books of account and estimated the income at 10 per cent of gross receipts. But the position was that the assessee was carrying on three kinds of contracts as in the earlier years, i.e., (i) own contracts, (ii ) contracts taken from the sub-contractors, (iii) contracts given to other parties on sub-contracts. The assessee had a higher rate of profit on the contracts executed by the assessee itself. In these contracts, the assessee agreed that its income was at 9 per cent of the gross receipts. Thus, the Assessing Officer was directed to estimate the income on the contracts executed by the assessee on its own at 9 per cent. In case of contracts taken by the assessee on sub-contract, the income was to be estimated at 8 per cent of the gross receipts. In case of contracts given by the assessee to the 3rd party on sub-contract, income was to be estimated at 4 per cent. This is because when the assessee gave contract to the other parties on sub-contract, it could not keep the same percentage of profit at 9 per cent. It had to forgo certain portion of the profit, i.e., around 5 per cent to the sub-contractors. Similar was the position in the case of contracts taken by the assessee on sub-contract from other parties. Further, the assessee was entitled to depreciation and remuneration, and interests to partners on the profit estimated by the Assessing Officer at applicable rates, because the income estimated as above of the assessee was before the depreciation and interest and remuneration of the partners. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer was to be directed to compute the income of the assessee afresh.

Another contention raised by the assessee was that once the books of account were rejected and income was estimated, the Assessing Officer was precluded from invoking provisions of section 40(a)( ia) to make further addition. The books of account of the assessee were not relied, these were rejected by the Assessing Officer and the same was confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as by the Tribunal. Now, placing reliance on the same books for the purpose of invoking the provisions of section 40(a)(ia ) was improper. The estimation of income took care of the irregularities committed by the assessee. Further addition by invoking section 40(a)(ia ) amounted to punishing the assessee for the same offence on double occasions, which was not permitted by law.

After coming to the conclusion that the trading results were not prone to verification, the Assessing Officer was left with only one alternative to estimate the income of the assessee in the most appropriate and reasonable manner. In such type of cases, the net profit rate or gross profit rate could be applied or the Assessing Officer could adopt any method of estimation and work out the income from profession or business. But the method adopted must be reasonable and logical. In all civil contract cases, if accounts are not maintained or defective accounts are maintained, a net rate of 10 per cent is applied which was admitted by the Commissioner (Appeals) in his order. In those cases neither depreciation nor interest nor any other expenditure debitable to profit and loss account are separately allowed. By allowing depreciation and interest, net profit rate of approximately 3.5 per cent had been applied consequent to the order of the Commissioner (Appeals). The rate itself was absolutely abnormal. There was no evidence on record whatsoever that there were abnormal conditions prevailing with the assessee to earn such a low net profit by executing the contract. Once net rate was applied it was not open to the Assessing Officer to allow any other claim debited to profit and loss account. Depreciation and interest were definitely items which were debited in profit and loss account before the net profit was arrived at. It could have been the case of the appellant to justify the net profit rate shown as .27 per cent or to justify the net profit rate applied by the Commissioner (Appeals) at 3.5 per cent approximately. But no such discussion was available on record. The logical conclusion of the circular of the CBDT regarding claim of depreciation that in case profits were estimated, the same should be made subject to the allowance of depreciation and the assessee should file complete details of the claim of depreciation. One has again to look into the power given by the statute to the Assessing Officer when he invoked proviso to section 145(1). The first proviso to section 145(1) gives power to the Assessing Officer to decide whether or not income can properly be deduced from the accounts maintained by the assessee, even if the accounts are correct and complete.

Keeping in view the law laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. British Paints India Ltd. [1991] 188 ITR 44/ 54 Taxman 499 the Assessing Officer has to adopt rationale and reasonable method in arriving at the estimate of income, after he gives finding that the accounts maintained by the appellant are neither prone to verification nor reliable. He can use his own method but his method should be rationale and reasonable. In the case of the assessee he had used rationale and reasonable method. The application of net rate is directly dependent on the net rate shown by other cases in the line of the business. Other cases of contractors are being applied net rate of profit without giving them advantage of depreciation some contractors debit various items which relate to profit & loss or trading account expenditure and claimed 100% of depreciation. This method creates an abnormal situation in the net profit. The Assessing Officer had, therefore, taken a proper course by ignoring depreciation and the interest and applied net rate of 10%. The second positive feature in the assessment of the ITO related to the observation that the net profit rate of the person who used heavy machinery was going to be more than the net profit of a person who was not using the mechanical aid for execution of civil work.

Hence, there was no infirmity in the method adopted by the Assessing Officer. The order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was reversed and the order of the Assessing Officer maintained.

The authority making a best judgment assessment must make an honest and fair estimate of the income of the assessee and though arbitrariness cannot be avoided in such estimate the same must not be capricious but should have a reasonable nexus to the available material and the circumstances of the case.

From the tender documents that were made available to the contractor and the terms and conditions of the "Lump Sum Contracts", two or three aspects emerged very clearly. In the first place, the contractor became aware that certain specified stores/materials would be supplied to him by the department at fixed rates for being used in the works to be undertaken by him for which he had not to pay from his pocket and it was on that footing that he submitted his tender quoting a particular figure for the entire work; secondly, such stores/material so supplied by the M.E.S. department had to be used, fixed or incorporated by the contractor in the works undertaken by him and the surplus, if any, that would remain after the completion of the work was to be returned to the department; thirdly, since for accounting purposes the initial supply was debited to the contractor at the specified fixed rates, credit for the balance of the stores/materials so returned was also given at the same rates, some adjustment being made in respect of the wear and tear of such stores/material but in regard to the stores/material out of such supply as was actually used, fixed or incorporated into the works, no accounting was done vis-a-vis the contract payment that is made to the contractor. In other words, in substance and in reality, such stores/material always remained the property of the department and the contractor had merely the custody of it and he fixed or incorporated the same into the works. It seemed clear that in such circumstances and having regard to the terms and conditions on which such supply of stores/materials was made there was not even a theoretical possibility of any element of profit being involved in the turnover represented by the cost of such stores/material. It was conceivable that when the contractor himself purchased materials in the open market and supplies the same to the department by using, fixing or incorporating the same in the works, as in the case of materials other than those specified in Schedule "B", some profit element would be embedded in the turnover represented by the cost of such material but when stores/material was supplied by the Government department at fixed rates for being used, fixed or incorporated in the work on terms indicated above, there would be no element of profit involved in the turnover represented by the cost of such material. It is true that, ordinarily, when a works contract is put through or completed by a contractor the income or profits derived by the contractor from such contract is determined on the value of the contract as a whole and cannot be determined by considering several items that go to form such value of the contract but in our view where certain stores/material is supplied at fixed rates by the department to the contractor solely for being used or fixed or incorporated in the works undertaken on terms and conditions mentioned above, the real total value of the entire contract would be the value minus the cost of such stores/material so supplied. Therefore, since no element of profit was involved in the turnover represented by the cost of stores/material supplied by the M.E.S. to the assessee-firm, the income or profits derived by the assessee firm from such contracts would have to be determined on the basis of the value of the contracts represented by the cash payments received by the assessee-firms from the M.E.S. department exclusive of the cost of the material/stores received for being used, fixed or incorporated in the works undertaken by them.

The appeal was, therefore, allowed.

The assessee is a contractor carrying out Government as well as private contracts. The assessee produced complete books of account before the Assessing Officer but without supporting vouchers. Even the unexplained credits/transfer entries/deposits in the bank account were inter deposits of business and these were nothing sort of cash credits or unexplained credits. Revenue could not explain how the entire addition was made and what was the basis for same. It only argued that since the books of account were not supported by vouchers, the Assessing Officer and Commissioner (Appeals) had disallowed the expenses, charges and unproved credits/transfers/deposits in the hands of the assessee. It is not the case of the revenue that these deposits /unproved credits/transfer were not related to business transaction, rather the assessee filed a complete chart stating that the entire deposits/transfers/credits were proved and these were related to business transactions only and out of contract receipts. In such circumstances, the assessment order or order of Commissioner (Appeals) cannot be upheld. [Para 6]

In the absence of supporting material of the books of account i.e., bills and vouchers, the assessing authority should have rejected books of account and should have framed assessment in terms of sections 144 and 145. For that the Assessing Officer must act honestly and not vindictively or capriciously because he must exercise judgment in the matter. However, from records it is evident otherwise. He must make what he honestly believes to be fair estimate of the proper figure of assessment, and for this purpose he must be able to take into consideration local knowledge and repute in regard to the assessee's circumstances, and his own knowledge of previous returns and assessments of the assessee and all other matters which he thinks will assist him in arriving at a fair and proper estimate; and though there must necessarily be guess-work in the matter, it must be honest guess-work. In making a best judgment assessment, the Assessing Officer does not possess absolutely arbitrary authority to assess at any figure he likes, and although he is not bound by strict judicial principles, he should be guided by rules of justice, equity and good conscience. At the same time, there is nothing in the language of section 144 or 145 for holding that an assessment made by an officer under these sections, without conducting a local enquiry and without recording the details and results of that enquiry, cannot have been made to the best of his judgment within the meaning of that section. In other words, the Assessing Officer, while making a best judgment assessment, should make an intelligent, well grounded estimate. Such estimate must be based on adequate and relevant materials. If more than one method or approach is possible, any alternative method can be restored to estimate the quantum in a best judgment assessment. The quantum to be made in a best judgment assessment should be rational and fair in all circumstances of the case. [Para 7]

The Tribunal confirmed the application of net profit at 5.35 per cent in earlier year i.e. in Assessment Year 2003-04. Keeping in view net profit of earlier years, a reasonable net profit i.e. at the rate of 8 per cent would meet the end of justice. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer is directed to recompute the assessee's income after deleting all the additions as made by him and enhanced by Commissioner (Appeals), but restrict the addition only at 8 per cent of gross contract receipts. It is also mentioned that this net profit rate at 8 per cent cannot be taken as reference to any other years, if facts are not identical or assessee claims that assessment be framed on the basis of accounts, if accounts are found correct. [Para 8]

It cannot be said that the assessee was not entitled to adopt percentage method of recognition of income for computation of income tax under accrual method of accounting. However, mere qualification in the Annual Report of the company containing the balance sheet and the profit and loss account by itself is not sufficient to conclude that the assessee has disclosed the percentage of the work completed during previous year relevant for the assessment year. [Para 33]

The assessee may have entered into several contracts with different clients with varied terms and conditions. These documents are required to be produced before the Assessing Officer at the time of assessments. The purpose of accounting under the Act, is to ascertain the taxable income and to determine the tax payable by an assessee. Therefore, these documents and other ancillary documents are required to be produced before an Assessing Officer during the assessment. [Para 34]

Further, a proper certification whether by an in-house department of the assessee or by an independent chartered engineer certifying the percentage of work completed under the contract was required to be produced by the assessee before the Assessing Officer for the purpose of assessment. [Para 35]

What was the term of the contract under which the revenue was generated on the bill raised on a client or a customer cannot be certified in the audited profit and loss account and the balance sheet. At best, they can corroborate what is there in the contract. Therefore, unless those supporting documents are produced, it cannot be said that there was full disclosure. [Para 36]

The enclosures filed before the Assessing Officer at the time of section 143(3) assessment do not indicate the same. Therefore, it cannot be said that there was true and full disclosure of all materials that were required for assessment before the Assessing Officer by the assessee. At the same time, it is to be noticed that the reasons given in the communications for reopening the respective assessment have merely questioned the method of accounting adopted by the assessee and show that it was issued in a mechanical manner. [Para 37]

As per Explanation I to section 147, production before the Assessing Officer of the account books or other evidence from which material evidence could with due diligence have been discovered by the Assessing Officer will not necessarily amount to disclosure within the meaning of section 147. [Para 38]

The conclusions arrived in the impugned communications overruling the objections of the assessee for the reopening of the assessments by the impugned notices are not conclusive. They are only prima facie views of the Assessing Officer. It is for the assessee to establish that it has correctly followed the accounting method by producing the supporting documents to substantiate the percentage of work that was completed for the purpose of proper determination of taxable turnover for payment of income tax. Mere disclosure in the profit and loss account and balance sheet is not sufficient. [Para 39]

Therefore, reassessment is directed to be completed after examining the documents to be produced by the assessee and pass reassessment orders on merits. [Para 40]

In the facts and circumstances of the instant case, it appeared that it was not possible to answer the questions referred without further findings on fact. It was not clear whether the lower authorities had seen or considered the terms and conditions of the contracts under which the assessee had carried on the work of construction. The terms and conditions as to supply of materials by the contractee were also not known.

Such terms were of some importance. It would be necessary to determine whether the materials to be supplied would be free of cost or price on the basis of market value or otherwise would be charged. On such facts it may be found that an element of profit was there on such supply (sic ). Whether the assessee submitted its tenders for the said contracts anticipating on being assured of supply of such materials were also not known. In this view, the matter was remanded back to the Tribunal. The Tribunal was directed to ascertain the terms and conditions of the contracts in question, if any, in respect of supply of materials and determine whether the assessee bid for such contracts taking into account such materials which were in fact supplied. If it was found on such facts that there was an element of profit involved in the materials supplied then the profits of the assessee will be estimated on the gross receipts of the assessee computed by including the value of the materials supplied to the net receipts. The Tribunal will be at liberty to take further evidence in the matter and will afford opportunity to the parties to adduce further evidence and to make further representations in the matter.

Note: Case remanded back.

see’s disclosed income for the assessment year 1996-97 was Rs. 1,51,29,500 and the income for the assessment year 1997-98 (broken period) was Rs. 51,81,310. This in fact, showed what profit the Assessing Officer had intended to adopt. The contention of the department that the annexure was prepared only to reconcile the figures to show as to how the ultimate undisclosed income had been arrived at, had no merit. As regards the contention of the revenue that for these two years the assessee had overstated the profits, there was no merit in the same. It was true that in earlier three years the profit of the assessee was quite small, but this did not give rise to the presumption that the assessee would have continued to show same lower profit for the assessment year 1996-97. For the assessment year 1996-97 the assessee showed a profit of Rs. 1,51,29,500 on contract receipts of Rs. 9,14,68,850. This gave an average of profit of 16.5 per cent. The profit for the broken period from 1-4-1996 to 8-8-1996 was 14.3 per cent. The profit for the rest of the period, i.e., 9-3-1996 to 31-3-1997 was Rs. 33.69 per cent. As pointed out by the assessee for the assessment year 1998-99, the assessee had filed its return of income in which its net contract receipts were Rs. 13,80,82,884 on which profit disclosed was Rs. 3,53,57,802 which gave profit at the rate of 25.6 per cent. Further, as pointed out by the assessee for the assessment year 1999-2000 for which the return was yet to be filed, the assessee had declared the profit of 24.2 per cent. Further, these figures had been considered for paying advance tax. This pattern of the profit shown for the subsequent year clearly indicated the assessee’s stand that the assessee would not have shown the lower profit as alleged, but would have shown much more improved profit genuinely worked out from the records maintained. A mere non-payment of advance tax did not lead to the conclusion that the assessee would have not shown any income. It was duly established from the documents available on record that the assessee would have disclosed the income for the assessment years 1996-97 and 1997-98. Therefore, there was no justification on the part of the Assessing Officer to treat Rs. 1,51,29,500 for the assessment year 1996-97 and Rs. 51,81,310 for the assessment year 1997-98 as undisclosed income of the block period. Therefore, the Assessing Officer was to be directed to treat the same as disclosed income and allow the deduction therefor and then compute the tax liability of the assessee in respect of the remainder undisclosed income.

In the instant case, the assessee-company had been consistently following a particular method of accounting. Its accounts were audited both under the Companies Act, 1956, as well as under section 44AB of the Income-tax Act. Such audited accounts were being filed with the Registrar of Companies as well as with the income-tax department for more than 7 years. The revenue had scrutinized the accounts and the method of accounting regularly employed and adopted by the assessee year after year had not been found fault with. The auditors of the company both under the Companies Act and the Income-tax Act had been consistently certifying that the assessee had been regularly following the method of accounting and that the annual profits could be properly deduced from such method of accounting employed by the assessee. The auditors over the years had also been certifying that the accounts were regularly maintained and were complete in the sense that there was no significant omission therein. This finding had been accepted by different Assessing Officers over a period of seven years. For rejecting the view taken for the earlier assessment years, there must be a material change in the fact situation. No doubt, the previous view will have no application even in cases where the law itself has undergone a change but before an earlier view can be upset or digressed from, one of the two must be demonstrated, namely, a change in the fact situation or a material change in law whether enacted or declared by the Supreme Court. [Para 5.7]

In the case of a civil contractor, who undertakes major works, a contract is spread over several years. The income arising from the same contract is spread over several assessment years and part of the profit of this contract is separately arrived at assessment year-wise and brought to tax.
