(2) The application shall be signed by a person authorised to make an application for registration. On receipt of the application, the assessing authority shall, after satisfying itself that the contents of the application are correct, allow the same and such contractor whose application is allowed shall be called lump sum contractor.

(3) The lump sum contractor shall be liable to make payment of lump sum monthly calculated at five per cent of the payments received or receivable by him during the month for execution of the contract. The payment of lump sum so calculated shall be made within twenty one days following the close of the month after deducting therefrom the amount paid by the contractee on behalf of the contractor under section 24 for that month. The treasury receipt in proof of payment made and certificate(s) of tax deduction and payment obtained from the contractee shall be furnished with the quarterly return.

(4) The lump sum contractor shall file returns at quarterly intervals in Form VAT-R6 within a month of the close of the quarter and shall pay lump sum, if any, due from him according to such return after adjusting the amount paid under sub-rule (3).

(5) The lump sum contractor shall be entitled to make purchase of goods for use in execution of the contract both on the authority of declaration in Central Form C as well as Form VAT-D1 prescribed under clause (a) of sub-section (3) of section 7 and for this purpose he shall be deemed to be a manufacturer.

(6) The lump sum contractor shall maintain complete account of, declarations in Central Form C and Form VAT-D1 used by him and, the utilisation of the goods purchased on the authority of these forms. He shall also keep complete account of, payments receivable by him for the execution of the contract and, the payments actually received by him.

(7) A lump sum contractor shall have to pay lump sum in respect of every works contract awarded to him after the award of the contract in respect of which he first elected to pay lump sum and he shall continue to pay tax in respect of contracts awarded before as if he is not a lump sum contractor.

(8) A lump sum contractor may at any time by appearing before the appropriate assessing authority himself or through an authorised agent express in writing his intention to opt out of the scheme of payment of lump sum in lieu of tax payable under the Act. Such contractor in respect of the contracts awarded to him thereafter shall not be liable to pay lump sum in lieu of tax payable under the Act but in respect of the other contract(s) he shall continue to pay lump sum in lieu of tax payable under the Act till the completion of each of such contract(s).

(9) A lump sum contractor may, when rate of lump sum is revised, opt out of the scheme of payment of lump sum in lieu of tax payable under the Act by appearing before the appropriate assessing authority himself or through an authorised agent within fifteen days of such revision and expressing in writing his intention to opt out of the scheme of payment of lump sum. In the assessment year 1983-84, the assessee, a civil works contractor, started construction work on behalf of Crompton Greaves Ambad and continued it up to the assessment year 1988-89.

The assessee adopted for its accounts the project completion method, by which the profit or loss was accounted for in the books of account of the year in which the project was completed.

However, the Commissioner, under section 263 set aside the assessments on the ground that income under construction work had not been computed correctly by taking into account the profits on the work-in-progress and that the method of accounting employed did not enable the income of the year to be properly deduced.

On appeal, before the Tribunal the following points were highlighted:

(a)Both the methods, the method adopted by the assessee and the method sought to be adopted by the Commissioner, are recognised methods.

(b)The profits of business must be computed in accordance with method of accounting regularly employed by the assessee. The choice of the method of accounting, like the choice of the previous year (Note: choice of previous year is no longer permitted) lies with the assessee.

(c)The assessee has been following the same method of accounting regularly in subsequent assessment years. Under the mandatory provisions of section 145, the department is bound by the assessee's choice of method which cannot be rejected as improper merely because it gives the assessee benefit in certain years even if this is assumed to be the case, or merely because, according to the department, another method is preferable.

(d)Independent Chartered Accountants have also found it appropriate to adopt the project completion method for the purpose of true and fair view of the financial position, including the profits earned.

(e)Merely because the profits of a project are postponed from the year of commencement of the project to the year of completion of the project, the same would not be the basis for considering the assessment made on that basis erroneous.

(f)When the rate of tax remains constant, it cannot also be said that the assessments adopting the project completion method are in any way prejudicial to the interests of revenue.

The Tribunal cancelled the orders passed by the Commissioner under section 263 and restored the assessments framed by the Assessing Officer.

Conclusion

(d)The Accounting Standard (AS-7) having been made mandatory for corporate entities from April 1, 1991 and non-corporate assessees from 1-4-1993, the accounting for construction contracts should strictly conform to the requirements of the Standard.

[1996] 85 TAXMAN 214 (ART) TAXATION OF PROFITS FROM CONSTRUCTION CONTRACTS EXTENDING OVER SEVERAL YEARS

R. Balasubramanian B. Sridhar

In certain types of contracts relating to construction of multi-storeyed buildings, dams, bridges, etc., the work is spread over a number of years and the question of determining profits therefrom on an annual basis bristles with difficulties. There are two basic recognised methods of accounting, viz., (i ) the 'percentage of completion' method and (ii ) the 'completed contract' method, available to an assessee-contractor to choose from, but once he has made his choice, he must stick to it for the duration of the contract. In this article, the author discusses some of the issues involved in detail and, on the basis of copious case-law cited by him, comes to the conclusion that the ITO need not wait for the completion of the contract to determine the taxable profits arising from the project and that he can determine such profits for any given assessment year on the basis of the regular method of accounting followed by the assessee - EDITOR

Introduction

1. Under section 145(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 ('the Act'), income chargeable under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession", is computed in accordance with the method of accounting regularly employed by the assessee. Even if the accounts are correct and complete, but the method employed is such that in the Assessing Officer's view the income cannot be properly be deduced therefrom, he may compute the income as he thinks best in the given circumstances. In contracts relating to construction of multi-storeyed building, bridges, dams, ships, etc., which entail operations for a number of years, a problem arises as to the allocation of revenues and related costs to various accounting periods over the duration of the contract. The determination of annual income in such cases for purposes of levy of tax under the tax statute bristles with difficulties.

Two basic types of contracts

2. According to the International Accounting Standard-(IAS-11) effective from January 1, 1980 and the Accounting Standard-7 (AS-7) of the Institute of Chartered Accountants made mandatory from April 1, 1991 in the case of companies and from April 1, 1993 in the case of non-companies, construction contracts, formulated in a variety of ways, generally fall into two basic types:

(i)fixed price contracts - the contractor agrees to a fixed contract price or rate, in some cases subject to cost escalation clauses;

(ii)cost plus contracts - the contractor is reimbursed for allowable or otherwise defined costs, and is also allowed a percentage of these costs or a fixed fee.

Two methods of accounting

3. Two methods of accounting for contracts generally followed by contractors are (i) the percentage of completion method and (ii) the completed contract method.

Under the percentage of completion method, revenue is recognised as the contract activity progresses based on the stage of completion reached. The costs incurred in reaching the stage of completion are matched with this revenue, resulting in reporting of results which can be attributed to the proportion of work completed.

Under the completed contract method, revenue is recognised only when the contract is completed or substantially completed; that is, when only minor work is expected other than warranty obligation. Costs and progress payments received are accumulated during the course of contract but revenue is not recognised until the contract activity is substantially completed.

Under both these methods, provision is made for losses for the stage of completion reached on the contract. In addition, provision is usually made for losses on the remainder of the contract. When a contractor uses a particular method of accounting for a contract, then, in respect of all other contracts that meet similar criteria, the same method is used.

Snam company case

4. In this case, which came to the notice of the Public Accounts Committee of the Parliament, a foreign company having world wide operations, entered into an agreement with Indian Refineries Ltd. for constructing pipe-line and erecting permanent stations and terminals and also supplying materials to be employed in the work. During the course of assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1964-65, the assessee-company approached the Commissioner, New Delhi for getting its assessments finalised on 'completed contract' basis. The reasons adduced for the request were the following:

(a)The assessee was receiving advance payments from its clients and incurring expenses in executing the contracts.

(b)The bills for the jobs done could not be evaluated till joint inspections by the parties as per the terms of the contracts.

(c)In the case of a contract work running over several years, it was often not possible to ascertain the profits earned during each year before the completion of the contract, because of absence of data for evaluation of the work-in-progress of the jobs actually completed during the year.

P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 124 ITR 31, the Supreme Court has observed that the provisions of the Act relating to the charge on income apply in relation to a specific assessment year and the provisions of the Act providing for the computation of the chargeable income apply, in the absence of anything to the contrary, in relation to the relevant previous year. Therefore, the profits and gains have to be computed for each accounting year separately.

Completed contract method - Its acceptability 4. In the case of completed contract method, the profits of a contract are determined on the completion of the contract and not every year. It may happen that a particular contract may take several years for its completion. Therefore, if an assessee has adopted the completed contract method of accounting, he will not be in a position to compute the profits of his contract business every year. In such a situation the Assessing Officer may invoke the provisions of the proviso to section 145(1) and hold that the method of accounting employed by the assessee is such that true profits of the business cannot be deduced therefrom.

It is, no doubt, true that the completed contract method is a recognized method of accounting as per the Accounting Standard issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India. However, the main defect of this method is that it does not enable an assessee to compute his income from the contract business every year. In para 10.2 of the aforesaid Accounting Standard this defect has been highlighted in the following words:

"The principal disadvantage of the completed contract method is that periodic reported income does not reflect the level of activity on contracts during the period. For example, when a few large contracts are completed in one accounting period but no contracts have been completed in the previous period or are to be completed in the subsequent period, the level of reported income can be erratic although the level of activity on contracts may have been relatively constant throughout. Even when numerous contracts are regularly completed in each accounting period, and reported income may appear to reflect the level of activity on contracts, there is a continuous lag between the time when work is performed and the related revenue is recognized."

Since under the Act, each year is a separate self-contained year and profits and gains have to be computed each year separately, the Assessing Officer may not accept the completed contract method, even if regularly employed by the assessee, on the ground that income cannot be properly deduced therefrom. He may invoke the provisions of section 145 and compute the income either by applying a flat rate on the contract receipts or by some other method.

Relevant case law

5. Here it will be relevant to refer to a few decided cases on the subject. In the case of Tirath Ram Ahuja (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1976] 103 ITR 15 , the Delhi High Court has held that in the case of contracts, in order to ascertain the income, one need not wait till the contract is completed, and that it is open to the revenue to estimate the profits on the basis of the receipts in each year of construction, although the contract is not complete. The same view has been taken by the Patna High Court in the case of Sri Sukhdeodas Jalan v. CIT [1954] 26 ITR 617. In this case a military contract extended beyond the accounting period and the accounts were closed only after the completion of the contract. The question for determination was whether the profits should be assessed only after the completion of the contract or whether the profits accruing during the accounting period could be assessed. The Patna High Court held that it is fallacious to argue that merely because the military contract was completed after the accounting period, no profits arose or accrued to the assessee in the accounting year and that in the case of an incomplete contract there is a well-established method of calculating profits accruing in the accounting year. In the case of P.M. Mohammed Meerakhan v. CIT [1969] 73 ITR 735 , the Supreme Court also has held that the profits of an adventure can be determined even if the adventure is not completed.

Conclusion

6. Although the completed contract method is a recognized method of accounting as per the Accounting Standard issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, it is not a suitable method of accounting from income-tax point of view, as it does not enable determination of the profits of the contract business every year. Since under the Act each year is a separate self-contained year, it is necessary to determine the profit of the contract business each year separately. For this purpose, it will be advisable to adopt the percentage of completion method, which is the other method recognized by the aforesaid Accounting Standard.

The claim of the assessee that no income was chargeable to tax was upheld by the Tribunal.

In the case of W.D. Estate (P.) Ltd. (supra) , the assessee engaged in construction work followed the project completion method of accounting and returned profits for assessment. No objection was raised by the revenue in regard to the method adopted by the assessee.

(vi) CIT v. Guttoffnungashutto Sterkrado [1992] 197 ITR 66 (Ori.)

Guttoffnungashutto Sterkvado (the assessee) was a non-resident (German) company and executed the work of installing a blast furnace in Rourkela Steel Plant during the period November 1963 to March 1968. The performance of the contract was spread over a number of years, and the assessee followed the 'complete contract' basis to ascertain the profits and to have them assessed. The accounts maintained regularly by the assessee in Germany were audited by qualified German Chartered Accountants. Copies of accounts as well as the required particulars for the entire contract period were submitted by the assessee before the Assessing Officer for the years 1965-66 and 1966-67. After ascertaining the net income for the entire contract period (i.e., assessment years 1965-66 to 1968-69) the assessee apportioned the income so computed for the two assessment years 1965-66 and 1966-67 and filed returns accordingly. The Assessing Officer accepted the profits determined under the 'complete contracts basis', and made the assessments for the two assessment years 1965-66 and 1966-67. The Commissioner, however, set aside the assessments under section 263, directing the Assessing Officer to re-do the same. The assessee preferred an appeal to the Tribunal which recorded a categorical finding that no defect in the accounts maintained by the assessee was pointed out by the Assessing Officer and, on the contrary, the profits of the assessee could be correctly determined from the method of accounting adopted by it. With these comments, the Tribunal restored the assessments made by the Assessing Officer. The department made a reference to the High Court.

In the meantime, the assessments for the assessment years 1967-68 and 1968-69 were taken up. The assessments were challenged before the appellate authority who set them aside with a direction for redoing them. While redoing them, the Assessing Officer, contending that the method of accounting adopted by the assessee was not correct, recomputed the net profits adopting a net profit rate of 10 per cent on the receipts, two-thirds of which were taxable in India. The Commissioner (Appeals) who was in possession of the Tribunal's orders for the first two assessment years, set aside the assessments for making fresh assessments and, on further appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the orders of the Commissioner. Against these orders also, the Department preferred a reference to the Orissa High Court.

[1993] 70 TAXMAN 106 (ART) LONG-TERM CONTRACTS - WHETHER PROFITS SHOULD BE DETERMINED ANNUALLY OR ON COMPLETION OF THE CONTRACTS

K.R. Gupta

In the case of long-term contracts, the determination of profits from the contract business annually is not an easy task. For this reason, a contractor executing a long-term contract may like to determine the profit of the contract only after the contract has been completed and to file his income-tax return on that basis. In this connection, a question that arises for consideration is whether under the Income-tax Act, 1961, it is permissible to adopt such a method of accounting in respect of the contract business. The author of this article discusses various aspects of this issue concluding that although the completed contract method is a recognized method of accounting as per the Accounting Standard issued by the institute of Chartered Accountants of India, it is not a suitable method of accounting from income-tax point of view - EDITOR

Difficulty in determining profits annually

1. In the case of long-term contracts, the determination of profits from the contract business annually is not an easy task. For this reason, a contractor executing a long-term contract may like to determine the profit of the contract only after the contract has been completed and to file his income-tax return on that basis. In this connection, a question that arises for consideration is whether under the Income-tax Act. 1961 ('the Act') it is permissible to adopt such a method of accounting in respect of the contract business.

Position from accountancy point of view

2. Before examining the matter from the income-tax angle, it will be appropriate to discuss the position in this regard from the accountancy point of view. The Accounting Standard of 'Accounting for construction contracts' issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India has recognized the following two methods of accounting for contracts :

(i)the percentage of completion method;

(ii)the completed contract method.

In para 7 of the Accounting Standard (AS-7) these methods have been described as under :

"7.2 Under the percentage of completion method, revenue is recognized as the contract activity progresses based on the stage of completion reached. The costs incurred in reaching the stage of completion are matched with this revenue, resulting in the reporting of results which can be attributed to the proportion of work completed. Although (as per the principle of 'prudence') revenue is recognized only when realised, under this method, the revenue is recognized as the activity progresses even though in certain circumstances it may not be realised.

7.3 Under the completed contract method, revenue is recognized only when the contract is completed or substantially completed; that is, when only minor work is expected other than warranty obligation.

Costs and progress payments received are accumulated during the course of the contract but revenue is not recognized until the contract activity is substantially completed."

It will be seen that from the accountancy point of view, the completed contract method is a recognized method of accountancy.

Under the Act the assessee has the choice of adopting whatever method of accounting he wants to adopt, provided he follows the method regularly for his own purposes. Section 145 of the Act clearly makes the method of accounting, if regularly employed by the assessee, a compulsory basis of computation unless, as provided in the first proviso to section 145(1), in the opinion of the Assessing Officer, the income, profits and gains cannot be properly deduced therefrom. If the true income, profits and gains cannot be ascertained on the basis of the assessee's method of accounting, the Assessing Officer has the power to compute the income on such basis and in such manner as he may determine.

Each year as a self-contained unit

3. Under the Act, for the purpose of computing the profits and gains, each year is a separate self-contained period of time. In the case of Mahamudabad Properties ( P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 124 ITR 31, the Supreme Court has observed that the provisions of the Act relating to the charge on income apply in relation to a specific assessment year and the provisions of the Act providing for the computation of the chargeable income apply, in the absence of anything to the contrary, in relation to the relevant previous year. Therefore, the profits and gains have to be computed for each accounting year separately.

(ii) Second illustrative case. - A public limited company, wholly owned by a State Government, undertook construction works exclusively for Government departments/undertakings, both on turnkey and non-turnkey basis and followed the mercantile system of accounting. The company followed the system of crediting the value of work done, measured by the company engineers up to 31st March every year at the rates approved by the clients and debiting all works and other expenses to the profit and loss account, irrespective of whether a certain piece of work was in the initial stage or nearing completion, since the rates for each item in the contract were quoted and accepted by the clients. The company charged the client for doing each piece of work on the basis of rate per metric cube of work done. Thus, the rate for each item of work quoted included material, labour, overheads and profit as an integral part of the rate itself.

Drawing the attention of the Committee to Accounting Standard-7(AS-7) on 'Accounting for Construction Contracts; paras 7.3 and 7.4 wherein it is mentioned that provision for losses should be made if the company anticipates that there is likelihood of losses in the remaining part of the contract, the company averred that if a contract extended for a period of three or four years, there was difficulty in quantifying the losses anticipated for the remaining portion of the contract as the reasons for possible losses like cost escalation in materials, labour, etc., and losses due to floods, fire, drought, etc., were unpredictable. Further, contracts which were not profitable in the first year might earn profit in the next year. The company felt that the system of crediting the value of work done at the rates approved by the clients and debiting all works and other expenses to the profit and loss account which it had followed from its inception and was accepted by the statutory auditors, would show a true and fair picture of the working of the company.

While reviewing a particular year's accounts, the Government auditors, however, insisted that the company should follow the procedure outlined in AS-7 and provide for anticipated losses and also should not take revenue in the contracts which were in progress.

In the circumstances, the company sought the opinion of the Expert Advisory Committee on the questions whether:

(b)the system outlined in AS-7 is mandatory and should be followed in the preparation of final accounts.

"9. Percentage of completion method.

9.1 Under the percentage of completion method, the amount of, revenue recognised is determined by reference to the stage of completion of the contract activity at the end of each accounting period. The advantage of this method of accounting for contract revenue is that it reflects revenue in the accounting period during which activity is undertaken to earn such revenue.

9.2 The stage of completion used to determine revenue to be recognised in the financial statements is measured in an appropriate manner. For this purpose no special weightage should be given to a single factor, instead, all relevant factors should be taken into consideration; for example, the proportion that costs incurred to date bear to the estimated total costs of the contract, by surveys which measure work performed and completion of a physical proportion of the contract work.

(ii)payments to sub-contractors to the extent that they do not reflect the amount of work performed under the sub-contract.

9.5 The application of the percentage of completion method is subject to a risk of error in making estimates. It is true that the Income-tax Act makes no express provision with regard to the value of stock. It charges for payment of tax the income, profits and gains which have to be computed in the manner provided by the Income-tax Act. In the case of a trading adventure the profits have to be calculated and adjusted in the light of the provisions of the Income-tax Act permitting allowances prescribed thereby. For that purpose it was the duty of the Income-tax Officer to find out what profit the business has made according to the true accountancy practice. Judicial decisions and decisions of Appellate Tribunal

6. The question of exigibility to tax of income from long-term contracts has been considered by the juridiciary as well as the Tribunal in a number of cases. To highlight their views on the issue, the gist of some of the decisions is set out below:

(i)( a)Sukhdeodas Jalan v. CIT [1954] 26 ITR 617 (Pat.)

(b) Tirath Ram Ahuja (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1976] 103 ITR 15 (Delhi)

A military contract entered into by the assessee Sukhdeodas Jalan extended beyond the accounting period and the accounts were closed only after the completion of the contract. The question arose for determination whether the profits should be assessed only after the completion of the contract or whether the profits accruing during the accounting period could be assessed. A Division Bench of the Patna High Court held that it was fallacious to argue that merely because the contract was completed after the accounting period, no profits arose or accrued to the assessee in the accounting year and that in the case of an incomplete contract there was a well established method of calculating profits accruing in the accounting year (vide page 971 of Batliboi's Advanced Accounting) . To quote from the High Court's decision:

"In the case of contracts, if accounts are maintained and completed on contract basis the profits or gains of the previous year cannot properly be extracted from the accounts, for a contract may take several years for being completed and payments in regard to it may also be received by the assessee in several years. It may be convenient from the point of view of the assessee that profit should be ascertained on the completion of the contract and assessment of the profit should take place after the completion of the contract. But section 3 imposes a charge of income-tax upon the profits and gains of the assessee for the accounting year and it is the duty of the income-tax authorities to ascertain the profits and gains accruing to the assessee in respect of the payment received during the accounting year.

It cannot be said that merely because a contract was completed after the accounting year, no profits arose or accrued to the assessee in the accounting year...." (p. 618)

The ratio of the decision supra was followed by the Delhi High Court in the case of Tirath Ram Ahuja (P.) Ltd. ( supra). It was held that in the case of contracts, one need not wait till the contract was completed in order to ascertain the income, and that it was open to the revenue to estimate the profit on the basis of the receipts in each year of construction, although the contract was not complete.

Revenue recognition according to the Expert Committee of the Institute of Chartered Accountants

5. Some illustrative cases dealt with by the Expert Advisory Committee of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India not only throw more light on the two methods of accounting, namely, (i) the percentage of completion method and (ii) the completed contract method of accounting, recommended for adoption in executing contracts running for a number of years, but also clarify the various issues involved in accounting for and taxation of profits. Three cases are discussed below in brief.

(i) First illustrative case. - A heavy engineering equipment manufacturing company sold equipment on turnkey basis. In almost all turnkey projects, the payments for supply and erection were received separately in instalments dependent on the stage of development. According to the terms agreed to, the final balance of 5 per cent of each, i.e., 10 per cent of the total cost, was receivable on successful commissioning and acceptance by the customer or on submission of bank guarantee covering the guarantee period.

The company was recognising sales at 100 per cent contract value on despatch of equipments to the site. Due to this, sales was taken at 100 per cent though the final 10 per cent became due only after 36 months, i.e., after commissioning. This accounting procedure had necessitated payment of income-tax on the portion of 10 per cent also taken as income in the year of despatch of equipment.

Considering the disadvantages from the taxation angle, the company sought the opinion of the Expert Advisory Committee as to whether the said 10 per cent of the contract price which was not due could be recognised as revenue in the year in which it fell due, i.e., after completion of the project, thereby deferring the tax liability.

The Expert Committee observed (April 1987) that according to AS-7,

"under the percentage of completion method, the amount of revenue recognised is determined by reference to stage of completion of the contract activity at the end of each accounting period (para 9.1)... The stage of completion used to determine revenue to be recognised in the financial statements, is measured in an appropriate manner. For this purpose no special weightage should be given to a single factor; instead, all relevant factors should be taken into consideration, for example, the proportion that costs incurred to date bear to the estimated total costs of the contract, by surveys which measure work performed and completion of physical proportion of the contract work (para 9.2) . . . progress payments and advances received from customers may not necessarily reflect the stage of completion ... (para 9.3)."

Further according to AS-9, "In a transaction involving the rendering of services, performance should be measured either under the completed service contract method or under the proportionate completion method, whichever relates the revenue to the work accomplished. Such performance should be regarded as being achieved when no significant uncertainty exists regarding the amount of the consideration that will be derived from rendering the service."

As the company was following the percentage of completion method for revenue recognition, the Committee opined that the company should recognise 100 per cent contract price as revenue in the year in which the entire equipment was despatched and the contract was performed to a substantial extent. However, the estimated liability of 10 per cent must be provided in the accounts for fulfilling possible claims. According to the Committee, the question of admissibility of the provision for possible claims as a deduction in computation of taxable income, was a separate question which had to be resolved keeping in view the facts and circumstances of each case, [vide page 12 of Vol. VII of Compendium of Opinions].

(ii) Second illustrative case. - A public limited company, wholly owned by a State Government, undertook construction works exclusively for Government departments/undertakings, both on turnkey and non-turnkey basis and followed the mercantile system of accounting.

. In addition to the billed amount the closing work-in-progress representing the value of goods and service transferred during the financial year but not billed, is added. For the same reason, the opening work-in-progress representing the value of goods and services transferred during the previous financial year and billed during the current financial year is reduced. Thus, the cost of goods and services transferred during the current financial year is arrived at for the computation of taxable turnover.

Thus, income to be recognized in a works contract is: For example, in the case of a works contract continuing over a period of 3 years, the income for the 1st year is to be recognized as the aggregate amount billed during this year and the value of closing work-in-progress. In the 2nd year, the aggregate of the amount billed during the year and the value of closing work-in-progress as reduced by the value of opening work-in-progress is the income to be recognized. In the 3rd year, the amount billed during that year as reduced by the opening work-in-progress is the income to be recognized. Any subsequent escalation or reduction in the bill subsequent to the financial year shall be adjusted in the returns by filing revised return for the period for which the change has occurred. The concept of percentage of completion of the work by recognizing the volume of work completed at any stage as asset of the contractor in AS-7 needs a reconsideration.

Profit or Loss

7. The profit or loss on works contract is derived by taking the income recognized as detailed above on the income side of the profit and loss account and the cost of goods and service is taken on the expenditure side of the profit and loss account. The cost of consumables, cost of design, consultation and technology, cost of hire charges, cost of finance, establishment charges and depreciation are taken on the expenditure side. The net result is the profit/loss of the contract work.

In case of bulk purchase during the first year, such part of goods not transferred while executing the work will be in the closing stock and that part of goods used in the work but not billed is in the work-in-progress. Whatever is transfer value of goods by involving in the execution of the works contract is recognized as income. Hence, bulk purchase of goods will not create an artificial loss in the profit and loss account.

Any amount received less than the measured and billed amount is to be treated as receivables and any amount received more than the measured and bill amount is to be treated as advance. Both amounts received and receivable are taken as the contract amount. Taxable turnover is determined by deducting the value of labour components and consumables from the contract amount as per the rules. The mobilization advance is to be treated as loan repayable as deduction from every subsequent bills. Hence, such mobilization advance is not part of the contract amount.

The above method remains unchanged in the fixed price contract and cost plus contract; since the measurement and billing on fixed price contract is based on the scheduled in the agreement and the cost plus contract adopts the measurement and billing on the basis of the cost of the contractor. Therefore, the AS-7 needs amendment accordingly.

As income taxable under the Income-tax Act, 1961 from manufacturing or trading is the income generated from such activities, the income from contract is the income generated from executing the contract work. Hence, estimation of income at the rate of proportionate work completed as per technical evaluation is a notional way, unwarranted in the presence of proper records. Taxable income is a truth and not to be estimated, unless the records are insufficient or incomplete and rejected by the Assessing Officer.

FAQ 56. Mr. A has opted for the presumptive scheme under Section 44AD in respect of one of his businesses. Is the auditor required to mention details of such business in the audit report?

Yes. He should report the nature of the presumptive business correctly in Clause 10(a) of Form No. 3CD. In case the profit and loss account of the assessee includes any profit declared under the presumptive scheme (Section 44AD, 44AE, 44AF, 44B, 44BB, 44BBA, 44BBB), then it is mandatory to mention the amount of such profit and the section under which the same is declared in Clause No. 12 of Form 3CD. FAQ 57. How to ensure that the profit has been computed correctly if the profit & loss account also includes the profit computed on a presumptive basis?

If the profit and loss account of the assessee also includes the presumptive income, the common business expenditure has to be apportioned to arrive at the correct amount of profit credited to the profit and loss account and assessable on a presumptive basis. The tax auditor, in such a situation, should arrive at a fair and reasonable estimate of such expenditure on the basis of evidence in possession of the assessee or by asking the assessee to prepare such an estimate, which should be checked by him.

It is also necessary to mention the basis of apportionment of common expenditure. However, if the tax auditor is not satisfied with the reasonableness of such apportionment, he should indicate such fact in Clause (3) of Form 3CA/Clause (5) of Form 3CB by way of a note.

Much can be said for and against the completed contract method but the chances of its acceptance by the assessing authorities are bleak in view of several judicial pronouncements against it. It is important to note that in most of the above-mentioned cases, profit has been estimated due to difficulty in estimation of work-in-progress. The other significant feature in building contracts is the point of time of revenue recognition, i.e., whether it is to be considered at the time of registration or handing over of physical possession or on payment of installments pursuant to agreement on estimated completion of construction. The answer to this question again depends on the method of accounting adopted and recognition of revenue on handing over of units of construction combined with a reasonable estimate of work-in-progress may be acceptable in income-tax assessments. 5. Controversies

5.1 Controversy relating to provision for foreseeable losses in construction contracts - The accounting practice of valuing unsold stocks at cost or net realisable value (market value) which is lower is widely accepted now. But when the same theory of prudence was applied to other anticipated losses in case of investments forming part of closing stock-in-trade, work-in-progress under construction contracts, fluctuations in foreign exchange transactions and other matters, litigations surfaced and persist till date.

In 1983, the Accounting Standards Board of the ICAI issued Accounting Standard (AS) 7, Accounting for Construction Contracts. Para 19 of the Standard stipulates as follows :

"19. A foreseeable loss on the entire contract should be provided for in the financial statements irrespective of the amount of work done and the method of accounting followed."

When the assessees started adopting the accounting practice envisaged in the above Accounting Standard (AS) 7, the tax authorities rejected the same. Following few cases are stated as examples.

In a case before The ITAT Mumbai Bench 'A' in Mazagon Dock Ltd. v. Jt. CIT [2009] 29 SOT 356 decided on February 18, 2009, the issue was whether as far as change in method of valuation of work-in-progress was concerned, in view of mandatory requirements of AS-7, it was a bona fide change, particularly in view of qualification made in this regard by statutory auditors as well as by the Comptroller & Auditor General of India. It was held as follows :

"The question that came up for consideration was as to whether the anticipated loss on the valuation of fixed price contract, in view of the mandatory requirements of the AS-7, was to be allowed in the year in which the contract had been entered into or it was to be spread over a period of contract, as was done by the assessee in earlier years. As far as the change in the method of valuation of work-in-progress was concerned, it could not be disputed that in view of mandatory requirements of the AS-7, it was a bona fide change in the method of valuation of work-in-progress, particularly in view of the qualification made in this regard by statutory auditors as well as by the Comptroller & Auditor General of India. Therefore, the observation of the Commissioner (Appeals) that the assessee had booked bogus loss was not correct. As far as the basis of estimation was concerned, the same was done on technical estimation basis and, therefore, merely because there were some variations in the figures furnished by the assessee at different stages, it could not be said that the estimated loss was not allowable. It was not disputed that the department in earlier years had allowed the loss on estimated basis having regard to the expenditure actually incurred in various years. Therefore, in principle, it was not disputed that the estimated loss under the present circumstances was an allowable deduction. However, merely because the change in method of accounting was bona fide, it could not lead to the inference that the income was also deducible properly under the Act. This aspect is very evident from the first proviso to section 145 as it stood prior to the amendment by the Finance Act, 1995 with effect from 1-4-1997. It could not be disputed that from the method adopted by the assessee, the assessee's income could not be deduced properly in the year in which the loss had been anticipated. As a matter of fact this aspect was not disputed by the Assessing Officer also. He had been swayed more by the revenue loss than by the correct principle to be applied. The matching principle of accounting was not of much significance in the present context because if the loss had been properly estimated in the year in which the contract had been entered into, then it had to be allowed in that very year and could not be spread over the period of contract. The matching principle is of relevance where income and expenditure, both are to be considered together. However, in the instant case, the effect of valuation of WIP would automatically affect the profits of subsequent years accordingly. Therefore, there was no reason for not accepting in principle the assessee's claim as being allowable."

The expression 'method of accounting' has reference to the pattern, system and principles on the basis of which the accounts of an assessee are maintained. The accounts maintained by the assessee constitute prima facie evidence for arriving at the income chargeable to tax during the relevant previous year. A presumption can, therefore, be made that the accounts provided by the assessee represent a fair picture of his income, unless strong evidence to the contrary is adduced.

Otherwise there will be no finality to the situation and the revenue may indulge in a witch-bunt. The power to compute profits under section 145(2) arises only where no method of accounting has been regularly employed by the assessee and where the method employed is such that the income, profits and gains cannot properly be deduced therefrom. It means that the method adopted by the assessee must, prima facie, prevail where it is regularly employed, though the Assessing Officer can reject it if the same is such that true profits cannot be correctly determined therefrom. In other words, even if the assessee has regularly employed a method of accounting, it can be discarded if the method does not show correct profits of the year - S.N. Namasivayam Chettiar v. CIT [1960] 38 ITR 579 (SC). The section does not compel the Assessing Officer to accept a balance sheet of cash receipts and outgoings prepared from the books of account. It is open to him under certain circumstances to compute the income on such basis and in such manner as he may determine – CIT v. A. Krishnaswami Mudaliar [1964] 53 ITR 122 (SC).

Fundamental nature of transaction important

5.3 The courts can always go into the fundamental nature of a transaction to determine its true impact and taxability. The courts may not accept the scheme of entries adopted by the assessee to record certain transactions. In the State Bank of Travancore v. CIT [1986] 158 ITR 102 , the Supreme Court has held that where interest has accrued and the assessee has debited the account of the debtor, the difficulty of recovery would not make its accrual non-accrual. There, the assessee, a banking company, maintained its accounts on the mercantile system of accounting. It used to charge interest on sticky advances by debiting the concerned parties. Instead of carrying the interest to the profit and loss account, the assessee credited it to a separate account called 'the interest suspense account'.

The assessee claimed that having regard to the bad and deteriorating financial condition of the parties concerned as well as the history of the accounts, the recovery of even the principal amounts of the debts had become improbable and doubtful and as such the interest thereon, though debited to the respective debtors, was taken to the 'interest suspense account' to avoid showing inflated profits by including hypo-thetical and unreal income. The contention of the assessee was that such interest on sticky advances was not real income and was not taxable in its hands. The Supreme Court held that interest on sticky advances had accrued according to the mercantile system of accounting and the assessee had debited the respective parties with the interest. After the close of the accounting year, the assessee, without giving up the interest as a bad debt, did not offer it for taxation, but carried it to the interest suspense account. Even if in given circumstances the amount might be taken to the interest suspense account for accounting purposes, that would not affect its taxability as such.

In Union Co-operative Insurance Society v. CIT [1967] 66 ITR 360 (SC)an insurance company was maintaining the accounts on mercantile basis. It claimed deduction of an item of expenditure that had been debited to profit and loss appropriation account on estimate basis. It was disallowed on the ground that by adopting this method the company had itself intended to treat it not as expenditure related to business but as disbursement made out of profit after it had accrued. It was held that by adopting that method the assessee-company did not seek to alter the character of expenditure. Hence, the same was not allowable as a deduction.

Tax credit illusory

6. It appears that cross settlement of input tax credit between the services and the goods is more on paper than real. Often the input tax credit for goods consumed in the service sector is obtained from dealers who cannot provide cenvatable invoices. The supply of goods is widespread among various dealers not all of whom provide cenvatable bills or cater to the requirements of the end-user who is a taxable service provider.

Similarly goods used in service contracts are not necessarily purchased from the first stage or second stage dealer or from the manufacturer directly. The input credit for goods consumed in service contracts is largely illusory as the output service provider purchases inputs from available sources of supply and on such terms as to credit and quantity which suit his business needs. The input credit for goods is thus not available as the cenvatable invoice essential for claiming the input credit is not there but only an ordinary purchase invoice to support the purchase of goods. Goods which are purchased under cenvatable invoices and undergoing further process not amounting to manufacture lose their cenvatable advantage when they are sold again in the processed stage; the processor is not a manufacturer of any new goods and the CENVAT chain is broken at his level and cannot be continued further into the hands of the next consumer.

The taxability of revenues and incomes in respect of construction contracts represents a vexed issue before the revenue authorities. There are conflicting decisions by the various Benches of the ITAT on the issue of allowance for foreseeable losses in the construction contracts. In this article the authors have examined the issue in details as per the Accounting Standards and have cited various case laws where decisions have been taken in favour or against such claims.

INTRODUCTION

1. The taxability of revenues and incomes in respect of construction contracts represents a vexed issue before the revenue authorities.

The accounting for construction contracts in the financial statements is governed by the Accounting Standard (AS)-7 - Construction Contracts issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI). As per AS-7, the contract revenue and contract costs are to be recognized as revenue and expenses, respectively, by reference to the stage of completion of the contract at the reporting date. This method of recognizing contract revenue and expenses with reference to stage of completion of the contract is popularly referred to as percentage of completion method (POCM). Hence, the revenue, expenses and profit with reference to a contract are reported based on the proportion of the work completed.

Accounting Standards issued by the ICAI advocate the view that financial results should be arrived at after considering the anticipated losses and expenses on the ground of 'prudence' and 'conservatism'. Inter alia, AS – 7 requires that an expected loss on the construction contract should be recognized as an expense immediately. The relevant paras 31, 32, 35 and 36 of AS-7 dealing with the recognition of loss in contract are reproduced hereinbelow:

"Para 31….. An expected loss on the construction contract should be recognised as an expense immediately in accordance with paragraph 35.

Para 32….. However, even though the outcome of the contract cannot be estimated reliably, it may be probable that total contract costs will exceed total contract revenue. In such cases, any expected excess of total contract costs over total contract revenue for the contract is recognised as an expense immediately in accordance with paragraph 35.

Para 35. When it is probable that total contract costs will exceed total contract revenue, the expected loss should be recognised as an expense immediately.

Para 36. The amount of such a loss is determined irrespective of:

(a) whether or not work has commenced on the contract;

(b) the stage of completion of contract activity; or

(c) the amount of profits expected to arise on other contracts which are not treated as a single construction contract in accordance with paragraph 8."

As per the above paras, the expected loss in contract is to be recognized immediately irrespective of the stage of completion of the contract or commencement of the work of contract. On this basis the contractors (particularly the large companies undertaking big infrastructure projects, telecom projects and other building contracts having high values) do make provision for foreseeable losses, if they are of the opinion that the project is likely to result in a loss initially while making the estimates of contract revenue and costs.

The recognition of loss in a contract is also provided by the Ind AS-11 on Construction Contract1.

Hence, the contractors create a provision for foreseeable losses, in case they are of the opinion that the project is likely to result in a loss. The provision is created while making an estimate of the contract cost and revenue in the initial stages of a contract.

FAQ 41. If shares of members of AOP are unknown during the previous year, is it required to be reported in Form 3CD?

If shares of members are unknown during the previous year, the auditor needs to disclose this fact in Clause 9(a) of Form 3CD.

FAQ 42. Is it mandatory to disclose the nature of all the businesses carried on by the assessee and any change therein? Clause 10 of Form 3CD mandates disclosure of the nature of every business or profession carried on by an assessee during the previous year. The codes for all main activities (principal line of each of the business or profession) shall be reported.

Any material change in the nature of business should be precisely disclosed. The change will include a change from manufacturer to trader and a change in the principal line of business. Any addition to or permanent discontinuance of a particular line of business may also amount to change requiring reporting. However, temporary suspension of the business may not amount to change and, therefore, need not be reported.

FAQ 43. Which address should be reported in Clause 11 if the books of accounts are maintained in a computerised system?

Clause 11(b) requires reporting the address at which the books so maintained are kept. As per the "Guidance Note on Tax Audit" issued by the ICAI, when the books of account are maintained and generated through a computer system, the auditor should obtain from the assessee the details of the address of the place where the server is located or the principal place of business/Head office or registered office by whatever name called and mention the same accordingly in clause 11(b). If the books of account are stored on the cloud or online, a unique IP address of the same may be reported. The auditor should also specify which books of account have been maintained in the computer system and which records have been maintained in hard copy form.

The Guidance does not provide any direction on reporting in Clause 11 if the IP Address is not unique but a dynamic IP address. In that situation, the name of the cloud should be mentioned.

FAQ 44. Mr. A has opted for the presumptive scheme under Section 44AD in respect of one of his businesses. Is the auditor required to mention details of such business in the audit report?

In case the profit and loss account of the assessee includes any profit declared under the presumptive scheme (Section 44AD, 44AE, 44AF, 44B, 44BB, 44BBA, 44BBB), then it is mandatory to mention the amount of such profit and the section under which the same is declared in Clause No. 12 of Form 3CD. The tax auditor is not required to indicate if the amount of presumptive income has been correctly computed under the relevant section relating to presumptive taxation. The reporting requirement is satisfied if the amount as per profit and loss account is reported.

FAQ 45. How to ensure that the profit has been computed correctly if the profit & loss account also includes the profit computed on a presumptive basis?

If the profit and loss account of the assessee also includes the presumptive income, the common business expenditure has to be apportioned to arrive at the correct amount of profit credited to the profit and loss account and assessable on a presumptive basis. The tax auditor, in such a situation, should arrive at a fair and reasonable estimate of such expenditure on the basis of evidence in possession of the assessee or by asking the assessee to prepare such an estimate, which should be checked by him.

It is also necessary to mention the basis of apportionment of common expenditure. However, if the tax auditor is not satisfied with the reasonableness of such apportionment, he should indicate such fact under this clause by a suitable note.

FAQ 46. An assessee has changed the method of accounting from mercantile to cash basis. What disclosure is required in Form 3CD?

Clause 13 of Form 3CD requires every assessee to report the method of accounting employed in the previous year. Further, if there was a change in the method of accounting employed in the immediately preceding previous year, then the same is to be reported. The assessee is also required to disclose the effect of a change in the method of accounting on the profit and loss. If it is not possible to quantify the effect of a change in the method of accounting, appropriate disclosure should be made under this clause.

5. Secondly, the amendment to section 145 presumes that all computations of business income are possible within the range of the cash or mercantile systems of accounting in prescribing computation according to them only. It is a fact that not every business activity takes place in the form of receipt or accrual for these accounting systems to record and measure. A casual perusal of balance sheets of non-banking financial companies engaged in hire purchase and leasing would show that myriad methods of accounting for such transactions are adopted by them and change of methods midway is not uncommon.

The above-mentioned transactions are usually spread over three to five years and the income is shown to ‘arise’ over the period of the contracts according to certain methods of accounting. The accounting methods employed to compute the income are neither cash nor mercantile but only determine the arisal of income embedded in such contracts in each year. So also in construction contracts and real estate development, the profits are ‘spreadover’ the period of the contract in relation to the job done. The spreadover is neither under the mercantile nor under the cash system of accounting but estimated. Under the mercantile system, the right to receive the income is essential whereas under the cash system, the receipt of income would make it taxable and none would operate during the period of execution of the contract when profits are indeterminate. It is relevant here to look into monographs on accounting issued by the ICAI for certain types of business.

In the monograph on accounting for poultry farming, 1980 edition, the issue of capital costs of chicken and the amortisation of their cost over a period is dealt with. Chicken are classified according to their age in batches and accounting starts with each batch as basis.

This measure deals with the profitability of the business from year to year and valid in normal business years when no natural calamity or disease strikes the poultry farm. The capital cost of a chicken is spread over its estimated egg lying period and the charge to each year is that proportion of the capital cost as the actual yield bears to the estimated total yield. The yielding period is not an accounting year but extends over 18 months. This accounting of cost of chicken depleted or used in the process of the business also directly affects the valuation of chicken on hand as at the end of the year. Added to the above is the valuation of natural accretion of new born chicken to the existing stock.

It is evident that income does not accrue in the form of a legal claim (due and receivable or payable) in this business, but it ‘arises’ or presents itself in each year if measured in the manner suggested in the monograph. The basic features, viz., the coming of age of chicks and their yielding period thereafter do not lend themselves to any precise annual measurement needed for accounting of the same and some estimated basis is used instead and this results in some kind of ‘spread over’ of profit or income over the effective life of a batch of chicken.

The monograph dealing with accounting in Rubber Plantations, 1983 edition offers another perspective. Rubber trees take six to eight years to develop from planting and their rubber yielding period spreads over many years. While the monograph recommends writing off of the capital cost of the trees over their productive life, it notes that business practice is different. While the write-off is not done, in lieu thereof, a rehabilitation reserve is built over 25 to 30 years sufficient to replant the area exploited and on that basis, the profits of the business are measured. For the practical businessman, what it takes to build or create a new asset after the existing asset exhausts itself is more important and, accordingly, he allocates so much out of each year’s revenue for such build-up and only the balance available is considered surplus.

So long as a recognised standard followed consistently from year to year, the results are to be accepted and even this does not prevent the Assessing Officer from questioning the correctness or completeness of the accounts. Deviations from the standards prescribed by the ICAI warrant qualificatory remarks from the auditor and the Assessing Officer will be well within his rights to probe into such issues and quantify the proper income while framing the assessment even under the existing provisions. By its very nature income from business or profession defies precision in computation. A mathematically correct income from a running business is not generally feasible to arrive at due to various factors affecting the business and such factors are not amenable to precise computation. Risks in business both in relation to completed transactions and those lying in the womb of future compel the businessman to estimate his income and not measure it mathematically. Conservatism is built into business computations and lurking fear of the unknown future influences business sentiment.

Any system of accounting will have to come to terms with the business realities and be acceptable from the business point of view for wide acceptance and implementation. A pedantic approach, however, scholarly it may seem, is unlikely to be widely followed unless it is realistic from the point of view of the businessman.

Certainly the ICAI has not come in for praise in the memorandum accompanying the Finance Bill for setting Accounting Standards after much research and debate. The standards are described as lacking requisite rigidity with too many alternatives, butter-fingered and so resulting in tax avoidance.

But the standards are mandatory and disclosed in published accounts compulsorily and when contravened, reported upon by the auditor. The user of such accounts now knows the effects of non-compliance with the standards of accounting prescribed by the ICAI, though such reporting may be in fine print. But the Assessing Officer is posted with this information and equipped with the Tax Audit Report under section 44AB of the Act, he can unravel the mystery in the accounts to assess the proper income.

In prescribing accounting standards for the entire field of business and industry and profession, a certain amplitude necessarily comes in. This is because of the different requirements of accounting for various types of business, but the underlying requirement in any business accounting is the true and fair view of the final results.

The accounting standards prescribed by the ICAI after due deliberation cannot, thus, be termed as ‘flexible’ with a connotation that they help avoid payment of tax. Nor can they be truncated in the name of standardisation as that would result in inadequate coverage.

Instead of venturing to set fresh standards under section 145, the Government would do well to adopt the standards set by the ICAI under the Income-tax Act as it has done for the companies under the recently promulgated Companies (Amendment) Ordinance, 1998. It would be wiser to align the measurement of income under section 145 with the scope of total income under section 5 to avoid potential litigation.

Issues in British Paints case (supra)

3. The main issues that came up for consideration before the Supreme Court in the case of British Paints India Ltd. (supra) were as follows :— Is the Assessing Officer bound to accept the system of accounting regularly and consistently employed by the assessee, the correctness of which had not been questioned in the past? Is the officer bound by the method followed in earlier years? Is there any estoppel in these matters? Should the Assessing Officer consider the question as to whether or not the books disclose the true state of accounts and whether correct income could be deduced therefrom? Whether in the case of an assessee, a paint manufacturer, valuing its goods in process and finished goods consistently at cost of raw materials, totally excluding overhead expenditure, rejection of such a system by the Assessing Officer was justified?

Facts of the case

4. The assessee’s goods in process and finished products were valued at raw materials cost which worked out to be 84.49 per cent of the total cost. The company had been following this practice and it had been accepted in the past on the basis of the contention that the goods being paints had limited storage life and if not quickly disposed of, they were liable to lose their market value. The contention of the assessee was rejected by the ITO on the ground that at no time had the assessee claimed any deduction on account of deterioration/damage to goods. The ITO held that there was no justification to recognise a practice, as claimed by the assessee, of valuing its stock otherwise than in accordance with the well-recognised principle of accounting which required the stock to be valued at either cost (raw material + expenditure) or market price, whichever was lower.

The AAC and Tribunal oh successive appeals, confirmad the ITO’s view that the goods were liable to be valued at 100 per cent of the cost which included the overhead expenditure and not at 84.49 per cent as claimed by the assessee. The Calcutta High Court, however, held in favour of the assessee by accepting the method as a valid method, having regard to the consistent practice of the assessee.

Supreme Court’s ruling

5. On the case coming up finally before it the Supreme Court ruled that it is not correct to say, as contended by the assessee, that the Assessing Officer is bound to accept a system of accounting regularly employed by the assessee, the correctness of which had not been questioned in the past. According to the Court, there is no estoppel in these matters and the officer is not bound by the method followed in the earlier years. The Supreme Court observed that any system of accounting, which excludes for the valuation of the stock-in-trade all costs other than the cost of raw material for the goods in process and finished products, is likely to result in a distorted picture of the true state of the business for the purpose of computing the chargeable income. Such a system may produce a comparatively lower valuation of the opening stock and the closing stock, thus, showing a comparatively low difference between the two. In a period of rising turnover and rising prices, such a system is apt to diminish the assessment of the taxable profit of a year. The profits of one year are likely to be shifted to another year which is an incorrect method of computing profits and gains for the year of assessment.

The Supreme Court opined that as each year is a self-contained unit and the taxes of a particular year are payable with reference to the income of that year as computed in terms of the Act, income cannot properly be deduced from such a method. In this view of the matter, the Supreme Court held that it is not only the right but the duty of the Assessing Officer to act in exercise of his statutory power under section 14S and reject the accounting system adopted by the assessee, as he has done in the instant case, for determining what in his opinion is the correct taxable income. Consequently the Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the Calcutta High Court. While coming to this conclusion, the Supreme Court considered various cases, Indian as well as foreign, having relevance to the issue at hand.

This judgment of the Supreme Court can have far-reaching implications. It can help the Assessing Officers to reject methods consistently followed in earlier years. However, such a rejection can take place only if the method adopted by the assessee has been found to be such that the income cannot properly be deduced therefrom. Perhaps one cannot question such an approach as otherwise the Assessing Officer will not be in a poistion to rectify the situation at all, being helpless against the ground of consistency.

In a works contract, the amount received or receivable from the awarder in consideration of executing the work includes consideration for transfer of goods and providing of service. The amount receivable as consideration is the billed amount less the amount received as advance. But the revenue recognition is to be based on the consideration for transfer of property in goods fixed by the contractor. Hence, the consideration receivable for the unbilled part of transfer of property in goods fixed by the contractor during the year is also to be included as revenue to be recognized for the year. The work-in-progress is to be taken as the unbilled part of transfer of property in goods fixed by the contractor during the year, valued on the end of the year; as being the part of work executed, but not charged by the contractor and unrecognized by the awarder. Thus, the aggregate of the billed amount and unbilled part of transfer of property in goods fixed by the contractor during the year as valued at the end of the year (work-in-progress) constitute the revenue to be recognized on the credit side of the profit and loss account for the relevant year. Any subsequent change in the contract amount recognized based on litigation or escalation results may be adjusted on accrual basis. Thus, the revenue to be recognized is to be based on the transfer of goods and providing of service during the year. Therefore, the contradiction in AS-7 is to be removed.

3.1 Indivisible Contract - A works contract is either a divisible contract or an indivisible contract. In the case of a divisible contract, the cost of materials and cost of service are separable and, hence, the levy of tax on sale of goods and services provided can be fixed easily. But in the case of indivisible and composite works contract, the computation of taxable turnover of goods is governed by rules in the VAT Law and value of taxable service is governed by Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006. The transfer value of goods and value of taxable services are to be divided for the levy of sales tax /VAT as per the direction of the Supreme Court of India in 88 STC 204 and the Rules framed by the States based on this judgment and for levy of service tax as per the Service tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006. The taxable turnover and taxable service are determined under this principle by deducting the value of labour component and consumables from the contract amount and, hence, it is not based on the percentage of completion of the work as stipulated by AS-7.

Apart from above, sub-section (3) lays down the consequences of not following the same. Sub-section (3) is attracted under any of the following three circumstances :

(a) Where the Assessing Officer is not satisfied about the correctness or completeness of the accounts of the assessee; or

(b) Where the method of accounting provided in sub-section (1) has not been regularly followed by the assessee; or

(c) Where accounting standards as notified under sub-section (2), have not been regularly followed by the assessee.

Not conceding, but assuming that an assessee maintains his accounts in accordance with the mandatory Accounting Standards issued by the ICAI and other authorised bodies but does not compute his taxable income in accordance with the Tax Accounting Standards. The Assessing Officer is satisfied about the correctness or completeness of his accounts. In this example, let us assume that an assessee fulfils the first two conditions envisaged in sub-section (3) of section 145 but does not satisfy the third condition. The three conditions are not cumulative. So, can it be argued that the third condition will have an overriding effect over the other two conditions and for non-compliance with the same, the consequences stipulated in sub-section (3) would follow. It is doubtful that the provisions of sub-section (3) would be attracted in such a situation.

It would be too early to say that notifications issued under section 145 of the Income-tax Act would receive judicial approval or not. But the following observations are equally noteworthy :

Method of stock valuation

4. Sub-section (1) of section 145 stipulates the need for a method of stock valuation and its being regularly employed by the assessee. It has been repeatedly pointed out by the Courts, that it is the assessee and not the department, that has the choice of the method of stock valuation.

An assessee's choice of the method, is influenced by various economic and commercial factors. Accounting and trade customs play a major role in the choice of method. Inventories are held in the expectation of deriving revenue directly or indirectly, from their sale or use. In order to determine the results of a business for a given period, it is necessary to carry forward the cost related to inventories, until the inventories are sold or consumed. However, if there is no reasonable expectation that the net realisable value would cover the cost incurred (as a result, for example, of deterioration, obsolescence or a change in demand), it is necessary that cost which cannot be recovered should be charged against the revenue of the current period. The inventories are, therefore, normally stated at the lower of historical cost and the net realisable value - Accounting Standard 2, Valuation of Inventories, Institute of Chartered Accountants of India. A system of accounting must, therefore, include an acceptable basis for valuing stock in trade too - Indo Commercial Bank Ltd. v. CIT [1962] 44 ITR 22 (Mad.). The method of accounting adopted by the assessee, should ordinarily be accepted by the department, unless it is either improper or patently false. It was aptly remarked by the Madras High Court in Chari and Ram's case (supra), that an assessee is entitled to compute the income, profits and gains, in accordance with the method of accounting regularly employed by the assessee and ordinarily this method must be accepted by the department, in the absence of anything to suggest that it is improper or patently false. This proposition has been later reiterated in a catena of decisions. The Act also imposes a statutory duty on the ITO to examine in every case, the method of accounting employed and to see, whether or not it has been regularly employed - CIT v. A. Krishna Swami Mudaliar [1964] 53 ITR 122 (SC).

The most common method of stock valuation, viz., cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower, has found universal acceptance with the Courts- Ramswarup Bengalimal v. CIT [1954] 25 ITR 17 (All.) and Chhaoni Lal Pragdas v. CIT [1957] 31 ITR 597 (All.). While anticipated loss is taken into account, anticipated profit in the shape of appreciated value of the closing stock, is not brought into account, as no prudent trader would care to show increased profits before actual realisation - Chainrup Sampatram's case (supra). The value of opening and closing stocks are essential factors in determining the profits of the year and wrong and arbitrary valuation cannot, therefore, be accepted as a system or method of accounting that may be adopted by an assessee. The Allahabad High Court in the case of Chhaoni Lal Pragdas ( supra) while recognising that stock must be valued at cost price or market value, rejected the assessee's stand of valuing stock arbitrarily and neither at cost nor market value. This does not in any way bar an assessee from adopting a mixed system of stock valuation, where some items are valued at market price and some at cost, so long as such method is regularly followed.

13.1 When current estimates of total contract costs and revenues indicate a loss, provision is made for the entire loss on the contract irrespective of the amount of work done and the method of accounting followed. 13.2 When a contract is of such magnitude that it can be expected to absorb a considerable part of the capacity of the enterprise for a substantial period, indirect costs to be incurred during the period of the completion of the contract are sometimes considered to be directly attributable to the contract and included in the calculation of the provisions for loss on the contract.

Notification of Accounting Standards by the Central Government 4. The Bill proposes to amend the Income-tax Act to empower the Central Government to prescribe by a Notification in the Official Gazette the accounting standard which an assessee will have to follow in computing the income under the head 'Profits and gains of business or profession' or 'Income from other sources'. The new section 145(2) provides for notification of accounting standards from time to time. Section 145(3) as brought in by the Finance Act, 1995 lays down that if the Assessing Officer is not satisfied about the correctness or completeness of the accounts of the assessee or where the method of accounting provided or the accounting standards notified have not been regularly followed by the assessee, the Assessing Officer may make an assessment in the manner provided in section 144 of the Act. This is the law applicable to the current assessment year 1997-98 and subsequent years. The amendment re moved the proviso to section 145 which enabled the Assessing Officer to compute the income on such basis and in such manner as he may determine wherever the method of accounting is such that income cannot be properly deduced therefrom. The removal of the proviso is no doubt a handicap to the Assessing Officers. As long as the accounting standards are followed, the Assessing Officer is bound to accept the results shown in the books of account.

Fifteen Standards running from AS-1 to AS-15 were issued by the ICAI.
