It is clear from the examples dealt with above, that income seldom accrues or is received in all cases and it would be an oversimplification to think that either the accrual system of accounting or the cash system of accounting would measure all business transactions and compute the income there from. On the contrary, almost in all cases, it is recognition of income at a stage or ‘arisal’ thereof and methods of recognition vary.

6. Flexibility in accounting standards prescribed by the ICAI is also cited as a reason for tax avoidance in the memorandum explaining the amendment to section 145. As pointed out supra, business transactions are not uniform to fall in line between the two systems of accounting and even within the two systems, different standards are set for different types of transactions. A blanket approach will not bring out the fair estimate of the profit of the year. So long as a recognised standard followed consistently from year to year, the results are to be accepted and even this does not prevent the Assessing Officer from questioning the correctness or completeness of the accounts. Deviations from the standards prescribed by the ICAI warrant qualificatory remarks from the auditor and the Assessing Officer will be well within his rights to probe into such issues and quantify the proper income while framing the assessment even under the existing provisions.

FAQ 32. How can tax auditor report payments referred to in section 43B if the same is unpaid as on the date of submission of tax audit report but paid before the due date of filing of return of income? Clause 26 of Form 3CD seek details of liability incurred in respect of any sum referred to in clause (a), (b), (c), (d), (e) or (f) of section 43B in the previous year and was paid or not paid on or before the due date for furnishing the Return of Income of the previous year.

Since the due date of filing of the tax audit report is one month before the due date of filing of return of income, it is practically not possible for the auditor to report if any payment is made after the filing of the tax audit report but before the due date of return of income.

To address this difficulty, the CBDT has inserted sub-rule (3) in Rule 6G. It provides that a person may get a revised audit report from an accountant and furnish it before the end of the relevant assessment year for which the report pertains. Thus, if there is payment after furnishing of the report, which necessitates a recalculation of disallowance under section 40 or section 43B, a revised report may be filed.

FAQ 33. If shares of members of AOP are unknown during the previous year, whether it is required to be reported in Form 3CD?

If shares of members are unknown during the previous year, the auditor needs to disclose this fact in Clause 9(a) of Form 3CD.

(Read more: Taxability of AOP/BOI on Taxmann.com/Practice)

FAQ 34. How does the auditor need to report the interest inadmissible under section 23 MSMED Act, 2006?

Clause 22 of Form 3CD seeks the disclosure of the amount of interest inadmissible under section 23 of the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006.The tax auditor needs to report the amount of interest inadmissible under section 23 of the MSMED Act, 2006 irrespective of whether the amount of such interest has been debited to profit and loss account or not.

The auditor should verify that the auditee has disclosed the information as required under section 22 of the MSMED Act, 2006 in the financial statements under audit. If the auditee makes no disclosure in the financial statements, the tax auditor should appropriately qualify his report in Form No. 3CB and also report the fact of non-disclosure in clause 22 of Form No. 3CD.

FAQ 35. Whether it is mandatory to disclose the nature of all the businesses carried on by the assessee and any change therein?

Clause 10 of Form 3CD mandates disclosure of the nature of every business or profession carried on by an assessee during the previous year.

Any material change in the nature of business should be precisely disclosed. The change will include a change from manufacturer to the trader as well as a change in the principal line of business. Any addition to or permanent discontinuance of a particular line of business may also amount to change requiring reporting. However, temporary suspension of the business may not amount to change and therefore need not be reported.

FAQ 36. Mr A has opted for the presumptive scheme under section 44AD in respect of one of his businesses. Whether auditor is required to mention details of such business in the audit report?

In case the profit and loss account of the assessee includes any profit declared under the presumptive scheme (section 44AD, 44AE, 44AF, 44B, 44BB, 44BBA, 44BBB), then it is mandatory to mention the amount of such profit and the section under which the same is declared in Clause No. 12 of Form 3CD.The tax auditor is not required to indicate whether the amount of presumptive income has been correctly computed under the relevant section relating to presumptive taxation. The reporting requirement is satisfied if the amount per profit and loss account is reported.

(Read more : Presumptive Taxation Schemes on Taxmann.com/Practice)

FAQ 37. How to ensure that the profit has been computed correctly if the profit & loss account includes the profit computed on a presumptive basis?

If the profit and loss account of the assessee also includes the presumptive income, the common business expenditure has to be apportioned to arrive at the correct amount of profit. The tax auditor, in such a situation, should arrive at a fair and reasonable estimate of such expenditure on the basis of evidence in possession of the assessee or by asking the assessee to prepare such estimate, which should be checked by him.

It is also necessary to mention the basis of apportionment of common expenditure. However, if the tax auditor is not satisfied with the reasonableness of such apportionment, he should indicate such fact under this clause by a suitable note.

Estimation of profits - Where the assessee has given a comparative instance of gross profit rate, it is necessary for the department to come to a finding as to the norm of the gross profit on the basis of comparative cases. Therefore, it is the duty of the AO to counter the comparative statement cited by the assessee before he can have the option to estimate the gross profit [CIT v. Eastern Commercial Enterprises [1994] 210 ITR 103 (Cal.)].

Even if the ITO considered the material placed before him by the assessee to be unreliable keeping in view the comparative statement of accounts of the previous years, he cannot proceed to make an arbitrary addition and base his conclusion purely on guesswork. He ought to have related his estimate to some evidence or material on the record as it is now well-settled that if the profits shown by the assessee in his return are not accepted, it is for the taxing authorities to prove that the assessee has made more profits than returned [International Forest Co. v. CIT [1975] 101 ITR 721 (J&K)].

The law says that the ITO shall make the assessment to the best of his judgment; it means that he must make it according to the rules of reason and justice, not according to private opinion, but according to law and not humour, and the assessment is to be not arbitrary, vague and fanciful, but legal and regular [Mysore Fertiliser Co. v. CIT [1966] 59 ITR 268 (Mad.)].

Estimation by the ITO of the assessee's gross profit on the basis of the fact that the other dealers doing the same business as that of assessee had made profits by selling goods in black market would not be justified unless the ITO proves that the assessee has also sold goods in black market [A. S. Sivan Pillai v. CIT [1958] 34 ITR 328 (Mad.)].

An assessment made by estimating the profits of the assessee on flat rate basis on the basis of comparable cases, without furnishing details of such cases to the assessee, is illegal [Joseph Thomas & Bros. v. CIT [1968] 68 ITR 796 (Ker.)].

Assessee to be given opportunity to rebut the estimated profits - Where, after rejecting the accounts of the assessee, an estimate of the turnover and gross profits is fixed to the detriment of the assessee, the assessee is entitled to know the basis and also to an opportunity to rebut the same [Yaggina Veeraraghavulu & Mavuleti Somaraju & Co. v. CIT [1966] 62 ITR 528 (AP)].

No best judgment assessment - Mere fact that there was a less rate of gross profit declared by an assessee as compared to the previous year would not by itself be sufficient to justify the addition [Aluminium Industries (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1995] 80 Taxman 184 (Gau.)].

1. An assessee engaged in Transport Business acquires a truck on 1st September for, say, Rs. 5 lakhs and the purchase is financed by borrowing about Rs. 3 lacs @ 18% p.a. The truck is leased to a public sector undertaking for a rent of Rs. 18,000 per month.

The income computation may work out as follows: The assessee can claim loss (and thus, declare a lower amount than the specified amount) by filing appropriate return, complying with other requirements (like, maintenance of books, audit, adduce evidence, etc.). He may have to produce evidence relating to:

Date of acquisition and when it was put to use.

Cost of acquisition of truck.

Proof of borrowing for acquisition of truck.

Amount borrowed was actually used for acquiring truck.

Agreement for lease.

Amount of rent and that no other consideration was received; and the truck was used by lessee only and was not given to any one else and that no other income arose from the truck.

2. An assessee engaged in civil construction business has agreed to carry out certain work relating to fixing tiles of particular brand. The cost of tiles is, say Rs. 18 per sq. ft. Total area is, say 20,000 sq.ft. It has got a fixed price contract of say Rs. 5,00,000, including cost of tiles, without escalation. Labour contract given is say @ Rs. 3 per sq. ft. His estimated profit was Rs. 80,000. The deemed profits were Rs. 40,000. After completing l/4th work, the tile manufacturer increases the rate of tiles by Rs. 4 per sq.ft. Thus, his profits went down to Rs. 20,000. He can return Rs. 20,000 as his income, and submit the following as evidence:

Fixed price contract.

Fact that no escalation was allowed to him.

Purchase costs.

Fact that he did purchase the 75% requirement after price increase.

Labour contract and its costs.

The evidence requirement stated above is only illustrative. However, it may be pointed out that it will have to be proved that profits earned were lower than the specified profits.

1.11-4 At what stage evidence should be produced? - Section 44AD(5)/44AE(6) reads:

"Nothing contained in... this section shall apply, where the assessee claims and proves that the profits ... are lower... and thereupon..." [Emphasis supplied]

Considering the language of the provisions, it is felt that evidence should be produced or filed along with the return/claim.

In practical life this may be difficult inasmuch as the degree of proof and satisfaction required are difficult to determine. Accordingly, an assessee will have to take an utmost care while making such claim.

If an assessee does not substantiate his claim and/or does not file evidence to prove the claim, it could be contended by the tax department that requirement of the above provisions are not complied with and, accordingly, it may apply the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 44AD and/or sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 44AE, as the case may be.

However, considering the practical difficulties, it is felt that the CBDT may lay down instructions in this behalf and may direct at least that an opportunity may be provided to an assessee to lead the evidence.

If no evidence is produced by the assessee, it is evident that the requirements cannot be considered to have been met and accordingly, AO may then be free to make an assessment based on prescribed amount(s) as per the New Provisions.

l.11-5 Effects of 'Claim for a lower amount' - Following effects of a 'claim for the lower amount' will ensue:

Once a claim for assessment at a lower amount of profits is made, the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 44AD/44AE would not apply, as a result of which, if the claim is accepted, the taxable profits may be the lower amount, subject to any addition or disallowance.

The profits computation will have to be made in accordance with the provisions of sections 28 to 43C.

Exemption from maintenance of books of account or audit would not be available. Accordingly, the provisions of section 44AA and/or section 44AB will have to be complied with.

As discussed in details above, the necessary evidence in support of lower profits will have to be produced.

The Assessing Officer will have to proceed to make assessment under section 143(3) which implies:

(a)

Notices under section 142 and/or under section 143(2) of the Act.

(b)

Formal hearing(s) at which the evidence may be produced by the assessee as also further evidence as may be required will have to be produced.

(c)

Consideration of all evidences and material.

(d)

On that basis, a written order of assessment of the income and determination of sum payable by the assessee.

Assessee, earning income from contract business and plying trucks, did not maintain any books of account and had been assessed on estimated profit basis. In assessment year in question he purchased two vehicles allegedly out of sale proceeds of old vehicles and taking some loan. Assessing Officer, however, found that source of Rs. 13,000 invested in purchase was unexplained and further several deposits in Canara Bank was found. Assessee explained that Rs. 13,000 had come from his contract business and deposits in Canara Bank were out of withdrawals from UCO Banks. Since it was a 'no account' case Assessing Officer disbelieving oral statement of assessee made an addition of Rs. 1,50,000 as income from unexplained sources. Held - Availability of funds in hands of assessee from sale proceeds as well as from contract work, being obvious no adverse inference could be drawn simply because assessee did not maintain books of account when income from contract business had been assessed on the basis of profit rate, and as such, there was no sufficient reason to require assessee to explain entries in the bank account. Though it was a 'no account' case but keeping in view that assessment had been made in respect of contract business, treating rate of profit at 12.5 per cent on total receipts, it could not be assumed that whatever deposits were made in bank account flowed from unexplained income. Therefore, addition was unjustified. - Mohinder Pal Singh v. ITO [1995] 83 Taxman 116 (Chd.) (Mag.)

Introduction

1.1 The Finance Act, 1994 inserts two new sections - 44AD and 44AE - in the Income-tax Act, 1961 ('the Act") to extend the concept of 'estimated/deemed income', for determination of profits and gains of the business of Civil Construction or Transport.

The objectives of the New Provisions are:

■ simplification;

■ minimizing compliance cost; and

■ minimizing undue harassment to tax payers.

The new provisions have been justified on two grounds:

■ Such a method is prevalent in several countries; and

■ Tax Reforms Committee has recommended gradual introduction of the method.

The above provisions come into force from the assessment year 1994-95 and thus, have a retrospective effect for the previous year ended on 31-3-1994.

■ ‘Transport Business' covers the business of plying, hiring or leasing of goods carriages owned by the assessee.

Consideration received on sale of fixed assets employed in the business cannot form part of the gross receipts on account of business, i.e., civil construction business. It arises on account of sale of assets employed in the business.

Any security or other deposits obtained from employees or sub contractors cannot form part of gross receipts. Works contract tax or sales tax collected would form part of the gross receipts.

Retention money may not be considered as part of gross receipts.

Receipts arising on account of sale of scrap, etc., would form part of gross receipts on account of business.

Any refund of sales tax or works contract tax, etc., may constitute a part of gross receipts on account of business. However, any income-tax refund or interest thereon would not constitute part of the gross receipts of business. Interest on refund would, however, be separately taxable.

In case of contract with material, where a part or the whole of it is supplied by the contractee, and is included in the value of contract, the value of materials supplied by the contractee would not form part of gross receipts of the assessee. In this connection, a reference may be made to the decision of the Supreme Court in Brij Bhushan Lal Parduman Kumar v. CIT [1978] 115 ITR 524.

The value of work in progress may not form part of gross receipts. However, if in respect of such work in progress, a bill/claim has been made and approved by the contractee, then to the extent of value billed, having regard to terms of contract, such value would form part of the gross receipts, as the accrued value. If in terms of the contract the work is approved, but, merely bill is not made, it is felt that value of such work in progress would form part of the gross receipts.

The value, if any, of stock-in-trade would not form part of gross receipts.

3.10

Percentage of Completion Method (POCM)

ICDS-III (Revised) requires a contractor to offer incomes from construction contracts to tax in accordance with the "percentage of completion method"(POCM). The recognition of contract revenue and contract costs by reference to the stage of completion of a contract is referred to as the percentage of completion method. Under this method, contract revenue is matched with the contract costs incurred in reaching the stage of completion, resulting in the reporting of revenue, expenses and profit which can be attributed to the proportion of work completed. Paras 18 and 19 of ICDS-III(Revised) explain how% of stage of completion of a contract as at reporting date is to be determined. Para 20 provides that percentage of completion method is not required to be followed during the early stages of a contract i.e. in case of a contract which has reached 25% or less stage of completion. In cases of contracts in early stage, where the outcome of the contract cannot be estimated reliably contract revenue is recognised only to the extent of costs incurred. In other words, neither profit nor loss on contracts in early stages shall be recognised.

In Dy. CIT v. Sri Jagannath Properties & Developers decided by ITAT-Cuttack on 31.08.2018 in [ITA No. 283/CTK/2017] it was held that while applying POCM as per ICDS-III, the question whether stage of completion of 25% has been reached or not is to be reckoned project-wise(contract-wise) and not by taking all projects (contracts) together on overall basis and revenue can be recognised in only those projects(contracts) where stage of completion has reached 25%.

Thus, POCM is to be applied contract-wise. There is a concept in accounts called the concept of Contract Accounts. To know the results of his operations, the contractor prepares what is called as Contract Account which is debited with various costs and which is credited with the revenue associated with a particular contract. Under the POCM, reasonable profit is calculated on the basis of the value of the work certified and the profit attributable to the work certified. For example, if the value of the work certified is one-fourth or more but less than half of the contract price, then a certain percentage of the profit accruing to the certified work is taken to the profit and loss account [CIT, Meerut v. Hyundai Heavy Industries Co. Ltd. [2007] 161 Taxman 191 (SC)]. Thus, for each construction contract, a separate contract account is to be opened and the contract costs and contract revenues related to it have to be debited and credited to it with reference to% of stage of completion reached in all individual contracts which have progressed to more than 25%. Where progress is 25% or less, contract account will be debited only with contract costs incurred and credited with contract revenue equal to contract costs incurred and contract account will neither reflect a profit nor a loss.

[It is assumed that the above method measures reliably the work performed in the facts of the case] In the above method of estimating stage of completion, only those contract costs that reflect work performed are included in costs incurred upto the reporting date. Hence, the stage of completion for year 2 (74%) is determined by excluding from contract costs incurred for work performed upto the reporting date, Rs. 100 of standard materials stored at the site for use in year 3.

The percentage of completion method is to be applied on a cumulative basis in each accounting period to the current estimates of contract revenue and contract costs. POCM has to be applied to year 1 as the work performed has crossed the 25% stage.

- the language of the provisions reflect a mandate:'... and there upon the Assessing Officer shall proceed to make an assessment of the total income ...' [Emphasis supplied],

■ Assessment at a higher amount exceeding the specified amount - The next issue is that in the computation made under sections 28 to 43C of the Act, on account of specific disallowance as well as on account of adjustment in gross profit, if an addition is required to be made, can AO make an assessment in excess of the specific profits, pursuant to the provisions of sections 143(3), 145 and other applicable provisions? For the purpose, one may consider the language of the provisions as well as certain illustrations and determine the effects of section 44AD(5), which reads as follow:

"Nothing contained in the foregoing provisions of this section shall apply where the assessee claims and produces evidence to prove ... and thereupon the Assessing Officer shall proceed to make an assessment... under sub-section (3) of section 143."

The New Provisions relating to assessment at specified amount or a higher amount would not apply, ... where the assessee claims and produces evidence to prove that the profits from the specified business are lower.

Thus, when a claim is made and evidence is produced, the provisions of normal assessment become applicable and thereafter whether the Assessing Officer accepts the same or not, as such, is of no consequence. In other words, once the claim for assessment at the lower profit is made, the New Provisions would not apply and the assessee would be governed by normal provisions and assessment at an amount higher than the specified amount is possible.

ILLUSTRATIONS

1. An assessee, while claiming the assessment at lower profit, omits to make certain disallowances under section 40A(2) or 40A(3) and in the course of assessment, an addition is required to be made under the aforesaid provisions. As a result, the profits ultimately required to be assessed exceed the amount of specified profits. Can the Assessing Officer make an assessment in excess of the specified profits ?

2. A truck operator carries out some work on a truck, to convert the same into a container carrier. He claims the expenditure as revenue expenditure and on that basis lower profits are returned.

3. A person is engaged in the business of civil construction, where the person had valued the work in progress at cost. The Assessing Officer considers that the correct method of valuation should be net realizable value and not cost and on account of the valuation difference the profits could exceed the specified profits.

4. In case of a person engaged in the business of civil construction, it is noticed that certain expenses claimed are inflated and as a result addition should be made which may exceed the specified profits.

In the situation considered in illustration (1) above, the additions are arising because of non-application of the provisions of the Act. The return as filed by the assessee is accepted. Thus, section 44AD(5)/44AE(6) apply and the profits have to be computed in accordance with sections 28 to 43C of the Act. Accordingly, AO can assess the profits at an amount higher than the specified amount.

3.16-1 Advance Tax & Return - For the purposes of payment of advance tax the assessee will have to choose the option available for declaring his income, namely, the specified amount or higher amount or lower amount and accordingly pay the advance tax. The consequences of failure to pay advance tax or short payment of advance tax would follow as per normal provisions of the Act.

3.16-2 Filing of Return - An assessee would be obliged to file the return of income before the due date applicable in his case and in the return declare income, based on his option, as said above.

As discussed earlier, under sections 44AD and 44AE of the Act, presumptive tax is charged in case of construction business or transport business. Form No. 2, the prescribed return of income, states that in case of persons governed by section 44AD/44AE they are required to give limited details, like, gross profits, rate of percentage prescribed, etc., which are necessary for arriving at profits and gains of the said business. As per the form, no other information or details are prescribed. Accordingly, even in respect of section 44AF, it could be presumed that if one opts to return profits at the specified amount or percentage no other details may have to be furnished.

3.16-3 Assessment provision - Note the following :

◆ If an assessee chooses to return the specified amount as his income in the return of income, unless he has some other income, the assessment may be completed by sending an intimation under section 143(1)(a) of the Act and there would be no cause for scrutiny as the amount of income is determined by the section itself.

◆ Further, as said above, the department would be bound to assess the assessee on the specified amount for assessing the tax liability.

◆ There cannot be any question of prima facie adjustment insofar as intimation is concerned except any arithmetical error.

◆ In a case where higher amount of income is returned, the same position would prevail, as the higher amount declared has to be adopted as the taxable income, in terms, of sub-section (1) of the new provisions. There would be no scope for any adjustment.

◆ Apparently, therefore, in any given situation, there may not be any liability to additional tax, inasmuch as adjustments would not be possible or permissible under the proviso to section 143(1)(a).

◆ As said above, where income returned is specified amount or a higher amount, possibly, there may not be any scrutiny assessment, unless the Assessing Officer wants to examine certain other information, like gross receipts, cash credits, sources of investment, claims for deductions, under Chapter VI-A, etc.

1.5-2a Profit computation linked with ownership period during the year -Section 44AE(1) provides:

"... in the case of an assessee who owns... and is engaged in the business... the income of such business... shall be deemed to be the aggregate of the profits and gains from all the goods carriage owned by him in the previous year, computed in accordance with the provisions of sub-section (2)." [Emphasis supplied]

Sub-section (2) reads as follows:

"for the purpose of sub-section (1), the profits and gains from each goods carriage—

(i)

being a heavy goods vehicle, shall be... for every month or part of a month during which the heavy goods vehicle is owned by the assessee in the previous year....;

(ii)

other than a heavy goods vehicle, shall be... for every month or part of a month during which the goods carriage is owned by the assessee in the previous year...." [Emphasis supplied]

A reading of the above provisions show that the profits computation has to be made in accordance with the period for which the goods carriage is owned during the previous year irrespective of the actual employment thereof in the business during the previous year. The memorandum explaining the provisions of the Finance Bill gives two illustrations, which are reproduced hereinbelow, which supports the above view, as well as explains the computation of profits for a part of the month:

"Illustration (1): An assessee owns a light commercial vehicle for 9 months 15 days, a medium goods vehicle for 9 months and a medium goods vehicle for 12 months during the previous year. His profits and gains from the three trucks shall be deemed to be (Rs. 1,800 × 10) + (Rs. 1,800 × 9) + (Rs. 1,800 × 12), i.e., Rs. 55,800.

Illustration (2) : An assessee owns a heavy goods vehicle for 9 months 7 days, a medium goods vehicle for 9 months and a light commercial vehicle for 12 months during the previous year. His profits and gains from the three trucks shall be deemed to be (Rs. 2,000 × 10) + (Rs. 1,800 × 9) + (Rs. 1,800 × "12), i.e., Rs. 57,800."

As per the illustrations, if a vehicle is owned even for 7 days, profits computation should be considered for a month.

Presumptive taxation in case of non-residents [Sections 44BB and 44BBB]

2.3 Under sections 44BB and 44BBB ('the said sections'), business income of non-residents engaged in the business of :

providing services or facilities in connection with, or supplying plant and machinery on hire used, or to be used, in the prospecting for, or extraction or production of, mineral oils (section 44BB);

civil construction or erection or testing or commissioning of plant or machinery in connection with a turnkey power project approved by the Government and financed under any international aid programme (section 44BBB),

is deemed to be 10% of the aggregate amounts paid or payable to the non-resident (hereinafter referred to as 'presumptive basis' or 'presumptive basis of taxation').

The above sections have now been amended with effect from assessment year 2004-05 to provide that the assessees covered by these sections will have an option to compute their income on a net income basis [, i.e., income shall be computed according to the provisions of the Act] (hereinafter referred to as 'net income basis' or 'net income basis of taxation'), provided the assessee:

maintains prescribed books of account;

gets the books of account audited; and

furnishes a tax audit report under section 44AB.

It is further provided that once a claim is made by the assessee for being governed by the net income basis of taxation, the Assessing Officer shall proceed to make an assessment of the total income under section 143(3) of the Act and determine the sum payable by, or refundable to, the assessee.

Further the presumptive tax rate of 10 per cent under section 44BBB will be applicable in those turnkey power projects also which are not financed under any international aid programme.

Consequential changes have been made in sections 44AA and 44AB of the Act relating to maintenance of accounts and audit of accounts, respectively.

2.3-1 Option - The alternative to follow the net income basis as business income is optional and hence, an assessee can continue to compute the business income on presumptive basis. Even if the assessee has maintained books of account and obtained an audit report, he may still opt to be governed by taxation on presumptive basis by not making the claim of being taxed on net income basis in the return of income.

2.3-2 Delay in filing the tax audit report - One of the pre-conditions for being governed by net income basis of taxation is that the assessee should furnish a tax audit report as required under section 44AB of the Act. Now, section 44AB of the Act provides that the tax audit report should be furnished on or before 31st October of the assessment year. Hence, on a strict literal interpretation, it appears that for the purpose of sections 44BB(3) and 44BBB(2) of the Act, the tax audit report has to be furnished before the said date and any delay may disentitle the assessee from making the claim to be governed by net income basis of taxation.

2.3-3 Loss - The sections provide that the Assessing Officer can make an assessment of the total income or loss. Such loss can be set off in accordance with the provisions of section 70 of the Act and carried forward and set off in accordance with provisions of section 72 of the Act. It appears that such carry forward loss can be set off against any business income, including presumptive income of the subsequent year, if the assessee decides to be so governed in that year.

2.3-4 Computation of income - In case the assessee opts to be governed by net basis of taxation, the computation of business income would be done by applying the provisions of sections 28 to 43B, including 40(a)(i), and also 44C of the Act. Further, the provisions of transfer pricing under sections 92 to 92F of the Act will also be applicable.

Calculation of value of property in goods involved in works contract, transferred works contract - In Vat, the dealer can pay Vat (or sales tax) either on value of material on actual basis or under composition scheme. If Vat or sales tax has been paid or payable on actual value of material, that amount will be deductible from total value of works contract to calculate value of taxable service.

The actual words used in the rule as follows - Where value added tax (Vat) has been paid or payable on the actual value of transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of the works contract, then, such value adopted for the purposes of payment of value added tax or sales tax, shall be taken as the value of transfer of property in goods transferred in the execution of the works contract for determining the value of works contract service under this clause [Rule 2A(i)(c) of Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006].

However, if the dealer has paid under composition scheme (i.e. at flat rate without separately calculating value of material), the value of material will have to be calculated on basis of actuals. Note that 'value' includes profit relating to goods also.

Vat or sales tax paid will not form part of value for service tax - Gross amount charged for the works contract shall not include value added tax or sales tax, as the case may be, paid, if any, on transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of the said works contract.

In Sobha Developers v. CCE (2010) 24 STT 425 (CESTAT), assessee was paying Vat on 70% of value of works contract as per Karnataka Vat Act and paid service tax on 30% of value as service tax. It was held that no differential service tax is payable, even if value of material is not shown separately in invoice. - departmental appeal against the decision has been admitted by SC for hearing - CCE v. Sobha Developers (2014) 47 GST 766 = 49 taxmann.com 595 (SC).

Splitting of contract permissible - In Essar Projects v. CCE (2014) 46 GST 582 = 47 taxmann.com 152 (CESTAT), assessee had entered into two different contracts - one for supply of material/equipment and other for erection/commissioning. There were a separate defect liability clauses for different contracts. Property in goods got transferred when equipment was supplied to customer. It was held that both cannot be treated as single contract for purpose of valuation under composition scheme of works contract.

16.3-2 Composition scheme for payment of service tax

Though service tax is legally payable only on value of service and Vat/sales tax is payable on value of goods, in a composite/indivisible contract, it is difficult to find value of goods and services. Hence, both under service tax and State Vat, a provision has been made for payment of tax under composition scheme.

In a composition scheme, tax can be paid on some ad hoc basis at the option of the tax payer.

In State of Kerala v. Builders Association of India 104 STC 134 = (1997) 2 SCC 183 = AIR 1997 SC 3640 = 1997 AIR SCW 977, the position was that a convenient, hassle-free and simple method, which was 'rough and ready method' was evolved by State Government for collection of sales tax on Works Contract. This was optional to assessee. It was held that Legislature can evolve such alternate, simplified and hassle-free methods of assessment, making it optional to assessee. - . - In the field of taxation, legislation must be allowed greater 'play in joints'. Allowance must be made for 'trial and error' by the legislature. - - Contractor who has opted to the alternate method of taxation cannot complain. Having voluntarily, and with the full knowledge of the alternate method of taxation, opted to be governed by it, a contractor cannot be heard to question the validity of relevant sub-sections or the rules - followed in Karnataka State Construction Corporation v. State of Karnataka (2004) 138 STC 75 (Kar HC DB) * Indian Oil Corp v. Prasanna Welding Industries (2007) 7 VST 101 (Gau HC).

In Mycon Construction v. State of Karnataka 2002 AIR SCW 2156 = 127 STC 105 (SC), it was held that a simplified composition scheme instead of regular assessment, can be evolved, if it is on optional basis. Validity of such provision has been upheld.

Government can make a provision allowing contractors option to opt for composition by paying a sum based on total consideration of contract. - Mytcon Construction v. State of Karnataka (1998) 111 STC 322 (Karn HC).

Finance Act, 2003

Presumptive taxation in case of non-residents [Sections 44BB and 44BBB]

2.3 Under sections 44BB and 44BBB ('the said sections'), business income of non-residents engaged in the business of :

providing services or facilities in connection with, or supplying plant and machinery on hire used, or to be used, in the prospecting for, or extraction or production of, mineral oils (section 44BB);

civil construction or erection or testing or commissioning of plant or machinery in connection with a turnkey power project approved by the Government and financed under any international aid programme (section 44BBB),

is deemed to be 10% of the aggregate amounts paid or payable to the non-resident (hereinafter referred to as 'presumptive basis' or 'presumptive basis of taxation').

The above sections have now been amended with effect from assessment year 2004-05 to provide that the assessees covered by these sections will have an option to compute their income on a net income basis [, i.e., income shall be computed according to the provisions of the Act] (hereinafter referred to as 'net income basis' or 'net income basis of taxation'), provided the assessee:

maintains prescribed books of account;

gets the books of account audited; and

furnishes a tax audit report under section 44AB.

It is further provided that once a claim is made by the assessee for being governed by the net income basis of taxation, the Assessing Officer shall proceed to make an assessment of the total income under section 143(3) of the Act and determine the sum payable by, or refundable to, the assessee.

Further the presumptive tax rate of 10 per cent under section 44BBB will be applicable in those turnkey power projects also which are not financed under any international aid programme.

Consequential changes have been made in sections 44AA and 44AB of the Act relating to maintenance of accounts and audit of accounts, respectively.

2.3-1 Option - The alternative to follow the net income basis as business income is optional and hence, an assessee can continue to compute the business income on presumptive basis. Even if the assessee has maintained books of account and obtained an audit report, he may still opt to be governed by taxation on presumptive basis by not making the claim of being taxed on net income basis in the return of income.

2.3-2 Delay in filing the tax audit report - One of the pre-conditions for being governed by net income basis of taxation is that the assessee should furnish a tax audit report as required under section 44AB of the Act. Now, section 44AB of the Act provides that the tax audit report should be furnished on or before 31st October of the assessment year. Hence, on a strict literal interpretation, it appears that for the purpose of sections 44BB(3) and 44BBB(2) of the Act, the tax audit report has to be furnished before the said date and any delay may disentitle the assessee from making the claim to be governed by net income basis of taxation.

2.3-3 Loss - The sections provide that the Assessing Officer can make an assessment of the total income or loss. Such loss can be set off in accordance with the provisions of section 70 of the Act and carried forward and set off in accordance with provisions of section 72 of the Act. It appears that such carry forward loss can be set off against any business income, including presumptive income of the subsequent year, if the assessee decides to be so governed in that year.

2.3-4 Computation of income - In case the assessee opts to be governed by net basis of taxation, the computation of business income would be done by applying the provisions of sections 28 to 43B, including 40(a)(i), and also 44C of the Act. Further, the provisions of transfer pricing under sections 92 to 92F of the Act will also be applicable.

Some of the issues in computation of such income were raised in N.V. Jan De Nul v. CIT [1999] 236 ITR 489. In this case, however, the authority refused to answer the questions !

Revision u/s 263 quashed as AO rightly accepted civil contractor’s voluntary 6% profit estimate, no error found: ITAT

IT: Where contract receipts and costs were accounted by assessee and were measurable, profit was to be computed based on actual revenue recognised (of which recovery was certain) and actual expenses incurred during financial year relevant to assessment year and not on basis of estimated costs

IT: Where assessee was fully engaged in labour oriented contract work and it had taken contracts from a construction company, which in turn had taken main contract from Government, Assessing Officer was directed to apply 5 per cent net profit on gross receipts of assessee

INCOME TAX : Where Assessing Officer rejected books of account of assessee under section 145(3) and applied 8 per cent net profit rate on total turnover and accordingly made addition as assessee failed to furnish relevant details, since even during appellate proceedings before CIT (Appeals) also assessee did not submit any submissions and CIT (Appeals) had decided appeal on basis of material available on record and merely upheld orders of Assessing Officer, matter was to be set aside to file of CIT (Appeals) to decide issue afresh

INCOME TAX: Where dispute was only with regard to rate of gross profit on income which was not disclosed by assessee, it could not be said that Assessing Officer erred in adopting gross profit at rate of 2 per cent on undisclosed income declared by assessee

HEADNOTE: Section 143, read with section 256, of Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 33, read with section 66, of Indian Income tax Act, 1922] - Assessment - General - Assessment year 1924-25 - In respect of contracts spread over a number of years, assessee produced accounts but accounts for relevant accounting year could not be separated - ITO assessed profit at a standard rate without informing assessee of information or evidence on which rate was based and without giving him any opportunity to produce evidence in rebuttal - Whether question of law arose out of order of ITO - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, a contractor, was assessed to income-tax for the relevant assessment year in respect of certain contracts which commenced in 1922 and were finished some time in 1924. The assessee produced his accounts, but the accounts for the relevant accounting year could not be separated. The ITO considered the accounts to be unreliable. He, therefore, assumed profit at the standard rate of 10 per cent for the purposes of his assessment. On appeal, the Assistant Commissioner concluded that in any case it was impossible to ascertain from the assessee’s accounts what the income had been for one year and, therefore, the only way of ascertaining it was to apply the usual rate of 10 per cent on the total payments received. On application under section 66(2) of the 1922 Act, the Commissioner declined to make any reference.

On application under section 66 (3) of the 1922 Act.

HELD: In the instant case the assessee did not allege that he derived no income at all from any contracts, nor did the assessment proceed definitely on the ground that the accounts were unreliable. The Assistant Commissioner adopted a standard rate for the assessment merely because no separate accounts were available for the accounting year. This was apparently due to the manner in which the accounting were kept. As the assessee failed to produce correct and complete accounts for the accounting year, it was open to the Income-tax Officer to make an assessment to the best of his judgment: vide section 23, read with section 11, of the 1922 Act. The Assistant Commissioner, however, gave no reasons for adopting what he called the usual rate of 10 per cent for the purposes of the assessment, and it was not known how that rate was arrived at. In the circumstances of the case, the point of law emerged for decision was whether in the case of a contract spread over a number of years when accounts for the year under assessment could not be separated, the ITO was legally justified in assessing profits at a flat rate without informing the assessee of the information or evidence on which the rate was based and without giving him any opportunity to produce evidence in rebuttal.

Accordingly, the petition was accepted and the Commissioner was directed to state the case and refer the point of law to the High Court for decision.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

Sardha Ram for the Assessee .

Jagan Nath Aggarwal for the Crown.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment years 1957-58 to 1962-63 - Assessee was a contractor and undertaking jobs of various Govt. departments - Books of account of assessee were rejected by ITO and he determined assessee's income on estimate - Terms and conditions as to supply of materials by contractee was not known - Element of profit on such supply if any was to be ascertained and it was also not known whether assessee had submitted its tenders for said contracts anticipating on being assured of supply of such materials - Whether case was to be remanded back to Tribunal to ascertain terms and conditions of contract - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a contractor and undertook jobs under various Government departments. The books of account were maintained by the assessee. The were not accepted by the ITO at the time of assessment and the assessee's income was determined on estimate. For the assessment years 1957-58 to 1959-60, estimated amounts were added to the net receipts of the assessee. For 1959-60, this figure was 10 per cent on account of the materials supplied by the Government departments. For the assessment years 1957-58 and 1958-59, lump sum additions were made on this account. For the assessment year 1962-63, the ITO went into the matter in detail. The assessee was called upon to produce certificates from various authorities under which he had carried on the work. Independent enquiries were also made from such authorities. On the basis of the aforesaid the ITO came to the conclusion that the total gross receipts during the said year would be Rs. 7,76,000 as against the amount of Rs. 5,25,000 as shown by the assessee. On such material, the ITO also reopened the proceedings for the earlier assessment years including the assessment years 1954-55, 1955-56 and 1956-57. On appeal, the AAC held that in all the years the assessee's income should be determined by applying a flat rate of 12.5 per cent on the net receipts of the assessee and that the value of materials supplied to the assessee by the departments concerned should not be included in such net receipts for the purpose of application of this flat rate. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that, on the facts and circumstances, the original assessment orders made for the assessment years 1957-58 to 1959-60 were correct and thus set aside the reassessments made under section 147. The Tribunal further held that in respect of the assessment year 1962-63, the assessment made by the ITO was correct and the total receipts for the purpose of estimation of the assessee's profits should include the cost of materials supplied by the contractees.

On reference :

HELD: In the facts and circumstances of the instant case, it appeared that it was not possible to answer the questions referred without further findings on fact. It was not clear whether the lower authorities had seen or considered the terms and conditions of the contracts under which the assessee had carried on the work of construction. The terms and conditions as to supply of materials by the contractee were also not known.

Such terms were of some importance. It would be necessary to determine whether the materials to be supplied would be free of cost or price on the basis of market value or otherwise would be charged. On such facts it may be found that an element of profit was there on such supply (sic ). Whether the assessee submitted its tenders for the said contracts anticipating on being assured of supply of such materials were also not known. In this view, the matter was remanded back to the Tribunal. The Tribunal was directed to ascertain the terms and conditions of the contracts in question, if any, in respect of supply of materials and determine whether the assessee bid for such contracts taking into account such materials which were in fact supplied. If it was found on such facts that there was an element of profit involved in the materials supplied then the profits of the assessee will be estimated on the gross receipts of the assessee computed by including the value of the materials supplied to the net receipts. The Tribunal will be at liberty to take further evidence in the matter and will afford opportunity to the parties to adduce further evidence and to make further representations in the matter.

Note: Case remanded back.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 13 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Method of accounting - Valuation of stock - Assessment year 1959-60 - While completing assessment ITO did not accept assessee's reasons for low profits at rate of 9% in respect of a contract undertaken by him and applied flat rate of 12Â½% profit - On appeal assessee had not derived before AAC that full quantitative details were not available in respect of stores of value of Rs. 1,30,000 - For subsequent assessment year assessee declared a profit of 9.9% - Whether on facts provisions of section 13 were applicable to assessee's case and therefore, Tribunal was justified in upholding addition in assessee's income - Held, yes

FACT: The business of the assessee was execution of construction contracts. The assessee commenced its business from 25-1-1958, and the accounts were closed for the first time on 25-1-1959. During the accounting year the assessee undertook three contracts with respect to which it submitted separate profit and loss statements.

The accounts in respect of the first two contracts were accepted by the authorities under the Act in toto but with regard to the accounts relating to the third contract the ITO declined to accept the assessee's reasons for low profits at the rate of 9% in respect of that contract. He, therefore, applied a flat rate of 12Â½% profit and made certain addition to the assessee's income.

On appeal, the AAC had accepted the assessee's reasons for the low profit of 9% but had sustained an addition of Rs. 10,000 on the ground that the assessee's representative had not denied before him that full quantitative details might not be available in respect of the stores of the value of over Rs. 1,30,000 consumed in the execution of the contract. When the case came up before the Tribunal the addition of Rs. 10,000 was found to be excessive and was reduced to Rs. 6,000.

On reference :

HELD: In the instant case there was material before the Tribunal on which its finding could be based: the assessee's representative had admitted before the AAC that full quantitative details in respect of the stores of the value of Rs. 1,30,000 consumed in the execution of that contract might not be available. In the circumstances, recourse to estimating the profits on the contract was inevitable. He, therefore, made an addition of Rs. 10,000 as against Rs. 26,434 added by the ITO. If the assessee wished to displace the AAC's estimate it was open to him to adduce evidence in support of its claim that the consumption of stores of the value of Rs. 1,30,000 was fully justified. This the assessee apparently did not do. For the subsequent year 1960-61 the assessee itself declared a net profit rate of 9.9% as against 9% declared in the assessment year in question. It could not be disputed that this was additional material which the Tribunal could take into consideration as it did. There was thus material before the Tribunal on which its estimate was based. The Tribunal's decision was, therefore, in conformity with the decision in the case of CIT v. Maharajadhiraj of Darbhanga [1933] 1 ITR 94 (P.C.).

The Tribunal was therefore justified in holding that the proviso to section 13 was applicable and there was material before it to sustain the aforesaid addition.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of revenue.

as he may determine.

In the case of a contractor, it cannot be said that merely because of incompleteness of the contract in the relevant accounting year profits of the assessee for that accounting year cannot be ascertained. It also cannot be said that merely because a contract was completed after the accounting year, no profit arose or accrued to the assessee in the accounting year. In the case of an incomplete contract there is a well-established method of calculating profits accruing in the accounting year. In the instant case, the Tribunal had found that for the assessment years 1939-40 and 1940-41 no accounts were kept for the contract the assessee had executed. For the assessment year 1943-44 he wrote a letter to the Income-tax Officer and admitted that he had no accounts to produce. For the assessment year 1944-45 he produced two sets of accounts. One was maintained for the two contracts he had taken from PWD but the profits of each contact was not separately worked out and there was one consolidated receipts and payments account for both the contracts. For the military contract he kept a separate set of accounts. These accounts were maintained from 14-4-1943 to 3-12-1944. The total value of contract was Rs. 3,78,766 and out of this the assessee received of Rs. 3,00,000 before 31-3-1944. He did not close the accounts on 31-3-1944, or prepare balance sheet but the accounts were kept open till 3-12-1944, when the execution of the contract was completed. It was argued on behalf of the assessee that the account are maintained on completed contract basis and the assessee had no objection if the income of the Hospital contract was taxed for the assessment year 1945-46 and that there was a single and indivisible contract for the Hospital and the work upon the entire contract was completed on 3-12-1944, and that was the proper date on which the profits should be ascertained. This argument was not acceptable if accounts are maintained and completed on contract basis the profits or gains of the previous year cannot properly be extracted from these accounts. For a contract may take several years for being completed. The payments in regard to the contract may also be received by the assessee in several years. It may be convenient for the assessee that profit should be ascertained on the completion of the contract and assessment of the profit should take place on the date of the completion of the contract. But section 3 imposes a charge of income-tax upon the profits and gains accruing to the assessee for the accounting year and it is the duty of the Income-tax authorities to make ascertainment of such profits and gains accruing to the assessee in respect of the payment received during the accounting year. Since the accounts maintained by the assessee did not correctly reflected the profits of the assessee for the accounting year the Tribunal was right in holding that the proviso to section 13 applied and that the ITO was entitled to discard the accounting method of the assessee and instead to make computation of the profits on such basis as he thought fit.

As regards the objection that the estimate of income on this formula would still be an estimate and would not be mathematically accurate, mathematical certainty is not demanded in a matter of this description.

The proviso to section 13 had been rightly applied by the Tribunal in regard to the accounts maintained for the contract business, which were not closed to profit at the end of each previous year but were closed to profit only after the completion of a contract.

PER AHMAD, J. (CONCURRENT VIEW ):

In the instant case the finding given by the Tribunal was that "the assessee never produced any account till the assessment in the present case and that no account was maintained by the assessee and therefore he had no method of accounting till 1943-44." On this finding of fact alone, therefore, the case attracted at once the operation of the rule of law laid down in the proviso, that is, it was the duty of the Income-tax Officer in such a state of facts to compute the income, profits and gains of the assessee upon such basis and in such manner as he thought best.

Even, however, if it be assumed in favour of the assessee, for which there was no evidence, that the account presented before the Income-tax Officer in the next year was one in accordance with a method regularly employed by the assessee, finding of fact given by the Tribunal that the method employed by the assessee in that account was such that the income, profits and gains could not properly be deduced there from. On that finding also the proviso to section 13 at once came into play and the duty was cast on the Income-tax Officer to compute the income, profit and gains of the assessee upon such basis and upon such manner as the income-tax Officer might determine.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 13 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment year 1959-60 - Assessee was a contractor who had undertaken construction of houses under a project for relevant assessment year - Assessee showed expenditure incurred on jobs during year at 
Rs 4,45,904 which was treated by assessee as work-in-progress and showed a sum of Rs 3,21,358 as received against contracts from executive engineer - Assessee did not show any profit or loss from jobs and claiming overhead expenses at Rs 12,764 a net loss was returned - ITO considered that a profit had to be calculated on basis of receipts from authorities and he accordingly computed gross profit of Rs. 40,169 at 12½ per cent of receipts - Before AAC, assessee claimed that since accounts were maintained on completed job basis which was recognised system of accounting, proviso to section 13 of 1922 Act could not be invoked - AAC did not accept assessee’s contention and upheld order of ITO in invoking provisions of section 13 of 1922 Act for computing assessee’s income - However, he computed gross profit by applying rate of 12½ per cent on gross value of work done and not on net payments received by assessee - Tribunal upheld order of AAC - Whether order of Tribunal was justified - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a contractor. In the year in question, the assessee had undertaken the construction of houses under a project. The expenditure incurred on the jobs during the year was shown at Rs. 4,45,904 and that was treated by the assessee as work-in-progress and a sum of Rs. 3,21,358 was shown as received against the contracts from the Executive Engineer. The assessee did not show any profit or loss from the jobs and, claiming overhead expenses at Rs. 12,764, a net loss was returned. The ITO considered that a profit had to be calculated on the basis of the receipts from the authorities and he had, accordingly, computed the gross profit of Rs. 40,169 at 12½ per cent of the receipts. The assessee appealed before the AAC. The assessee claimed that the accounts were maintained on what was known as the completed job basis which was the recognised system of accounting and that the accounts having been maintained in a proper manner, the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act could not be invoked. The AAC did not accept the assessee's contention. According to the AAC, the tax had to be levied on the total income of the previous year and not on the total income of a period of 2, 3, 4 or more years, the period that would be required for completing any contracted work. Accordingly, he upheld action of the ITO in invoking the provisions of section 13 of the 1922 Act, for computing the assessee’s income, however, the AAC, held that the rate was to be applied on the gross value of the work done and not on the net payments received by the assessee and accordingly computed the gross profits at Rs. 1,04,926 by applying the rate of 12½ per cent on Rs. 8,29,412 as the gross value of the work done during the previous year. On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order of the AAC.

On reference:

HELD: In the instant case, the assessee contractor had not been able to satisfy the lower authorities as to what were the terms of the contract with the contractee and in what terms and consideration the materials were supplied by the contractee to the contractor. Furthermore, in the instant case the total amount of profit had to be computed by applying the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act. The rate of profit had also to be determined by applying the proviso to section 13 of the 1922, Act. As the Tribunal had pointed out that if the normal experience and expectation of a contractor as to how the profit would vary, were taken into consideration and in the circumstances where the contractor had not been actually able to satisfy the terms of the contract and where the estimates were to be based by applying the provisions to section 13 of the 1922 Act, it could not be said that the Tribunal was not justified in upholding the decision of the AAC in the manner as it did. In cases where there was clear and unambiguous evidence that there was contract which provided sufficient limit, beyond which the tender could not be quoted and there was a stipulation that the contract was to be quoted at a particular rate, excluding the cost of materials, to be supplied by the contractee, other considerations might apply.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

should be taxed on year-to-year basis. It is a dangerous proposition to recognise that the profit accrues only after the completion of a contract, Such a proposition is liable to be abused by dishonest taxpayers. It is a judicially recognised proposition that in the case of a contract in order to ascertain the income one need not wait till the contract is completed and that it is open to the revenue to estimate the profit on the basis of receipts in each year of construction, although the contract is not complete. Section 3 makes each previous year a distinct unit of time for the purpose of assessment and the profits made before or after that unit of time are entirely immaterial in assessing the profits of that year. In the case of contracts, if accounts are maintained and completed on contract basis, the profits or gains of the previous year can not properly be extracted from the accounts, for a contract may take several years for being completed and payment in regard to it may also be received by the assessee in several years. It may be convenient from the point of view of the assessee that profit should be ascertained on the completion of the contract and assessment of the profit should take place after the completion of the contract. But section 3 imposes a charge of income-tax upon the profits and gains of the assessee for the accounting year and it is the duty of the ITO to ascertain the profits and gains accruing to the assessee in respect of the payment received during the accounting year. It cannot be said that merely because a contract is completed after the accounting year, no profit arises or accrues to the assessee in the accounting year. In the case of an incomplete contract, there is a well-established method of calculating profits accruing in the accounting year. In such a contract, the long-term contract method is adopted in respect of contracts which have to be completed by stages over a course of years, such as, building contracts or building schemes by co- operative or private enterprise, or contracts entered into with public authorities such as public works, military, etc. The ascertainment of the profit in the execution of such contracts cannot be deferred till the completion of the entire constructions which may take several years. Each year’s profit shall have to be, in the nature of things, computed on an estimate, having regard to the work completed during the year. There are recognised methods of estimating with reasonable accuracy the profits accrued from time to time on uncompleted contracts. The fact that the contracts have not been completed or the accounts thereof have not been closed, is not sufficient reason for not estimating the profit of each year though absolute accuracy may not be reached. Thus, in a contract running over several years, the entire profits cannot be attributed to a single last year in which the contract was completed. The fact that it is not convenient or easy to allocate receipts or expendi- ture as against various items of trading assets is no reason for uphold- ing that profits emerge only after the entire expenditure on the assets has been recouped; the allocation of expenditure and receipts must somehow be made on a reasonable basis and the debts and trading assets valued on the closing date. In such cases, a workable method is for the revenue to assess on the basis of gross receipts of each year at a flat rate of profit on such receipts. The assessment in the case of a building

contractor, therefore, need not be postponed till the completion of the contract.

If the profits could reasonably be arrived at from year to year, such profit should be assessed from year to year only. In the instant case, the assessee had not correctly valued the closing work-in-progress and, therefore, it was the duty of the Assessing Officer to correctly value the closing work-in-progress: and arrive at the true picture of the profit. Thus, in the case of a building contractor, the revenue need not wait till the completion of the contract and the reasonable profit can be estimated from year to year and brought to tax.

Regarding the estimate of profits at 8 per cent there was no material on record to show that the estimate of profit at 8 per cent was excessive and unreasonable having regard to the facts of the case. However, the profit at 8 per cent estimated for these three years was only a mere estimate and the true profit of the entire project would be arrived at when the contract was complete. The assessee was, therefore, entitled to the adjustment of profit or loss in the year of completion of the contract. Hence, the estimate of profit at 8 per cent was reasonable.

HEADNOTE: Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income (In case of estimation of profit) - Assessment year 1995-96 - Assessee was a contractor and assessee declared its income at an estimated 3 per cent of contract receipts - Search took place in assessee's premises and in view of seized materials Assessing Officer gave due opportunity to assessee to justify disclosed income and explain discrepancies noticed by special auditor - Assessee was also permitted to inspect seized documents - Despite that assessee could not explain said discrepancies - Accordingly Assessing Officer resorted to estimation of profits by adopting 11 per cent on gross contract receipts and initiated penalty proceedings - Whether there was gross or wilful negligence on part of assessee in failing to return correct income, penalty would be levied under section 271(1)(c) - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of revenue]IT: Where assessee could not explain discrepancies noticed by special auditor and disclosed a lesser income than what it actually earned, penalty under section 271(1)(c) was to be levied

FACT: The assessee, a contractor undertaking projects of Indian Railways on turnkey basis, filed its return of income.

On the basis of the materials gathered by the income-tax authorities in the course of a search carried out in the assessee's premises as well as in the premises of the directors and trusted persons, the Assessing Officer referred the matter to a special audit in terms of section 142(2A). The special audit report, inter alia, reported that there were large number of transactions in which several discrepancies were noticed.

In response to the queries raised by the Assessing Officer on the basis of the special audit report the assessee could not give any proper explanation and wherever an explanation was sought to be given, it was found to be evasive. The assessee was also allowed inspection of the seized documents and was supplied photocopies of the seized records. Despite such opportunity, no convincing reason was given by the assessee.

The Assessing Officer proceeded to estimate the net profit of the assessee at 11 per cent of the gross receipts from the contracts. The Assessing Officer also found that some income from business activities was not included in the aforesaid receipts and the profit from such activity was taken at Rs.13.34 lakhs. Demands were accordingly raised.

Penalty proceedings were initiated by the Assessing Officer for concealment of income and after rejecting the assessee's explanation, a penalty was imposed for concealment of income under section 271(1)(c).

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) cancelled the penalty order on the ground that the Assessing Officer has not stated the basis of this estimate nor did he give an opportunity to the assessee to rebut the proposal to estimate the profits at 11 per cent of the gross receipts. He held that the assessee made a counter proposal which was a conditional offer as to the taxability of the profits and even if it is assumed that there was an agreement on the part of the assessee for being taxed at the rate of 11 per cent of the gross receipts, it does not follow automatically that the assessee concealed its income.

On second appeal by Revenue, the Tribunal dismissed it.

On appeal to the High Court:

HELD: The assessee is not right in his contention that whenever an assessment is made by applying a flat rate of profit to the declared turnover or receipts, which is higher than the rate adopted by the assessee in the return of income, there can be no inference that the assessee concealed his profits. [Para 9]

HEADNOTE: Section 144, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Best judgment assessment - Assessment year 1974-75 - Whether while making a best judgment assessment, though there must necessarily be guess work in matter, it must not be arbitrary - Held, yes - Assessee-contractor did not main books of account - He filed his return of income on estimate basis by computing profit at flat rate of 10 per cent on gross receipts - ITO, however, computed net profit at rate of 15 per cent - Revision petition filed by assessee was dismissed by Commissioner - Whether since neither ITO nor Commissioner had referred to any material for applying flat rate of 
15 percent while estimating net profits, impugned orders passed by them deserved to be set aside - Held, yes

FACT: The petitioner assessee, who was carrying on business as a contractor filed his return on estimated basis by computing the profit at a flat rate of 10 per cent, on gross receipts, as he did not maintain any books of account. The ITO, however, computed the net profit at 15 per cent, on the contract payments received by the assessee. The revision petition filed under section 263 was dismissed by the Commissioner.

On writ:

HELD: It is now well settled that while making a best judgment assessment, though there must necessarily be guess-work in the matter, it must not be arbitrary. In the instant case, the basis on which the computation was made was not disclosed in the order.

Neither the ITO nor the Commissioner had referred to any material for applying the flat rate of 15 per cent while estimating the net profits.

In such circumstances, the assessment order could not but be held to be arbitrary. The order passed by the ITO and that passed by the Commissioner, therefore, deserved to be set aside. The petition was allowed accordingly.

Note: The case has been decided in favour of the petitioner-assessee.
