S.C. Bagdiya for the Respondent.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 13, Proviso to the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Method of accounting - Works contract - Assessment year 1944-45 - Whether merely because a contract was completed after relevant accounting year, it could not be said that no profits arose or accrued to assessee in that accounting year - Held, yes - Assessee was a contractor - As contracts entered into by assessee were not completed during accounting year in question, no income therefrom was declared on ground that no profits accrued on incomplete contracts - Assessee maintained no accounts till accounting year relevant to assessment year 1943-44 and accounts maintained for accounting year relevant to assessment year 1944-45 were not closed on 31-3-1944 but were kept open till execution of contract was completed - These accounts did not reflect profits of assessee for accounting year in question - Whether in instant case proviso to section 13 was applicable and ITO was entitled to discard accounting method of assessee and estimate profits on such basis as he thought fit - Held, yes - Whether objection of assessee that estimate of income on his formula would still be an estimate and would not be mathematically accurate had no substance as mathematical certainty is not demanded in a matter of this description - Held, yes

FACT: During the accounting year ending on 31-3-1944 the assessee-HUF carried on contract business. It obtained contracts from PWD and from the Defence Department. The work of contracts with PWD was taken up on 14-4-1943, and completed on 12-5-1944. For the Defence Department the work of the hospital was started on 14-4-1943, and was closed on 3-12-1944. In the return for the assessment year 1944-45 the assessee did not declare any income from contract on the ground that they were not closed within the accounting year. The ITO held that during the accounting year the assessee had realized a net income of Rs. 19,683 from the PWD contracts. For the military contract he held that the entire contract had been completed within the accounting year and the assessee had received Rs. 3,67,578 from the military authorities. In view of the defective state of the account books produced by the assessee he considered that the profits should be estimated at 15 per cent of this amount. He determined the net income from the military contract as Rs. 55,135 and included it in the total income. On appeal, it was argued that the military contract was not fully executed before 31-3-1944, and that the ITO was not justified in holding that the income therefrom should be included in the return of the assessee for the accounting year in question. This argument was accepted by the AAC who directed the ITO to exclude the profit from the military contract. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal held that the account maintained by the assessee did not reflect the true profits of the assessee. It accepted the case of the assessee that the military contract was executed on 3-12-1944 nevertheless, it held that 9/10th of the contract work had been done in the accounting year and the assessee had received from the military department about Rs. 3,00,000 on that account and, thus, the proviso to section 13 was applicable and the profits for the accounting year should be determined by the ITO by estimate.

On reference :

HELD: Per Ramaswami, J.

The scheme and structure of the Income-tax Act, read with the Finance Act is to make the tax an annual tax for the purpose of assessment. Section 3 makes each "previous year" a distinct unit of time for the purpose of assessment and the profits made before or after that unit of time are entirely immaterial in assessing the profits of that year. If section 3 is read in the context of section 13, it is clear that the accounts maintained by the assessee must correctly show or reflect the profits of the preceding year. If the method of accounting adopted by the assessee does not reflect the true profits of the preceding year the proviso to section 13 will apply and the ITO would be entitled to compute the profits upon such basis and in such manner as he may determine.

In the case of a contractor, it cannot be said that merely because of incompleteness of the contract in the relevant accounting year profits of the assessee for that accounting year cannot be ascertained. It also cannot be said that merely because a contract was completed after the accounting year, no profit arose or accrued to the assessee in the accounting year. In the case of an incomplete contract there is a well-established method of calculating profits accruing in the accounting year.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimate of profits - Assessment year 1985-86 - Assessee, a contractor, did not maintain regular books of account - Assessee had only estimated cash profit with reference to gross receipts and, thus, quantum of gross receipt was only intended to serve as a basis to measure cash profit retained - Assessee contended that tax deducted at source by Government could not be considered as an outgoing for year - Whether there was substance in plea of assessee that tax deducted at source could not be considered as having to come out of profits thus estimated - Held, yes

FACT: On a search of the assessee’s premises under section 132 certain investments hitherto not disclosed were found. The Assessing Officer called for year-wise statements of receipts and outgoings for all the assessment years from 1980-81 and on the basis of such statements, he determined the assessee’s income. The assessee did not maintain regular books of account for his business in contract work and the income was admitted from year to year on the basis of estimates and assessed also on the basis of estimates. The assessee furnished statements of funds flow referred to as cash flow statements for various years. The total income determined for the assessment year 1985-86 was Rs. 6,10,070. On appeal, the assessee contended that the tax deducted at source by the Government could not be considered as an outgoing for the year. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, dismissed the assessee’s plea.

On second appeal :

HELD: The revenue would certainly be right in its submission if only the assessee had taken the gross receipts and set them off against all the outgoings including the tax deducted at source and the expenditure incurred or laid out on the contract work in earning the gross receipts before arriving at the profit in contract business. This method was not adopted by the assessee. The assessee had only estimated the ‘cash profits’ with reference to the gross receipts and thus the quantum of gross receipts was only intended to serve as a basis to measure the cash profit retained. This method of estimating the cash profit is a method known to income-tax and often resorted to in the assessment of contractors and as a matter of fact such reckoning of the cash profit has been made in the assessee’s own case in the past several years. From the cash profit so ascertained, depreciation was allowed to be deducted in determining the taxable income of the assessee as would be seen from the computation of the income furnished by the assessee for the assessment years 1980-81 onwards. Therefore, there was substance in the plea of the assessee that the tax deducted at source could not be considered as having come out of the profits thus estimated.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment years 1964-65 and 1965-66 - Assessee was carried on business of executing contracts for Government - He received gross amounts of bills for assessment years 1964-65 and 1965-66 from Government - As assessee did not maintain any books of account, ITO applied net profit rate of 12.6 per cent on gross bill amounts and computed total income for two years - Assessee contended that cost of materials supplied by Government should have been deducted before applying net profit rate - Tribunal held that assessee though tendered contract as a whole, it must have included cost of material which were supplied by Government as an element of profit in respect of cost of material also - Whether since there was no evidence on record to show that assessee did not know about supply of material by Government to be made or at what price and furthermore gross profit had been computed on total gross bill of assessee, it could not be said that Tribunal was indulging in any surmise, or acting without any proper evidence - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was carrying on business of executing contracts for the Government. He received gross amounts of bills amounting to Rs. 4,93,995 for the assessment year 1964-65 and Rs. 4,43,982 for the assessment year 1965-66 from the Government. As the assessee did not maintain any books of account, the ITO applied net profit rate of 12.6 per cent on the gross bill amounts received by the assessee in each of the two years under consideration and computed the total income for the two years. The assessee being aggrieved by the said order filed appeals before the AAC and contended that the cost of the materials supplied by the Government should have been deducted before applying the net profit rate and that there was no element of profit in the cost of materials supplied. The AAC found that the Government had supplied cement, iron rods, etc., costing Rs. 1,44,408 and Rs. 1,99,383 in the respective two years under consideration and held that the assessee did earn profits on the cost of materials supplied because certain materials were supplied by the Government from the market at the prevailing prices.

On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order of the AAC.

On reference :

HELD: In the instant case the assessee had not maintained any books of account and the revenue applied a rate of profit of 12.6 per cent on the gross amounts of bills received by the assessee. The assessee had tendered for the contract as a whole including the cost of materials which were subsequently supplied by the Government. There was no evidence on record to show that the assessee did not know about the supply of materials by the Government to be made or at what price. Furthermore, the gross profit had been computed on the total gross bill of the assessee. In the aforesaid background the Tribunal had come to the conclusion that the assessee, though tendered the contract as a whole, it must have included the cost of materials which were supplied by the Government as an element of profit in respect of cost of materials also. In the aforesaid background, it could not be said that the Tribunal was indulging in any surmise or acting without any proper evidence. Therefore, the Tribunal was justified in holding that a net profit rate as applied by the departmental authorities on the gross amounts of bills without deducting the cost of materials supplied by the Government was legally justified for the assessment years 1964-65 and 1965-66.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

But neither he can exercise this authority in caprice, nor has he an unrestricted, unlimited, unconditional or absolute right in this matter. It was undisputed that the ITO had completed the assessments of the assessee’s income for the assessment years 1978-79 to 1981-82 on a flate rate basis observing, inter alia, that in the absence of maintenance of vouchers and receipts for the expenditure incurred by the assessee, the books of account were not acceptable. Now to examine whether the books of account kept in all the years inclusive of the year under appeal were maintained in the same manner or not, the trading and profit and loss accounts were the best available guide on which one should rely. There was no difference in the manner in which they had been kept in any of the assessment years inclusive of the assessment year under appeal. However, it was strange that though the assessee was a big contractor and executions of many of the contracts were spread in these years, no work-in-progress or closing stock had been recorded in the trading account. In view of the circumstances, it was not possible for the ITO to presume that the true profit could be computed on the basis of the books of account. He had overlooked the orders for the assessment years 1978-79 to 1981-82 framed by his predecessors. As a matter of fact, his finding was not very much different. In the instant case, the ITO arrived at the figure on the basis of the receipts extending over three accounting year. He took the sum total of these receipts to be the base for the net income that had accrued to the assessee during the accounting year 1943-44 as the entire contract work had been completed during that year. Mere execution of the contract work will not necessarily entitle the contractor to make a demand for payment until it is ascertained that the works are up to the standard agreed upon between the parties. Some parts of such work may be wholly rejected and like bad debts in every earning may be ignored in computing the gains or profits. It might have been open to the ITO, in exercise of his discretion, to make an enquiry into whether and when the bills for payment became due to the assessee. Much depended upon the terms in the contract, and the manner of its performance. Even as a basis of guess work, which the Income-tax Officer was entitled to do, the basis could not be said to be in consonance with honest guess work. The ITO did not seem to have taken into consideration why the payments which, according to him, were due to the assessee in the accounting year were not fully paid till three years after. Sometimes the payments to the contractors are withheld on account of unsatisfactory execution and they are held entitled to payments only if and when they replace the rejected work by acceptable and accepted ones. The bare possibility of such contingency could not be wholly eliminated in the instant case. If the ITO, in arriving at the figure for assessment, left out these considerations, he certainly could not be said to have exercised his judgment which he was none the less called upon to do in making the assessment in cases of assessee's default under sections 23(4) and 13 proviso of the 1922 Act. Any method of accounting adopted by the ITO acting under the proviso of section 13 of 1922 Act can be rejected if the method in fact does not show the true income, profits and gains. In this view of the matter, the Appellate Tribunal was right in asking the ITO to assess the assessee on receipt basis with regard to contracts carried out and completed during the year of accounting, there being every presumption that the incomes were paid as soon as they became due. At any rate, the Tribunal's decision might be upheld on the ground that when two methods of guess work are available for the purpose of assessment, the one which is more just to the assessee and which involves a much less margin of chance of uncertainty should be taken as the basis.

In the result, the Tribunal was right in asking the ITO to assess the assessee on receipts basis with regard to contracts carried on and completed during the year of account.

As regards the reduction of flat rate, the Appellate Tribunal had arrived at the lesser flat rate on the basis of their decisions in similar cases in the district. Their opinions were not receivable evidence in the instant case. The decisions in different cases must have been based upon different facts and different inferences deducible from such facts. In this connection, it might be observed that the ITO had been very fair to the assessee bearing in mind the difference between the gross value and net value of the bills. The Appellate Tribunal, therefore, did commit a mistake of law in arriving at a finding for which there was no relevant evidence to support.

Therefore, the reduction of the estimated profit rate from 40 per cent adopted by the ITO to 30 per cent by the Tribunal on the ground that 30 per cent was the general rate adopted by it in the cases of other assessees doing the same kind of contract works during the same assessment year was not legal.

Note : The case was partially decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 3 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 2(11) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Previous year - Assessment year 1959-60 - In respect of a contract work for which no accounts were maintained till completion is for a period of 2 years and 8 months, ITO adopted 30th September as accounting year, for assessment year 1958-59, as was done by assessee in respect of other sources of income - Succeeding ITO however relying on section 2(11)(i) of 1922 Act, took year ending 31st March as previous year and apportioned profits between assessment years 1958-59 and 1959-60 - Whether words “previous year" ordinarily means a period from 1st April to 31st March but if assessee wants to adopt any other period, then his accounts must be made up for that period and if, those accounts are not made up for that period, he cannot ask for that period - Held, yes - Whether since accounts had not been made up for over a period of 2 years and 8 months, assessee could not adopt any other period than 1st April to 31st March - Held, yes - Whether, therefore adoption by ITO of accounting period from October to September for year of assessment 1958-59, could not be conclusive, nor could next ITO be barred from adopting correct accounting period in terms of section 2(11)(i)(a) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether questions about estimation of profit on gross amount instead of on net amount received by assessee after deduction of costs of material supplied by Government or about apportionment of profit to be made over a period of 4 years instead of 2 years, not having been raised at any stage of assessment proceedings, could not be gone into - Held, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 1959-60, the assessee, an individual contractor, having other sources of income also, had undertaken to complete the building contract work, the contract having been undertaken much earlier. The contract started on 1-1-1957 and was completed on 30-8-1959. Accounts maintained for this business were, however, closed only once i.e., when the contracts were completed; so much so, the profit from the contracts was ascertained for the entire period from 1-1-1957, to 30-8-1959, when the accounts were so closed and not periodically with reference to any previous year. For the assessment year 1-1-1957 to 30-8-1959, the ITO had adopted the previous year as the year ending with 30th September, because the assessee was maintaining accounts from October to September in respect of his other businesses, such as film exhibition business, medical stores, etc., and this was also the accounting period which he preferred for the earlier assessment year in respect of the contract business.

For the assessment year 1959-60, the succeeding ITO, however, adopted the accounting period ending on 31st March as the previous year, and apportioned the profits as between the two assessment years 1958-59 and 1959-60. He further estimated the profit on the gross amount and not on the net amount received by the assessee after deduction of costs of material supplied by the Government. On second appeal, the Tribunal upheld the ITO’s assessments.

On reference :

HELD: The adoption by the ITO of the previous year, October to September, for the assessment year 1958-59, was wrongly adopted, because it did not satisfy the requirements of section 2(11)(i)(a ). It was only in cases where the assessee could adopt a different period to the financial year, 1st April to 31st March, that any other period could be adopted, which would invariably mean a period of twelve months. This was also subject to the requirement of the section.

"Previous year" ordinarily means a period from 1st April to 31st March. But if the assessee wanted to adopt any other period, then his accounts must be made up for that period. If, however, those accounts were not made up for that period, he could not ask for that period. In the instant case, admittedly the accounts had not been made up for over a period of 2 years and 8 months, so that the assessee could not adopt any other period than 1st April to 31st March. In these circumstances, the adoption by the ITO of the accounting period from October to September for year of assessment 1958-59, could not be conclusive, nor could the next ITO be barred from adopting the correct accounting period in terms of section 2(11)(i )(a).

On further appeal by the revenue: HELD: In the instant case the assessee as sub-contractor to execute the civil construction works awarded by the principals, which was a small part of the projects executed by the principals. On the contract receipts, the principals had also deducted the tax under section 194C. Besides, the assessee was also engaged in the business of trading of sarees. It was also a fact that the assessee filed duly audited profit and loss account and balance sheet along with its annexure. It also produced the audited books of account, bills/vouchers and bank statements before the Assessing Officer as admitted by him in the assessment order. Besides, it further produced all the details and explanations called for by the Assessing Officer from time to time. It also produced labour registers before the Assessing Officer. However, he was of the opinion that the said registers had not been maintained in a conventional manner and according to him, there were no signatures or thumb impressions of all the recipients. Because of the aforesaid observations, the Assessing Officer rejected the audited books of account of the assessee and estimated the net profit. The Assessing Officer gave the examples of net profit earned by three companies and, thereafter, he relied on the provisions of section 11AD and estimated the net profit at the rate of 8 per cent of gross receipts. Now the assessee argued that the estimation of net profit at the rate of 8 per cent by relying on provisions of section 44AD was totally incorrect and without any basis for the reason that the assessee was sub-contractor and its profit margin was low in comparison to the contractors. Further, the Assessing officer had compared the profit of the assessee with the companies whose turnover and business paraphernalia was huge in comparison to the assessee. Further, the assessee had executed the part of work of civil construction for these companies and, therefore, it was not correct to compare the profit of those companies with the profit margin of the assessee. In fact the profit margin of those companies was also less than the margin which had been estimated by the Assessing Officer in the case of assessee. In the case of assessee as per audited books of account, the net profit margin for assessment years 2007-08, 2008-09, 2009-10 and 2010-11 was 1.94 per cent, 0.67 per cent, 0.20 per cent and 0.09 per cent respectively. Now, the assessee argued that the Assessing Officer had failed to appreciate that the profit margins of contractors and sub-contractors could not be same. In the assessment order he had worked out the average profit margins in the case of those three companies at 5.93 per cent, 6.15 per cent and 5.19 per cent respectively and in the case of assessee he had estimated the profit at the rate of 8 per cent, whereas, in the case of assessee the profit margin would be much less than in these companies being a sub-contractor of these companies. [Para 5]

In view of the above factual position and comparative figures given by assessee of its principal, wherein the net profit was ranging from 5.19 per cent to 6.15 per cent, it was held that definitely there would be lower profit in the case of sub-contractor, i.e., the assessee and, hence, the Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly estimated the net profit rate at 4 per cent. Accordingly, the order of Commissioner (Appeals) and this issue of revenue's appeal was dismissed. [Para 6]

FACT: The assessee was a works contractor, who in addition to the said income had income from a firm, house property and other sources.

The Commissioner (Appeals) though held that for the assessment year 1998-99, income declared at the rate of 9.08 per cent before depreciation and 8.5 per cent for the assessment year 1999-2000 as reasonable. However, he has given different finding for the assessment year 2001-02 and for the period from 1-4-2001 to 20-12-2001. The assessee explained the reasons for low profit as to that the company has been in the construction industry for more than two decades. The company for quite some years focused its core activity in civil works consisting of mostly industrial/housing structures. Besides such civil contracts, the company diversified its activities into cement industry, wind power, manufacture of cylinders and other incidental jobs. Heavy losses resulted in closure of its cement division during financial year 1999-2000. The company also started focusing on infrastructure projects because of its line of business in construction and contracts. Hence, in the initial years, the company had undertaken some of the smaller projects especially the road works outside the State of Andhra Pradesh. To intrude into the competitive section like this, and to withstand the obvious competition from the established giants and multinationals, obviously the company had to quote the price in tenders either without a profit or with nominal profit. During the financial years 2000-01 and 2001-02 (up to 31-12-2001) the company has incurred losses in certain major projects. [Para 39]

the contrary, as against the standard norm of 25 per cent labour charges amounting to Rs. 91.13 lakhs, the assessee had actually incurred only Rs. 75.37 lakhs, which worked out to be at 20.67 per cent. Income-tax provisions nowhere either authorize the Assessing Officer or cast an obligation on the assessee to prove the negative result, i.e., to prove as to why he had failed to make a profit at a particular rate. The accounts may be rejected as unreliable if important entries and transactions are omitted therefrom or if proper particulars and vouchers, bills, etc., are not forthcoming or if they do not include entries relating to particular class of business transaction. Reasons for rejecting wages record as commented by the Assessing Officer related to full address of the labour, which was not given on the muster roll register. The wages record had been kept by the assessee as per regulation known as 'Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970. The addresses of the labourers to whom wages had been paid were not mentioned, since the labourers stayed in the Jhugi Jhoperies at a work site itself and to that effect the assessee had already replied to the Assessing Officer vide its letter dated 23-3-2001, through which site of construction where labourers resided was given which was, however, not taken notice of by the Assessing Officer and the same was sent to him by courier and was found to be duly received by the Assessing Officer. The Assessing Officer had also alleged that the actual date of payment was not mentioned by the payee receiving the wages. The date on which the entry had been made in the wages register was the actual date of payment. As per the nature of the contract work executed by the assessee, he had got a contract to carry out a particular job or a contract for which the material was supplied by the CPWD/DOT and the labour was provided by the assessee-contractor. The assessee used to make payments to the labourers on the basis of mandays put in by the labourers and not on the basis of work performed by them on each day. Therefore, there was no merit in the allegations of the Assessing Officer that work performed by the labour was not mentioned on the payment vouchers and in making them as basis for rejection of books of account. The payment to the assessee-contractor was also made on the basis of work completed which was measured by the department itself and not on the basis of what the labourer had done. The bills for such a contract were prepared, which were not verified by the engineers of contractee before making payments. On the basis of those bills which were finally approved by the Government engineers/contractee, the payment was given to the assessee-contractor after deducting TDS. Thus, it was humanly not possible to provide the details as to what work a particular labourer had done at the site. Further, the Assessing Officer had also not indicated any defect in the system of accounting regularly followed by the assessee, or its correctness, nor was there any change in the method of accounting during the year under consideration as compared to the earlier years to indicate any intention of the assessee to show low profit.

While examining the books of the assessee, the Assessing Officer has to consider the following aspects : (i) whether the assessee has regularly employed a method of accounting; (ii) even if regular adoption of a method of accounting is there, whether the annual profits can properly be deduced from the method employed; (iii ) whether the accounts have been correctly maintained; (iv) whether the accounts maintained are complete in the sense that there is no significant omission therein. If the answers to above four questions would be in the affirmative, then the assessee's profits would be computed on the basis of his accounts. In such cases, proviso to section 145(1) or section 145(2) cannot be invoked. On the perusal of the materials placed on record in the instant case, it was found that the answers to all the above four questions were in the affirmative. No finding had been recorded by either of the lower authorities as to the unacceptability of the method and to the irregularity of the accounts kept by the assessee. It is well-settled that in the absence of such a finding recorded by the authorities, the book results cannot be ignored or brushed aside.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits Assessment year 1964-65 - Assessee was a military contractor - Finding some irregularities in accounts, ITO assessed profits of assessee from military contracts by applying flat rate of 10 per cent on total receipts - Tribunal held that price of stores supplied by Government was to be excluded while applying flat rate to assessee's contract receipts - Whether order passed by Tribunal was justified - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a military contractor. During the relevant accounting period, the assessee took three military engineering service contracts. The ITO found that the expenditure of the assessee was not supported by vouchers and he detected some other mistakes also in the accounts. After applying the provisions of section 145(1), the ITO assessed the profit from these contracts by applying a flat rate of 10 per cent on the total receipts. The AAC allowed the appeal of the assessee and held that no rate of profit could be applied on the value of the stores supplied by the Government and this order was upheld by the Tribunal.

On reference, the Division Bench noticed the divergent views taken by the various High Courts and particularly because of the challenge laid to the correctness of the judgment in Brij Bhushan Lal v. CIT [1971] 81 ITR 497 (Punj.) and, thus, referred the matter for decision of the Full Bench.

HELD: The Supreme Court in Brij Bhushan Lal Parduman Kumar v. CIT [1978] 115 ITR 524 (SC) reversed the said judgment of the High Court (supra) and held that the assessment was to be made excluding the cost of material and stores received for being used in the works undertaken by the contractor. Following, the aforesaid decision, it was to be held in the instant case that the Tribunal was justified in holding that price of stores supplied by Government was not to be included while applying the flat rate to the assessee's contract receipts.

Note : The decision was in favour of assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Rejection of accounts - Assessment years 1981-82 to 1983-84 - Assessee was engaged in construction of flats and since project was not complete, it claimed that no profit accrued during the construction period and that in case of a building contractor profits should not be assessed on year-to-year basis but at end of contract work - Assessing Officer held that method of accounting followed by assessee was defective and, consequently, by applying provisions of section 145 computed assessee’s business income at 8 per cent of receipts - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) upheld computation of business income - Whether in case of building contractor, profits should be assessed on year-to-year basis, and, thus, in absence of material to the contrary, profit at 8 per cent estimated by Assessing Officer was neither excessive nor unreasonable - Held, yes

Section 40A(8) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business disallowance - Interest payments - Assessment years 1981-82 to 1983-84 - Whether where business profits are estimated under section 145 they should be deemed to include disallowable interest under section 40A(8) - Held, no - Whether interest under section 40A(8) can be separately added even if the profit in the case of assessee has been estimated under section 145 - Held, yes

Section 5 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income - Accrual of - Assessment years 1981-82 to 1983-84 - Whether profit in a building contract accrues from year to year - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company had undertaken a project of construction of a multi-storeyed building. For the assessment years 1981-82 to 1983-84, it had realised certain amounts as the sale proceeds of a few flats. However, the assessee had filed ‘nil’ return for all the three years on the plea that in the case of a building contractor the profits should not be assessed on year-to-year basis and the ascertainment of the profit could be done only after the contract work was completed. The Assessing Officer, however, was of the view that the method of accounting followed by the assessee being defective and incomplete, did not lead to the correct computation of income. According to him, the assessee would put on credit side any amount in order to bring the profit to ‘nil’. The Assessing Officer accordingly applied the provisions of section 145 and computed the business income of the assessee at 8 per cent of the receipts. In addition, he disallowed the interest payment under the provisions of section 40A(8). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the determination of business income at 8 per cent, being reasonable. He,

however, deleted the addition in respect of interest payments on the ground that the business profit of the assessee had been estimated under section 145, and, therefore, such estimate should be deemed to include the disallowable interest under section 40A(8).

On cross-appeals:

HELD: The profit in a long-term contract should be taxed on year-to-year basis. It is a dangerous proposition to recognise that the profit accrues only after the completion of a contract, Such a proposition is liable to be abused by dishonest taxpayers. It is a judicially recognised proposition that in the case of a contract in order to ascertain the income one need not wait till the contract is completed and that it is open to the revenue to estimate the profit on the basis of receipts in each year of construction, although the contract is not complete.

HEADNOTE: Section 145, read with section 36(1)(iia) and section 32, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits - Assessment year 1992-93 - Assessee carried on contract business of construction of roads by obtaining contracts from Government departments - Books maintained by assessee were not verifiable - Assessee filed his return of income along with tax audit report under section 44AB - During assessment proceedings, assessee was asked to prove genuineness of transactions with various parties from whom raw material had been purchased - Assessee filed confirmation letters from parties but failed to produce them in person before Assessing Officer for verification - Assessing Officer rejected books of assessee and estimated profits - Assessing Officer also made disallowance on account of labour payments holding that payments were excessive and inflated - Further, Assessing Officer disallowed depreciation - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) held that assessee had not maintained verifiable accounts and he applied net profit rate of 10 per cent on receipt - He also granted depreciation after applying net profit rate - Whether in absence of verifiable accounts maintained by assessee, Assessing Officer should have examined past history of assessee and should have adopted net profit rate instead of making additions on account of purchases in raw materials - Held, yes - Whether since department itself had accepted net profit rate in case of same assessee in different years at 8 per cent to 8.25 per cent on receipt after deducting material and sales tax in past, looking to past history and comparable cases, it would be reasonable and appropriate if net profit rate of 8 per cent on receipts after deducting cost of material supplied by Government department was applied in instant case - Held, yes - Whether keeping in view past history of assessee in which depreciation was allowed, Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in allowing depreciation after applying net profit rate - Held, yes - Whether assessee was entitled to deduction of interest paid to third parties after applying net profit rate - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee carried on contract business of construction of roads by obtaining contracts from the Government departments. For the assessment year 1992-93, the assessee filed the return of income along with the tax audit report under section 44AB. It was accepted that the books maintained by the assessee were not verifiable. During the course of the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer asked the assessee to furnish the names and addresses of the parties and sundry creditors from whom raw material for construction of the roads had been purchased. The assessee furnished the addresses and the Assessing Officer issued letters of enquiry under section 133(6). However, the letters sent to 17 parties returned unserved to the Assessing Officer. The assessee was directed to prove the genuineness of the transactions made with the parties. The assessee filed copies of the accounts and copies of the confirmation letters stated to have been obtained from the parties before the Assessing Officer. However, the Assessing Officer did not agree with the confirmation letters as the letters sent to the parties had returned unserved. The assessee was asked to prove the genuineness of those parties but could not prove except filing confirmation letters from those parties. The Assessing Officer further pointed out that there might be standard specification but it was difficult to arrive at a definite conclusion in the absence of specific formula for construction of roads of various thickness and it was further observed that in the absence of details, general statement would not support any measurement and it was not possible to arrive at the exact consumption of raw material. He therefore, made certain additions to income of the assessee on that account.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits - Assessment years 1970-71 and 1971-72 - Assessee carried on business of undertaking public works contracts - It received cement, steel, bricks etc. from public works department - Its case before ITO was that since it had not earned any profits on value of materials received, no profit should be charged from it - ITO, however, estimated gross profit at five per cent on value of materials - On appeal Tribunal however, referred matter back to ITO with a view to examine tenders and find out as to whether assessee had calculated its profits on value of materials while submitting tenders - If that was so, ITO could estimate reasonable profit on such value - If, on other hand, it was seen that assessee had understanding with department that it would supply materials for execution of contracts and assessee adjusted its rate on that basis, profit on value of material supplied could not be estimated - Whether, on facts, order passed by Tribunal was correct - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm carried on business of undertaking contracts under the public works department authorities. For the relevant assessments year, it received certain amount on account of work done from the authorities concerned. Apart from the payments on account of work done, the assessee had also received cement, steel and bricks from the concerned department. The assessee’s case before the ITO was that since it had not earned any profit on the value of the materials received by it from the Government, no profit should be charged from it. That contention was not accepted by the ITO and he estimated the gross profit at five per cent on value of materials also. The assessee's appeals before the AAC on this question having failed, it took up the matter in further appeal before the Tribunal. The Tribunal referred the matter back to the ITO with a view to examine the tenders and find out as to whether the assessee had calculated its profit on the value of the materials while submitting the tenders and, if that was so, then estimate the reasonable profit on such value. If, on the other hand, it was found that the assessee was under an understanding that the department concerned would supply the required materials to it for the execution of those contracts and the assessee adjusted its rates on that basis, then there would not arise any occasion for estimating any profit on the value of the materials supplied. For that reason, the Tribunal remanded the case to the ITO.

On reference :

HELD: The view taken by the Tribunal was correct.

the observations, it was to be held that when the Assessing Officer offered to apply a net profit rate of more than 11 per cent, the assessee had only alternatively given a counter-proposal which, in fact, was not acted upon by the Department and as such, such an offer made thereof by the appellant was of no consequence and the same did not bind the assessee in any manner and, accordingly, it could not be validly held that the instant assessment was an agreed assessment. Having come to the conclusion that the proposal made by the assessee was not a binding proposal and as such not an agreed assessment, the next question for consideration was as to what could be the reasonable profit that could have been applied on the basis of material on record and the submissions of the parties. On that issue, the observations of the Accountant Member as well as the findings for arriving at the conclusion for application of profit rate of 8 per cent were contained in his order. The Bench fully agreed with the findings as well as the observations contained in the orders of the Accountant Member. As pointed out by the Accountant Member, the Assessing Officer himself had analysed each and every transaction with reference to the reply furnished by the assessee and he was of the firm opinion that the assessee could justify only a few transactions and the Assessing Officer, however, did not bring any material with respect to any remaining transactions with which he was not satisfied though admittedly the reply thereto was duly furnished by the assessee; that merely because some of the sub-contractors could not be produced at the relevant time could not lead to the conclusion of application of exorbitant rate of 11 per cent, that too without giving a finding that the expenditure so claimed was not for business necessity or that it did not relate wholly and exclusively for the purpose of business or the carrying on of business as required under section 37; and that, in fact, the Assessing Officer did ask the assessee through various queries to give explanation but he had not stated basis of its estimate nor given chance to the assessee to rebut basis for or the application of arriving at the precision rate of 11 per cent.

As observed by the Accountant Member, assessment is a quasi-judicial proceeding in which the personal will or rough estimation does not have any place, that the Assessing Officer is bound to disclose the mental process through which he arrived at a particular figure of income as his orders are being subjected to appeal and, therefore, should be speaking one. The Accountant Member observed that it was evident from the past history of the appellant that never a profit rate of more than 7 per cent was applied in the case of the appellant, more particularly when two of the past assessments had already been completed as a consequence of the search and incriminating documents as alleged in the year under appeal were also available with the Assessing Officer in those assessments; that keeping in view the peculiar circumstances like nature of business, expenses on public issue, etc., in the year under appeal, the assessee’s own history for the earlier years, over all facts, findings and circumstances of the case, suppression of profits having not been established, allegations having not been proved, explanation rendered by the appellant and the legislative history, that there was no justification in applying or confirming net profit rate of 11 per cent and that the ad-hoc application of 8 per cent net profit rate subject to allowability of depreciation and interest thereon in the case of the assessee was justified.

The department referred to the statement of ‘S’, in reply to a query as to what was the income of the company from the contract work usually. He replied that it was 10 per cent to 15 per cent to the total receipts. That statement was taken at the time of search without confronting ‘S’ with the books of account or any contract work specifically. The question posed to him was not in respect of the specific income of the year under consideration nor do the income from total contract work of the assessee. There was no clarification sought by the authorized officer or by the Assessing Officer as to the fact whether the said ‘S’ was stating so in respect of any of a single venture forming part of the one and individual business of the appellant comprised of several contract works secured by it, for which the assessee had maintained a combined profit and loss account or it was only a hypothetical calculation. The affidavit filed before the Assessing Officer of the same person was also not found false. The statement so given before the authorized officer was, thus, not a conclusive statement as the same was not based on any material on record but was only on approximation basis and not relevant to the facts of the case. The statement also did not quantify any correct rate as to whether it should be 10 per cent or 11 per cent or any higher rate. Thus, the statement so given by ‘S’ was of no credence and the same could not be used against the assessee for applying a profit rate of 11 per cent, which was not supported by any material or basis and was contrary to the facts of the case.

He thus rejected books of account under the provisions of section 145(3) and estimated net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts net of all deductions. In addition to estimation of net profit, the Assessing Officer made separate additions towards income from other sources being interest earned on fixed deposits.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal: HELD: The Assessing Officer has rejected books of account for the reason that the assessee has failed to produce necessary bills and vouchers in respect of expenditure. The Assessing Officer has observed that most of the expenditure are supported by self-made vouchers. Although, the assessee claims that it has produced bills and vouchers in respect of major expenditure, fails to substantiate the claim with necessary evidences. The assessee failed to controvert the findings of the Assessing Officer with any positive evidence to come to the conclusion that the books of account maintained by him gave a true and correct profit from the business. The Assessing Officer was therefore right in rejecting books of account under the provisions of section 145(3) of the Act. [Para 8]

Having said, one has to examine, on facts and circumstances of the case whether the Assessing Officer was right in adopting net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts. There is no dispute with regard to the facts that the assessee is in the business of execution of works contracts. It is also an admitted fact that the assessee had disclosed 6.73 per cent to 7.44 per cent net profit, in the earlier period. For the assessment year 2007-08 in the scrutiny assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer has estimated net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts for which the assessee has not preferred any appeal. Estimation of net profit from the business is one of the accepted method of determination of income from business. But, there is no hard and fast rule for estimation of income.

The department is following estimation of net profit on various rates depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case. But, while estimating net profit from the business, there should be a basis for adopting a particular rate of net profit, either based on comparable cases of similar nature of business or assessee's own book results for earlier years. When there is no possibility of getting a comparable cases, and there is no possibility of reference to assessee's own book results for earlier periods, a reference to the provisions of section 44AD can be made, wherein the Act provides for estimation of net profit from the specified businesses subject to certain conditions. [Para 9]

The provisions of section 44AD provide for estimation of net profit of 8 per cent on gross receipts, in case where the assessees are involved in specified businesses and turnover from the business does not exceed specified limit. Although, the assessee's case does not fall within the ambit of the provisions of section 44AD of the Act, as its contract receipts exceed the specified limit, the analogy provided in the provisions of section 44AD can be adopted for estimation of net profit because of nature of business carried out by the assessee. The nature of business carried on by the assessee was squarely fit into the specified businesses referred to in the provisions of section 44AD of the Act. The presumptive rate of net profit of 8 per cent incorporated in section 44AD, reflects the legislative approved rate of net profit, which can be considered as fair and reasonable to estimate income from civil contract business, where the books of account are not found reliable by the Assessing Officer.

In this case, admittedly, the Assessing Officer had rejected books of account for the reason that the assessee has failed to produce supporting bills and vouchers in respect of expenditure. It is also an admitted fact that the assessee himself has admitted about 8 per cent net profit in the earlier period net of all deductions including depreciation. Therefore, considering the overall facts and circumstances of the case, the rate of net profit adopted by the Assessing Officer appears to be fair and reasonable. Hence, estimation of net profit of 8 per cent on total receipts net of all deductions including depreciation is upheld. [Para 10]

In so far as separate deductions towards depreciation is concerned, the assessee submitted that when estimation of net profit is made, separate deductions towards depreciation should be allowed, as depreciation is a notional deduction for normal wear and tear of the assets.

In this case, the assessee is involved in the business of execution of main works which carries more profit than sub-contract works and hence, the Assessing Officer has rightly adopted reasonable net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts and accordingly, further deductions towards depreciation is not allowed. Whether separate deductions can be allowed towards depreciation or not is a fact which is to be decided based on the facts and circumstances of each case and also based on the rate of net profit adopted for estimation of profit.

HEADNOTE: Section 145, read with section 144, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Rejection of accounts - Assessment years 1993-94 to 1997-98 - Assessee-firm was engaged in work of civil construction in Public Works Department (PWD) - Assessing Officer, after rejecting books of account, made assessment determining 8 per cent profit at flat rate - Commissioner (Appeals) reduced rate of profit from 8 per cent to 5 per cent on ground that since turnover of assessee exceeded Rs. 40 lakhs, it was bound to incur more expenses and rate of profit would be less - Further, Tribunal reduced profit rate to 4 per cent on ground that assessee was doing work for PWD and normally, profit rate was much less for work of PWD, as contract work had to be done under certain specifications and under supervision of PWD authorities - Whether rate of profit cannot be assumed, merely on assumptions or surmises and conjectures - Held, yes - Whether since Assessing Officer as well as Commissioner (Appeals) as also Tribunal had not recorded any finding based on any material and findings recorded were merely based on surmises and conjectures, findings of rate of profit could not be sustained and 
 matter deserved to be remanded to assessing authority for re-determination thereof - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm which was engaged in the work of civil construction in public works department, filed returns for the assessment years 1993-94 to 1997-98. The Assessing Officer on the analogy of section 44AD, after rejecting the books of account, made best judgment assessment determining 8 per cent profit at flat rate. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) reduced the rate of profit from 8 per cent to 5 per cent, mainly on the ground that since the turnover of the assessee exceeded Rs. 40 lakhs, it was bound to incur more expenses and rate of profit would be less. On further appeal, the Tribunal reduced the rate of profit to 4 per cent on the ground that the assessee was doing the work for PWD and normally the net profit rate was much less for the work of PWD, as the contract work had to be done under certain specifications and under the supervision of the PWD authorities.

On appeal :

HELD: A bare perusal of the findings recorded by the Assessing Officer would indicate that he had applied the principles determining the profit vide section 44AD, whereas the aforesaid provision was not at all applicable in the case of assessee in the relevant assessment years. This factual position was not being disputed by either of the parties. That being so, the question arose as to what should be the profit rate for the purpose of determining the profit accrued or gained by the parties. Since the Assessing Officer, had not dealt with this question independent of section 44AD, the rate of profit could not be upheld. [Para 3]

So far as the determination of profit of 5 per cent by the Commissioner (Appeals) was concerned, the Commissioner (Appeals) had also not given any reason nor any material was placed before the Commissioner (Appeals), or for that matter before the Assessing Officer for arriving at a conclusion about the rate of profit. Merely on assumption that since the assessee was performing the work for the PWD and as the contract work had to be done under certain specifications and under supervision of the PWD authorities, the rate of profit would be low or merely because the turnover exceeded Rs. 10 lakhs, it would incur more expenses, the aforesaid rate of profits could not have been arrived at. Neither the Commissioner (Appeals) nor the Tribunal had taken into consideration the relevant material or facts which might be necessary for arriving at such a conclusion. [Para 4]

The rate of profit cannot be assumed merely on assumptions or surmises and conjectures. It is the first liability of the assessee to produce such records, evidence and material so as to substantiate his plea about the rate of profit that he claims and in case the books of account have been rejected , the onus shifts on to the Assessing Officer to determine the rate of profit on consideration of the material which may be brought before him or even on making such inquiry, which may be necessary and which may include the requirement of having any information from the assessee also during the course of determination of such rate of profit, namely, during the assessment proceedings. In no case, simply because the turnover was more than Rs. 40 lakhs or the assessee was performing civil construction work for Public Works Department, neither the rate of profits could be determined nor it could be taken to be less nor it could be reduced nor could be arrived at any presumptions. [Para 5]

-contractors totalling to Rs. 68,43,650. The Assessing Officer, therefore, treated the entire award amount as income of the assessee. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) sustained the rejection of accounts but adopted a different method of estimating the income by directing the Assessing Officer to adopt 8 per cent of the gross receipt as the income. On further appeal, by the department, the Tribunal confirmed the order passed by the first appellate authority.

On appeal : HELD: The main reason for rejecting the books of account was that the Assessing Officer, after considering the statements and depositions of the seven sub-contractors, was of the view that they were only name lenders. It was in the above circumstances that the claim of deduction of a sum of Rs. 68,43,650 was not allowed as deduction from the gross receipt. The Assessing Officer was also of the view that there was nothing to be deducted from the gross receipt of the sum of Rs. 87,51,092 received under the award of the arbitrator. It was in that view of the matter he had treated the entire sum of Rs. 87,51,092 as income of the assessee. The first appellate authority had adverted to the contentions of the assessee with reference to the payments made to the sub-contractors. However, the first appellate authority had taken the view that the instant case was at the most a case for rejection of the account and that if the accounts were rejected, the income had to be estimated. The first appellate authority was of the view that when the income was being estimated, there was no question of making separate additions. He therefore, after rejecting the books, had resorted to the estimation of the income on percentage basis. It was to be noted that the first appellate authority did not thereafter make any reference to the books of account and other documents relied upon by the assessee for the purpose of estimation of income. In other words, he had totally discarded the materials available in the form of books of account and other documents. He had resorted to the estimation on percentage basis. The first appellate authority was not justified in the facts of instant case to totally discard the books of account and other documents relied upon by the assessee in the matter of estimation of income. As held by the Supreme Court in CST v. Girja Shanker Awanish Kumar [1997] 104 STC 130, even after rejection of the books of account for technical and other reasons, it is for the Assessing Officer on the facts of each case to consider the materials disclosed to ascertain as to what extent the books of account can be relied upon for determination of the turnover. The Tribunal in the instant case had adverted to the findings of the Assessing Officer and the first appellate authority. However, the Tribunal did not consider aforesaid aspect of the matter even though it found it difficult to accept the case of the assessee regarding payment to the sub-contractors. The Tribunal had adverted to the award passed by the arbitrator and found that the amount awarded represented the value of the extra work done, which also represented interest at the rate of 12 per cent. The Tribunal was of the view that even if the additional work was not got done through sub-contractors, it might have been done by the assessee itself, which aspect had not been considered. The Tribunal, however, observed that it was not possible to say that the entire amount of award was a profit to the assessee and taxable as contended by the department. In such circumstances, it was for the Tribunal to remit the matter to the Assessing Officer or at any rate to the first appellate authority to consider the matter afresh. However, the Tribunal had agreed with the first appellate authority that the instant case was a case which called for estimation of the profit on percentage basis. No reason was, however, stated by the Tribunal for justifying the estimate made on profit basis. Apart from the general observations made by the Tribunal on the merits of the matter, there was no due consideration of the case of the assessee or of the department in regard to the acceptance of the books of account or the estimation of the income with reference to all the materials available on record including the books of account and documents. [Para 5]

The first appellate authority, without considering the case of the assessee, based on the books of account and other records, had straightaway thought that it was a fit case for estimation of profit on percentage basis. In the facts of the instant case, the first appellate authority was not justified in adopting such a course. The Tribunal had also committed the mistake in approving the estimation of income adopted by the first appellate authority. In such circumstances the question of estimation of income from the contract receipt was a matter to be considered by the Assessing Officer himself in accordance with law in the light of the observations made in the instant judgment. [Para 6]

HEADNOTE: Section 145, read with section 143 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 13, read with section 23 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits - Assessment years 1945-46 and 1946-47 - Whether in case to which proviso to section 13 of 1922 Act applies, Income-tax Officer is bound to disclose in his order basis and manner of computation of income, gains or profits and to disclose data on which he arrives at result - Held, yes - Whether if assessee fails to satisfy Income-tax Officer as to correctness of percentage of profits returned by him, it is open to Income-tax Officer to take higher percentage consistent with state of trade in locality or with any special circumstances of assessee which warrant higher rate of profits - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was carrying on business in cloth and yarn. The method of accounting employed by the assessee was such that, income, profits and gains could not be properly deduced therefrom. The ITO accordingly applied the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act and determined the profits for the assessment years 1941-42 and onwards under this proviso. The Income-tax Officer had not informed the assessee how he was going to compute the assessee’s income from his business. The Tribunal concluded that once an assessee’s books of accounts are rejected, the best that the ITO can do is to make a reasonable estimate, having regard to all the circumstances of the case.

On reference :

HELD: The proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act does not entitle the Income-tax Officer to have a leap in the dark but requires him to compute the income ‘upon such basis and in such manner as the Income-tax Officer may determine.’ He has therefore to find out ‘the basis and the manner of computation’. The assessment is under section 23(3) of the 1922 Act after hearing such evidence as the assessee may produce and such other evidence as the Income-tax Officer may require on specified points. The Income-tax Officer may use material not placed before him by the assessee; but in such a case natural justice demands that he should give the assessee an opportunity of showing, if he can, that the material is incorrect, though the officer is not bound to disclose the source of his information. It may be that there is an adequate explanation against the information sought to be used against the assessee or that the Income-tax Officer might be misinformed. Although there is no express provision in the Act to require the Income-tax Officer to make such disclosure, it is necessary on the principles of natural justice.

The order is appealable and must stand scrutiny by an appellate court. It must, therefore, be a speaking order. If the basis and manner of computation are not disclosed in the order, the assessee’s right of appeal may be illusory unless the appellate authority refers the matter back to the Income-tax Officer to disclose the basis and manner of his computation. If the profits are computed under this proviso upon a basis determined by the Income-tax Officer, profits included in such computation cannot be included again in the assessment for any subsequent year. The burden is on the assessee to prove that the profits sought to be assessed were included in the assessment for any preceding year. This burden cannot be adequately discharged unless the assessment orders disclose the basis and manner of computation. If after rejecting the method of accounting employed by the assessee, the Income-tax Officer were simply to add a particular amount to the income returned or to disallow a part of the business expenses properly incurred by the assessee and allowable under section 10 of the 1922 Act, he would not be acting under the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act. The Income-tax Officer would be acting contrary to law if he were to disallow such business expenses or make an addition of a lump sum simply on the ground that the trading profits cannot be properly determined from the books of account. The Income-tax Officer is not entitled to discard the evidence of the books of account altogether merely because the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act is attracted.

It is certainly not a "leap in the dark". The Income-tax Officer is not entitled to make a guess without evidence.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits - Assessment year 1984-85 - Assessee-firm was carrying on construction business - During period relevant to assessment year under consideration, it had taken a contract for construction of hotel building - Assessee contended that it was only on completion of project that profitability 
 or otherwise of contract could be judged - Assessing authority, however, found that there was no day-to-day maintenance of accounts and, therefore, concluded that profit from return could not be ascertained and, accordingly, estimated profit at 8 per cent of gross receipts which was reduced to 5 per cent by Commissioner (Appeals) - Whether in absence of properly maintained accounts, authorities were bound to follow accepted method of calculating profits on yearly basis and ‘project-completion-method’ was inapplicable - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm was in the business of building and construction. During the year relevant to the assessment year under consideration, there were some small contracts which were completed more or less in a year and there was a big contract which was to continue for many years. During assessment proceedings, the assessing authority found that there was no day-to-day maintenance of accounts and, therefore, he came to the conclusion that the profits from the return could not be ascertained and, accordingly, estimated the profit. In appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the assessee’s contention that it was only on the completion of the contracts that profitability or otherwise of the same could be judged. He directed the assessing authority that in respect of the said big contract, the profit be assessed on ad hoc basis at 5 per cent of gross receipts. On further appeal, the Tribunal disapproved the Commissioner (Appeals)’s order and directed the assessing authority to determine the profit only on the year of completion of the project.

On reference :

HELD: There were no proper contract accounts whatsoever. Therefore, there was no way in knowing as to what were the receipts and the spendings on the part of the assessee. Therefore, if the Commissioner (Appeals) adopted the method of yearly accounting in pursuance of his powers under section 144, then there was nothing wrong. The Tribunal had clearly gone wrong in ignoring the fact that there was no accounting at all and the method suggested by it could stand justified only if there were proper accounts maintained by the assessee. In the absence of properly maintained accounts, the authorities were bound to follow the accepted method of calculating the profits on yearly basis, which the appellate authority had done. The order of the appellate authority was a correct order and the order of the Tribunal holding to the contrary and introducing method of calculating profits only after the completion of the contract was not correct.

HEADNOTE: Section 147 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income escaping assessment - In formation - Position prior to 1-4-1989 - Assessment year 1970-71 - Whether an audit note can be a source of information - Held, yes - ITO having noted that assessee had not maintained quantity stock register and other relevant registers, estimated income by considering profits made in earlier assessment years - subsequently, ITO received an audit note which pointed out that account books of assessee disclosed more profit than estimated by ITO - On basis of said information ITO reopened assessment and estimated gross profit at higher rate - Whether on facts, reopening of assessment on basis of audit note was valid - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a building contractor. It had entered into certain contracts in 1966 and also in 1970 respectively. The 1966 contracts were described as old contracts and the 1970 contracts as new contracts. It had filed a consolidated trading account and profit and loss account disclosing gross profit at 10.2 per cent. The ITO noticed that the assessee had not maintained quantity stock register and other relevant registers and a work-in-progress account which would have enabled him to verify the correctness of the book result and, therefore, decided to estimate the income by considering the profits made in earlier assessment years. He noticed that the assessee itself in the previous year had disclosed gross profits at the rate of 15.4 per cent. The ITO, therefore, after considering the explanation of the assessee that the old contracts were in the last stages of completion, assessed the gross profit in respect of the old contracts at 12 per cent, and at the rate of 15 per cent in respect of the new contracts. The assessee did not prefer any appeal. Thereafter, the ITO received an audit note wherein it was pointed out that in respect of the one of the old contract, the account books of the assessee disclosed a profit of 14.5 per cent. On the basis of the said information, the ITO reopened the assessment under section 147(b) and computed the gross profit in respect of that contract at 15 per cent. The AAC allowed the assessee’s appeal and annulled the order of assessment. But the Tribunal held that the reopening of the assessment was valid.

On reference :

HELD: It was no doubt true that the account books of the assessee were before the ITO when he made the original assessment. But, the ITO doubted the correctness of the accounts maintained by the assessee and, therefore, without adopting the account books as the basis, he estimated the profit on the basis of the margin of profits normally earned by persons in such types of business and the rate of profit earned by the assessee in the previous year. Thus, the ITO had not considered this material while estimating the profit of the old contracts at 12 per cent. Since the ITO had not considered the said material, it had not come to his notice that the account books of the assessee showed that in respect of the one of the old contract, the assessee had earned profit at the rate of 14.5 per cent. That an audit note can be a source of information is no longer in dispute now.

The relevant material in the shape of book result was not considered by the ITO on the ground that the books of account were not properly maintained by the assessee. Thus, this was not a case where it could be said that the ITO had considered the material while making the original assessment. This was a case where the ITO had not considered the said material and only subsequently he came to know about that material when his attention in that behalf was drawn by the audit note. Thus, this case would squarely fall within the scope of section 147(b).

The reopening of the assessment under section 147(b ) was thus valid.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 145, read with section 256 of the Income-tax Act 1961 - Method of accounting - Rejection of accounts - Assessment years 1967-68 to 1969-70 - ITO rejected assassee's accounts and applied flat rate of profit - Tribunal found that neither ITO nor AAC had tried to examine details of expenses claimed by assessee - Tribunal further noticed that none of expenses claimed by assessee was inadmissible and accordingly, directed AAC to accept trading result disclosed by assessee - Whether, on facts, no question of law arose from Tribunal's order - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee undertook execution of contracts and a large proportion of its work was executed through sub-contractors. The ITO rejected accounts of the assessee and completed the assessment by calculating the assessee’s income at flat rate. The AAC gave some relief to the assessee. On second appeal, the Tribunal found that the expenses related to materials, wages, labour organisation, transport charges, stores, water charges, freight and demurrage, electric charges, etc. and these were prima facie allowable expenditure against the receipts disclosed by the assessee. Neither the ITO nor the AAC had tried to examine the details of expenses claimed by the assessee and found that any of the items of expenditure were either not genuine or inadmissible.

The Tribunal therefore, held that the expenditure claimed as per books of account should have been allowed and there was no justification for resorting to estimate when the AAC had admitted the fact that the assessee having had the necessity to maintain establishment for various activities enumarated in his order. Accordingly the Tribunal directed acceptance of trading results disclosed by the assessee including the expenses claimed by it and delete the additions sustained in each of the years.

On application under section 256(2).

HELD: The Tribunal concluded as a fact that the assessee's claim for acceptance was acceptable and the book result should not have been disturbed. Upon these findings of pure fact, no question of law arose.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

A. Pasayat for the Respondent.

HEADNOTE: Section 28 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Assessee, carrying contract work under government departments, did not maintain proper account books - Whether net profit could be estimated at a flat rate on gross receipts including value of material supplied by government - Held, on facts, yes

FACT: The assessee, a firm of contractors, executed certain contracts given by the State Government during the assessment years 1972-73 and 1973-74. For the assessment years 1972-73 and 1973-74, the total gross receipts under the work contract respectively amounted to Rs. 19,41,472 and Rs. 22,86,353 out of which a sum of Rs. 1,27,215 and Rs. 4,82,527 was deducted, being the value of materials supplied by the Government. Since the assessee did not maintain proper account books or any stock book or material issue register, the ITO determined the net profit under the proviso to section 145(1) by applying a flat rate of 10 per cent on the aforesaid gross receipts without excluding the value of the materials supplied by the Government. The AAC, however, directed that for determining the net profit, flat rate was to be applied only on the net receipts. The Tribunal could not ascertain: (i) the actual position regarding the materials obtained from the department and; (ii) whether the same remained under the control of the department or of the assessee. It, accordingly, restored the ITO's order.

On reference:

HELD: 1. No hard and fast rule could be laid down as to whether the value of the materials should or should not be included in a contractor's gross turnover from business for determining his net profits. It depended upon the manner in which the materials were obtained and used in the execution of the contract. The contracts could be generally classified as (i) contract for labour supply; (ii) a lump sum contract; and (iii) where the material supplied by the department was either an outright sale or was specifically meant to be used in the work allotted. In the types of contracts mentioned in (i) and (iii), the profit had to be calculated on the gross receipts, including the value of the material supplied either by the Government or by the assessee. Whereas, in the case of the other items at (ii) and (iii), profit would be determined en the basis of only the net amount without taking into consideration the value of the materials. In the instant case, in the absence of any stock register or issue register, it was not known whether the materials were supplied by the department as an outright sale to the assessee or it remained under the control of the department throughout and that the same was never under the control of the contractor except for using it in the constitution.

2. The Tribunal was, accordingly, correct in holding that the profit was to be calculated on the gross receipts excluding the recoveries for the material supplied by the Government department.

Kashi Nath Jain, Rameshwar Prasad and A.B. Prasad for the Petitioner. B.P. Rajgarhia and S.K. Sharan for the Respondent.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961- Method of accounting - Estimation of profits - Assessment years 1985-86 to 1988-89. Assessee was engaged in construction work - It took a huge project in 1980 which had to take several years to complete . It adopted ‘Project Completion Method’ as its method of accounting and contended that it should be treated to have earned no profits till assessment year 1985-86. During a search on 11-5-1987 department found some incriminating materials - Assessee declared unaccounted profit of Rs. 66 lakhs as ‘on money’ and wanted that Rs. 26 lakhs should be assessed in assessment year 1987-88 and Rs. 40 lakhs in assessment year 1988-89 - Two employees of assessee deposed that it was charging 30 to 40 per cent ‘on money’ and one of directors stated that it was charging 15 to 20 per cent ‘on money’- Because of unaccounted ‘on money’ Assessing Officer concluded that accounts were not properly kept so that income could be properly deduced therefrom and, therefore, rejected method of account followed by assessee.
