He worked out ‘on money’ receipts on basis of statements of employees and version of director - He also applied rate of profit at 25 per cent on total receipts and allocated profits in different years - Whether Assessing Officer had rightly rejected method followed by assessee and assessed income in each assessment year by application of provisions of section 145(2) - Held, yes Whether rate of profit at 25 per cent was correctly applied on total receipts and not on receipts after deducting profits - Held, yes - Whether Assessing Officer was justified in rejecting assessee’s version that ‘on money’ was received only in last two assessment years and, therefore, was justified in spreading it in all assessment years under consideration and preceding years - Held, yes

) cannot be invoked. On the perusal of the materials placed on record in the instant case, it was found that the answers to all the above four questions were in the affirmative. No finding had been recorded by either of the lower authorities as to the unacceptability of the method and to the irregularity of the accounts kept by the assessee. It is well-settled that in the absence of such a finding recorded by the authorities, the book results cannot be ignored or brushed aside. In the instant case, the assessee had been regularly maintaining the percentage of profit between 1 per cent to 2 per cent. Such profit had actually been worked out at higher figure, if one took only labour charges as a contract receipt insofar as the material was supplied by the Government, on which there was no question of any profit being earned by the assessee. From the record, it was also found that out of total contract receipts of Rs. 3.64 crores, the material used, supplied by the Government amounted to Rs. 1,60,35,409 as per the certificate of chartered accountant placed on the record. There was no question of any profit being earned by the assessee on the amount of Rs. 1.60 crores of materials being supplied by the Government/'contractee' to the assessee-firm for being used in the contract assigned to the assessee by the Government departments. It was also not the case of the Assessing Officer that any part of the contract receipt had not been entered in the books of account or that the assessee had accounted for expenses more than what had actually been incurred.

In view of the above facts and circumstances of the case and the materials placed on record there was no valid reason and justification for rejection of audited books of account and the method of accounting regularly and consistently followed by the assessee for accounting for the contract receipts. Thus, there was no justification in estimating the profit at 8 per cent by disregarding the book results.

HEADNOTE: Section 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Rejection of accounts (Estimation of profit) - Assessment year 2014-15 - Assessee was engaged as civil contractor - Assessing Officer being not satisfied with explanation of assessee regarding decline in net profit rejected account books and estimated net profit at rate of 10 per cent of turnover - Whether in light of various defects/deficiencies/irregularities along with assessee’s evasive approach towards explanation sought by Assessing Officer, allegation that rejection of books was done in arbitrary manner did not hold any ground and, thus, rejection of books of account was justified - Held, yes - Whether however, in absence of any comparative instances of similar assessees in same line of business, it was appropriate to estimate profit at a percentage worked out on basis of preceding three years profit of assessee herself - Held, yes [Paras 10 and 12] [Partly in favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where explanation of assessee-contractor regarding decline in net profit was evasive and there were various defects in books of account of assessee, rejection of books of account was proper; however, in absence of any comparative instances of similar assessees in same line of business, it was appropriate to estimate profit at a percentage worked out on basis of preceding three years profit of assessee herself

Section 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Rejection of accounts (Estimation of profit) - Assessment year 2014-15 - Assessee was engaged as civil contractor - Assessing Officer being not satisfied with explanation of assessee regarding decline in net profit rejected account books and estimated net profit at rate of 10 per cent of turnover - Whether in light of various defects/deficiencies/irregularities along with assessee’s evasive approach towards explanation sought by Assessing Officer, allegation that rejection of books was done in arbitrary manner did not hold any ground and, thus, rejection of books of account was justified - Held, yes - Whether however, in absence of any comparative instances of similar assessees in same line of business, it was appropriate to estimate profit at a percentage worked out on basis of preceding three years profit of assessee herself - Held, yes [Paras 10 and 12] [Partly in favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee was engaged as civil contractor.

■

The Assessing Officer being not satisfied with the explanation of the assessee regarding decline in gross profit and net profit rejected the account books by invoking the provisions of section 145(3) and estimated the net profit at the rate of 10 per cent of the turnover before allowing interest expenses and depreciation.

■

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the action of the Assessing Officer rejecting account books and scaled down the estimation of net profit to 6 per cent.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal :

HELD: ■

On a perusal of the assessment order, it is observed that while rejecting the books of account the Assessing Officer had pointed out defects in the books of account of the assessee, which are again thoroughly discussed by the Commissioner (Appeals). The issue regarding rejection of books of account has been dealt and deliberated by the Commissioner (Appeals) at length and has noted that in light of various defects/deficiencies/irregularities along with assessee’s evasive approach towards explanation sought by the Assessing Officer, the allegation that the rejection of books was done in arbitrary manner does not hold any ground. Such observations of the Commissioner (Appeals) are worth accepting for the reason that in absence of requisite details of non-maintenance of certain prescribed records necessary to find out the true and fair picture of the books of account, it is not possible for the Assessing Officer to work out the correct profit of the assessee. Accordingly the rejection of books under section 145(3) on account of dissatisfaction of the Assessing Officer was justified, which has led the Assessing Officer to estimate the profit of the assessee. [Para 10]

■

Apropos ground regarding estimation of profit by the Assessing Officer at 10 per cent before allowing interest and depreciation, which was scaled down by the Commissioner (Appeals) to 6 per cent, the Bench finds force in the contention of the assessee that the estimation should be on a logical basis, might be on the basis of comparable instances and in case no comparable instances available then the best ratio to be adopted should be the past performance of the assessee itself. [Para 11]

■

the account books could not be relied upon, he came to the conclusion that the assessee's income could be determined only on the basis of the income made by similar businessmen. Therefore, on the basis of independent enquiries made by him, he was of opinion that in the year under account manufacturers of dyed and printed cloth made bumper profits going up to 50 per cent accordingly the ITO assessed the assessee. On appeals both AAC and the Tribunal confirmed the order of ITO.

On reference : HELD: The proviso to section 13 empowers the ITO to assess the profits on such basis and in such manner as he thinks proper where he comes to the conclusion that the income and profits could not be properly deduced from the accounts of the assessee. But it has to be observed that the power of the ITO under this proviso is not an arbitrary power. He must exercise his discretion and judgment judicially and reasonably. Further, if the ITO proposes to use against the assessee the result of any private enquiry made by him, he should put him in possession of the full particulars and gave him an opportunity to meet the same. Although the assessing authority, having had no other means of arriving at the correct amount of profit by reason for the accounts, of the assessee being unsatisfactory, could have recourse to the method of independent enquiries about profits made by like concerns doing similar business, he cannot come to his own conclusions without affording an opportunity to the assessee to be able to satisfy the income-tax authorities that the cases relied upon by him were not comparable cases and were distinguishable on various grounds. The ITO cannot be said to make an assessment to the best of his judgment if he is not guided by the dictates of justice and fair-play. Natural justice demands that he should draw the attention of the assessee to the particular cases the authority had in view. The income-tax authority is not competent to make a random assessment based on his private enquiries which may not be revealed to the assessee. Local enquiry and the placing on record a note of the results of such enquiry are essential to sustain an ex-parte assessment. If the ITO proposes to act upon information collected by him independently on private enquiries, he should disclose to the assessee the nature of that information to rebut it. There ought to be an opportunity to the assessee to displace the Taxing Officer's estimate by adducing evidence. In the instant case, it was not shown that any attempt was made by the ITO to draw the attention of the assessee to the material collected by him on private enquiry and which formed the basis for his conclusions. He merely felt content on the circumstance that in the year of account the manufactures of dyed and printed cloth like the assessee made bumber profits shooting up to 50 per cent and over. It was all the more necessary in a business of the kind that the assessee firm was doing that the information gathered with regard to other manufacturers should have been placed before the assessee, because in a business of this kind there could be no two truly comparable cases. The assessee's business consisted of (a) buying mill cloth and selling it in the market as cloth, (b) buying handloom cloth, getting it dyed and printed in his own karkhana and selling them same, and (c) buying mill cloth and handloom cloth and getting it dyed and printed elsewhere and selling final dyed and printed cloth in the market.

The profit in business (a) was bound to be different from the profit made in business (b), likewise the percentage of the profit in business (c) could not be the same in business (d). These factors had necessarily to be taken into consideration in arriving at the amount of profit. There could not be a rule of thumb in these matters. The Tribunal seemed to have taken it for granted that the assessee would have made as such profit as the others, because of the boom period, without going into the matter as to whether such profit could be made in the particular variety of business undertaken by the assessee.

The result was that the order of the Tribunal was set aside and the case was remanded to it with the direction to disclose the material gathered from private enquiries to the assessee and give full opportunity to the assessee to place any relevant material to meet the substance of the private enquiry.

Note : [Case remanded]

by assessee and assessed income in each assessment year by application of provisions of section 145(2) - Held, yes Whether rate of profit at 25 per cent was correctly applied on total receipts and not on receipts after deducting profits - Held, yes - Whether Assessing Officer was justified in rejecting assessee’s version that ‘on money’ was received only in last two assessment years and, therefore, was justified in spreading it in all assessment years under consideration and preceding years - Held, yes FACT: The assessee, engaged in construction work, had started a project for construction of 30 buildings in 1980 which was to take several years for completion. Hence, it adopted ‘Project Completion Method’ as its method of accounting. According to this method the profits could be worked out only when the project was complete or at least substantially complete. Therefore, for the assessment year 1981-82, the assessee filed its return at nil income, which was accepted. However, similar returns were not accepted for the assessment years 1982-83 to 1985-86, and the Assessing Officer estimated the income by applying the profit rate at 10 per cent to 15 per cent. There was a search in the premises of the assessee on 11-5-1987 where some incriminating materials were found. The assessee declared unaccounted profit of Rs. 66 lakhs as ‘on money’ sought to be assessed in assessment years 1987-88 and 1988-89. On the basis of that, the assessment for the assessment year 1985-86 was completed where the Assessing Officer, besides making estimate of profit at the rate of 15 per cent, made a separate addition of Rs. 73,19,200 pursuant to offer of the assessee of taxing Rs. 66 lakhs as ‘on money’ receipts which were stated to have been entered in the books of account for assessment years 1987-88 and 1988-89. On appeal, the addition of estimated profit was deleted by the Commissioner (Appeals) but the addition of Rs. 73,19,200 was set aside. For the assessment year 1986-87, the assessment was completed at Rs. 55,11,859 against returned income of Rs. 7,96,450. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the assessment and directed to complete it afresh. However, in spite of repeated notices for hearing, no compliance was made and thus, the Assessing Officer completed the assessment again taking into account (i) the quantum of ‘on money’ received by the assessee, and (ii) the year in which that ‘on money’ should be taxed. For dealing with these issues, the Assessing Officer took into account the statement of ‘J’, one of the directors of the assessee-company who had stated that the assessee had been charging 15 per cent to 20 per cent ‘on money’ and no ‘on money’ was charged from institutions like BML, Dena Bank and some educational trusts. He also took into account the statements of one M, accountant, and ‘S’, supervisor, of the assessee recorded during the course of search, wherein the ‘on money’ charged was stated to be 30 per cent to 40 per cent. The above statements were taken in the presence of independent Panchas at the time of search, who had certified that no untoward incident had taken place during the course of search. Therefore, the assessee’s plea that those persons had retracted from their statements as they were stated to have been recorded under threat or duress, was rejected by the Assessing Officer. The Assessing Officer also took into account statement on oath of one ‘I’ who had deposed to the effect that he had paid 40 per cent as ‘on money’ on the shop purchased by him from the assessee in 1983. On the basis of these evidence, the Assessing Officer estimated that ‘on money’ received by the assessee could be 25 per cent of the total consideration received. The Assessing Officer, therefore, estimated ‘on money’ at Rs. 1,25,78,000 for the assessment years 1981-82 to 1988-89 against which the assessee had offered for taxation Rs. 26 lakhs in the assessment year 1987-88 and Rs. 40 lakhs in the assessment year 1988-89. The AO held that ‘on money’ was unaccounted receipt, that there was no provision in law to assess unaccounted money arbitrarily in two years only, that the contention of the assessee that it had been following project completion method of ac-counting was not correct and added Rs. 25,42,000 in the assessment year 1986-87. For the assessment year 1987-88, the assessee had filed its return of income declaring total income at Rs. 28,87,260. The assessment was completed by the Assessing Officer on a total income of Rs. 29,80,712. For the assessment year 1988-89, the assessee filed its return of income at Rs. 35,82,987 after taking into account the ‘on money’ of Rs. 40 lakhs offered to be assessed this year

HEADNOTE: Section 145, read with section 28(i), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Work contracts - Whether in case of contractor before estimating profits it has to be determined whether control of materials supplied by Government was with assessee or with Government - Held, yes

FACT: During the previous year relevant to the assessment year in question, the assessee-firm was paid certain amount towards the works executed on contract for one H. The AAC divided the amount paid to the assessee under two categories. First was the value of materials supplied by H to the assessee. In the balance amount, the AAC had taken 12½ per cent as profit of the assessee. In regard to the value of materials supplied by H, the AAC assessed profit at the rate of 5 per cent. The Tribunal upheld the AAC's order.

On reference :

HELD: It was held by this Court in Ramesh Chandra Chaturvedi v. CIT [1980] 121 ITR 116 that there could not be any hard and fast rule to determine the question as to whether the value of the materials should or should not be added to the gross turnover of the assessee, who is a contractor, for determining his net profits. It all depends upon manner in which the materials has to be used in the execution of the contract. Thus, although the contract document might be showing that the materials always remained the property of the department, yet in actual practice it might not be so and, therefore, the department has to consider whether as a fact the contractor has control over the materials or the department has the control. The matter has to be examined in that light. The matter was, therefore, remanded back to the Tribunal to reconsider and decide in the light of the above principle.

HEADNOTE: Section 145,  read with section 44AD, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (Gross profit rate) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Assessee was engaged in business of execution of civil works contract - He filed his return of income for relevant assessment year declaring certain taxable income - In course of assessment, Assessing Officer noted that assessee had kept self-made vouchers in support of major expenditure and, accordingly, opined that books of account maintained by assessee were not amenable for verification - He thus rejected books of account under provisions of section 145(3) and estimated net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts net of all deductions - Whether since assessee failed to controvert findings of Assessing Officer with any positive evidence to come to conclusion that books of account maintained by him gave a true and correct profit from business, Assessing Officer was right in rejecting books of account - Held, yes - Whether as regards rate of profit, since assessee had disclosed 6.73 per cent to 7.44 per cent net profit in earlier period, impugned estimation made by Assessing Officer was justified - Held, yes - Whether even otherwise, since nature of business carried on by assessee was squarely fit into specified business referred to in provisions of section 44AD, estimation of net profit at rate of 8 per cent of gross receipts specified in said section was rightly adopted - Held, yes [Paras 8, 9 and 10] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where assessee had kept self-made vouchers in support of major expenditure and books of account maintained by him did not give true and correct profit from business, Assessing Officer was justified in rejecting said books of account and estimating net profit of 8 per cent of gross receipts  IT : Where Assessing Officer had adopted reasonable rate of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts, further deduction towards depreciation could not be allowed as it would result into determination of total income below income returned by assessee   IT : Where there was no nexus between interest receipts and works contracts executed by assessee, interest on fixed deposits was separately assessable under head 'Income from other sources'

Section 32 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Depreciation - Allowance/Rate of (In case of estimated income) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether in view of facts stated under heading 'Method of accounting - Estimation of income', since Assessing Officer had adopted reasonable rate of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts, further deductions towards depreciation could not be allowed as it would result into determination of total income below income returned by assessee - Held, yes [Para 11] [In favour of revenue]

Section 56 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income from other sources - Chargeable as (Interest) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Whether in view of facts stated under heading 'Method of accounting - Estimation of income', since there was no nexus between interest receipts and works contracts executed by assessee, interest on fixed deposits was separately assessable under head 'Income from other sources' - Held, yes [Para 14] [In favour of revenue]

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the business of execution of civil works contract. He filed his return of income for the relevant assessment years declaring certain taxable income.

During the course of assessment proceedings, on verification of books of account and other details filed by the assessee, the Assessing Officer noticed that most of the expenditure in respect of labour charges, work expenses, mess charges and other indirect expenses were not supported by proper bills and vouchers. The Assessing Officer further observed that the assessee had kept self-made vouchers in support of major expenditure and, accordingly, opined that the books of account maintained by the assessee were not amenable for verification.

He thus rejected books of account under the provisions of section 145(3) and estimated net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts net of all deductions. In addition to estimation of net profit, the Assessing Officer made separate additions towards income from other sources being interest earned on fixed deposits.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal:

HEADNOTE: I. Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit (Net profit rate) - Assessment years 2012-13 to 2014-15 - Assessing Officer disallowed total expenses claimed in profit and loss account and sale consideration from immovable property and passed an ex parte order under section 144 - Commissioner (Appeals) based on his observation that purchase made by assessee in past were in dispute and genuineness of same had not been proved, computed net profit applying rate of 8 per cent on total revenue - However, it was found that net profit rate of 0.4 per cent had been accepted by this Tribunal in one of sister concern of assessee and even in scrutiny proceedings, revenue authorities in assessee's own case had estimated net profit below rate of 1 per cent - Whether therefore, looking to fact that there was no change of business during all these years, books of account were duly audited and no specific error had been pointed out by both lower authorities, estimating net profit at rate of 8 per cent could not be justified - Held, yes - Whether thus, application of net profit rate of 0.6 per cent on turnover of contract business during year would be proper - Held, yes [Paras 9.3 and 9.5] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where revenue authorities in assessee's own case in earlier year had estimated net profit below rate of 1 per cent, there being no change of business during relevant assessment years, estimating net profit at rate of 8 per cent could not be justified  INCOME TAX : Where business of earning commission from purchase and sale of land was being consistently carried out by assessee in previous year also and same was regularly entered in books of account and commission income earned from such transactions had been duly disclosed in financial statements and offered to tax, alleged amount of sale consideration of immovable property being just one of many transactions of sale of property executed by assessee on behalf of purchaser, could not be added to income of assessee  INCOME TAX : Where advances as appearing in audited financial statement were trade advances for execution of contract work which were transferred to sub-contractor and assessee was only conduit between work awarder and sub-contractor and transaction was made through banking channel, Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in deleting addition made by Assessing Officer under section 68

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the business of construction of building bridges. It filed its return of income on 30-9-2012 declaring income of Rs. 35.09 lakhs. Notices under sections 143(2) and 142(1) were issued but there was no compliance. Since the Assessing Officer had not received necessary information pursuant to notices issued under sections 143(2) and 142(1), he disallowed the total expenses claimed in the profit and loss account and sale consideration from immovable property and passed an ex parte order under section 144.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) applied the net profit rate of eight per cent on the gross business turnover for the assessment year 2012-13 and set aside the finding of the Assessing Officer of denying the claim of total expenses incurred during the year.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: It is noted that the audited financial statements were available before the Assessing Officer but without disputing the sales turnover during the year he disallowed the total expenses including the purchase of material towards contract work undertaken by the assessee during the year. When the matter travelled before the Commissioner (Appeals) he observed in the impugned order that the net profit rate for assessment years 2009-10 to 2011-12 disclosed by the assessee in its regular audited books of account is 0.22 per cent, 0.17 per cent and 0.25 per cent. Even during the course of scrutiny proceeding for assessment years 2009-10 to 2011-12 net profit rate applied by the Assessing Officer was 0.16 per cent, 0.93 per cent and 0.18 per cent. Though the Commissioner (Appeals) appreciated the fact that undisputed revenue just could not have come without incurring an expenditure, but based on his observation that the purchase made by the assessee in the past were in dispute and genuineness of the same had not been proved, the Commissioner (Appeals) computed the net profit applying the rate of 8 per cent on the total revenue for the year of Rs. 87.46 crores.[Para 9]

The revenue has challenged the relief given by the Commissioner (Appeals) and the assessee is agitating for the higher net profit rate applied by the Commissioner (Appeals) and ignoring past net profit track of the assessee.[Para 9.1]

HEADNOTE: Section 249 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Commissioner (Appeals)/Deputy Commissioner (Appeals) - Condonation of delay - Assessment years 1983- 84 and 1984-85 - Appeal was filed by assessee belatedly with application for condonation of delay of one month allegedly caused in Chartered Accountant’s office - Chartered Accountant filed affidavit explaining delay - Whether Chartered Accountant’s affidavit being categorical about entrustment of work in time and delay being caused due to staff problem in his office, delay deserved to be condoned and Commissioner (Appeals) was unjustified in not condoning it - Held, yes

Section 143 of the Income-tax, Act, 1961 - Assessment - Additions to - Assessment years 1993-84 and 1984-85 -Whether profit disclosed by assessee- contractor in succeeding year can be taken to be a sure guide for determining profit for preceding year - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, where assessee-contractor had disclosed net profit at 8.4 per cent in assessment year in question, it would be incorrect to raise it to 12 per cent merely on ground that in succeeding year net profit returned was at 12.8 per cent - Held, yes - Whether lower authorities were unjustified in not allowing separate deduction for depreciation after estimating profits on gross receipts - Held yes - Whether, on consideration of facts, it would be appropriate to estimate net profits in instant case at 11.5 per cent with separate deduction for depreciation - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, a civil contractor, showed his gross receipts less cost of material at Rs. 25 lakhs and disclosed a net profit of 8.4 per cent. The Assessing Officer estimated net profit at 12 per cent on the ground that in the succeeding year the assessee had disclosed a net profit of 12.8 per cent. While doing so, the Assessing Officer did not allow any separate deduction by way of depreciation. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessment order.

On second appeal :

HELD: In the instant case, the net profit was to be estimated at 11.5 per cent of about Rs. 25 lakhs. The reduction of 1 /2 per cent was given for the reason that the assessee’s turnover of Rs. 25 lakhs was not very high as compared to others in this line of business. The reduction was granted for the further reason that as the work progressed from year to year, the assessee would be gaining experience and expertise as a result of which economy would be affected in the later years. Therefore, the profit of 12.8 per cent disclosed by the assessee in the succeeding year could not be taken to be a sure guide for determining the profit for the preceding year. The net profit was, therefore, estimated at 11.5 per cent of the receipts of Rs. 25 lakhs (approximately). This determination of net profit was only on the working of the contract by the assessee and depreciation (the correct amount was to be quantified by the Assessing Officer after verification) which was an allowance granted under the Act, should be viewed as a separate deduction. Another reason for considering depreciation for separate deduction was that in some cases of contracts, huge machines may have to be employed; whereas in some other cases Labour intensive devices would be employed. Therefore, in order to have a uniform estimate of profit, it is desirable that profit is estimated first ignoring the depreciation and then granting depreciation separately. Then and then only true profit can be ascertained as bet been persons employing high cost machinery and persons employing Labour intensive devices. Therefore, depreciation should be separately deducted from the profit thus estimated.

HEADNOTE: Section 145(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Assessment year 1989-90 - Assessee was in business of construction of ownership flats - He got part of work done through sub-contractors and claimed deduction of payment made to them but failed to produce them for examination - Details of payment of salary, etc., to staff were also not furnished - Basis of valuing work-in-progress was also not given -Whether on facts ITO was justified in invoking provisions of section 145(1) and making an estimated addition of Rs. 30,000 to be returned net profit - Held, yes.

FACT: The assessee commenced business of construction of ownership flat on 1-9-1987 and filed income-tax returns for the transitional previous year for 19 months up to 31-3-1989. He had taken up two projects and handed over the civil works to two sub-contractors by agreements dated 29-4-1988 and 7-10-1988. In the profit and loss account, a sum of Rs. 13,70,740 was debited and was shown as having been paid to these two sub-contractors. Before the ITO the assessee filed details of sub- contract payments but was unable to produce the two sub-contractors. The ITO observed that the assessee was unable to derive his correct profit in respect of the period taking Into account the progress of the work till 31-3-1989 and payments actually to be made and payments made, and that there was no basis for work in progress estimated by the assessee at Rs. 14,116, He also noted that the profit and loss account included items like development charges, registration charges, etc., that details for salaries and staff welfare debited at Rs. 18,747 were not available on record. Considering all these defects and the ad hoc nature of payments made to sub-contractors. the Assessing Officer made a round sum addition of Rs. 30,000 to the income returned, making the assessment order under section 143(3).

On appeal, the Dy. Commissioner (Appeals) held that the Assessing Officer had not noticed any specific defect which would have amounted to a wrong statement of income and, deleted the addition of Rs. 30,000 made by the ITO.

On appeal by the revenue:

HELD: Payment in excess of the amount which an assessee is liable to pay under the terms of an agreement is not an allowable deduction under section 37(1). The accounts of the assessee had not disclosed the correct profit derived by him in respect of the accounting period in question, taking into consideration the works so far done till 31-3-1989 and the payments to be made and actually made by the assessee. The burden to prove the sub- contracts, to bring the sub-contractors and examine them with reference to the sub-contracts entered into by them with the assessee, as also to satisfied the Assessing Officer with regard to the various payments received by them under the sub-contracts, lay squarely upon the assessee and not the department. Despite several opportunities granted to the assessee, he had failed to produce them, and, therefore, the Assessing Officer had reason to doubt the payments said to have been made under the sub-contracts. Further, the details for salaries and staff welfare expenses debited at Rs. 18,747 were not available on record and they were also not produced before the ITO. For these reasons, it was a case of estimate of profit under the proviso to section 145(1).

The order of Deputy Commissioner (Appeals) was, therefore, reversed and that of the ITO was restored.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment years 1965-66 to 1967-68 - Assessee was executing constructional contract works under military authorities - He was not maintaining any account books - Military authorities had supplied certain materials to assessee - Tribunal found that there was no element of profit on cost of materials supplied by authorities - Whether having regard to Tribunal is finding, cost of materials supplied by military authorities was not liable to be included in total receipts of assessee for calculating his net profit - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was doing business of executing constructional contract works under the military authorities but he did not produce any books of account before the ITO on the ground that he was not maintaining any account books.

The assessee had received some material supplied by the M.E.S. department and the value of such materials was deducted from the contract bills. In the absence of accurate figures furnished by the assessee regarding the value of materials supplied by the M.E.S. Department, the ITO estimated 10 per cent of the net contract payments on account of the value of materials supplied by the M.E.S. department for which deductions were made from the bills and added this amount to the net contract value to arrive at the gross value of the work executed by the assessee during that year. On that gross receipt, the ITO estimated the net profit. The AAC rejected the assessee's appeals. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that there was no element of profit on the cost of materials supplied by the department and, therefore, only net receipts should be taken into consideration for all purposes.

On reference :

HELD: The Tribunal had clearly held that there was no element of profit so far as the value of the materials supplied by the M.E.S. department to the assessee in performing the construction works was concerned.

The Tribunal was justified in holding that the cost of materials supplied by the M.E.S. department was not liable to be included in the total receipts of the assessee for calculating its net profits.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

to show that the estimate of profit at 8 per cent was excessive and unreasonable having regard to the facts of the case. However, the profit at 8 per cent estimated for these three years was only a mere estimate and the true profit of the entire project would be arrived at when the contract was complete. The assessee was, therefore, entitled to the adjustment of profit or loss in the year of completion of the contract. Hence, the estimate of profit at 8 per cent was reasonable. Regarding the interest payments under section 40A(8) the computation of income in the case of a contractor is normally made under section 145 if the books of account are incomplete and the true profit cannot be deduced therefrom. Such an estimate of profit under the provisions of section 145 cannot include all the other statutory disallowance like section 40A(8), section 40(b) or other such disallowances. The disallowance under section 40A(8) is provided for a specific purpose and if such a disallowance is deemed to be included in the estimate of profit under section 145, this would defeat the very purpose for which the provisions of section 40A(8) are enacted. Therefore, the interest under section 40A(8) can be separately added even if the profit in the case of the assessee has been estimated under section 145. Thus, the Commissioner (Appeals) was in error in deleting the addition under section 40A(8).

HEADNOTE: I. Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting (Rejection of books of account) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Where there was non-maintenance of inventory of items purchased, some purchases not supported by bills/vouchers, payments to labourers made in cash and no supporting evidence being maintained, non-furnishing of site-wise details of expenses and non-maintenance of day-to-day stock register and quantitative details of stock consumption, books of account of assessee were defective and, therefore, were rightly rejected - Held, yes - Whether since current year was only second year of assessee in contract business and assessee declared better NP rate of 7.02 per cent than first year, addition made by Assessing Officer by applying higher NP rate of 8.5 per cent as declared by others in similar line of business was not justified - Held, yes [Para 3.6] [Partly in favour of assessee]IT : Where relevant year was second year of assessee's contract business and he had shown better results than preceding year, even if assessee's books of account were rejected for certain defects, no addition could be made on account of low NP rate  IT : In absence of any positive material to show that assessee had made undisclosed investment in plot purchased in name of partnership firm of which he was partner, no addition could be made in hands of assessee under section 69B  IT : Inquiries conducted or material gathered behind back of assessee cannot be used against assessee to make addition under section 69B without providing opportunity of confrontation to assessee

FACT: The assessee was engaged in civil construction work. He filed return declaring certain net profit which was 7.02 per cent of gross contract receipts.

The Assessing Officer observed that the books of account of the assessee consisted defects like non-maintenance of inventory of items purchased, some purchases not supported by bills/vouchers, payments to labourers made in cash and no supporting evidence being maintained, i.e., complete postal address of labourers and non-maintenance of muster-roll and wages register, non-maintenance of salary register, payments of some expenses through self-made vouchers, non-maintenance of telephone call register, non-furnishing of site-wise details of expenses and non-maintenance of day-to-day stock register and quantitative details of stock consumption. He held that due to above defect the correct profit of the assessee could not be ascertained from books of account of the assessee. Hence, he rejected the books of account of the assessee by invoking the provisions of section 145(3) and estimated profit by applying the NP rate of 8.5 per cent of total turnover of the assessee by holding that other assessees carrying out similar business activities declared this net profit rate.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld rejection of books of account but reduced addition made by the Assessing Officer by estimating net profit at 8.25 per cent.

On second appeal, the assessee contended that the defects pointed out by the Assessing Officer were of general in nature and were not serious defects on basis of which books of account could be rejected. He also contended that the rejection of books of account did not give unfettered power to the Assessing Officer to estimate the profit at his whims and fancy specially when relevant year was the second year of the assessee in contract business and the NP rate of the assessee was better than last year.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment year 1966-67 - ITO rejected books produced by assessee, a liquor contractor and estimated sales - Thereafter, taking into consideration case of another liquor contractor of very same area for an earlier year, profit was estimated at 7½ per cent on estimated sale - Whether in absence of better material revenue was well justified in taking into consideration case relating to another liquor contractor of very area in respect of earlier year - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, rate of profit at 7½ per cent was justifiably applied on turn over of assessee - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, a liquor contractor for Mandi Dabwali, returned an income for the relevant assessment year. The ITO rejected the books produced by the assessee and estimated the sales at a higher amount as against the amount shown in the books and estimated the profit at 7½ per cent of the total estimated sales.

On appeal, the AAC arrived at the figure of 7½ per cent after taking into consideration the case of another company, which was assessed for the year 1964-65 in respect of their income as liquor contractors for Mandi Dabwali. The further appeal to the Tribunal was also dismissed.

On reference:

HELD: In the absence of better material the revenue was well justified in taking into consideration the case relating to a liquor contractor of the very area in respect of an earlier year. That was the best material available and if there was anything to be said against it, it was open to the assessee to raise the necessary ground before the Tribunal. Nothing was said against taking into consideration the case of the other liquor contractor for the assessment year 1964-65. All that was said before the Tribunal was that there was a slump in sales because of the Indo-Pakistan war in 1965. From the facts and figures as mentioned in the Tribunal's order it did not appear that there was any particular slump after September, 1965, though there appeared to be some slump in September, 1965, only. In fact it was in December, 1965, that there were peak sales of the assessee. The sales of the contractor for the year 1964-65 amounted to Rs. 4,70,000 only. Therefore, the assessee's sales, which even according to him, amounted to Rs. 10,78,898 were not in any manner hit by the Indo-Pakistan war.

Therefore, the rate of profit at 7½ per cent on the turnover was justifiably applied by the Tribunal on the turnover of the assessee.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

Bhagirath Dass for the Applicant.

D.N. Awasthy for the Respondent.

HEADNOTE: Section 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (GP/NP Rate) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee, a joint venture, was formed for purpose to bid and execute construction work - It declared net profit at rate of 1 per cent of contractual receipts - Assessing Officer having noticed that assessee had failed to establish its claim of 1 per cent net profit by producing any evidence to that effect rejected book results and estimated net profit at rate of 4 per cent of total contractual receipts - Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed appeal on ground that assessee did not pursue its appeal before him - Whether matter required to be remanded back to Commissioner (Appeals) to decide issue on merit after affording reasonable opportunities of being heard to assessee - Held, yes [Para 11] [Matter remanded]INCOME TAX : Where assessee was engaged in construction work and Assessing Officer rejected book results and estimated net profit at rate of 4 per cent of total contractual receipts as against 1 per cent declared by assessee and Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed appeal ex parte, matter was to be remanded back to Commissioner (Appeals) to decide issue on merit

Section 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (GP/NP Rate) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee, a joint venture, was formed for purpose to bid and execute construction work - It declared net profit at rate of 1 per cent of contractual receipts - Assessing Officer having noticed that assessee had failed to establish its claim of 1 per cent net profit by producing any evidence to that effect rejected book results and estimated net profit at rate of 4 per cent of total contractual receipts - Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed appeal on ground that assessee did not pursue its appeal before him - Whether matter required to be remanded back to Commissioner (Appeals) to decide issue on merit after affording reasonable opportunities of being heard to assessee - Held, yes [Para 11] [Matter remanded]

FACT: ■

The assessee, a joint venture, was formed by two co-ventures for the purpose to bid and execute the construction work.

■

For the relevant assessment year, the assessee declared the net profit at the rate of 1 per cent of the contractual receipts.

■

The Assessing Officer having noticed that the assessee had failed to establish its claim of 1 per cent net profit by producing any evidence to that effect and similarly placed assessees in the same line of business activity as the assessee were offering taxable income ranging from 5 per cent to 10 per cent of the gross contractual receipts rejected the book results of the assessee by invoking section 145 and estimated the net profit at rate of 4 per cent of the total contractual receipts.

■

The Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed the appeal on the ground that the assessee did not pursue its appeal before him and did not furnish any supporting evidence or written submission despite having been given sufficient opportunity of being heard.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal :

HELD: ■

It is proper to remand the matter back to the file of the Commissioner (Appeals) to decide the issue on merit after affording reasonable opportunities of being heard to the assessee considering the non-compliance due to Covid-19 Pandemic. The assessee is also directed to make compliance before the Commissioner (Appeals) and explain its case on merit. [Para 11]

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of Accounting Estimation of Profit -  Assessment year 1965-66 - Assessee carried on business of constructing buildings and doing work of maintenance of buildings, inter alia for railways - As per specific terms of contract entered into with railway authorities cement and iron had to be supplied them for execution of work and no accounting of cost of those materials was to be done while making bill in respect of contract payment - Whether value of materials supplied by railway authorities could not be included in total receipt of assessee for purpose of calculating net profit by application of rate - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee carried on business of construing buildings and doing the work of maintenance of buildings, inter alia, for railways. As per the specific terms of the contract entered into with the railway authorities, cement and iron had to be supplied by them for execution of the work and no accounting of the cost of these materials was to be done while making the bill in respect of contract payment. The assessee did not maintain books of account. In the absence of the books of account, the ITO estimated not profit at the rate of 15 per cent on total receipts, in which the ITO included the value of materials supplied by the railway authorities.

On appeal the AAC reduced the rate of net profit to 12.5 per cent of the total receipts and held that the ITO was not justified in including the value of the materials supplied by the railway authorities in the total receipts for the purpose of calculating the net profit by application of the rate.

The Tribunal held that the value of the materials supplied by the railway authorities should be included in the receipts for the purpose of ascertaining the net profits by applying the percentage rate.

The Tribunal however held that the profit should be calculated on the basis of 10 per cent.

On reference :

HEADNOTE: Section 143 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Assessment - Addition to income - Assessment year 1993-94 - Assessing Officer disallowed 1 per cent of labour payments and material purchase expenses on ground that in respect of internal vouchers genuineness could not be ascertained for want of details - Assessee contended that complete details with bills, vouchers, labour registers, etc., were produced but no comments were made by Assessing Officer and that percentage of gross profit on sales had actually gone up as compared to previous year - Assessing Officer had not made any averment that books of account were not correct or defective - Whether since additions made were not based on any cogent material nor any basis given for arriving at figure of one per cent, first appellate authority had rightly deleted addition - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a contractor. The Assessing Officer noticed that for the assessment year 1993-94, the net profit from contract came to less than 1 per cent of the net receipt which was more than rupees one crore. The Assessing Officer was of the view that in respect of materials purchased and labour payments, which were based on several internal vouchers, the genuineness could not be ascertained in the absence of complete details. He, therefore, disallowed 1 per cent of the expenses relating to the above as inflated expenses and added the same to the total income of the assessee. The assessee contended that the disallowance was arbitrary and based on assumptions, conjectures and surmises; that complete details of all purchases along with bills, vouchers, etc., and full details of labour payments with labour registers were being maintained and the same were also produced before the Assessing Officer but no comments were made by the Assessing Officer; that the percentage of the gross profit on sales in the assessment year under appeal had actually gone up as compared to the earlier year. The first appellate authority deleted the addition.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: The revenue had not brought any material on record to controvert the submission of the assessee. The additions made by the Assessing Officer were not based on cogent material. The Assessing Officer had not given any basis for arriving at the figure of 1 per cent of the expenses shown by the assessee on account of material purchases and labour payments. There was no averment by the Assessing Officer that the books of account maintained by the assessee were not correct or contained any defect. The Assessing Officer did not adopt any basis for increase made by him. As held by the Supreme Court in the case of State of Orissa v. Maharaja Sri B.P. Singh Deo [1970] 76 ITR 690 that the mere fact that the material placed by the assessee before the assessing authorities was unreliable did not empower the authorities to make an arbitrary order. In view of the above facts and for the reasons stated hereinabove, the assessee’s contention was to be upheld.

Sampat Kr. Jain and K.K. Jain for the Appellant. S.K. Malakar for the Respondent.

headnotes.text: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment years 1957-58 to 1962-63 - Assessee was a contractor and undertaking jobs of various Govt. departments - Books of account of assessee were rejected by ITO and he determined assessee's income on estimate - Terms and conditions as to supply of materials by contractee was not known - Element of profit on such supply if any was to be ascertained and it was also not known whether assessee had submitted its tenders for said contracts anticipating on being assured of supply of such materials - Whether case was to be remanded back to Tribunal to ascertain terms and conditions of contract - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment years 1964-65 and 1965-66 - Assessee was carried on business of executing contracts for Government - He received gross amounts of bills for assessment years 1964-65 and 1965-66 from Government - As assessee did not maintain any books of account, ITO applied net profit rate of 12.6 per cent on gross bill amounts and computed total income for two years - Assessee contended that cost of materials supplied by Government should have been deducted before applying net profit rate - Tribunal held that assessee though tendered contract as a whole, it must have included cost of material which were supplied by Government as an element of profit in respect of cost of material also - Whether since there was no evidence on record to show that assessee did not know about supply of material by Government to be made or at what price and furthermore gross profit had been computed on total gross bill of assessee, it could not be said that Tribunal was indulging in any surmise, or acting without any proper evidence - Held, yes

Section 143, read with section 256, of Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 33, read with section 66, of Indian Income tax Act, 1922] - Assessment - General - Assessment year 1924-25 - In respect of contracts spread over a number of years, assessee produced accounts but accounts for relevant accounting year could not be separated - ITO assessed profit at a standard rate without informing assessee of information or evidence on which rate was based and without giving him any opportunity to produce evidence in rebuttal - Whether question of law arose out of order of ITO - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 13, Proviso to the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Method of accounting - Works contract - Assessment year 1944-45 - Whether merely because a contract was completed after relevant accounting year, it could not be said that no profits arose or accrued to assessee in that accounting year - Held, yes - Assessee was a contractor - As contracts entered into by assessee were not completed during accounting year in question, no income therefrom was declared on ground that no profits accrued on incomplete contracts - Assessee maintained no accounts till accounting year relevant to assessment year 1943-44 and accounts maintained for accounting year relevant to assessment year 1944-45 were not closed on 31-3-1944 but were kept open till execution of contract was completed - These accounts did not reflect profits of assessee for accounting year in question - Whether in instant case proviso to section 13 was applicable and ITO was entitled to discard accounting method of assessee and estimate profits on such basis as he thought fit - Held, yes - Whether objection of assessee that estimate of income on his formula would still be an estimate and would not be mathematically accurate had no substance as mathematical certainty is not demanded in a matter of this description - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits - Assessment years 1970-71 and 1971-72 - Assessee carried on business of undertaking public works contracts - It received cement, steel, bricks etc. from public works department - Its case before ITO was that since it had not earned any profits on value of materials received, no profit should be charged from it - ITO, however, estimated gross profit at five per cent on value of materials - On appeal Tribunal however, referred matter back to ITO with a view to examine tenders and find out as to whether assessee had calculated its profits on value of materials while submitting tenders - If that was so, ITO could estimate reasonable profit on such value - If, on other hand, it was seen that assessee had understanding with department that it would supply materials for execution of contracts and assessee adjusted its rate on that basis, profit on value of material supplied could not be estimated - Whether, on facts, order passed by Tribunal was correct - Held, yes

Section 145, read with section 144, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Rejection of accounts - Assessment years 1993-94 to 1997-98 - Assessee-firm was engaged in work of civil construction in Public Works Department (PWD) - Assessing Officer, after rejecting books of account, made assessment determining 8 per cent profit at flat rate - Commissioner (Appeals) reduced rate of profit from 8 per cent to 5 per cent on ground that since turnover of assessee exceeded Rs. 40 lakhs, it was bound to incur more expenses and rate of profit would be less - Further, Tribunal reduced profit rate to 4 per cent on ground that assessee was doing work for PWD and normally, profit rate was much less for work of PWD, as contract work had to be done under certain specifications and under supervision of PWD authorities - Whether rate of profit cannot be assumed, merely on assumptions or surmises and conjectures - Held, yes - Whether since Assessing Officer as well as Commissioner (Appeals) as also Tribunal had not recorded any finding based on any material and findings recorded were merely based on surmises and conjectures, findings of rate of profit could not be sustained and 
 matter deserved to be remanded to assessing authority for re-determination thereof - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income- Assessment year 2010-11 - Where despite various opportunities given, assessee, civil contractor failed to produce books of account and relevant vouchers and there had been a lot of variation in profit rate of assessee during different years, Assessing Officer was justified in rejecting audited balance-sheet filed by assessee and making assessment by applying net profit rate of 12 per cent [In favour of revenue]

Section 144, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Best judgment assessment - Assessment year 1974-75 - Whether while making a best judgment assessment, though there must necessarily be guess work in matter, it must not be arbitrary - Held, yes - Assessee-contractor did not main books of account - He filed his return of income on estimate basis by computing profit at flat rate of 10 per cent on gross receipts - ITO, however, computed net profit at rate of 15 per cent - Revision petition filed by assessee was dismissed by Commissioner - Whether since neither ITO nor Commissioner had referred to any material for applying flat rate of 
15 percent while estimating net profits, impugned orders passed by them deserved to be set aside - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment year 2001-02 - Assessee, a labour contractor, failed to produce books of account and vouchers to justify expenses made against gross receipts - Therefore, Assessing Officer estimated net profit rate at 8 per cent against 1.52 per cent shown by assessee - On appeal, Tribunal reduced net profit rate to 6.5 per cent - Whether there was any justification to interfere with order passed by Tribunal - Held, no

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment year 1966-67 - ITO rejected books produced by assessee, a liquor contractor and estimated sales - Thereafter, taking into consideration case of another liquor contractor of very same area for an earlier year, profit was estimated at 7½ per cent on estimated sale - Whether in absence of better material revenue was well justified in taking into consideration case relating to another liquor contractor of very area in respect of earlier year - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, rate of profit at 7½ per cent was justifiably applied on turn over of assessee - Held, yes

Section 145, read with section 263, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (Revision) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee was a works contractor, who in addition to said income had income from a firm, house property and other sources - Assessing Officer rejected account books of assessee on premise that it had failed to produce bills and vouchers of materials purchased and estimated net profit at 6 per cent on gross receipts of assessee to which other incomes were added - Commissioner took revisional proceedings against assessee and having found that sundry creditors of assessee having not been examined by Assessing Officer held assessment order to be erroneous - It was noted that whether unexplained sundry credits are added to contract receipts or as income from other sources definitely tax payable by assessee would be higher than that paid by a mere estimation of net profit - Whether since sundry creditors having been not examined by Assessing Officer, estimation of profit on contract receipts alone would be an erroneous exercise and it caused prejudice to interests of revenue - Held, yes [Para 13] [In favour of revenue]

Section 145, read with section 263, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (Revision) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee was a works contractor, who in addition to said income had income from a firm, house property and other sources - Assessing Officer rejected account books of assessee on premise that it had failed to produce bills and vouchers of materials purchased and estimated net profit at 6 per cent on gross receipts of assessee to which other incomes were added - Commissioner took revisional proceedings against assessee and having found that sundry creditors of assessee having not been examined by Assessing Officer held assessment order to be erroneous - It was noted that whether unexplained sundry credits are added to contract receipts or as income from other sources definitely tax payable by assessee would be higher than that paid by a mere estimation of net profit - Whether since sundry creditors having been not examined by Assessing Officer, estimation of profit on contract receipts alone would be an erroneous exercise and it caused prejudice to interests of revenue - Held, yes [Para 13] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where assessee was a works contractor and had income from various sources and Assessing Officer rejected assessee's account books and estimated net profit at 6 per cent on gross receipts, since sundry creditors of assessee was not examined by Assessing Officer, estimation of profit on contract receipts alone would be an erroneous exercise and it caused prejudice to interest of revenue

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Rejection of accounts - Assessment years 1981-82 to 1983-84 - Assessee was engaged in construction of flats and since project was not complete, it claimed that no profit accrued during the construction period and that in case of a building contractor profits should not be assessed on year-to-year basis but at end of contract work - Assessing Officer held that method of accounting followed by assessee was defective and, consequently, by applying provisions of section 145 computed assessee’s business income at 8 per cent of receipts - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) upheld computation of business income - Whether in case of building contractor, profits should be assessed on year-to-year basis, and, thus, in absence of material to the contrary, profit at 8 per cent estimated by Assessing Officer was neither excessive nor unreasonable - Held, yes

Section 145, read with section 144 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income - Civil contract work - Assessment year 2007-08 - In view of non-maintenance of proper books of account by assessee-contractor, revenue authorities estimated its net income at 8 per cent of gross receipts - It was found that assessee made purchases more than 80 per cent which were billed and were forming part of gross receipts from contractees - Whether remaining amount could not fetch 8 per cent as per provisions of section 44AD when assessee rendered civil contract work without material - Held yes - Whether it was also not case of assessee to make profit of 8 per cent on material cost and in this view of matter, it would be reasonable to estimate income on gross receipts at rate of 6 per cent - Held, yes [Para 8] [In favour of assessee]

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income - Civil contract work - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessing Officer estimated assessee's income at 8 per cent of gross receipts - He made additions on account of disallowance of sundry creditors which had increased not in proportion to increase in material cost thereby indicating that assessee had raised bills on contractees when material cost was still to be borne by assessee - Whether, estimation of 8 per cent after deleting additions and disallowance was not proper and 7 per cent profit on gross receipts would be reasonable - Held, yes [Para 8] [In favour of assessee]

Section 28 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business income - Assessee, carrying contract work under government departments, did not maintain proper account books - Whether net profit could be estimated at a flat rate on gross receipts including value of material supplied by government - Held, on facts, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Rejection of accounts (Illustrations) - Assessment year 2010-11 - Assessee was a contractor - Assessing Officer rejected books of account of assessee on ground that assessee failed to verify genuineness of opening and closing balance of labour charges payable and, accordingly, assessed net profit at 12 per cent - Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed rejection of books of account but reduced net profit rate from 12 per cent to 5 per cent - It was found that assessee failed to verify genuineness of opening and closing balance of labour payable or furnish details called for by Assessing Officer or justify quantitative and qualitative details of closing stock - Further, queries raised by Assessing Officer were not properly addressed and assessee was not able to rebut findings given by Assessing Officer - Whether, therefore, rejection of books of account was justified - Held, yes - Whether since true picture of profits earned by assessee could not be found out due to substantial defects in maintenance of books of account, it was reasonable to estimate profit of assessee by applying net profit rate of 8 per cent - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 12] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where assessee failed to verify genuineness of opening and closing balance of labour charges payable or furnish details called for by Assessing Officer, rejection of books of account was justified

u Section 145 of Income-tax Act, 1961
Where assessee, a construction company, did not maintain any books of account and it was also an undisputed fact that the assessee did not produce before the Assessing Officer the vouchers or any other documentary evidence to support the correctness of various expenses shown in the profit and loss account submitted long with the returns of income, Assessing Officer was justified in estimating assessee’s profits by applying net profit rate
Eastern Construction Co. v. ITO [1997] 59 TTJ (Delhi) 723
It is true that the assessing Officer, while making the best judgment, has to make a fair, just and reasonable estimate of income. Such estimation of profit in a fair and just manner could be done by the Assessing Officer either by applying a net profit rate on the contract receipts or he could also estimate the profit in any other manner which can be regarded as fair and reasonable. 
Where assessee, a construction company, did not maintain any books of account and it was also an undisputed fact that the assessee did not produce before the Assessing Officer the vouchers or any other documentary evidence to support the correctness of various expenses shown in the profit and loss account submitted long with the returns of income, and the Assessing Officer completed assessment by resorting to section 145 and he estimated profits by applying net profit rate of 12.5 per cent : 
Held that, on the facts of the case, it was incumbent upon by the Assessing Officer to have resorted to estimation of profit from the contract business. It could not, therefore, be said that the method of computing the taxable income adopted by the Assessing Officer while making the best judgment was patently erroneous or invalid. The year under consideration was the first accounting year of the firm. The contention that the income ought to have been assessed on the basis of past assessed history was, therefore, not relevant and justified on the facts of the present case.

Section 3 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 2(11) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Previous year - Assessment year 1959-60 - In respect of a contract work for which no accounts were maintained till completion is for a period of 2 years and 8 months, ITO adopted 30th September as accounting year, for assessment year 1958-59, as was done by assessee in respect of other sources of income - Succeeding ITO however relying on section 2(11)(i) of 1922 Act, took year ending 31st March as previous year and apportioned profits between assessment years 1958-59 and 1959-60 - Whether words “previous year" ordinarily means a period from 1st April to 31st March but if assessee wants to adopt any other period, then his accounts must be made up for that period and if, those accounts are not made up for that period, he cannot ask for that period - Held, yes - Whether since accounts had not been made up for over a period of 2 years and 8 months, assessee could not adopt any other period than 1st April to 31st March - Held, yes - Whether, therefore adoption by ITO of accounting period from October to September for year of assessment 1958-59, could not be conclusive, nor could next ITO be barred from adopting correct accounting period in terms of section 2(11)(i)(a) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether questions about estimation of profit on gross amount instead of on net amount received by assessee after deduction of costs of material supplied by Government or about apportionment of profit to be made over a period of 4 years instead of 2 years, not having been raised at any stage of assessment proceedings, could not be gone into - Held, yes

Section 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Rejection of accounts (Estimation of profit) - Assessment year 2014-15 - Assessee was engaged as civil contractor - Assessing Officer being not satisfied with explanation of assessee regarding decline in net profit rejected account books and estimated net profit at rate of 10 per cent of turnover - Whether in light of various defects/deficiencies/irregularities along with assessee’s evasive approach towards explanation sought by Assessing Officer, allegation that rejection of books was done in arbitrary manner did not hold any ground and, thus, rejection of books of account was justified - Held, yes - Whether however, in absence of any comparative instances of similar assessees in same line of business, it was appropriate to estimate profit at a percentage worked out on basis of preceding three years profit of assessee herself - Held, yes [Paras 10 and 12] [Partly in favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where explanation of assessee-contractor regarding decline in net profit was evasive and there were various defects in books of account of assessee, rejection of books of account was proper; however, in absence of any comparative instances of similar assessees in same line of business, it was appropriate to estimate profit at a percentage worked out on basis of preceding three years profit of assessee herself

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimate of profits - Assessment year 1985-86 - Assessee, a contractor, did not maintain regular books of account - Assessee had only estimated cash profit with reference to gross receipts and, thus, quantum of gross receipt was only intended to serve as a basis to measure cash profit retained - Assessee contended that tax deducted at source by Government could not be considered as an outgoing for year - Whether there was substance in plea of assessee that tax deducted at source could not be considered as having to come out of profits thus estimated - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits - Assessment year 1992-93 - Assessee-contractor declared profit rate of 9.3 per cent - Assessing Officer in view of higher profit rate in earlier two years enhanced it to 11.5 per cent - However, no comparable case was cited - Assessee explained that fall in profit rate was due to execution of huge pending works of earlier year and price hike of materials as a result of gulf war - Whether having regard to specific reasons given by assessee for fall of gross profit rate in assessment year in question together with fact that in assessee’s own case for assessment year 1986-87, Tribunal held profit rate 9 per cent to be reasonable, conclusion/finding of Commissioner (Appeals) in treating profit rate of 9.3 per cent in current year was reasonable, proper and justified - Held, yes

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (Rate of income) - Assessment year 2007-08 - Assessee was a contractor and undertook works for municipal corporation - Assessee declared a net taxable income which represented his share of profit from a firm, in addition to his own income from proprietary concern - During course of assessment proceedings, Assessing Officer made enquiries into loans taken, purchases made, genuineness of some sub-contracts awarded by assessee and penalty paid by him - Assessing Officer treated said sums as income of assessee - Commissioner (Appeals) took cognizance of several irregularities in accounts of assessee and estimated income of assessee at 8 per cent of turnover - On cross-appeals, assessee contended that rate of estimated income was to be 6.5 per cent whereas revenue contended that estimated rate of income by Commissioner (Appeals) was on lower side - Tribunal concluded that in comparable cases net profit rate had varied from 2.93 per cent to 9.96 per cent; but these were big concerns, which maintained proper accounts and also maintained quality standards and in instant case accounts were not reliable and, hence, estimation of net profit at 8 per cent was justified - Whether since estimation of net profit by Assessing Officer was on higher side, Tribunal's order was to be upheld - Held, yes [Paras 7 and 8] [Partly in favour of assessee]IT : Where Tribunal after referring to comparable cases applied net profit at 8 per cent, since estimation of net profit by Assessing Officer was on higher side, order passed by Tribunal was justified

Section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Penalty - For concealment of income (In case of estimation of profit) - Assessment year 1995-96 - Assessee was a contractor and assessee declared its income at an estimated 3 per cent of contract receipts - Search took place in assessee's premises and in view of seized materials Assessing Officer gave due opportunity to assessee to justify disclosed income and explain discrepancies noticed by special auditor - Assessee was also permitted to inspect seized documents - Despite that assessee could not explain said discrepancies - Accordingly Assessing Officer resorted to estimation of profits by adopting 11 per cent on gross contract receipts and initiated penalty proceedings - Whether there was gross or wilful negligence on part of assessee in failing to return correct income, penalty would be levied under section 271(1)(c) - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of revenue]IT: Where assessee could not explain discrepancies noticed by special auditor and disclosed a lesser income than what it actually earned, penalty under section 271(1)(c) was to be levied

Section 145(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Assessment year 1989-90 - Assessee was in business of construction of ownership flats - He got part of work done through sub-contractors and claimed deduction of payment made to them but failed to produce them for examination - Details of payment of salary, etc., to staff were also not furnished - Basis of valuing work-in-progress was also not given -Whether on facts ITO was justified in invoking provisions of section 145(1) and making an estimated addition of Rs. 30,000 to be returned net profit - Held, yes.

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 13 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Method of accounting - Rejection of accounts - Assessment year 1943-44 - Whether while making assessment under section 23(3), it is open to ITO to take into account other materials that may come to his knowledge apart from accounts submitted by assessee but principles of natural justice require that assessee should be given opportunity to rebut any inference that may be drawn against him from such other material and though for that purpose he is not bound to disclose actual source of information he should indicate to assessee that he intended to use additional material against him and give him opportunity to have his say regarding it - Held, yes - In his books of account, assessee had disclosed a profit of 7½ per cent - ITO, however, notived that neighbournig shopkeepers who were also dealing with same kind of goods showed a profit of 15 percent for period in question - He thus, rejected assessee’s accounts and assessed him at a profit of 12½ per cent - Whether since assessee was given an opportunity  to rebut inference arising against him from high profits shown by neighbouring shop-keepers and he did put forward an explanation which was rejected by lower authorities, there was no illegality in assessment under section 23(3) of 1922 Act on basis of profits of neighbouring shop-keepers - Held, yes
