On appeal to the Tribunal.

The assessee was a contractor executing contract works under various Government departments.

The Assessing Officer verified the profit and loss account and found that the assessee had claimed huge expenses under heads 'freight', 'salaries and wages', 'travelling expenses' and 'other expenses'. The assessee was asked to produce salary and wage register and evidences of the above expenses. The assessee did not produce the same. The Assessing Officer rejected the book profit and estimated the profit at 8 per cent of the gross contract receipts.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the order of the Assessing Officer.

On appeal :

The assessee was a contractor. In the year in question, the assessee had undertaken the construction of houses under a project. The expenditure incurred on the jobs during the year was shown at Rs. 4,45,904 and that was treated by the assessee as work-in-progress and a sum of Rs. 3,21,358 was shown as received against the contracts from the Executive Engineer. The assessee did not show any profit or loss from the jobs and, claiming overhead expenses at Rs. 12,764, a net loss was returned. The ITO considered that a profit had to be calculated on the basis of the receipts from the authorities and he had, accordingly, computed the gross profit of Rs. 40,169 at 12½ per cent of the receipts. The assessee appealed before the AAC. The assessee claimed that the accounts were maintained on what was known as the completed job basis which was the recognised system of accounting and that the accounts having been maintained in a proper manner, the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act could not be invoked. The AAC did not accept the assessee's contention. According to the AAC, the tax had to be levied on the total income of the previous year and not on the total income of a period of 2, 3, 4 or more years, the period that would be required for completing any contracted work. Accordingly, he upheld action of the ITO in invoking the provisions of section 13 of the 1922 Act, for computing the assessee’s income, however, the AAC, held that the rate was to be applied on the gross value of the work done and not on the net payments received by the assessee and accordingly computed the gross profits at Rs. 1,04,926 by applying the rate of 12½ per cent on Rs. 8,29,412 as the gross value of the work done during the previous year. On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order of the AAC.

On reference:

The assessee was engaged in the business of civil contract works and during the assessment year, executed contract works with different Government departments.

During assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer asked the assessee to produce the books of account, bills and vouchers for verification, but the assessee could not produce the complete books of account, even the cash book.

Therefore, the Assessing Officer rejected the books of account by applying the provisions of section 145(3) and estimated the profit at rate of 10 per cent on the gross bills subject to that assessee would not be allowed the interest and salary claimed to have been paid to the partners.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld rejection of books of account but reduced net profit rate from 10 per cent to 8 per cent.

On second appeal:

The assessee carried on contract business of construction of roads by obtaining contracts from the Government departments. For the assessment year 1992-93, the assessee filed the return of income along with the tax audit report under section 44AB. It was accepted that the books maintained by the assessee were not verifiable. During the course of the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer asked the assessee to furnish the names and addresses of the parties and sundry creditors from whom raw material for construction of the roads had been purchased. The assessee furnished the addresses and the Assessing Officer issued letters of enquiry under section 133(6). However, the letters sent to 17 parties returned unserved to the Assessing Officer. The assessee was directed to prove the genuineness of the transactions made with the parties. The assessee filed copies of the accounts and copies of the confirmation letters stated to have been obtained from the parties before the Assessing Officer. However, the Assessing Officer did not agree with the confirmation letters as the letters sent to the parties had returned unserved. The assessee was asked to prove the genuineness of those parties but could not prove except filing confirmation letters from those parties. The Assessing Officer further pointed out that there might be standard specification but it was difficult to arrive at a definite conclusion in the absence of specific formula for construction of roads of various thickness and it was further observed that in the absence of details, general statement would not support any measurement and it was not possible to arrive at the exact consumption of raw material. He therefore, made certain additions to income of the assessee on that account.

As regards the payments made to the labourers, the assessee had submitted samples and muster rolls before the Assessing Officer. They were examined by the handwriting expert, which indicated that the thumbs’ impressions were not of different parties and the Assessing Officer observed that it could be easily deduced that the labour payments were excessive and inflated and, accordingly, made certain disallowance. However, the Assessing Officer allowed depreciation to the assessee as per profit and loss account. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee had not maintained verifiable accounts and as such, net profit rate should be applied. The consumption of the raw material claimed was within the parameters laid down by the laboratories for particular type of road construction. He also held that the Assessing Officer had not made out a fool-proof case for addition on account of bogus purchases and the road constructed by the assessee during the year was found up to the specification by the principals while making payment to the contractor and it could not be held that the assessee had not utilized grit and had not paid the wages for construction of roads. Accordingly, the Commissioner (Appeals) applied net profit rate of 10 per cent on the receipts as against 8 per cent applied in the immediately preceding year, keeping in view the discrepancy pointed out in the maintenance of the books of account. However, the Commissioner (Appeals) granted the depreciation after applying net profit rate as allowed by the Assessing Officer also.

On further appeal :

For the assessment year 1989-90, the assessee, a contractor, had shown net profit before depreciation and financial charges at the net profit rate of 6 per cent as against the net profit rate at 9.6 per cent in the preceding year. The Assessing Officer found that the assessee had not maintained stock register for purchase and consumption nor the details of work-in-progress were verifiable. The stock of material at site had not been taken into account,besides certain unverifiable credit on account of miscellaneous receipts. He, therefore, applied section 145(2) and estimated the net profit at the rate of 9 per cent. On appeal,the commissioner (Appeals) upheld the rejection of book results but applied a reduced net profit rate of 8 per cent.

On second appeal :

The assessee-firm had undertaken a Government contract for construction of canals, etc. In execution of the aforesaid work, the Government supplied cement and other materials to the assessee for being directly utilised in the completion of the work. After the completion of the contract, the Government made payment of the gross amount due to the assessee after deducting the value of the materials supplied to the assessee. At the time of assessment, the ITO rejected the books of account maintained by the assessee on the ground that they suffered from certain defects and applied a net profit rate of 12½ per cent. The AAC, while maintaining the estimate of net profits at the rate of 12½ per cent in respect of the contracts directly executed by the assessee, applied 7½ per cent profit rate in respect of the contracts which were supervised by the other persons employed by the assessee. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the estimates of net profit arrived at by the AAC were fair and reasonable. However, it held that the amount of the bills relating to the value of the material supplied by the Government should have been excluded from the gross receipts of the assessee.

On reference:

The Assessing Officer noted that there was delay in filing the return for the assessment year 1997-98. The Assessing Officer also noted that books of account were neither found during the search nor were produced during block assessment proceedings. As such the income was worked out on the basis of accounts filed alongwith the return. The assessee was engaged in contract work related to the construction of roads. The Assessing Officer applied net profit rate of 8 per cent by stating that the nature of job of the assessee was more or less the same as that of a civil contractor and determined the total income of the assessee. After allowing the claim of the assessee on account of depreciation, the income was worked out and it was treated as undisclosed income for that assessment year. For the subsequent assessment year also the Assessing Officer estimated the net profit and after allowing half of the depreciation claimed by the assessee, treated the income as undisclosed income and the same was added to the income of the assessee.

During the course of assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer noted that the assessee had shown liabilities under ‘crusher payable’ and ‘labour payable’ for different years but had not produced any evidence for settlement of payment in the future years. The Assessing Officer worked out the peak difference of crusher payable only for various assessment years and made addition of same. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the action taken by the Assessing Officer.

The assessee was engaged in the business of execution of civil works contract. He filed his return of income for the relevant assessment years declaring certain taxable income.

During the course of assessment proceedings, on verification of books of account and other details filed by the assessee, the Assessing Officer noticed that most of the expenditure in respect of labour charges, work expenses, mess charges and other indirect expenses were not supported by proper bills and vouchers. The Assessing Officer further observed that the assessee had kept self-made vouchers in support of major expenditure and, accordingly, opined that the books of account maintained by the assessee were not amenable for verification.

He thus rejected books of account under the provisions of section 145(3) and estimated net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts net of all deductions. In addition to estimation of net profit, the Assessing Officer made separate additions towards income from other sources being interest earned on fixed deposits.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal:

The assessee was a works contractor, who in addition to the said income had income from a firm, house property and other sources.

The Assessing Officer looked at the account books and directed the assessee to produce the bills and vouchers of the materials purchased.

The assessee having failed to produce the same, the Assessing Officer rejected the account books and estimated the net profit at 6 per cent on the gross receipts of the assessee to which the other incomes were added.

Subsequently the Commissioner took revisional proceedings against the assessee and having found that non payment into the treasury of tax deducted at source by the assessee having not been verified by the Assessing Officer and the sundry creditors of the assessee especially when no bills and vouchers were produced having not been examined by the Assessing Officer held the assessment order to be erroneous.

The Tribunal allowed the appeal of the assessee.

On appeal to the High Court by revenue:

The assessee carried on business of construing buildings and doing the work of maintenance of buildings, inter alia, for railways. As per the specific terms of the contract entered into with the railway authorities, cement and iron had to be supplied by them for execution of the work and no accounting of the cost of these materials was to be done while making the bill in respect of contract payment. The assessee did not maintain books of account. In the absence of the books of account, the ITO estimated not profit at the rate of 15 per cent on total receipts, in which the ITO included the value of materials supplied by the railway authorities.

On appeal the AAC reduced the rate of net profit to 12.5 per cent of the total receipts and held that the ITO was not justified in including the value of the materials supplied by the railway authorities in the total receipts for the purpose of calculating the net profit by application of the rate.

The Tribunal held that the value of the materials supplied by the railway authorities should be included in the receipts for the purpose of ascertaining the net profits by applying the percentage rate.

The Tribunal however held that the profit should be calculated on the basis of 10 per cent.

On reference :

The petitioner assessee, who was carrying on business as a contractor filed his return on estimated basis by computing the profit at a flat rate of 10 per cent, on gross receipts, as he did not maintain any books of account. The ITO, however, computed the net profit at 15 per cent, on the contract payments received by the assessee. The revision petition filed under section 263 was dismissed by the Commissioner.

On writ:

The assessee was a contractor undertaking project of Indian Railways on turnkey basis. A search action under section 132 was carried out at the assessee's premises. As the assessee, at the relevant point of time, was not able to collect information about such contracts or produce relevant personnel, it proposed for fixing net profit rate at 11 per cent. The Assessing Officer, accordingly, applied net profit rate at the rate of 11 per cent on the total contract receipts on estimate basis which however, was reduced to 8 per cent by the Tribunal. A penalty under section 271(1)(c) was also levied upon the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the penalty on the ground that the estimation of income by applying flat net profit ratio did not tantamount to concealment or filing inaccurate particulars of income.

On revenue's appeal:

The assessee civil contractor doing sub-contractor’s work returned his income for the assessment year 1994-95. The percentage of profit as per the said return worked out to 5 per cent as against 7.1 per cent and 8.7 per cent in the assessment years 1992-93 and 1991-92, respectively. During the assessment proceedings the Assessing Officer from a scrutiny of the books of account noticed six payments received by the assessee during the first quarter itself, payments made to a certain person in cash while payment vouchers indicated less than bills received, and other irregularities in payment of labour charges as well as claim of transportation charges, etc. Considering these defects the Assessing Officer rejected the books of account under section 145(2) and applying the provisions of section 44AD estimated the net profits at 8 per cent of the contract receipts.

The matter was taken in appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) by the assessee contending that the Assessing Officer was not justified in applying the provisions of section 44AD inasmuch as the profits and gains of the business in question were lower and supported by proper evidence. The assessee filed a comparative chart of the gross profits and explained the fall in GP rate by arbitrary reduction of agreed rate by his contractor which resulted in reduction of 18.5 per cent in profits of total turnover. He further contended that the labour payments were made as per the norms of the BSP and the assessee had no choice. The Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee’s pleas and the estimation of income under section 44AD was held unjustified and the Assessing Officer was directed to accept the income from business returned by the assessee.

On revenue’s appeal :

The assessee was a civil contractor. In the absence of details and there being no proper books of account maintained, the Assessing Officer estimated the assessee's income from contract business at 8 per cent of the gross contract receipts by invoking the provisions of section 44AD.

The Commissioner (Appeals) held that net profit of assessee was to be assessed at 5 per cent of contractual receipts.

The Tribunal finding that the assessee had not filed profit and loss account or balance sheet for the relevant years and that the returns and the vouchers produced were defective in nature, confirmed the order of the assessment thereby taking 8 per cent of the gross turnover as the income of the assessee.

On appeal:

The assessee-firm was in the business of building and construction. During the year relevant to the assessment year under consideration, there were some small contracts which were completed more or less in a year and there was a big contract which was to continue for many years. During assessment proceedings, the assessing authority found that there was no day-to-day maintenance of accounts and, therefore, he came to the conclusion that the profits from the return could not be ascertained and, accordingly, estimated the profit. In appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the assessee’s contention that it was only on the completion of the contracts that profitability or otherwise of the same could be judged. He directed the assessing authority that in respect of the said big contract, the profit be assessed on ad hoc basis at 5 per cent of gross receipts. On further appeal, the Tribunal disapproved the Commissioner (Appeals)’s order and directed the assessing authority to determine the profit only on the year of completion of the project.

On reference :

During the previous year relevant to the assessment year 1958-59, the assessee-firm executed MES contract for the construction of a part of an air-field and received total payment of Rs. 26,32,361 comprising Rs. 17,02,824 in cash and Rs. 9,29,437 representing value of material supplied free of cost. It included in its tax returns the profit computed only with reference to cash receipts of Rs. 17,02,824 by showing a gross profit rate of 18 per cent. The ITO, however, included the said value of the material also while computing the total income which was pitched up by applying a gross profit rate of 26 per cent after invoking the proviso to section 13, as the account books were not reliable. The AAC confirmed the ITO's order. The Tribunal, however, reduced the profit rate.

On reference :

The assessee-firm carried on business of undertaking contracts under the public works department authorities. For the relevant assessments year, it received certain amount on account of work done from the authorities concerned. Apart from the payments on account of work done, the assessee had also received cement, steel and bricks from the concerned department. The assessee’s case before the ITO was that since it had not earned any profit on the value of the materials received by it from the Government, no profit should be charged from it. That contention was not accepted by the ITO and he estimated the gross profit at five per cent on value of materials also. The assessee's appeals before the AAC on this question having failed, it took up the matter in further appeal before the Tribunal. The Tribunal referred the matter back to the ITO with a view to examine the tenders and find out as to whether the assessee had calculated its profit on the value of the materials while submitting the tenders and, if that was so, then estimate the reasonable profit on such value. If, on the other hand, it was found that the assessee was under an understanding that the department concerned would supply the required materials to it for the execution of those contracts and the assessee adjusted its rates on that basis, then there would not arise any occasion for estimating any profit on the value of the materials supplied. For that reason, the Tribunal remanded the case to the ITO.

On reference :

The assessee was a registered firm carrying on various kinds of business including the taking of contracts for making constructions. The assessee was called upon to make a return of its income for the year 1934-35 and in the return submitted by it, it was stated that the assessee had in the year in question undertaken a contract for the construction of certain buildings. A certain sum was due in respect of the said contract for which a suit for recovery was pending in the Civil Court. The assessee maintained that as the amount spent by it in making the constructions was in excess of the amount received from the party it must be taken that the assessee had made no profit from the contract referred to above. This contention of the assessee was overruled by the ITO.

The ITO further held that the accounts submitted by the assessee were incomplete and accordingly he estimated the profits from the contract of building at a flat rate of 15 per cent. on the outlay. The assessee appealed to the Assistant Commissioner who affirmed the assessment made by the ITO.

The assessee then applied to the Commissioner under section 66(2) of the 1922 Act for reference of certain questions of law to this Court. The Commissioner rejected the application.

On application under section 66(3) of 1922 Act.

The assessee, an interior decorator, had declared an income of Rs. 8,80,300 against gross contractual receipts amounting to Rs. 1,97,58,476. He debited job work charges amounting to Rs. 92,55,404 to the profit and loss account. The Assessing Officer required the assessee to produce the five parties to whom job work payments had been made in cash, along with relevant account books and bank pass books for examination. Only one party appeared before the Assessing Officer. After examination the Assessing Officer accepted the job work given to him as genuine. The other four parties were neither produced nor confirmations were filed. Therefore, the Assessing Officer added to the income of the assessee entire job work payments amounting to Rs. 44,14,495 allegedly paid to the parties. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), accepting the alternative plea of the assessee that he would agree to the application of net profit rate of 8 per cent on gross contractual receipts as has been prescribed under section 44AD for computing profits and gains of business of civil construction, applied the provisions of section 44AD and net profit of 8 per cent was applied on gross receipts.

On appeal by the revenue :

The petitioner derived his income mostly from contracts and he undertook the contract of construction; the work for construction was started on November 4, 1943, and was completed some time in May, 1944; during the time when the work was in progress, the petitioner received part of the payments in the financial year 1943-44, and the remaining in the financial year 1944-45. The ITO made an assessment of the petitioner for the assessment year 1944-45, but as some of the income was relevant to construction work which was not completed, the said assessment was made on tentative basis subject to adjustment in the year when the construction was completed. The petitioner filed appeals to the AAC and subsequently to the Tribunal objecting to application of rate of profit at 18 per cent were dismissed.

After the completion of the contract, the ITO fixed the petitioner’s total income at Rs. 55,403 which he apportioned between the two assessment years 1944-45 and 1945-46.

The point that has been urged in the instant was that since the Income-tax Officer has in his assessment order for the year 1945-46; arrived at a total profit for the entire contract at Rs. 4,119 and has apportioned only a sum of Rs. 1,818 as profits for the assessment year 1944-45, it was the duty of the Income-tax Officer to revise the assessment made by him for the assessment year 1944-45 and to substitute the figure of Rs. 1,818 in the place of Rs. 44,214, arrived at as profits for the assessment year 1944-45.

The assessee was engaged in civil construction work. He filed return declaring certain net profit which was 7.02 per cent of gross contract receipts.

The Assessing Officer observed that the books of account of the assessee consisted defects like non-maintenance of inventory of items purchased, some purchases not supported by bills/vouchers, payments to labourers made in cash and no supporting evidence being maintained, i.e., complete postal address of labourers and non-maintenance of muster-roll and wages register, non-maintenance of salary register, payments of some expenses through self-made vouchers, non-maintenance of telephone call register, non-furnishing of site-wise details of expenses and non-maintenance of day-to-day stock register and quantitative details of stock consumption. He held that due to above defect the correct profit of the assessee could not be ascertained from books of account of the assessee. Hence, he rejected the books of account of the assessee by invoking the provisions of section 145(3) and estimated profit by applying the NP rate of 8.5 per cent of total turnover of the assessee by holding that other assessees carrying out similar business activities declared this net profit rate.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld rejection of books of account but reduced addition made by the Assessing Officer by estimating net profit at 8.25 per cent.

On second appeal, the assessee contended that the defects pointed out by the Assessing Officer were of general in nature and were not serious defects on basis of which books of account could be rejected. He also contended that the rejection of books of account did not give unfettered power to the Assessing Officer to estimate the profit at his whims and fancy specially when relevant year was the second year of the assessee in contract business and the NP rate of the assessee was better than last year.

The assessee had been carrying on business of the execution of contracts. The total income of the assessee for the assessment year 1962-63 was computed at Rs. 6,380. In respect of the assessment year under consideration assessment was made on estimate by the ITO acting under section 145. After deducting from the total income of Rs. 6,380 the tax of Rs. 3,190, the distributable surplus was worked out at Rs. 3,190. Therefore, the assessee ought to have declared a dividend of Rs. 1,914, being 60 per cent of the said amount of distributable surplus of Rs. 3,190. The ITO, held that the gross profit of the year had been determined by application of section 145 and there was no other addition in determining the assessable income and as such the point of commercial profits had no relevance. On appeal, the AAC held that there was no commercial profit for distribution as dividend and, therefore, he cancelled the ITO’s order under section 104. On second appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order of the AAC holding that in determining the commercial profits of the assessee-company for the year for the purpose of section 104, no estimated profit was to be taken into account in respect of the contracts that were partly executed by the end of the year when the accounts were maintained on the basis of completed contracts.

On reference, the revenue contended that the question, as to, whether the method of maintaining of the assessee's accounts was correct or not or whether the profit of the assessment year 1962-63 was correctly and properly calculated on the basis of the estimate under section 145 or not, was a question which related to assessment proceeding and its correctness could be determined only in appeal or reference, arising out of the assessment order for the said year and not in appeal or reference arising out of an order made under section 104.

The assessee was carrying on business of executing contracts for the Government. He received gross amounts of bills amounting to Rs. 4,93,995 for the assessment year 1964-65 and Rs. 4,43,982 for the assessment year 1965-66 from the Government. As the assessee did not maintain any books of account, the ITO applied net profit rate of 12.6 per cent on the gross bill amounts received by the assessee in each of the two years under consideration and computed the total income for the two years. The assessee being aggrieved by the said order filed appeals before the AAC and contended that the cost of the materials supplied by the Government should have been deducted before applying the net profit rate and that there was no element of profit in the cost of materials supplied. The AAC found that the Government had supplied cement, iron rods, etc., costing Rs. 1,44,408 and Rs. 1,99,383 in the respective two years under consideration and held that the assessee did earn profits on the cost of materials supplied because certain materials were supplied by the Government from the market at the prevailing prices.

On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order of the AAC.

On reference :

Two persons 'S' and B constituted an unregistered firm sharing the profits and losses in the proportion of 9-as and 7-as respectively. The business, of which the profits and gains were the subject of assessment, consisted of aerodrome work under the Central Public Works Department, certain katcha building constructions under the Military Engineering Service and small supply of potatoes to Garrison Engineer. During the accounting year 1942-43, the assessee received a sum of Rs. 2,92,256. During the next year, that is 1-4-1943 to 31-3-1944, they received a sum of Rs. 86,434 and during the following accounting year of 1-4-1944 to 31-3-1945, they received a sum of Rs. 25,703. Besides it appeared, there were certain estimated outstanding bills to the credit of the assessee which had been excluded from assessment. On firm's failure to produce, books of account, the ITO took the sum total of the above sums received in course of three years, that is Rs. 4,54,948, as the basis of his assessment. He deducted the income at Rs. 1,18,975, on the ratio of 40 per cent, a flat rate on the gross receipts. Deducting the excess profits tax of Rs. 1,13,317 the assessable income was set at Rs. 65,659 which was reduced by the AAC by a sum of Rs. 28,270 by way of rectification of an error in calculation of Rs. 24,270 and deducting the profits of Rs. 4,000 representing 40 per cent of the estimated outstanding bills. The AAC, on appeal, came to the conclusion that since it was a question of determination of that year's income, in the absence of account books and since this was the first assessment in the case, the proviso to section 13 came into operation and no question of cash basis could arise.

The Tribunal, however, thought that in the circumstances of the case, the ITO should have applied the rate of profit to the annual receipts instead of to the total receipts and that by amalgamating the receipts under one assessment the ITO raised the tax liability of the assessee which was not fair. The Tribunal, therefore, set aside the basis of the said assessment and remanded the case back to the ITO to assess the income on the basis of the receipts during each year.

On the question of the flat rate, the Tribunal reduced the estimate of 40 per cent to 30 per cent.

On reference :

The assessee-firm which was engaged in the work of civil construction in public works department, filed returns for the assessment years 1993-94 to 1997-98. The Assessing Officer on the analogy of section 44AD, after rejecting the books of account, made best judgment assessment determining 8 per cent profit at flat rate. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) reduced the rate of profit from 8 per cent to 5 per cent, mainly on the ground that since the turnover of the assessee exceeded Rs. 40 lakhs, it was bound to incur more expenses and rate of profit would be less. On further appeal, the Tribunal reduced the rate of profit to 4 per cent on the ground that the assessee was doing the work for PWD and normally the net profit rate was much less for the work of PWD, as the contract work had to be done under certain specifications and under the supervision of the PWD authorities.

On appeal :

During the relevant previous year, the assessee, a cable work contractor, had executed various contracts in the names of various concerns and received labour contract receipts. In the course of the assessment, the Assessing Officer determined the total income of the assessee at Rs. 50.95 lakhs as against declared by the assessee at Rs. 1.82 lakhs. While computing the assessee's income, the Assessing Officer had adopted the net profit rate of 30 per cent on gross labour contract receipts. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the assessment order and directed the Assessing Officer to re-decide the correct quantum of receipts after considering the explanation of the assessee. Further, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed the Assessing Officer to adopt the net profit rate of 15 per cent of labour contract receipts for completing the set aside assessment. Against the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) in respect of adopting 15 per cent of the labour contract receipts as profit as against 30 per cent of the gross receipts adopted by the Assessing Officer, the Department filed an appeal before the Tribunal. Meanwhile, the Assessing Officer completed the set aside assessment under section 143, read with section 250, adopting 15 per cent of the gross receipts as net profit. In said proceedings, the Assessing Officer found that the assessee had concealed the particulars of income by way of not declaring certain receipts of labour contract. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer initiated the penalty proceedings under section 271(1)(c) by issue of notice under section 274, read with section 271(1)(c), directing the assessee to submit his explanation with regard to concealing the particulars of income and also for furnishing inaccurate particulars of income. The assessee's explanation included lack of knowledge of law, blame on the CA and the main contractors, etc. The Assessing Officer rejected the assessee's explanation and imposed penalty under section 271(1)(c). In the meantime, the Tribunal passed order in quantum appeal directing the Assessing Officer to adopt 6 per cent of gross contract receipts as the net profit in place of 15 per cent. Thus, on appeal filed by the assessee in the penalty proceedings, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the imposition of penalty but at the same time he directed the Assessing Officer to impose penalty at the rate of 200 per cent of the tax on the income which must be estimated at the rate of 6 per cent of the gross receipts in tune with the order of the Tribunal.

On cross appeals :

The assessee, a railway contractor, was in the field of conversion of old traditional signaling system to the modern colour light signaling system for various divisions of Indian Railways It was also manufacturing railway signaling equipments. The accounts maintained by the assessee were audited by the firm of Chartered Accountants. The assessee returned income which stood revised within the statutory period.

The Assessing Officer noticed that the assessee did not maintain stock register, site-wise expenses vouchers, payment vouchers and attendance or labour control register. Since true profits could not be deduced from the books of account of the assessee, he after applying provisions of section 145(3), estimated its income by applying gross profit rate at 8 per cent and, thus, made trading addition.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the rejection of books of account but directed the Assessing Officer to apply net profit rate of 7 per cent on gross contract receipts and sustained addition accordingly following earlier decision of Tribunal in assessee's own case.

On second appeal:

The assessee-company had undertaken a project of construction of a multi-storeyed building. For the assessment years 1981-82 to 1983-84, it had realised certain amounts as the sale proceeds of a few flats. However, the assessee had filed ‘nil’ return for all the three years on the plea that in the case of a building contractor the profits should not be assessed on year-to-year basis and the ascertainment of the profit could be done only after the contract work was completed. The Assessing Officer, however, was of the view that the method of accounting followed by the assessee being defective and incomplete, did not lead to the correct computation of income. According to him, the assessee would put on credit side any amount in order to bring the profit to ‘nil’. The scheme and structure of the Income-tax Act, read with the Finance Act is to make the tax an annual tax for the purpose of assessment. Section 3 makes each "previous year" a distinct unit of time for the purpose of assessment and the profits made before or after that unit of time are entirely immaterial in assessing the profits of that year. If section 3 is read in the context of section 13, it is clear that the accounts maintained by the assessee must correctly show or reflect the profits of the preceding year. If the method of accounting adopted by the assessee does not reflect the true profits of the preceding year the proviso to section 13 will apply and the ITO would be entitled to compute the profits upon such basis and in such manner as he may determine.

In the case of a contractor, it cannot be said that merely because of incompleteness of the contract in the relevant accounting year profits of the assessee for that accounting year cannot be ascertained. It also cannot be said that merely because a contract was completed after the accounting year, no profit arose or accrued to the assessee in the accounting year. In the case of an incomplete contract there is a well-established method of calculating profits accruing in the accounting year.

In the instant case, the Tribunal had found that for the assessment years 1939-40 and 1940-41 no accounts were kept for the contract the assessee had executed. For the assessment year 1943-44 he wrote a letter to the Income-tax Officer and admitted that he had no accounts to produce. For the assessment year 1944-45 he produced two sets of accounts. One was maintained for the two contracts he had taken from PWD but the profits of each contact was not separately worked out and there was one consolidated receipts and payments account for both the contracts. For the military contract he kept a separate set of accounts. These accounts were maintained from 14-4-1943 to 3-12-1944. The total value of contract was Rs. 3,78,766 and out of this the assessee received of Rs. 3,00,000 before 31-3-1944. He did not close the accounts on 31-3-1944, or prepare balance sheet but the accounts were kept open till 3-12-1944, when the execution of the contract was completed. It was argued on behalf of the assessee that the account are maintained on completed contract basis and the assessee had no objection if the income of the Hospital contract was taxed for the assessment year 1945-46 and that there was a single and indivisible contract for the Hospital and the work upon the entire contract was completed on 3-12-1944, and that was the proper date on which the profits should be ascertained. This argument was not acceptable if accounts are maintained and completed on contract basis the profits or gains of the previous year cannot properly be extracted from these accounts. For a contract may take several years for being completed. The payments in regard to the contract may also be received by the assessee in several years. It may be convenient for the assessee that profit should be ascertained on the completion of the contract and assessment of the profit should take place on the date of the completion of the contract. But section 3 imposes a charge of income-tax upon the profits and gains accruing to the assessee for the accounting year and it is the duty of the Income-tax authorities to make ascertainment of such profits and gains accruing to the assessee in respect of the payment received during the accounting year. Since the accounts maintained by the assessee did not correctly reflected the profits of the assessee for the accounting year the Tribunal was right in holding that the proviso to section 13 applied and that the ITO was entitled to discard the accounting method of the assessee and instead to make computation of the profits on such basis as he thought fit.

As regards the objection that the estimate of income on this formula would still be an estimate and would not be mathematically accurate, mathematical certainty is not demanded in a matter of this description.

The proviso to section 13 had been rightly applied by the Tribunal in regard to the accounts maintained for the contract business, which were not closed to profit at the end of each previous year but were closed to profit only after the completion of a contract.

It is true that there is no res judicata in the income-tax law and that the ITO has authority to take a different view from what has been taken in an earlier year. But neither he can exercise this authority in caprice, nor has he an unrestricted, unlimited, unconditional or absolute right in this matter. It was undisputed that the ITO had completed the assessments of the assessee’s income for the assessment years 1978-79 to 1981-82 on a flate rate basis observing, inter alia, that in the absence of maintenance of vouchers and receipts for the expenditure incurred by the assessee, the books of account were not acceptable. Now to examine whether the books of account kept in all the years inclusive of the year under appeal were maintained in the same manner or not, the trading and profit and loss accounts were the best available guide on which one should rely. There was no difference in the manner in which they had been kept in any of the assessment years inclusive of the assessment year under appeal. However, it was strange that though the assessee was a big contractor and executions of many of the contracts were spread in these years, no work-in-progress or closing stock had been recorded in the trading account. In view of the circumstances, it was not possible for the ITO to presume that the true profit could be computed on the basis of the books of account. He had overlooked the orders for the assessment years 1978-79 to 1981-82 framed by his predecessors. As a matter of fact, his finding was not very much different. He had also overlooked his own letter dated 16-2-1985 addressed to the assessee. Accordingly, the reasoning of the ITO to change the mode of assessment could not be accepted and the estimate of profit at a flat rate method as adopted in earlier years in the same circumstances should also apply in the assessment year under appeal, except that, in view of the finding that a large amount of expenses claimed was unestablished, the profit rate to be applied should be 12½ per cent instead of 10 per cent adopted for the earlier years.

The profit in a long-term contract should be taxed on year-to-year basis. It is a dangerous proposition to recognise that the profit accrues only after the completion of a contract, Such a proposition is liable to be abused by dishonest taxpayers. It is a judicially recognised proposition that in the case of a contract in order to ascertain the income one need not wait till the contract is completed and that it is open to the revenue to estimate the profit on the basis of receipts in each year of construction, although the contract is not complete.

Section 3 makes each previous year a distinct unit of time for the purpose of assessment and the profits made before or after that unit of time are entirely immaterial in assessing the profits of that year. In the case of contracts, if accounts are maintained and completed on contract basis, the profits or gains of the previous year can not properly be extracted from the accounts, for a contract may take several years for being completed and payment in regard to it may also be received by the assessee in several years. It may be convenient from the point of view of the assessee that profit should be ascertained on the completion of the contract and assessment of the profit should take place after the completion of the contract. But section 3 imposes a charge of income-tax upon the profits and gains of the assessee for the accounting year and it is the duty of the ITO to ascertain the profits and gains accruing to the assessee in respect of the payment received during the accounting year. It cannot be said that merely because a contract is completed after the accounting year, no profit arises or accrues to the assessee in the accounting year. In the case of an incomplete contract, there is a well-established method of calculating profits accruing in the accounting year. In such a contract, the long-term contract method is adopted in respect of contracts which have to be completed by stages over a course of years, such as, building contracts or building schemes by co- operative or private enterprise, or contracts entered into with public authorities such as public works, military, etc. The ascertainment of the profit in the execution of such contracts cannot be deferred till the completion of the entire constructions which may take several years. Each year’s profit shall have to be, in the nature of things, computed on an estimate, having regard to the work completed during the year. There are recognised methods of estimating with reasonable accuracy the profits accrued from time to time on uncompleted contracts. The fact that the contracts have not been completed or the accounts thereof have not been closed, is not sufficient reason for not estimating the profit of each year though absolute accuracy may not be reached. Thus, in a contract running over several years, the entire profits cannot be attributed to a single last year in which the contract was completed. The fact that it is not convenient or easy to allocate receipts or expendi- ture as against various items of trading assets is no reason for uphold- ing that profits emerge only after the entire expenditure on the assets has been recouped; the allocation of expenditure and receipts must somehow be made on a reasonable basis and the debts and trading assets valued on the closing date. In such cases, a workable method is for the revenue to assess on the basis of gross receipts of each year at a flat rate of profit on such receipts. The assessment in the case of a building

contractor, therefore, need not be postponed till the completion of the contract.

If the profits could reasonably be arrived at from year to year, such profit should be assessed from year to year only. In the instant case, the assessee had not correctly valued the closing work-in-progress and, therefore, it was the duty of the Assessing Officer to correctly value the closing work-in-progress: and arrive at the true picture of the profit. Thus, in the case of a building contractor, the revenue need not wait till the completion of the contract and the reasonable profit can be estimated from year to year and brought to tax.

Regarding the estimate of profits at 8 per cent there was no material on record to show that the estimate of profit at 8 per cent was excessive and unreasonable having regard to the facts of the case. However, the profit at 8 per cent estimated for these three years was only a mere estimate and the true profit of the entire project would be arrived at when the contract was complete. The assessee was, therefore, entitled to the adjustment of profit or loss in the year of completion of the contract. Hence, the estimate of profit at 8 per cent was reasonable.

It is no doubt true that in the case of a contractor, work-in-progress has to be brought into accounts in order to show the profits earned in respect of the work turned out and the profit embedded in the receipts received during the year. The concept of bringing to accounts the work-in-progress is no different from the concept of bringing into accounts the closing in the case of a trader or a manufacturer. But unlike the case of a trader or a manufacturer, in the case of a contractor the workin-progress cannot be exactly arrived at with reference to any particular books because there are so many components which go to make up the work-in-progress and which have to be estimated. Therefore, estimate in arriving at the work-in progress was necessary and there was bound to be certain amount of approximation and guess work. Merely on the ground that the work-in-progress is estimated, it cannot be said that the book results were not to be accepted and that proviso to section 145 is applicable unless it is shown that the work-in-progress was arrived in such a way as to be too far from reality. In the instant case, the ITO attempted to prove the unreliability of the amount of work-in-progress arrived at by pointing out that the closing stock ought to have been Rs. 3,82,000 as against Rs. 1 lakh shown by the assessee. The basis for this was the assumption that normally the advance was given at 75 per cent of the material lying at site. There was no basis for this assumption nor any figure were given to show that this hypothesis could be accepted as correct. It was mere ipsi dixit of the ITO, without any basis to support it. The advance could be given at 75 per cent. It could be more, it could be less. This was, therefore, a surmise and conjecture.

As regards the receipts, following the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Brij Bhushan Lal Parduman Kumar v. CIT [1978] 115 ITR 524 , in the instant case, the value of the material supplied by the Government must be excluded. So the balance of receipts should come to only Rs. 14.63 lakhs shown by the assessee. The estimate of the income at Rs. 1,50,000 on those receipts of Rs. 14.63 lakhs would work out to about 10.4 per cent. In none of the previous years, the assessee had shown such a high rate of profit nor had the department estimated the profit at such a rate nor the books of account were ever rejected. The previous results are only the points of reference, in relation to which the results of subsequent years are to be judged and reasons for variations are investigated. The range of profit would be discernible from the previous records. The lowest rate of net profit rate shown and accepted by the department was 2.8 per cent. In the immediately preceding assessment year rate of net profit shown and accepted was 2.75 per cent and the gross profit was 11.75 per cent. The estimate made by the ITO in the year in question of the profit at 10.5 per cent was very excessive and unreasonable. The ITO had not shown the basis for determining the income of Rs. 1,50,000. It is now the settled law that whenever estimates of income are resorted to in order that they are not arbitrary, unreasonable and unjustified, the ITO must show the basis on which and the method by which and the manner in which the estimate was made. These are the safeguards provided to act as an insurance against arbitrary estimates. None of these guidelines settled by the law of the land was disclosed by the ITO except leaving one to infer that because of the variations in the closing stock, he determined to fix the income at Rs. 1,50,000. Therefore, the estimate made by the ITO was not justified.

A fair estimate of the income has to be made. Further, the Jurisdictional High Court held that Guesswork is inevitable; but, it cannot be wild guess; the guesswork should have a reasonable nexus to the available material and the circumstances of each case. In the instant case, the ITO arrived at the figure on the basis of the receipts extending over three accounting year. He took the sum total of these receipts to be the base for the net income that had accrued to the assessee during the accounting year 1943-44 as the entire contract work had been completed during that year. Mere execution of the contract work will not necessarily entitle the contractor to make a demand for payment until it is ascertained that the works are up to the standard agreed upon between the parties. Some parts of such work may be wholly rejected and like bad debts in every earning may be ignored in computing the gains or profits. It might have been open to the ITO, in exercise of his discretion, to make an enquiry into whether and when the bills for payment became due to the assessee. Much depended upon the terms in the contract, and the manner of its performance. Even as a basis of guess work, which the Income-tax Officer was entitled to do, the basis could not be said to be in consonance with honest guess work. The ITO did not seem to have taken into consideration why the payments which, according to him, were due to the assessee in the accounting year were not fully paid till three years after. Sometimes the payments to the contractors are withheld on account of unsatisfactory execution and they are held entitled to payments only if and when they replace the rejected work by acceptable and accepted ones. The bare possibility of such contingency could not be wholly eliminated in the instant case. If the ITO, in arriving at the figure for assessment, left out these considerations, he certainly could not be said to have exercised his judgment which he was none the less called upon to do in making the assessment in cases of assessee's default under sections 23(4) and 13 proviso of the 1922 Act. Any method of accounting adopted by the ITO acting under the proviso of section 13 of 1922 Act can be rejected if the method in fact does not show the true income, profits and gains. In this view of the matter, the Appellate Tribunal was right in asking the ITO to assess the assessee on receipt basis with regard to contracts carried out and completed during the year of accounting, there being every presumption that the incomes were paid as soon as they became due. At any rate, the Tribunal's decision might be upheld on the ground that when two methods of guess work are available for the purpose of assessment, the one which is more just to the assessee and which involves a much less margin of chance of uncertainty should be taken as the basis.

In the result, the Tribunal was right in asking the ITO to assess the assessee on receipts basis with regard to contracts carried on and completed during the year of account.

Their opinions were not receivable evidence in the instant case. The decisions in different cases must have been based upon different facts and different inferences deducible from such facts. In this connection, it might be observed that the ITO had been very fair to the assessee bearing in mind the difference between the gross value and net value of the bills. The Appellate Tribunal, therefore, did commit a mistake of law in arriving at a finding for which there was no relevant evidence to support.

Therefore, the reduction of the estimated profit rate from 40 per cent adopted by the ITO to 30 per cent by the Tribunal on the ground that 30 per cent was the general rate adopted by it in the cases of other assessees doing the same kind of contract works during the same assessment year was not legal.

As per provisions of section 158BB, the block assessment is to be made based on evidence before the Assessing Officer. The word 'Evidence' has to be construed in a comprehensive manner and it includes all circumstantial evidence also. The material or evidence with the Assessing Officer on which assessment may be based is not confined to direct testimony by witnesses. Such evidence need not only be evidence found during the course of search but also material gathered by him. The Assessing Officer was not fettered by the Technical rules of evidence and the like and he may act on material which may not strictly speaking, be accepted as an evidence in the Court of law. It may be circumstantial evidence or assessment based on the preponderance of probabilities judged by human conduct. For this purpose, the past history of the case, and general market conditions will constitute relevant material for the purpose of assessment. For the purpose of block assessment under Chapter XIV-B, in view of amendment by Finance Act, 2002 to section 158BC(b) of the Income-tax Act which is effective retrospectively from 1-7-1995 wherein there is insertion of section 145 for the purpose of determining the undisclosed income. As per amendment to section 158BC(b ), the section 145 could also be invoked by Assessing officer for determining the undisclosed income. [Para 37]

However, it is to be made clear that if no material was found during the search which could show suppression of income, no estimation of undisclosed income of block period by resorting to section 145 could be made. In other words, where there is a material, such an estimation of income can be made. It is not necessary that addition should be limited to what is found during the search. [Para 38]

Adverting to the facts of the instant case, assessment was made by applying the flat rate of net profit at the rate of 10 per cent for the Assessment years 1998-99 and 1999-2000 for which no reasons has been given except stating that considering the nature of contract works executed by the assessee-company and the percentage of income admitted for the assessment years 1996-97, 1997-98 and 2000-01 and also for the percentage of income admitted by other contractors viz., M/s Prasad & Co. (PW) and M/s SEW Construction Ltd., income was estimated before depreciation at the rate of 10 per cent for the assessment years 1998-99, 1999-2000, 2001-02 and for the period 1-4-2001 to 20-12-2001 and treated the difference of income estimated and the income admitted as undisclosed income of the assessee-company for such assessment year. The Commissioner (Appeals) though held that for the assessment year 1998-99, income declared at the rate of 9.08 per cent before depreciation and 8.5 per cent for the assessment year 1999-2000 as reasonable. However, he has given different finding for the assessment year 2001-02 and for the period from 1-4-2001 to 20-12-2001. The assessee explained the reasons for low profit as to that the company has been in the construction industry for more than two decades. The company for quite some years focused its core activity in civil works consisting of mostly industrial/housing structures. Besides such civil contracts, the company diversified its activities into cement industry, wind power, manufacture of cylinders and other incidental jobs. Heavy losses resulted in closure of its cement division during financial year 1999-2000. The company also started focusing on infrastructure projects because of its line of business in construction and contracts. Hence, in the initial years, the company had undertaken some of the smaller projects especially the road works outside the State of Andhra Pradesh. To intrude into the competitive section like this, and to withstand the obvious competition from the established giants and multinationals, obviously the company had to quote the price in tenders either without a profit or with nominal profit. During the financial years 2000-01 and 2001-02 (up to 31-12-2001) the company has incurred losses in certain major projects. [Para 39]

It was clear from the narration of the facts hereinabove set out that the books of account were not found reliable and correct by the ITO. Under section 145(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, since the ITO was not satisfied about the correctness or the completeness of the accounts of the assessee, he could make an assessment in the manner provided in section 144. Section 144 provides for best judgment assessment and it enables the ITO, after taking into account all relevant material which he has gathered, to make the assessment of the total income or loss to the best of his judgment and determine the sum payable by the assessee or refundable to the assessee on the basis of such assessment. Thus, section 144 provides for best judgment assessment and if the conditions mentioned in section 145(2) are satisfied, as they were satisfied in the instant case, the best judgment assessment could be made by the ITO.

It must be pointed out that the best judgment assessment referred to in section 144 is regarding the figure of income, which, in the opinion of the ITO, is the proper figure of income and he makes the assessment of the total income to the best of his judgment after taking into account all relevant material which he has gathered.

It might be mentioned at the outset that, in the instant case, as shown by the material papers filed, it was obligatory on the part of the assessee to obtain the cement required for the work from the railway authorities on the conditions laid down in the contract and that bazaar cement was not allowed to be used.

Certificates issued by railway engineers did indicate exactly how the contract was entered into and on what basis the railway authorities and the assessee dealt with each other. It was clear that, if the ITO had to assess the income of the assessee to the best of his judgment and since, in the instant case, he had to arrive at the figure of profits or gains from the business of the assessee to the best of his judgment he must arrive at the figure of profits which the assessee was said to have earned from his contract with the railway authorities. The very fact that some materials, viz., cement, iron and steel, were to be supplied by the railway authorities and it was not open to the assessee-contractor, to purchase cement, iron and steel from outside or to use cement, iron and steel other than those supplied by the railway authorities, clearly showed that these items could never have entered into the making of profit by the assessee. It could not be said that the cement, iron and steel supplied by the railway authorities contributed to the profit made by the assessee. The question, therefore, arose as to whether, it could be said that the cost of materials in cases like the instant one must be excluded before the profits were ascertained on the best judgment assessment.

The facts and circumstances of each case would determine as to whether the cost of materials can or cannot be taken into consideration in determining the profits of a particular contractor on the best judgment assessment basis. It must be borne in mind that what the ITO has to determine is the profit of the assessee and the question whether the assessee was not maintaining his accounts properly. The question was of determining the profits which the assessee could be said to have earned and if the cost of materials supplied by the department concerned was never intended to contribute to the profits earned or to be earned by the contractor, and, in fact, had not resulted in any profit for the assessee, it was difficult to understand how the cost of materials supplied by the other party to the contract could be taken into consideration for estimating the profit earned by the contractor.

Therefore, on the facts and in the circumstances of this case, it was held that the value of the materials supplied by the railway authorities could not be taken into consideration for estimating the net income for the assessment years 1964-65 to 1967-68. Hence, the Tribunal was justified in law in giving directions to the AAC that the value of the materials supplied by the railway authorities should not be taken into consideration for estimating the net income for the assessment years 1964-65 to 1967-68.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

Assessee's books of account stand rightly rejected by Assessing officer

The assessee is admittedly not maintaining any stock register, so that there is no basis to verify the material consumption, which constitutes a very significant part of its operating cost. Not only that, it is admittedly following the 'method' of writing off its purchases for the year to the operating statement, treating the same as consumed. Now there is no basis to state that the material is actually consumed as soon as it is purchased, or that the assessee maintains no inventory thereof. The accounts as maintained are thus admittedly inconsistent with the actual, obtaining state of affairs, which the books of account of any entity or enterprise are supposed to reflect. There is no basis whatsoever, either in law or in accountancy; the law only upholding the accepted principles of commercial accounting, for the said concocted and/or arbitrary method of accounting being followed by the assessee. That the method has been followed from year to year, does not in any manner mitigate the defect, or justify its adoption. The assessee's books of account, as maintained, are thus not amenable to yielding correct operating results, so that the same stand rightly not accepted by Assessing Officer, applying section 145(3). [Para 3.1]

Continuing further, there is no basis in the Assessing Officer's estimation of material consumption at 36 per cent. Equally unjustifiable is his separate addition toward closing stock, which arises as a by-product to the finding of an actual lower material consumption. In fact, neither any separate addition can be sustained nor there is any warrant for allowing the assessee, as claimed by it, credit for the closing stock. The assessee would also have, similarly, opening stock, which has to be necessarily taken into account in determining the profit of the year. In fact, the opening stock being taken at nil, i.e., the value of the closing stock as reflected and accepted for the immediately preceding year, no opening stock for the year could be taken without first sustaining an addition toward the same under section 69/69A. [Para 3.2]

Presumptive statutory rate under section 44AD provides a good guideline for estimation of income

Section 145(3) mandates for making the assessment in the manner as provided in section 144, i.e., according to the best judgment of the assessing authority, taking all the relevant material into account. The assessee has relied on case law, i.e., Kesharbhai Ghamarbhai Chaudhary v. ITO [2012] 23 taxmann.com 273 (Ahd.), to the effect that under the circumstance of rejection of books of account, the prescription of section 44AE; the assessee in that case being a transport operator, is a good guideline for the purpose of estimation of income. The presumptive provision in the case of civil contractors is section 44AD, which provides for a net profit rate of 8 per cent. The matter is purely factual, though the prescribed presumptive statutory rate, applicable for assessees with a turnover of up to Rs. 40 lakh, without doubt provides a good guideline. The Apex Court in Brij Bushan Lal Parduman Kumar v. CIT [1978] 115 ITR 524 approved a profit rate of 10 per cent. The Tribunal has in such cases upheld profit rates varying from 8 per cent upwards to as much as 20 per cent, or even higher. A net profit rate of 10 per cent on the assessee's contract receipt of Rs. 360.86 lakh, i.e., involving material consumption, would be a reasonable estimate. Qua its labour receipt of Rs. 82.95 lakh, a net profit rate of 20 per cent, in view of a much lower base, as appropriate under the given facts and circumstances of the case. The Assessing Officer is directed to work out the assessee's income for the year by applying the said percentages. No other addition is sustainable. [Para 3.3]

In the instant case, the assessee contractor had not been able to satisfy the lower authorities as to what were the terms of the contract with the contractee and in what terms and consideration the materials were supplied by the contractee to the contractor. Furthermore, in the instant case the total amount of profit had to be computed by applying the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act. The rate of profit had also to be determined by applying the proviso to section 13 of the 1922, Act. As the Tribunal had pointed out that if the normal experience and expectation of a contractor as to how the profit would vary, were taken into consideration and in the circumstances where the contractor had not been actually able to satisfy the terms of the contract and where the estimates were to be based by applying the provisions to section 13 of the 1922 Act, it could not be said that the Tribunal was not justified in upholding the decision of the AAC in the manner as it did. In cases where there was clear and unambiguous evidence that there was contract which provided sufficient limit, beyond which the tender could not be quoted and there was a stipulation that the contract was to be quoted at a particular rate, excluding the cost of materials, to be supplied by the contractee, other considerations might apply.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

In the instant case there was material before the Tribunal on which its finding could be based: the assessee's representative had admitted before the AAC that full quantitative details in respect of the stores of the value of Rs. 1,30,000 consumed in the execution of that contract might not be available. In the circumstances, recourse to estimating the profits on the contract was inevitable. He, therefore, made an addition of Rs. 10,000 as against Rs. 26,434 added by the ITO. If the assessee wished to displace the AAC's estimate it was open to him to adduce evidence in support of its claim that the consumption of stores of the value of Rs. 1,30,000 was fully justified. This the assessee apparently did not do. For the subsequent year 1960-61 the assessee itself declared a net profit rate of 9.9% as against 9% declared in the assessment year in question. It could not be disputed that this was additional material which the Tribunal could take into consideration as it did. There was thus material before the Tribunal on which its estimate was based. The Tribunal's decision was, therefore, in conformity with the decision in the case of CIT v. Maharajadhiraj of Darbhanga [1933] 1 ITR 94 (P.C.).

The Tribunal was therefore justified in holding that the proviso to section 13 was applicable and there was material before it to sustain the aforesaid addition.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of revenue.

The Tribunal on various dates directed the assessee to file details of the length of road, quantity of store and grit and basis of evidence for consumption of the raw material and the details of the sales-tax and TDS certificate issued on that account. The assessee could not give evidence regarding the consumption of the dalla grit in the construction of the road, but applying the test of human probabilities to the explanation and the material on record and that the books account had not been rejected and that the assessee had also filed audit report showed that considerable purchases of raw material were used in the construction of the road, but it was difficult to arrive at definite conclusion about exact consumption of raw material in the absence of specific evidence. It was also established fact from the past history of the assessee that in the preceding years and subsequent years, income of the assessee was computed and assessed by the department on the basis of estimation by applying the net profit rate of 8 per cent to 8.25 per cent and the matters had become final.
