1.3 Section 44AC (as existed prior to assessment year 1993-94), which deemed a certain amount of profits related to purchase price, as assessable profits from the business of trading in certain goods, was challenged, inter alia, on a ground that the provisions raised a conclusive presumption of law that the assessee will make a net taxable income of the specified amount and this presumption was not allowed to be rebutted. The Kerala High Court upheld the vires of the provisions in T.K Aboobacker v. Union of India [1989] 177 ITR 358. The Andhra Pradesh High Court in A. Sanyasi Rao v. Government of Andhra Pradesh [1989] 178 ITR 31 held the provisions to be constitutional by reading it down and observing that it would be upon assessee to prove in the assessment proceedings his real assessable income.

The new provisions incorporate a provision permitting a rebuttal of the presumption. Accordingly, it is felt that the new provisions may stand the test, in case of a challenge of its vires.

Applicability of the new provisions

1.4 The new provisions are applicable to all assessees, irrespective of the residential status or the status as a person or whether old or new assessee.

Thus, the new provisions would apply to:

■ resident as well as non-resident assessees;

■ all categories of persons, corporate or non-corporate (including a firm or a trust or an AOP or a BOI); and

■ whether new or old assessees, (that is, an assessee already engaged in the specified business or proposing to engage in the specified business as also a person who is presently liable to tax or not).

1.4-1 Applicability of New Provisions in case of Civil Construction business - Explanation to section 44AD, for the purpose of the New Provisions, explains 'Civil Construction' inclusively as:

■ Construction or repair of any building, bridge, dam or other structure or of any canal or road ('specified structure'); and

■ The execution of any 'works contract'.

The expression 'civil construction', as such, is not defined or explained but, apparently, has been used as nomenclature for grouping certain activities as part of the Civil Construction business.

The expression 'civil construction', as such, does not have any technical meaning. In the common parlance, it is expressed to connote or denote certain activity relating to construction of any building, bridge, etc., and works relating thereto as distinct from mechanical engineering or electrical engineering, etc. In the common parlance, it relates to creation of a structure made up of RCC or any other materials and related work (which imparts functional capability to the structure).

To comprehend the meaning of the expression 'civil construction', as well as to ascertain which types of activities would be considered as part of Civil Construction business, one may consider dictionary meaning of certain words used in the Explanation, namely:

CHAPTER ONE

Introduction

1.1 The Finance Act, 1994 inserts two new sections - 44AD and 44AE - in the Income-tax Act, 1961 ('the Act") to extend the concept of 'estimated/deemed income', for determination of profits and gains of the business of Civil Construction or Transport.

The objectives of the New Provisions are:

■ simplification;

■ minimizing compliance cost; and

■ minimizing undue harassment to tax payers.

The new provisions have been justified on two grounds:

■ Such a method is prevalent in several countries; and

■ Tax Reforms Committee has recommended gradual introduction of the method.

The above provisions come into force from the assessment year 1994-95 and thus, have a retrospective effect for the previous year ended on 31-3-1994.

Provisions in brief

1.2 Following points need be noted:

■ Sections 44AD and 44AE ('the New Provisions') are applicable to all assessees engaged in the business of Civil Construction and/or Transport ('the specified business').

■ 'Civil Construction' business, as defined, will include the construction or repairs of buildings, dams, bridges, or other structures or roads or canals. It will also include the execution of any works contract.

■ ‘Transport Business' covers the business of plying, hiring or leasing of goods carriages owned by the assessee.

The scheme is optional. A person can claim that his income in respect of the specified business is lower than the specified profit. He must produce necessary evidence to prove his case in the course of scrutiny and/or regular assessment. Constitutional validity of the new provisions

1.3 Section 44AC (as existed prior to assessment year 1993-94), which deemed a certain amount of profits related to purchase price, as assessable profits from the business of trading in certain goods, was challenged, inter alia, on a ground that the provisions raised a conclusive presumption of law that the assessee will make a net taxable income of the specified amount and this presumption was not allowed to be rebutted. The Kerala High Court upheld the vires of the provisions in T.K Aboobacker v. Union of India [1989] 177 ITR 358. The Andhra Pradesh High Court in A. Sanyasi Rao v. Government of Andhra Pradesh [1989] 178 ITR 31 held the provisions to be constitutional by reading it down and observing that it would be upon assessee to prove in the assessment proceedings his real assessable income.

The new provisions incorporate a provision permitting a rebuttal of the presumption. Accordingly, it is felt that the new provisions may stand the test, in case of a challenge of its vires.

Thus, the new provisions would apply to:

resident as well as non-resident assessees;

all categories of persons, corporate or non-corporate (including a firm or a trust or an AOP or a BOI); and

whether new or old assessees, (that is, an assessee already engaged in the specified business or proposing to engage in the specified business as also a person who is presently liable to tax or not).

3.10

Percentage of Completion Method (POCM)

ICDS-III (Revised) requires a contractor to offer incomes from construction contracts to tax in accordance with the "percentage of completion method"(POCM). The recognition of contract revenue and contract costs by reference to the stage of completion of a contract is referred to as the percentage of completion method. Under this method, contract revenue is matched with the contract costs incurred in reaching the stage of completion, resulting in the reporting of revenue, expenses and profit which can be attributed to the proportion of work completed. Paras 18 and 19 of ICDS-III(Revised) explain how% of stage of completion of a contract as at reporting date is to be determined. Para 20 provides that percentage of completion method is not required to be followed during the early stages of a contract i.e. in case of a contract which has reached 25% or less stage of completion. In cases of contracts in early stage, where the outcome of the contract cannot be estimated reliably contract revenue is recognised only to the extent of costs incurred. In other words, neither profit nor loss on contracts in early stages shall be recognised.

In Dy. CIT v. Sri Jagannath Properties & Developers decided by ITAT-Cuttack on 31.08.2018 in [ITA No. 283/CTK/2017] it was held that while applying POCM as per ICDS-III, the question whether stage of completion of 25% has been reached or not is to be reckoned project-wise(contract-wise) and not by taking all projects (contracts) together on overall basis and revenue can be recognised in only those projects(contracts) where stage of completion has reached 25%.

Thus, POCM is to be applied contract-wise. There is a concept in accounts called the concept of Contract Accounts. To know the results of his operations, the contractor prepares what is called as Contract Account which is debited with various costs and which is credited with the revenue associated with a particular contract. Under the POCM, reasonable profit is calculated on the basis of the value of the work certified and the profit attributable to the work certified. For example, if the value of the work certified is one-fourth or more but less than half of the contract price, then a certain percentage of the profit accruing to the certified work is taken to the profit and loss account [CIT, Meerut v. Hyundai Heavy Industries Co. Ltd. [2007] 161 Taxman 191 (SC)]. Thus, for each construction contract, a separate contract account is to be opened and the contract costs and contract revenues related to it have to be debited and credited to it with reference to% of stage of completion reached in all individual contracts which have progressed to more than 25%. Where progress is 25% or less, contract account will be debited only with contract costs incurred and credited with contract revenue equal to contract costs incurred and contract account will neither reflect a profit nor a loss.

[It is assumed that the above method measures reliably the work performed in the facts of the case] In the above method of estimating stage of completion, only those contract costs that reflect work performed are included in costs incurred upto the reporting date. Hence, the stage of completion for year 2 (74%) is determined by excluding from contract costs incurred for work performed upto the reporting date, Rs. 100 of standard materials stored at the site for use in year 3.

The percentage of completion method is to be applied on a cumulative basis in each accounting period to the current estimates of contract revenue and contract costs. POCM has to be applied to year 1 as the work performed has crossed the 25% stage.

For the purpose, one may consider the language of the provisions as well as certain illustrations and determine the effects of section 44AD(5), which reads as follow:

"Nothing contained in the foregoing provisions of this section shall apply where the assessee claims and produces evidence to prove ... and thereupon the Assessing Officer shall proceed to make an assessment... under sub-section (3) of section 143."

The New Provisions relating to assessment at specified amount or a higher amount would not apply, ... where the assessee claims and produces evidence to prove that the profits from the specified business are lower.

Thus, when a claim is made and evidence is produced, the provisions of normal assessment become applicable and thereafter whether the Assessing Officer accepts the same or not, as such, is of no consequence. In other words, once the claim for assessment at the lower profit is made, the New Provisions would not apply and the assessee would be governed by normal provisions and assessment at an amount higher than the specified amount is possible.

3.16-1 Advance Tax & Return - For the purposes of payment of advance tax the assessee will have to choose the option available for declaring his income, namely, the specified amount or higher amount or lower amount and accordingly pay the advance tax. The consequences of failure to pay advance tax or short payment of advance tax would follow as per normal provisions of the Act.

As discussed earlier, under sections 44AD and 44AE of the Act, presumptive tax is charged in case of construction business or transport business. ◆ Further, as said above, the department would be bound to assess the assessee on the specified amount for assessing the tax liability.

1.5-2 In case of transport business - Computation provisions are discussed below :

1.5-2a Profit computation linked with ownership period during the year -Section 44AE(1) provides:

"... in the case of an assessee who owns... and is engaged in the business... the income of such business... shall be deemed to be the aggregate of the profits and gains from all the goods carriage owned by him in the previous year, computed in accordance with the provisions of sub-section (2)." [Emphasis supplied]

Sub-section (2) reads as follows:

"for the purpose of sub-section (1), the profits and gains from each goods carriage—

(i)

being a heavy goods vehicle, shall be... for every month or part of a month during which the heavy goods vehicle is owned by the assessee in the previous year....;

(ii)

other than a heavy goods vehicle, shall be... for every month or part of a month during which the goods carriage is owned by the assessee in the previous year...." [Emphasis supplied]

A reading of the above provisions show that the profits computation has to be made in accordance with the period for which the goods carriage is owned during the previous year irrespective of the actual employment thereof in the business during the previous year. The memorandum explaining the provisions of the Finance Bill gives two illustrations, which are reproduced hereinbelow, which supports the above view, as well as explains the computation of profits for a part of the month:

"Illustration (1): An assessee owns a light commercial vehicle for 9 months 15 days, a medium goods vehicle for 9 months and a medium goods vehicle for 12 months during the previous year. His profits and gains from the three trucks shall be deemed to be (Rs. 1,800 × 10) + (Rs. 1,800 × 9) + (Rs. 1,800 × 12), i.e., Rs. 55,800.

Illustration (2) : An assessee owns a heavy goods vehicle for 9 months 7 days, a medium goods vehicle for 9 months and a light commercial vehicle for 12 months during the previous year. His profits and gains from the three trucks shall be deemed to be (Rs. 2,000 × 10) + (Rs. 1,800 × 9) + (Rs. 1,800 × "12), i.e., Rs. 57,800."

As per the illustrations, if a vehicle is owned even for 7 days, profits computation should be considered for a month.

As per section 2(30)of the Motor Vehicle Act, 1988 'owner' is defined as follows:

' "Owner" means a person in whose name a motor vehicle stands registered, and where such person is a minor, the guardian of such minor, and in relation to a motor vehicle which is the subject of a hire-purchase, agreement, or an agreement of lease or an agreement of hypothecation, the person in possession of the vehicle under that agreement';

In the context of the New Provisions it is felt that ownership should be construed in the same manner as construed for the purposes of section 32 of the Act.

Accordingly, it is felt that the date on which the Motor Vehicle is registered or person obtains possession of the vehicle, whichever is earlier, would be considered as the date from which the assessee should be regarded as an owner.

Section 44BBB

Finance Act, 2003

Presumptive taxation in case of non-residents [Sections 44BB and 44BBB]

2.3 Under sections 44BB and 44BBB ('the said sections'), business income of non-residents engaged in the business of :

providing services or facilities in connection with, or supplying plant and machinery on hire used, or to be used, in the prospecting for, or extraction or production of, mineral oils (section 44BB);

civil construction or erection or testing or commissioning of plant or machinery in connection with a turnkey power project approved by the Government and financed under any international aid programme (section 44BBB),

is deemed to be 10% of the aggregate amounts paid or payable to the non-resident (hereinafter referred to as 'presumptive basis' or 'presumptive basis of taxation').

The above sections have now been amended with effect from assessment year 2004-05 to provide that the assessees covered by these sections will have an option to compute their income on a net income basis [, i.e., income shall be computed according to the provisions of the Act] (hereinafter referred to as 'net income basis' or 'net income basis of taxation'), provided the assessee:

maintains prescribed books of account;

gets the books of account audited; and

furnishes a tax audit report under section 44AB.

It is further provided that once a claim is made by the assessee for being governed by the net income basis of taxation, the Assessing Officer shall proceed to make an assessment of the total income under section 143(3) of the Act and determine the sum payable by, or refundable to, the assessee.

Further the presumptive tax rate of 10 per cent under section 44BBB will be applicable in those turnkey power projects also which are not financed under any international aid programme.

Consequential changes have been made in sections 44AA and 44AB of the Act relating to maintenance of accounts and audit of accounts, respectively.

2.3-1 Option - The alternative to follow the net income basis as business income is optional and hence, an assessee can continue to compute the business income on presumptive basis. Even if the assessee has maintained books of account and obtained an audit report, he may still opt to be governed by taxation on presumptive basis by not making the claim of being taxed on net income basis in the return of income.

2.3-2 Delay in filing the tax audit report - One of the pre-conditions for being governed by net income basis of taxation is that the assessee should furnish a tax audit report as required under section 44AB of the Act. Now, section 44AB of the Act provides that the tax audit report should be furnished on or before 31st October of the assessment year. Hence, on a strict literal interpretation, it appears that for the purpose of sections 44BB(3) and 44BBB(2) of the Act, the tax audit report has to be furnished before the said date and any delay may disentitle the assessee from making the claim to be governed by net income basis of taxation.

2.3-3 Loss - The sections provide that the Assessing Officer can make an assessment of the total income or loss. Such loss can be set off in accordance with the provisions of section 70 of the Act and carried forward and set off in accordance with provisions of section 72 of the Act. It appears that such carry forward loss can be set off against any business income, including presumptive income of the subsequent year, if the assessee decides to be so governed in that year.

2.3-4 Computation of income - In case the assessee opts to be governed by net basis of taxation, the computation of business income would be done by applying the provisions of sections 28 to 43B, including 40(a)(i), and also 44C of the Act. Further, the provisions of transfer pricing under sections 92 to 92F of the Act will also be applicable.

Application Guide-ICDS-III (Revised) - How to apply ICDS-III (Revised) in computation of income

This ICDS may be applied as under:

(a)

Identify each construction contract for which separate contract account needs to be opened.

(b)

Identification of each separate construction based on the definition of 'construction contract' [Para 3.5.] and combining and segmenting construction contracts in accordance with their substance [Paras 3.11 to 3.13]

(c)

The exercise in (a) and (b) above will serve dual purpose-for accounting as per AS) 7 and for computation of income as per section 43CB and this ICDS.

(d)

Apply percentage of completion method [Para 3.10] for each construction contract separately as per steps (e) to (p) below

(e)

Identify contract revenues and contract costs separately for each separate construction contract identified as above for which separate contract account has been opened. [Paras 3.14 to 3.35]

(f)

Determine stage of completion of each construction contract separately [Para 3.35-1]

(g)

Recognise contract costs and contract revenues with reference to% of completion for each construction contract which has crossed the 25% completion stage. Thus contract profit/contract loss would get recognised proportionate to% of completion. Add up such proportionate profits and losses and deduct period costs and other deductions from the aggregate of proportionate profits and losses to determine taxable income [Para 3.35-1]

(h)

If stage of completion of any construction contract is 25% or less, recognise contract costs already incurred and recognise contract costs equal to contract costs incurred [Para 3.35-1]

(i)

Where, on any contract which has crossed 25% stage of completion, full anticipated loss has been provided as per (AS) 7 instead of proportionate loss as per(g) above, make adjustment for the difference in computation of income in order to comply with ICDSs.

(j)

Where proportionate profit has not been recognised in accounts as per AS 7 in respect of a contract that has crossed 25% completion stage on the grounds that outcome of contract cannot be estimated reliably, add proportionate profit as per (g) above to net profit/loss as per P&L in computation of income.

(k)

Where on any contract which has not crossed 25% stage of completion full anticipated loss has been provided as per (AS) 7, make adjustment for the loss so provided in computation of income in order to comply with ICDSs.

(l)

Where proportionate profit was offered to tax in any past FY/FYs as per (g) above though no profit was recognised in accounts as outcome of contract could not be reliably estimated and the same has been booked in accounts of current period as per AS 7 since outcome could now be reliably estimated,deduct such profit amount booked in accounts in current period.

(m)

In case of Ind AS companies, following need to be added to net profit as per Ind ASP&L in statement of computation of total income

(i)

Profits from contracts which have crossed 25% stage of completion but Contract revenues recognition postponed due to applicability of at a point in time basis.

(ii)

Proportionate profit not recognised in accounts on POCM basis in respect of construction contracts which have crossed 25% stage of completion.

(iii)

Anticipated Loss in excess of proportionate loss recognised in respect of construction contracts which have crossed 25% stage of completion.

(iv)

Finance element computed by discounting to NPV (difference between contract revenues and NPV of contract revenues).

(n)

In case of Ind AS companies, following need to be deducted from net profit:

(i)

Profit recognised in accounts in current FY on point in time basis in respect of contracts from which profit was offered to tax in past FYs on POCM basis as per ICDS III.

(ii)

Finance element computed by discounting to NPV (difference between contract revenues and NPV of contract revenues)pertaining to current year.

(o)

Adjustments for complying with this ICDS as per (i) to (k) above are not to be made in accounts but in computation of income.

(p)

The adjustments to be made to profit or loss in computation of income for complying with ICDS-III(Revised) to be disclosed against items (d) & (e) of clause 13 of Form No. 3CD.

Calculation of value of property in goods involved in works contract, transferred works contract - In Vat, the dealer can pay Vat (or sales tax) either on value of material on actual basis or under composition scheme. If Vat or sales tax has been paid or payable on actual value of material, that amount will be deductible from total value of works contract to calculate value of taxable service.

The actual words used in the rule as follows - Where value added tax (Vat) has been paid or payable on the actual value of transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of the works contract, then, such value adopted for the purposes of payment of value added tax or sales tax, shall be taken as the value of transfer of property in goods transferred in the execution of the works contract for determining the value of works contract service under this clause [Rule 2A(i)(c) of Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006].

However, if the dealer has paid under composition scheme (i.e. at flat rate without separately calculating value of material), the value of material will have to be calculated on basis of actuals. Note that 'value' includes profit relating to goods also.

Vat or sales tax paid will not form part of value for service tax - Gross amount charged for the works contract shall not include value added tax or sales tax, as the case may be, paid, if any, on transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of the said works contract.

In Sobha Developers v. CCE (2010) 24 STT 425 (CESTAT), assessee was paying Vat on 70% of value of works contract as per Karnataka Vat Act and paid service tax on 30% of value as service tax. It was held that no differential service tax is payable, even if value of material is not shown separately in invoice. - departmental appeal against the decision has been admitted by SC for hearing - CCE v. Sobha Developers (2014) 47 GST 766 = 49 taxmann.com 595 (SC).

Splitting of contract permissible - In Essar Projects v. CCE (2014) 46 GST 582 = 47 taxmann.com 152 (CESTAT), assessee had entered into two different contracts - one for supply of material/equipment and other for erection/commissioning. There were a separate defect liability clauses for different contracts. Property in goods got transferred when equipment was supplied to customer. It was held that both cannot be treated as single contract for purpose of valuation under composition scheme of works contract.

16.3-2 Composition scheme for payment of service tax

Though service tax is legally payable only on value of service and Vat/sales tax is payable on value of goods, in a composite/indivisible contract, it is difficult to find value of goods and services. Hence, both under service tax and State Vat, a provision has been made for payment of tax under composition scheme.

In a composition scheme, tax can be paid on some ad hoc basis at the option of the tax payer.

In State of Kerala v. Builders Association of India 104 STC 134 = (1997) 2 SCC 183 = AIR 1997 SC 3640 = 1997 AIR SCW 977, the position was that a convenient, hassle-free and simple method, which was 'rough and ready method' was evolved by State Government for collection of sales tax on Works Contract. This was optional to assessee. It was held that Legislature can evolve such alternate, simplified and hassle-free methods of assessment, making it optional to assessee. - . - In the field of taxation, legislation must be allowed greater 'play in joints'. Allowance must be made for 'trial and error' by the legislature. - - Contractor who has opted to the alternate method of taxation cannot complain. Having voluntarily, and with the full knowledge of the alternate method of taxation, opted to be governed by it, a contractor cannot be heard to question the validity of relevant sub-sections or the rules - followed in Karnataka State Construction Corporation v. State of Karnataka (2004) 138 STC 75 (Kar HC DB) * Indian Oil Corp v. Prasanna Welding Industries (2007) 7 VST 101 (Gau HC).

In Mycon Construction v. State of Karnataka 2002 AIR SCW 2156 = 127 STC 105 (SC), it was held that a simplified composition scheme instead of regular assessment, can be evolved, if it is on optional basis. Validity of such provision has been upheld.

Government can make a provision allowing contractors option to opt for composition by paying a sum based on total consideration of contract. - Mytcon Construction v. State of Karnataka (1998) 111 STC 322 (Karn HC).

Reimbursement of expenses, if any, incurred by the assessee may not be includible. Consideration received on sale of fixed assets employed in the business cannot form part of the gross receipts on account of business, i.e., civil construction business. It arises on account of sale of assets employed in the business.

Any security or other deposits obtained from employees or sub contractors cannot form part of gross receipts.

Works contract tax or sales tax collected would form part of the gross receipts.

Retention money may not be considered as part of gross receipts.

Receipts arising on account of sale of scrap, etc., would form part of gross receipts on account of business.

Any refund of sales tax or works contract tax, etc., may constitute a part of gross receipts on account of business. However, any income-tax refund or interest thereon would not constitute part of the gross receipts of business. Interest on refund would, however, be separately taxable.

In case of contract with material, where a part or the whole of it is supplied by the contractee, and is included in the value of contract, the value of materials supplied by the contractee would not form part of gross receipts of the assessee. In this connection, a reference may be made to the decision of the Supreme Court in Brij Bhushan Lal Parduman Kumar v. CIT [1978] 115 ITR 524.

The value of work in progress may not form part of gross receipts. However, if in respect of such work in progress, a bill/claim has been made and approved by the contractee, then to the extent of value billed, having regard to terms of contract, such value would form part of the gross receipts, as the accrued value. If in terms of the contract the work is approved, but, merely bill is not made, it is felt that value of such work in progress would form part of the gross receipts.

The value, if any, of stock-in-trade would not form part of gross receipts.

EFFECTS OF LOWER GROSS RECEIPTS: Following may be noted:

The specified amount would reduce and would be accordingly assessable.

It could result into lower tax liability, refund of tax, if any, paid in excess, interest thereon, etc.

This may be done by passing an order under section 143(3).

EFFECT OF HIGHER GROSS RECEIPTS : Following may be noted:

If it is below Rs. 40 lakhs after adjustments:

-

The specified amount would increase and accordingly, the tax liability.

-

It may involve payment of interest, if any, for shortfall in payment of advance tax.

-

It could result into penalty, if any, under section 271(l)(c), depending on the facts of the case.

This may be done by passing an order under section 143(3).

If it is above Rs. 40 lakhs, after adjustments:

-

The case would not fall under section 44AD and accordingly, all the provisions thereof would not apply.

-

The computation of profits from the specified business would be made in accordance with normal provisions of sections 28 to 43C.

The new provision does not confer exemption from other provisions as in the case of assessees governed by erstwhile Chapter XII-C of the Act, where upon furnishing the relevant statement and payment of taxes, the assessees were absolved from all other obligations.

Filing of Return

4.14-11An assessee would be obliged to file the return of income before the due date applicable in his case and in the return declare income, based on his option, as said above.

As discussed earlier, under existing sections 44AD, 44AE and 44AF of the Act, presumptive tax is charged in case of construction business or transport business, or retail business. ITR 4, the prescribed return of income, states that in case of persons governed by sections 44AD, 44AE and 44AF they are required to give limited details. As per the form, no other information or details are prescribed.

Accordingly, even in respect of new section 44AD, it could be presumed that if one opts to return profits at the specified amount or percentage no other details may have to be furnished.

4.14-11a Assessment provision - Note the following:

If an assessee chooses to return the specified amount as his income in the return of income, unless he has some other income, the assessment may be completed by sending an intimation under section 143(1)(a) of the Act and there would be no cause for scrutiny as the amount of income is determined by the section itself.

Further, as said above, the department would be bound to assess the assessee on the specified amount for assessing the tax liability.

There cannot be any question of prima facie adjustment insofar as intimation is concerned except any arithmetical error.

In a case where higher amount of income is returned, the same position would prevail, as the higher amount declared has to be adopted as the taxable income, in terms, of sub-section (1) of section 44AD. There would be no scope for any adjustment.

As said above, where income returned is specified amount or a higher amount, possibly, there may not be any scrutiny assessment, unless the Assessing Officer wants to examine certain other information, like gross receipts, cash credits, sources of investment, claims for deductions under Chapter VI-A, etc.

4.14-11b Advance tax - Sub-section (4) provides that an eligible assessee is not obliged to pay advance tax in respect of income relating to eligible business.

It implies that the exemption from payment of advance tax is restricted to profits and gains of eligible business. In respect of the other income of an eligible assessee, he would be liable to pay advance tax thereon, in terms of the provisions of Chapter XVII-C of the Act.

4.14-12 Consequential amendments

4.14-12a section 44AA - Section 44AA obliges an assessee to maintain accounts in case specified in sub-section (2).

Sub-section (2)(iii) obliged an assessee claiming lower profits in Civil construction or Retail or Transport business, in terms of the provisions of sections 44AD, 44AE and 44AF of the Act, to maintain books of account. Consequent to the amendments, section 44AD is substituted and 44AF is made inoperative, effective from 1-4-2011. Accordingly the sub-section is amended to omit references to sections 44AD and 44AF, effective from 1-4-2011.

In sub-section (2), clause (iv) is inserted from 1-4-2011 to provide that where an eligible assessee claims that the profit of the eligible business is lower than the specified amount, and his income exceeds the maximum amount which is not chargeable to tax, he shall maintain books of account.

4.14-12b section 44AB - Section 44AB obliges an assessee to have its accounts audited and furnish a report thereon as specified therein.

Clause (c) thereof obliged an assessee claiming lower profits in Civil construction or Retail or Transport business, in terms of the provisions of sections 44AD, 44AE and 44AF of the Act, to have the accounts audited and furnish report thereon. Consequent to the amendments, sections 44AD is substituted and 44AF is made inoperative, effective from 1-4-2011. Accordingly the clause is amended to omit references to sections 44AD and 44AF, effective from 1-4-2011.

Section 44BB

Finance Act, 2003

Presumptive taxation in case of non-residents [Sections 44BB and 44BBB]

2.3 Under sections 44BB and 44BBB ('the said sections'), business income of non-residents engaged in the business of :

providing services or facilities in connection with, or supplying plant and machinery on hire used, or to be used, in the prospecting for, or extraction or production of, mineral oils (section 44BB);

civil construction or erection or testing or commissioning of plant or machinery in connection with a turnkey power project approved by the Government and financed under any international aid programme (section 44BBB),

is deemed to be 10% of the aggregate amounts paid or payable to the non-resident (hereinafter referred to as 'presumptive basis' or 'presumptive basis of taxation').

The above sections have now been amended with effect from assessment year 2004-05 to provide that the assessees covered by these sections will have an option to compute their income on a net income basis [, i.e., income shall be computed according to the provisions of the Act] (hereinafter referred to as 'net income basis' or 'net income basis of taxation'), provided the assessee:

maintains prescribed books of account;

gets the books of account audited; and

furnishes a tax audit report under section 44AB.

It is further provided that once a claim is made by the assessee for being governed by the net income basis of taxation, the Assessing Officer shall proceed to make an assessment of the total income under section 143(3) of the Act and determine the sum payable by, or refundable to, the assessee.

Further the presumptive tax rate of 10 per cent under section 44BBB will be applicable in those turnkey power projects also which are not financed under any international aid programme.

Consequential changes have been made in sections 44AA and 44AB of the Act relating to maintenance of accounts and audit of accounts, respectively.

2.3-1 Option - The alternative to follow the net income basis as business income is optional and hence, an assessee can continue to compute the business income on presumptive basis. Even if the assessee has maintained books of account and obtained an audit report, he may still opt to be governed by taxation on presumptive basis by not making the claim of being taxed on net income basis in the return of income.

2.3-2 Delay in filing the tax audit report - One of the pre-conditions for being governed by net income basis of taxation is that the assessee should furnish a tax audit report as required under section 44AB of the Act. Now, section 44AB of the Act provides that the tax audit report should be furnished on or before 31st October of the assessment year. Hence, on a strict literal interpretation, it appears that for the purpose of sections 44BB(3) and 44BBB(2) of the Act, the tax audit report has to be furnished before the said date and any delay may disentitle the assessee from making the claim to be governed by net income basis of taxation.

2.3-3 Loss - The sections provide that the Assessing Officer can make an assessment of the total income or loss. Such loss can be set off in accordance with the provisions of section 70 of the Act and carried forward and set off in accordance with provisions of section 72 of the Act. It appears that such carry forward loss can be set off against any business income, including presumptive income of the subsequent year, if the assessee decides to be so governed in that year.

2.3-4 Computation of income - In case the assessee opts to be governed by net basis of taxation, the computation of business income would be done by applying the provisions of sections 28 to 43B, including 40(a)(i), and also 44C of the Act. Further, the provisions of transfer pricing under sections 92 to 92F of the Act will also be applicable.

Some of the issues in computation of such income were raised in N.V. Jan De Nul v. CIT [1999] 236 ITR 489. In this case, however, the authority refused to answer the questions !

HEADNOTE: Section 143, read with section 256, of Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 33, read with section 66, of Indian Income tax Act, 1922] - Assessment - General - Assessment year 1924-25 - In respect of contracts spread over a number of years, assessee produced accounts but accounts for relevant accounting year could not be separated - ITO assessed profit at a standard rate without informing assessee of information or evidence on which rate was based and without giving him any opportunity to produce evidence in rebuttal - Whether question of law arose out of order of ITO - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, a contractor, was assessed to income-tax for the relevant assessment year in respect of certain contracts which commenced in 1922 and were finished some time in 1924. The assessee produced his accounts, but the accounts for the relevant accounting year could not be separated. The ITO considered the accounts to be unreliable. He, therefore, assumed profit at the standard rate of 10 per cent for the purposes of his assessment. On appeal, the Assistant Commissioner concluded that in any case it was impossible to ascertain from the assessee’s accounts what the income had been for one year and, therefore, the only way of ascertaining it was to apply the usual rate of 10 per cent on the total payments received. On application under section 66(2) of the 1922 Act, the Commissioner declined to make any reference.

On application under section 66 (3) of the 1922 Act.

HELD: In the instant case the assessee did not allege that he derived no income at all from any contracts, nor did the assessment proceed definitely on the ground that the accounts were unreliable. The Assistant Commissioner adopted a standard rate for the assessment merely because no separate accounts were available for the accounting year. This was apparently due to the manner in which the accounting were kept. As the assessee failed to produce correct and complete accounts for the accounting year, it was open to the Income-tax Officer to make an assessment to the best of his judgment: vide section 23, read with section 11, of the 1922 Act. The Assistant Commissioner, however, gave no reasons for adopting what he called the usual rate of 10 per cent for the purposes of the assessment, and it was not known how that rate was arrived at. In the circumstances of the case, the point of law emerged for decision was whether in the case of a contract spread over a number of years when accounts for the year under assessment could not be separated, the ITO was legally justified in assessing profits at a flat rate without informing the assessee of the information or evidence on which the rate was based and without giving him any opportunity to produce evidence in rebuttal.

Accordingly, the petition was accepted and the Commissioner was directed to state the case and refer the point of law to the High Court for decision.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

Sardha Ram for the Assessee .

Jagan Nath Aggarwal for the Crown.

Court for decision, viz.h (1) whether the Assistant Commissioner was legally justified in assessing the petitioner's profits at a standard rate of 10 per cent, on the advances received during the calendar year 1923 on the ground that the accounts for that year could not be separated; (2) whether the Assistant Commissioner has erred in law in holding items of expenditure amounting to Rs. 31,864 as inadmissible merely because no details were given in full in the cash book. It will appear from the order of the Assistant Commissioner referred to above that the second point does not really arise at all. It is true that the Assistant Commissioner was inclined to consider items of expenditure aggregating to Rs. 31,864 as suspicious, but he did not base his decision to assess the profits at the standard rate of 10 per cent, on that ground. The decision was merely based on the ground that the accounts for the year 1923 could not be separated. So the only point which requires decision is No. 1 stated above. The Commissioner of Income-tax apparently treated this as a question of accountancy and not of law. On behalf of the petitioner it is urged, on the other hand, that the question is one of law and not merely of accountancy. The following authorities were cited in support of the contentions : In re, Bishnu Priya Chowdhurani 1 ITC 261 and M. Sankar Iyer v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Madras 1 ITC 395 . In the former case the assessee had declared that he had no bastu income, but his statement was disbelieved and his bastu income was assessed at Rs. 1,528-6-4, at the rate of 2½ per cent, on the gross rental, without there being any evidence to show that the assessee had, as a matter of fact, derived any bastu income. It was held that when the assessee had declared that he had no bastu income at all, it was for the Income-tax Officers to prove that he had any such income, but not for him to prove the reverse. The question whether, in the absence of any reliable data as to the income of an assessee from a certain source, the Income-tax Officer is justified in making an assessment based on a formula which had been found in practice generally applicable was referred to the High Court, but no opinion was expressed on it as the other point was considered sufficient for disposal of the reference. In Sankar Iyer v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Madras 1 ITC 395 , the assessee's accounts were held to be unreliable and his income was assessed at a certain figure by the Income-tax Officer without any materials before him. On application by the assessee, the High Court directed the Commissioner to state a case for the determination of the following question :

"Whether in cases where the Income-tax Officer is not prepared to act on the accounts produced or the statement or evidence of the assessee, he can assess without any evidence on the record, or whether he is bound to inform the assessee as to how he proposes to assess him and the information on which he proposes to act and to call evidence so as to allow the assessee an opportunity of showing that such information or evidence is incorrect and ought not to be acted upon."

It will appear from the, above that the facts in both the cases are distinguishable. In the present case the assessee does not allege that he derived no income at all from any contracts, nor does the assessment proceed definitely on the ground that the accounts were unrealiable. Srinivasa Iyengar, J.—These two references under section 256(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, relate to the assessment year 1964-65 (accounting year ending 31st March, 1964). The first one arises out of the assessment proceedings for the said year and the other one in respect of a penalty imposed under section 271(1)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961.

The facts lie within a narrow compass. The assessee is a contractor at Udipi. During the year of account he had taken up contracts which included the construction of a hospital at Udipi and construction of roads. The Income-tax Officer dealt with these several contracts under three headings. The first one was with regard to the building of a hospital at Udipi and construction of a garage and certain other items. Items Nos. 2 and 3 related to the construction of roads. The assessee did not maintain any accounts. In regard to the contract of item No. 1, he disclosed a profit of 8 per cent. of the receipts on estimate. The Income-tax Officer was of opinion that the profit disclosed was low. He estimated the profits in respect of the building contract at 10 per cent. of the total receipts. In arriving at the total receipts, he also made an addition of 10 per cent. of the total receipts as cost of materials. This was made on the basis of an estimate as the assessee had not taken into account the cost of materials. So far as the road works were concerned, he was of opinion that the profit in respect of such contracts would be higher than in regard to a building contract. Accordingly, he estimated the profits at 12½ per cent. in respect of such items in item No. 1 and at 12 per cent. in respect of other items comprised in items Nos. 2 and 3. The assessee went up in appeal against these assessments. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the assessment as made by the Income-tax Officer. Feeling aggrieved by this, the assessee went up in appeal to the Tribunal. The Tribunal, after considering the entire facts, reduced the addition in regard to item No. 1 to a sum of Rs. 3,000 only. In regard to the other two items of contracts the case of the assessee was that he had given them out on sub-contracts and the profit derived by him was only three per cent. The Income-tax Officer did not accept this contention. He held that the so-called sub-contractors were mere name-lenders to the assessee and the entire profit has to be assessed in the hands of the assessee. The same view was upheld both by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal. It, however, gave a further relief in a sum of Rs. 1,500 in respect of these two contracts.

The questions referred for the opinion of this court are three in number. They are:

"1.Whether, on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the inclusion of any sum as profit on the estimated cost of materials supplied by P.W.D. to the assessee is right in law ?

2.Whether in estimating the assessee's profit at 10% in the case of one work and 12% in the case of another work, and in rejecting the assessee's estimate of 8%, the Tribunal acted arbitrarily on mere conjectures, suspicions and surmises; and whether such an estimate is correct in law ?

3.Whether the inference drawn by the Tribunal that the income of the sub-contractors should be regarded as the income of the assessee is erroneous in law by reason of misplacement of the burden of proof and whether such inference was justified in law on the admissible evidence on record?"

H.N. Seth, J.—The Income-tax Appellate Tribunal, "B" Bench, Allahabad, has, at the instance of the Commissioner of Income-tax, made this reference under section 256 (1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961.

The assessee in this case is K.S. Wazir Mohd. and Sons, a registered firm, carrying on business of building contractors and the assessment year involved is the year 1965-66.

Brief facts as they emerge from the statement of the case read along with the annexures attached thereto are that in the relevant accounting year the assessee derived income from two sets of contract businesses, described as the Kanpur set and the Lucknow set, as also by way of interest on certain fixed deposits in the savings bank. For the purposes of this case, the income derived by way of interest on fixed deposits is not material. In its income-tax return, the assessee showed its total receipts from the two sets of contract businesses as Rs. 12,45,000 resulting in a net profit of Rs. 42,209. The Income-tax Officer proceeded to make the assess­ment under section 143(3) of the Income-tax Act. He thought that the amount of profit disclosed by the assessee, which came to slightly more than 3.3% of the total receipts, was very low. Accordingly, he scrutinized the books of the assessee and found that neither the cash book had been written from day to day, nor had the daily balance been struck. Although the assessee had mentioned that it had furnished the particulars of its closing stock in its trading account, yet that had not been done. Subsequently, the assessee estimated its closing stock at Rs. 1,549, but did not disclose the basis for estimating or valuing the same. The expenses claimed by the assessee were mostly unvouched and they had not been debited correctly. Some of the car expenses which should not have been debited in the material account were found debited therein. He, accordingly, found the account books of the assessee to be unreliable and after rejecting them proceeded to make the assessment on the basis of the material available on the record.

In respect of the business relating to the Kanpur set the assessee showed its total receipts as Rs. 6,29,554 which included a sum of Rs. 5,72,621 in respect of two contracts and some miscellaneous receipts, resulting in a net profit amouting to Rs. 27,765, i.e., about 4% of the receipts. In the opinion of the Income-tax Officer, the profit disclosed was too low. The assessee attempted to explain the low rate of profit by stating that ever since the contracts in question had been entered, the price of material and wages had increased. In this connection the Income-tax Officer observed :

"Assessee's condition of accounts, however, as disclosed above is very unsatisfactory. In view of this, however, a net rate of 8% will be applied so as to give an income of Rs. 50,364. The assessee received raw material of Rs. 27,766 on which a not rate of 5% will be applied so as to give an income of Rs. 1,388. Income from this set thus comes to Rs. 51,752 subject to depreciation."

While dealing with the business relating to the Lucknow set, the Income-tax Officer found that the assessee had disclosed its total receipts and net profit as Rs. 6,18,145 and Rs. 14,444. The rate of profit thus came to about 2% which, in his opinion, was absurd. Again, the assessee attempted to explain the low rate of profit by alleging that the contracts in question had been entered into in the year 1962. It was expected that the work under those contracts would be completed within one year. However, the work continued right up to the year 1964 by which time the cost of material and wages had shot up. While dealing with this point of the case the Income-tax Officer observed:

"There is some force in the assessee's contention. Looking, however, to the fact that this remains unproved in the absence of proper account net rate of 8% will be applied on payments of Rs. 6,18,145 so as to give a profit of Rs. 49,452. A net rate of 5% will be applied on raw material received on Rs. 39,400 so as to give a profit of Rs. 1,970. The income from this set comes to Rs. 51,422."

What happened with regard to the assessment year 1945-46 is fully set out in the judgment of a Bench of the Punjab High Court in S. Sewa Singh Gill v. Commissioner of Income-tax [1962] 46 ITR 152 , already referred to. It will appear from that judgment that after the Appellate Assistant Commissioner remanded the matter concerning the assessment year 1945-46, the Income-tax Officer inquired into the matter and prepared a draft order in February, 1954, though it was not signed by him and dated by him. The question before the High Court was whether that unsigned and undated order could be said to be the final order of, the Income-tax Officer in relation to the assessment year 1945-46. The Bench of the Punjab High Court in that case came to the conclusion that the said draft order was in effect the assessment order and consequently, issuing further notice under section 24(4) of the Act to the petitioner was illegal. The point that has been urged before me is that since the Income-tax Officer has in his assessment order for the year 1945-46 made in February, 1954, arrived at a total profit for the entire contract at Rs. 4,119 and has apportioned only a sum of Rs. 1,818 as profits for the assessment year 1944-45, it is the duty of the Income-tax Officer to revise the assessment made by him on January 25, 1945, for the assessment year 1944-45 and to substitute the figure of Rs. 1,818 in the place of Rs. 44,214, arrived at as profits for the assessment year 1944-45.

Jaganmohan Reddy, CJ.—These two references arise from the same transactions entered into by the assessee, namely, renovation and repairs to what is known as "Rashtrapathi Nilayam" at Bolarum, and the period of assessment is in respect of the "previous year" 1959-60. Two questions are before us, the one referred by the Tribunal under section 66(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, viz.,

"Whether, on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the 'previous year' for the assessment year 1959-60 in respect of the contract business was correctly taken as the year ending on the 31st day of March, 1959?"

and the second question referred by the Tribunal as required by us, under section 66(2) in R.C. No. 36 of 1966, namely :

"Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, estimation of profit on the gross amount instead of estimating on the net amount received by the assessee after deduction of costs of material supplied by the Government is justified in law."

The assessee is an individual contractor and has several sources of income, such as interest on securities, income from house property and income from business. In the previous year, relating to the assessment year 1959-60, he had undertaken to complete the building contract work. In fact, this building contract was undertaken by him even earlier to the previous year. But the question that has been referred is only confined to the previous year relating to the assessment year 1959-60. It is, however, stated in the statement of the case that the contract actually started on 1st January, 1957, and was completed on 30th August, 1959. Accounts maintained for this business were, however, closed only once, i.e., when the contracts were completed ; so much so, the profit from the contracts was ascertained for the entire period from 1st January, 1957, to 30th August, 1959, when the accounts were so closed and not periodically with reference to any previous year. For the assessment year 1st January, 1957, to 30th August, 1959, the Income-tax Officer had adopted the previous year as the year ending with 30th September, because the assessee was maintaining accounts from October to September in respect of his other businesses, such as film exhibition business, medical stores, etc., and this was also the accounting period which he preferred for the earlier assessment year in respect of the contract business. But when it came to 1959-60, it was found by the next Income-tax Officer that the assessee could not so adopt and, therefore, he apportioned the entire profits as between the two assessment years 1958-59, and 1959-60 for which the previous years are 1957-58 and 1958-59 in the proportion of 3:1. The basis for doing so as appears from the Income-tax Officer's report is the receipts in each of the above assessment years, which according to him justify the fixing of that proportion.

Mr. Ramachandra Rao contends that once a year of assessment has been adopted by the Income-tax Officer, he cannot give a go-by to that period and adopt another. As a proposition of law it is unexceptionable. But in this case the adoption by the Income-tax Officer of the previous year, October to September, for the assessment year 1958-59, was wrongly adopted, because it does not satisfy the requirements of section 2(11)(i)( a) of the Income-tax Act. It is only in cases where the assessee could adopt a different period to the financial year, 1st April to 31st March, that any other period could be adopted, which would invariably mean a period of twelve months. This is also subject to the requirement of the section. Section 2(11)(i)(a ) is as follows :

"2. (11) 'previous year' means—

(i)in respect of any separate source of income, protits and gains—

(a)the twelve months ending on the 31st day of March next preceding the year for which the assessment is to be made, or, if the accounts of the assessee have been made up to a date within the said twelve months in respect of a year ending on any date other than the said 31st day of March, then, at the option of the assessee, the year ending on the date to which his accounts have been so made up."

The facts are not in dispute. The relevant assessment year is 1959-60. The business of the assessee is execution of construction contracts. The assessee commenced its business from January 25, 1958, and the accounts were closed for the first time on January 25, 1959. During the accounting year the assessee undertook three contracts with respect to which it submitted separate profit and loss statements disclosing the following net profit:— The accounts in respect of the first two contracts were accepted by the authorities under the Income-tax Act in to but with regard to the accounts relating to the third contract the Income-tax Officer declined to accept the assessee's reasons for low profits at the rate of 9% in respect of that contract. He, therefore, applied a flat rate of 12Â½% profit and made an addition of Rs. 22,558 to the assessee's income. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax agreed that some addition was called for but he felt that the addition made by the Income-tax Officer was definitely on the high side. He, therefore, held that it would meet the ends of justice if the addition was restricted to Rs. 10,000 in round figures. On further appeal to the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal, the addition was restricted to Rs. 6,000 only as against Rs. 10,000 sustained by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The question that has been mooted before us by the learned counsel for the assessee is whether the Tribunal was right in rejecting the assessee's application for submitting a statement of case and referring to this court the three questions as set out at the beginning of this order.

The argument advanced by Mr. Bajaj is that the Appellate Assistant Commissioner had accepted the assessee's reasons for the low profit of 9% but had nevertheless sustained an addition of Rs. 10,000 on the ground that the assessee's representative had not denied before him that full quantitative details might not be available in respect of the stores of the value of over Rs. 1,30,000 consumed in the execution of the contract. When the case came up before the Tribunal the addition of Rs. 10,000 was found to be excessive and was reduced to Rs. 6,000. Mr. Bajaj contended that it was not open to the Tribunal to sustain an addition of Rs. 6,000 unless there was material for the same. The order passed by the Tribunal, however, did not disclose any such material.

In this connection our attention was drawn by the learned counsel to a Full Bench decision of the Madras High Court in Gunda Subbayya v. Commissioner of Income-tax [1939] 7 ITR 21 (Mad.) [FB], where it was held that recourse to section 13 could certainly be had if the method of accounting employed by the assessee was one which did not properly disclose the income, profits and gains of the assessee. In such a case the Income-tax Officer could adopt his own method but in doing so it was imperative that he should refer to the accounts before him as section 13 did not contemplate the rejection of the accounts. It was also said in that case that section 13 neither added to nor took anything away from section 23(3) and, therefore, when an assessment was made under section 23(3) it became incumbent upon the Income-tax Officer to draw the assessee's attention to the material on which he proposed to act and give him an opportunity to show that the opinion formed by the officer was wrong. The Income-tax Officer should also indicate in his order the material on which he had made his assessment as an order under section 23(3) was appealable. Basing himself on the above observations, Mr. Bajaj argued that the same applied to the Tribunal and that before any addition was made to the income of the assessee on the ground that recourse to section 13 was necessary the material on which that addition was contemplated should have been disclosed to the assessee.

Since the order of the Tribunal did not disclose any such material, it did give rise to the questions formulated by the assessee.

Reliance was also placed on the judgment of the Supreme Court in Dhakeswari Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax [1954] 26 ITR 775; [1955] 1 SCR941 (SC) and on the decision of the Kerala High Court in S. Veeriah Reddiar v. Commissioner of Income-tax [1960] 38 ITR 152 (Ker.). Particular stress was laid by the learned counsel on the judgment of the Kerala High Court in which it was held that low profits and absence of a regular stock register were not sufficient reasons or material on the strength of which the accounts of the assessee could be rejected under the proviso to section 13 of the Income-tax Act and an assessment made therein. In any case it was argued that the question whether the proviso to section 13 applied to the facts of the present case was a question of law which did arise out of the order of the Tribunal. Likewise, the question whether there was any material or evidence before the Tribunal to sustain the addition of Rs. 6,000 in round figures in respect of Srinagar contract was a question of law which ought to have been referred to this court.

Bhide, J.—The petilioner R.B. Panna Lal, a contractor of Ambala, was assessed to income-tax for the year 1924-25 in respect of certain contracts which commenced in 1922 and were finished some time in 1924. The petitioner produced his accounts, but the accounts for the year 1923 (which was the accounting year for the purpose of the assessment for 1924-25) could not be separated. The Income-tax Officer also considered the accounts to be unreliable. He, therefore, "assumed profit at the standard rate of 10 per cent." for the purposes of his assessment. An appeal was preferred to the Assistant Commissioner who had the accounts re-examined. The Assistant Commissioner also found that the accounts for the year 1923 could not be separated. The assessee showed receipts and expenditure amounting to Rs. 2,57,946 and Rs. 2,54,775 respectively, during the entire period of the contracts and a net profit of Rs. 3,171 only. The Assistant Commissioner, however, considered items of expenditure amounting to Rs. 31,864 to be of a suspicious character as they were not supported by any details in the assessee's "books of original entry". The assessee produced certain other books giving details in respect of some of the larger items, but these books were produced only at a late stage and after several adjournments. If the items amounting to Rs. 31,864 were excluded altogether the contracts would have shown a profit of 14 per cent. The Assistant Commissioner concluded as follows :—

"In any case it is impossible to ascertain from the assessee's accounts what the income has been for one year and I, therefore, agree with the Income-tax Officer that the only way of ascertaining it is to apply the usual rate of 10 per cent, on the total payments received."

The petitioner then applied to the Commissioner of Income-tax, for a review and, in the alternative, prayed that certain points of law may be referred to this Court under section 66(2) of the Income-tax Act. The Commissioner held that the points raised were questions of fact and not of law and, therefore declined to make any reference. The petitioner has now applied under section 66(3) of the Act for the issue of a mandamus to the Commissioner to refer the following alleged points of law to this Court for decision, viz.h (1) whether the Assistant Commissioner was legally justified in assessing the petitioner's profits at a standard rate of 10 per cent, on the advances received during the calendar year 1923 on the ground that the accounts for that year could not be separated; (2) whether the Assistant Commissioner has erred in law in holding items of expenditure amounting to Rs. 31,864 as inadmissible merely because no details were given in full in the cash book.

(a)the twelve months ending on the 31st day of March next preceding the year for which the assessment is to be made, or, if the accounts of the assessee have been made up to a date within the said twelve months in respect of a year ending on any date other than the said 31st day of March, then, at the option of the assessee, the year ending on the date to which his accounts have been so made up." The crucial point to note about this section is the making up of accounts. "Previous year" ordinarily means a period from 1st April to 31st March. But if the assessee wants to adopt any other period, then his accounts must be made up for that period. If, however, those accounts are not made up for that period, he cannot ask for that period. In this case, admittedly the accounts had not been made up for over a period of 2 years and 8 months, so that the assessee could not adopt any other period than 1st April to 31st March. In these circumstances, the adoption by the Income-tax Officer of the accounting period from October to September for year of assessment 1958-59, cannot be conclusive, nor can the next Income-tax Officer be barred from adopting the correct accounting period in terms of section 2(11)(i)(a ).

The next question that has been urged before us is that the apportionment ought to have been made over a period of 4 years instead of 2 years, because the receipts were spread over those 4 years. We would have considered this question but for the fact that it was not urged at any stage of the assessment proceedings, nor is it the subject-matter of the assessment. Nor for the same reason can we assist the assessee in respect of his further argument that the whole of the amount was not received in those two assessment years and, therefore, the proportion of the 3/4ths and 1/4ths was not a correct proportion to be adopted as a basis for assessment of the tax. In this view, our answer to the first question is in the affirmative and in favour of the department.

In respect of the second question also, the answer must be in favour of the department, inasmuch as the contentions now urged have not been raised before the Tribunal nor has the assessee adduced any evidence in respect of this contention, nor does the statement of case refer to this contention. We cannot, therefore, go into that question. The contention of Mr. Ramachandra Rao is that the contract which the assessee has entered into with the Central Government was only to build and repair "Rashtrapathi Nilayam" and that the value of the contract does not include the materials which the Government supplied. Notwithstanding this, he says, the cost of the materials supplied was also included for the purposes of ascertaining the net profits on percentage basis. We do not know whether the contract was for the whole of the work including the materials and the Government gave a rebate of the cost of materials. There is, however, an indication in the finding of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner that the latter is the case. In the statement of the case, the following observations of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner were extracted, which we may also usefully give below :

"The contention that profit rate should be adopted only in respect of the net receipts cannot be accepted because admittedly the appellant had received the gross amount and had to furnish the materials himself. A profit ratio had been adopted. The material supplied by the departmental authorities were of such a nature that they could not be obtained by the appellant in the open market at the rates at which the Government supplied them, even if he could obtain them in the open market. It is not also the case of the appellant that he had enough funds that he could stock those materials when the prices were low and utilise them when prices were high. The percentage of net profit of 12.5 per cent. adopted by the Income-tax Officer also is quite reasonable. In fact, in respect of the contract relating to Rashtrapathi Nilayam, the Income-tax Officer himself adopted the net profit at 10 per cent., accepting the appellant's plea that the appellant had been alloted only a part of the work and that more profitable items of the contract were given to other contractors."

This above extract gives an indication that the assessee was to receive the gross amount and had to furnish the materials himself but since the Government furnished the materials, an inference would arise that they must have deducted those amounts from the payments, in which case the basis cannot be challenged.

Our answers to both the questions are, therefore, in the affirmative and in favour of the department, with costs in R.C. No. 52 of 1962.

FACT: The business of the assessee was execution of construction contracts. The assessee commenced its business from 25-1-1958, and the accounts were closed for the first time on 25-1-1959. During the accounting year the assessee undertook three contracts with respect to which it submitted separate profit and loss statements.

The accounts in respect of the first two contracts were accepted by the authorities under the Act in toto but with regard to the accounts relating to the third contract the ITO declined to accept the assessee's reasons for low profits at the rate of 9% in respect of that contract. He, therefore, applied a flat rate of 12Â½% profit and made certain addition to the assessee's income.

On appeal, the AAC had accepted the assessee's reasons for the low profit of 9% but had sustained an addition of Rs. 10,000 on the ground that the assessee's representative had not denied before him that full quantitative details might not be available in respect of the stores of the value of over Rs. 1,30,000 consumed in the execution of the contract. When the case came up before the Tribunal the addition of Rs. 10,000 was found to be excessive and was reduced to Rs. 6,000.

On reference :

HELD: In the instant case there was material before the Tribunal on which its finding could be based: the assessee's representative had admitted before the AAC that full quantitative details in respect of the stores of the value of Rs. 1,30,000 consumed in the execution of that contract might not be available. In the circumstances, recourse to estimating the profits on the contract was inevitable. He, therefore, made an addition of Rs. 10,000 as against Rs. 26,434 added by the ITO. If the assessee wished to displace the AAC's estimate it was open to him to adduce evidence in support of its claim that the consumption of stores of the value of Rs. 1,30,000 was fully justified. This the assessee apparently did not do. For the subsequent year 1960-61 the assessee itself declared a net profit rate of 9.9% as against 9% declared in the assessment year in question. It could not be disputed that this was additional material which the Tribunal could take into consideration as it did. There was thus material before the Tribunal on which its estimate was based. The Tribunal's decision was, therefore, in conformity with the decision in the case of CIT v. Maharajadhiraj of Darbhanga [1933] 1 ITR 94 (P.C.).

The Tribunal was therefore justified in holding that the proviso to section 13 was applicable and there was material before it to sustain the aforesaid addition.

Mukharji J. held that where there was a contract which provided sufficient limit beyond which the tender could not be quoted and there was a stipulation that the contract was to be quoted at a particular rate excluding the cost of materials to be supplied by the con-tractee then in such a case the principles laid down in Commissioner of Income-tax v. In the Income-tax Reference No. 198 of 1971 [Rakhal Chandra Banerjee v. Commissioner of Income-tax [1978] 113 ITR 419 (Cal) (Appendix No. 1)] Mukharji J. again held that where the assessee had tendered for the contract as a whole including the cost of materials which were subsequently supplied by the Government and there was no evidence on record to show that the assessee did not know of such supply of materials to be made by the Government and the price thereof, then the gross profits of the assessee could be computed on his total gross bills and there was no question of excluding the cost of the materials supplied. If it is found on such facts that there was an element of profit involved in the materials supplied then the profits of the assessee will be estimated on the gross receipts of the assessee computed by including the value of the materials supplied to the net receipts. The Tribunal will be at liberty to take further evidence in the matter and will afford opportunity to the parties to adduce further evidence and to make further representations in the matter.

Commissioner of Income-tax [1973] 92 ITR 92 (Ker) fall within the first category that we have mentioned above and we are in respectful agreement with the conclusion reached by the Madras and the Kerala High Courts regarding contracts of this type which we have referred to as the contract in the first category. In Brij Bushan Lal v. Commissioner of Income-tax [1971] 81 ITR 497 (Punj), the facts before the Punjab High Court were that the assessee, who did building work on contract for the M.E.S. department, was assessed on the basis of net profits determined at 10 per cent., 12.5 per cent., 12.5 per cent. and 10 per cent. of the amounts received by the assessee from the M.E.S. department in the four years in question. Subsequently, on the ground that the cost of materials supplied by the military authorities to be used in the building works by the assessee had not been disclosed, the Income-tax Officer issued notices to the assessee under section 34 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, and made orders of reassessment by adding profits at the same rates on the cost of the building materials supplied to him. Question No. (3) referred to the High Court at the instance of the assessee was: "Whether, on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Tribunal was justified in holding that the price of the stores supplied by the military authorities was to be included before applying the flat rate to the assessee's receipts?" The Punjab High Court held that if an assessee does not produce his accounts to satisfy the Income-tax Officer as to the true profits or income made by him from a contract and leaves it to him to determine, on the best judgment basis, the profits or income made by the assessee, the Income-tax Officer naturally will calculate and determine the net income assessable on the basis of the value of the contract as a whole and not on the value of the contract after deducting the cost of the materials supplied by the department. With respect, we are unable to agree with this conclusion of the learned judges of the Punjab High Court. The question that has to be determined even in best judgment basis is as to what is the profit from this particular construction work which the particular assessee has earned and in determining these profits, the main question is what was in substance the contract between the parties. It is that substance of the contract which matters and if, as we have pointed out in sub-category of category No. (1), the agreement between the parties right from the beginning is that certain materials are to be supplied by the other party to the contract, that is, the Government department, or the authority concerned, then it is obvious that the contract was entered into on the footing that no profit would be made by the building contractor in respect of the supply of those materials.

It may be pointed out that in a subsequent decision in Commissioner of Income-tax v. Brij Bhushan Lal, Ramesh Kumar [1976] 102 ITR 430 (Punj), the Punjab High Court followed its earlier decision and held that the cost of materials supplied by the Government must be included while estimating the profit of the contractor.
