On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) sustained the rejection of accounts but adopted a different method of estimating the income by directing the Assessing Officer to adopt 8 per cent of the gross receipt as the income. On further appeal, by the department, the Tribunal confirmed the order passed by the first appellate authority.

On appeal : HELD: The main reason for rejecting the books of account was that the Assessing Officer, after considering the statements and depositions of the seven sub-contractors, was of the view that they were only name lenders. It was in the above circumstances that the claim of deduction of a sum of Rs. 68,43,650 was not allowed as deduction from the gross receipt. The Assessing Officer was also of the view that there was nothing to be deducted from the gross receipt of the sum of Rs. 87,51,092 received under the award of the arbitrator. It was in that view of the matter he had treated the entire sum of Rs. 87,51,092 as income of the assessee. The first appellate authority had adverted to the contentions of the assessee with reference to the payments made to the sub-contractors. However, the first appellate authority had taken the view that the instant case was at the most a case for rejection of the account and that if the accounts were rejected, the income had to be estimated. The first appellate authority was of the view that when the income was being estimated, there was no question of making separate additions. He therefore, after rejecting the books, had resorted to the estimation of the income on percentage basis. It was to be noted that the first appellate authority did not thereafter make any reference to the books of account and other documents relied upon by the assessee for the purpose of estimation of income. In other words, he had totally discarded the materials available in the form of books of account and other documents. He had resorted to the estimation on percentage basis. The first appellate authority was not justified in the facts of instant case to totally discard the books of account and other documents relied upon by the assessee in the matter of estimation of income. As held by the Supreme Court in CST v. Girja Shanker Awanish Kumar [1997] 104 STC 130, even after rejection of the books of account for technical and other reasons, it is for the Assessing Officer on the facts of each case to consider the materials disclosed to ascertain as to what extent the books of account can be relied upon for determination of the turnover. The Tribunal in the instant case had adverted to the findings of the Assessing Officer and the first appellate authority. However, the Tribunal did not consider aforesaid aspect of the matter even though it found it difficult to accept the case of the assessee regarding payment to the sub-contractors. The Tribunal had adverted to the award passed by the arbitrator and found that the amount awarded represented the value of the extra work done, which also represented interest at the rate of 12 per cent. The Tribunal was of the view that even if the additional work was not got done through sub-contractors, it might have been done by the assessee itself, which aspect had not been considered. The Tribunal, however, observed that it was not possible to say that the entire amount of award was a profit to the assessee and taxable as contended by the department. In such circumstances, it was for the Tribunal to remit the matter to the Assessing Officer or at any rate to the first appellate authority to consider the matter afresh. However, the Tribunal had agreed with the first appellate authority that the instant case was a case which called for estimation of the profit on percentage basis. No reason was, however, stated by the Tribunal for justifying the estimate made on profit basis. Apart from the general observations made by the Tribunal on the merits of the matter, there was no due consideration of the case of the assessee or of the department in regard to the acceptance of the books of account or the estimation of the income with reference to all the materials available on record including the books of account and documents. [Para 5]

The first appellate authority, without considering the case of the assessee, based on the books of account and other records, had straightaway thought that it was a fit case for estimation of profit on percentage basis. In the facts of the instant case, the first appellate authority was not justified in adopting such a course. The Tribunal had also committed the mistake in approving the estimation of income adopted by the first appellate authority. In such circumstances the question of estimation of income from the contract receipt was a matter to be considered by the Assessing Officer himself in accordance with law in the light of the observations made in the instant judgment. [Para 6]

HEADNOTE: Section 145, read with section 143 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 13, read with section 23 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits - Assessment years 1945-46 and 1946-47 - Whether in case to which proviso to section 13 of 1922 Act applies, Income-tax Officer is bound to disclose in his order basis and manner of computation of income, gains or profits and to disclose data on which he arrives at result - Held, yes - Whether if assessee fails to satisfy Income-tax Officer as to correctness of percentage of profits returned by him, it is open to Income-tax Officer to take higher percentage consistent with state of trade in locality or with any special circumstances of assessee which warrant higher rate of profits - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was carrying on business in cloth and yarn. The method of accounting employed by the assessee was such that, income, profits and gains could not be properly deduced therefrom. The ITO accordingly applied the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act and determined the profits for the assessment years 1941-42 and onwards under this proviso. The Income-tax Officer had not informed the assessee how he was going to compute the assessee’s income from his business. The Tribunal concluded that once an assessee’s books of accounts are rejected, the best that the ITO can do is to make a reasonable estimate, having regard to all the circumstances of the case.

On reference :

HELD: The proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act does not entitle the Income-tax Officer to have a leap in the dark but requires him to compute the income ‘upon such basis and in such manner as the Income-tax Officer may determine.’ He has therefore to find out ‘the basis and the manner of computation’. The assessment is under section 23(3) of the 1922 Act after hearing such evidence as the assessee may produce and such other evidence as the Income-tax Officer may require on specified points. The Income-tax Officer may use material not placed before him by the assessee; but in such a case natural justice demands that he should give the assessee an opportunity of showing, if he can, that the material is incorrect, though the officer is not bound to disclose the source of his information. It may be that there is an adequate explanation against the information sought to be used against the assessee or that the Income-tax Officer might be misinformed. Although there is no express provision in the Act to require the Income-tax Officer to make such disclosure, it is necessary on the principles of natural justice.

The order is appealable and must stand scrutiny by an appellate court. It must, therefore, be a speaking order. If the basis and manner of computation are not disclosed in the order, the assessee’s right of appeal may be illusory unless the appellate authority refers the matter back to the Income-tax Officer to disclose the basis and manner of his computation. If the profits are computed under this proviso upon a basis determined by the Income-tax Officer, profits included in such computation cannot be included again in the assessment for any subsequent year. The burden is on the assessee to prove that the profits sought to be assessed were included in the assessment for any preceding year. This burden cannot be adequately discharged unless the assessment orders disclose the basis and manner of computation. If after rejecting the method of accounting employed by the assessee, the Income-tax Officer were simply to add a particular amount to the income returned or to disallow a part of the business expenses properly incurred by the assessee and allowable under section 10 of the 1922 Act, he would not be acting under the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act. The Income-tax Officer would be acting contrary to law if he were to disallow such business expenses or make an addition of a lump sum simply on the ground that the trading profits cannot be properly determined from the books of account. The Income-tax Officer is not entitled to discard the evidence of the books of account altogether merely because the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act is attracted.

It is certainly not a "leap in the dark". The Income-tax Officer is not entitled to make a guess without evidence.

The assessee-firm had undertaken a Government contract for construction of canals, etc. In execution of the aforesaid work, the Government supplied cement and other materials to the assessee for being directly utilised in the completion of the work. After the completion of the contract, the Government made payment of the gross amount due to the assessee after deducting the value of the materials supplied to the assessee. At the time of assessment, the ITO rejected the books of account maintained by the assessee on the ground that they suffered from certain defects and applied a net profit rate of 12½ per cent. The AAC, while maintaining the estimate of net profits at the rate of 12½ per cent in respect of the contracts directly executed by the assessee, applied 7½ per cent profit rate in respect of the contracts which were supervised by the other persons employed by the assessee. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the estimates of net profit arrived at by the AAC were fair and reasonable. However, it held that the amount of the bills relating to the value of the material supplied by the Government should have been excluded from the gross receipts of the assessee.

On reference:

The Assessing Officer noted that there was delay in filing the return for the assessment year 1997-98. HEADNOTE: Section 147 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income escaping assessment - In formation - Position prior to 1-4-1989 - Assessment year 1970-71 - Whether an audit note can be a source of information - Held, yes - ITO having noted that assessee had not maintained quantity stock register and other relevant registers, estimated income by considering profits made in earlier assessment years - subsequently, ITO received an audit note which pointed out that account books of assessee disclosed more profit than estimated by ITO - On basis of said information ITO reopened assessment and estimated gross profit at higher rate - Whether on facts, reopening of assessment on basis of audit note was valid - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a building contractor. It had entered into certain contracts in 1966 and also in 1970 respectively. The 1966 contracts were described as old contracts and the 1970 contracts as new contracts. It had filed a consolidated trading account and profit and loss account disclosing gross profit at 10.2 per cent. The ITO noticed that the assessee had not maintained quantity stock register and other relevant registers and a work-in-progress account which would have enabled him to verify the correctness of the book result and, therefore, decided to estimate the income by considering the profits made in earlier assessment years. He noticed that the assessee itself in the previous year had disclosed gross profits at the rate of 15.4 per cent. The ITO, therefore, after considering the explanation of the assessee that the old contracts were in the last stages of completion, assessed the gross profit in respect of the old contracts at 12 per cent, and at the rate of 15 per cent in respect of the new contracts. The assessee did not prefer any appeal. Thereafter, the ITO received an audit note wherein it was pointed out that in respect of the one of the old contract, the account books of the assessee disclosed a profit of 14.5 per cent. On the basis of the said information, the ITO reopened the assessment under section 147(b) and computed the gross profit in respect of that contract at 15 per cent. The AAC allowed the assessee’s appeal and annulled the order of assessment. But the Tribunal held that the reopening of the assessment was valid.

On reference :

HELD: It was no doubt true that the account books of the assessee were before the ITO when he made the original assessment. But, the ITO doubted the correctness of the accounts maintained by the assessee and, therefore, without adopting the account books as the basis, he estimated the profit on the basis of the margin of profits normally earned by persons in such types of business and the rate of profit earned by the assessee in the previous year. Thus, the ITO had not considered this material while estimating the profit of the old contracts at 12 per cent. Since the ITO had not considered the said material, it had not come to his notice that the account books of the assessee showed that in respect of the one of the old contract, the assessee had earned profit at the rate of 14.5 per cent. That an audit note can be a source of information is no longer in dispute now.

The relevant material in the shape of book result was not considered by the ITO on the ground that the books of account were not properly maintained by the assessee. Thus, this was not a case where it could be said that the ITO had considered the material while making the original assessment. This was a case where the ITO had not considered the said material and only subsequently he came to know about that material when his attention in that behalf was drawn by the audit note. Thus, this case would squarely fall within the scope of section 147(b).

The reopening of the assessment under section 147(b ) was thus valid.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

The assessee carried on business of construing buildings and doing the work of maintenance of buildings, inter alia, for railways. In the assessment year 1983-84, the assessee, a civil works contractor, started construction work on behalf of Crompton Greaves Ambad and continued it up to the assessment year 1988-89.

The assessee adopted for its accounts the project completion method, by which the profit or loss was accounted for in the books of account of the year in which the project was completed.

The Assessing Officer, accepting the method of accounting of the assessee, completed the assessments for the assessment years 1983-84 and 1984-85 under section 143(3) after observing that the profit or loss would be accounted for on completion of project. However, the Commissioner, under section 263 set aside the assessments on the ground that income under construction work had not been computed correctly by taking into account the profits on the work-in-progress and that the method of accounting employed did not enable the income of the year to be properly deduced.

On appeal, before the Tribunal the following points were highlighted:

(a)Both the methods, the method adopted by the assessee and the method sought to be adopted by the Commissioner, are recognised methods.

(b)The profits of business must be computed in accordance with method of accounting regularly employed by the assessee. The choice of the method of accounting, like the choice of the previous year (Note: choice of previous year is no longer permitted) lies with the assessee.

(c)The assessee has been following the same method of accounting regularly in subsequent assessment years. Under the mandatory provisions of section 145, the department is bound by the assessee's choice of method which cannot be rejected as improper merely because it gives the assessee benefit in certain years even if this is assumed to be the case, or merely because, according to the department, another method is preferable.

(d)Independent Chartered Accountants have also found it appropriate to adopt the project completion method for the purpose of true and fair view of the financial position, including the profits earned.

(e)Merely because the profits of a project are postponed from the year of commencement of the project to the year of completion of the project, the same would not be the basis for considering the assessment made on that basis erroneous.

(f)When the rate of tax remains constant, it cannot also be said that the assessments adopting the project completion method are in any way prejudicial to the interests of revenue.

The Tribunal cancelled the orders passed by the Commissioner under section 263 and restored the assessments framed by the Assessing Officer.

7. From the foregoing discussion, the following guiding principles emerge:

(a)Where contracts for execution of works extend over a number of years, the Assessing Officer can estimate the profit on the basis of receipts in a year and bring the yearly profits to tax as contemplated in section 3 of the Act; the Assessing Officer need not wait for the completion of contract to charge tax on the profits.

(b)The 'completed contract basis' and the 'percentage of completion method' or the 'project completion method' are recognised methods to ascertain annual profits for purposes of levy of tax; the choice of method is that of the assessee; the choice has to be carefully made.

(c)The method adopted should be followed regularly in all years till the particular contract is over.

(d)The Accounting Standard (AS-7) having been made mandatory for corporate entities from April 1, 1991 and non-corporate assessees from 1-4-1993, the accounting for construction contracts should strictly conform to the requirements of the Standard.

In the aforesaid background, it could not be said that the Tribunal was indulging in any surmise or acting without any proper evidence. The adoption by the ITO of the previous year, October to September, for the assessment year 1958-59, was wrongly adopted, because it did not satisfy the requirements of section 2(11)(i)(a ). It was only in cases where the assessee could adopt a different period to the financial year, 1st April to 31st March, that any other period could be adopted, which would invariably mean a period of twelve months. This was also subject to the requirement of the section.

"Previous year" ordinarily means a period from 1st April to 31st March. But if the assessee wanted to adopt any other period, then his accounts must be made up for that period. If, however, those accounts were not made up for that period, he could not ask for that period. In the instant case, admittedly the accounts had not been made up for over a period of 2 years and 8 months, so that the assessee could not adopt any other period than 1st April to 31st March. In these circumstances, the adoption by the ITO of the accounting period from October to September for year of assessment 1958-59, could not be conclusive, nor could the next ITO be barred from adopting the correct accounting period in terms of section 2(11)(i )(a).

Therefore, the ‘previous year’ for the assessment year 1959-60 in respect of the contract business was correctly taken as the year ending on 31-3-1959.

The second question whether estimation of profit on the gross amount instead of estimating on the net amount received by the assessee after deduction of costs of material supplied by the Govt. was justified, must be answered in favour of the department inasmuch as the contentions now urged had not been raised before the Tribunal nor had the assessee adduced any evidence in this respect. Therefore, this question could not be gone into.

HELD: 1. No hard and fast rule could be laid down as to whether the value of the materials should or should not be included in a contractor's gross turnover from business for determining his net profits. It depended upon the manner in which the materials were obtained and used in the execution of the contract. The contracts could be generally classified as (i) contract for labour supply; (ii) a lump sum contract; and (iii) where the material supplied by the department was either an outright sale or was specifically meant to be used in the work allotted. In the types of contracts mentioned in (i) and (iii), the profit had to be calculated on the gross receipts, including the value of the material supplied either by the Government or by the assessee. Whereas, in the case of the other items at (ii) and (iii), profit would be determined en the basis of only the net amount without taking into consideration the value of the materials. In the instant case, in the absence of any stock register or issue register, it was not known whether the materials were supplied by the department as an outright sale to the assessee or it remained under the control of the department throughout and that the same was never under the control of the contractor except for using it in the constitution.

2. The Tribunal was, accordingly, correct in holding that the profit was to be calculated on the gross receipts excluding the recoveries for the material supplied by the Government department.

On reference :

The proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act does not entitle the Income-tax Officer to have a leap in the dark but requires him to compute the income ‘upon such basis and in such manner as the Income-tax Officer may determine.’ He has therefore to find out ‘the basis and the manner of computation’. The assessment is under section 23(3) of the 1922 Act after hearing such evidence as the assessee may produce and such other evidence as the Income-tax Officer may require on specified points. The Income-tax Officer may use material not placed before him by the assessee; but in such a case natural justice demands that he should give the assessee an opportunity of showing, if he can, that the material is incorrect, though the officer is not bound to disclose the source of his information. It may be that there is an adequate explanation against the information sought to be used against the assessee or that the Income-tax Officer might be misinformed. Although there is no express provision in the Act to require the Income-tax Officer to make such disclosure, it is necessary on the principles of natural justice.

The order is appealable and must stand scrutiny by an appellate court. It must, therefore, be a speaking order. If the basis and manner of computation are not disclosed in the order, the assessee’s right of appeal may be illusory unless the appellate authority refers the matter back to the Income-tax Officer to disclose the basis and manner of his computation. If the profits are computed under this proviso upon a basis determined by the Income-tax Officer, profits included in such computation cannot be included again in the assessment for any subsequent year. The burden is on the assessee to prove that the profits sought to be assessed were included in the assessment for any preceding year. This burden cannot be adequately discharged unless the assessment orders disclose the basis and manner of computation. If after rejecting the method of accounting employed by the assessee, the Income-tax Officer were simply to add a particular amount to the income returned or to disallow a part of the business expenses properly incurred by the assessee and allowable under section 10 of the 1922 Act, he would not be acting under the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act. The Income-tax Officer would be acting contrary to law if he were to disallow such business expenses or make an addition of a lump sum simply on the ground that the trading profits cannot be properly determined from the books of account. The Income-tax Officer is not entitled to discard the evidence of the books of account altogether merely because the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act is attracted.

It is certainly not a "leap in the dark". The Income-tax Officer is not entitled to make a guess without evidence.

The Tribunal did not make a distinction between an assessment under section 23(3) of the 1922 Act where the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 Act is invoked, and an assessment "to the best of judgment" under section 23(4) of the 1922. If the Income-tax Officer has made "best judgment assessment" under section 23(3) of the 1922 Act in the instant case, they were bad in law. Under section 23(3) of the 1922 Act the Income-tax Officer has to determine the income on the evidence before him produced by the assessee or collected by him, while under sub-section (4) he acts in the absence of such evidence because the assessee is in default in supplying information.

It was, therefore, held that in a case to which the proviso to section 13 of the 1922 applies, the ITO is bound to disclose in his order the basis and the manner of computation of the income, gains or profits and to disclose the date on which he arrives at the result.

As regards the question whether there was any material on record to warrant the estimate of the profits at the several rates adopted in this case unfortunately the statement of the case was not satisfactory. This was evidently due to the view of the Tribunal that the assessment was a leap in the dark. Instead of referring the case back under section 66(4) of the 1922 Act and wasting considerable time, the Court proposed to examine the orders of the Income-tax Officer to see if there was any material on record to warrant the estimate of profits at the several rates adopted by the Income-tax Officer.

On reference : HELD: The proviso to section 13 empowers the ITO to assess the profits on such basis and in such manner as he thinks proper where he comes to the conclusion that the income and profits could not be properly deduced from the accounts of the assessee. But it has to be observed that the power of the ITO under this proviso is not an arbitrary power. He must exercise his discretion and judgment judicially and reasonably. Further, if the ITO proposes to use against the assessee the result of any private enquiry made by him, he should put him in possession of the full particulars and gave him an opportunity to meet the same. Although the assessing authority, having had no other means of arriving at the correct amount of profit by reason for the accounts, of the assessee being unsatisfactory, could have recourse to the method of independent enquiries about profits made by like concerns doing similar business, he cannot come to his own conclusions without affording an opportunity to the assessee to be able to satisfy the income-tax authorities that the cases relied upon by him were not comparable cases and were distinguishable on various grounds. The ITO cannot be said to make an assessment to the best of his judgment if he is not guided by the dictates of justice and fair-play. Natural justice demands that he should draw the attention of the assessee to the particular cases the authority had in view. The income-tax authority is not competent to make a random assessment based on his private enquiries which may not be revealed to the assessee. Local enquiry and the placing on record a note of the results of such enquiry are essential to sustain an ex-parte assessment. If the ITO proposes to act upon information collected by him independently on private enquiries, he should disclose to the assessee the nature of that information to rebut it. There ought to be an opportunity to the assessee to displace the Taxing Officer's estimate by adducing evidence. In the instant case, it was not shown that any attempt was made by the ITO to draw the attention of the assessee to the material collected by him on private enquiry and which formed the basis for his conclusions. He merely felt content on the circumstance that in the year of account the manufactures of dyed and printed cloth like the assessee made bumber profits shooting up to 50 per cent and over. It was all the more necessary in a business of the kind that the assessee firm was doing that the information gathered with regard to other manufacturers should have been placed before the assessee, because in a business of this kind there could be no two truly comparable cases. The assessee's business consisted of (a) buying mill cloth and selling it in the market as cloth, (b) buying handloom cloth, getting it dyed and printed in his own karkhana and selling them same, and (c) buying mill cloth and handloom cloth and getting it dyed and printed elsewhere and selling final dyed and printed cloth in the market.

The profit in business (a) was bound to be different from the profit made in business (b), likewise the percentage of the profit in business (c) could not be the same in business (d). These factors had necessarily to be taken into consideration in arriving at the amount of profit. There could not be a rule of thumb in these matters. The Tribunal seemed to have taken it for granted that the assessee would have made as such profit as the others, because of the boom period, without going into the matter as to whether such profit could be made in the particular variety of business undertaken by the assessee.

The result was that the order of the Tribunal was set aside and the case was remanded to it with the direction to disclose the material gathered from private enquiries to the assessee and give full opportunity to the assessee to place any relevant material to meet the substance of the private enquiry.

HELD: It was held by this Court in Ramesh Chandra Chaturvedi v. CIT [1980] 121 ITR 116 that there could not be any hard and fast rule to determine the question as to whether the value of the materials should or should not be added to the gross turnover of the assessee, who is a contractor, for determining his net profits. It all depends upon manner in which the materials has to be used in the execution of the contract. Thus, although the contract document might be showing that the materials always remained the property of the department, yet in actual practice it might not be so and, therefore, the department has to consider whether as a fact the contractor has control over the materials or the department has the control. Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit (Net profit rate) - Assessment years 2012-13 to 2014-15 - Assessing Officer disallowed total expenses claimed in profit and loss account and sale consideration from immovable property and passed an ex parte order under section 144 - Commissioner (Appeals) based on his observation that purchase made by assessee in past were in dispute and genuineness of same had not been proved, computed net profit applying rate of 8 per cent on total revenue - However, it was found that net profit rate of 0.4 per cent had been accepted by this Tribunal in one of sister concern of assessee and even in scrutiny proceedings, revenue authorities in assessee's own case had estimated net profit below rate of 1 per cent - Whether therefore, looking to fact that there was no change of business during all these years, books of account were duly audited and no specific error had been pointed out by both lower authorities, estimating net profit at rate of 8 per cent could not be justified - Held, yes - Whether thus, application of net profit rate of 0.6 per cent on turnover of contract business during year would be proper - Held, yes [Paras 9.3 and 9.5] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where revenue authorities in assessee's own case in earlier year had estimated net profit below rate of 1 per cent, there being no change of business during relevant assessment years, estimating net profit at rate of 8 per cent could not be justified  INCOME TAX : Where business of earning commission from purchase and sale of land was being consistently carried out by assessee in previous year also and same was regularly entered in books of account and commission income earned from such transactions had been duly disclosed in financial statements and offered to tax, alleged amount of sale consideration of immovable property being just one of many transactions of sale of property executed by assessee on behalf of purchaser, could not be added to income of assessee  INCOME TAX : Where advances as appearing in audited financial statement were trade advances for execution of contract work which were transferred to sub-contractor and assessee was only conduit between work awarder and sub-contractor and transaction was made through banking channel, Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in deleting addition made by Assessing Officer under section 68

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the business of construction of building bridges. It filed its return of income on 30-9-2012 declaring income of Rs. 35.09 lakhs. Notices under sections 143(2) and 142(1) were issued but there was no compliance. Since the Assessing Officer had not received necessary information pursuant to notices issued under sections 143(2) and 142(1), he disallowed the total expenses claimed in the profit and loss account and sale consideration from immovable property and passed an ex parte order under section 144.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) applied the net profit rate of eight per cent on the gross business turnover for the assessment year 2012-13 and set aside the finding of the Assessing Officer of denying the claim of total expenses incurred during the year.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: It is noted that the audited financial statements were available before the Assessing Officer but without disputing the sales turnover during the year he disallowed the total expenses including the purchase of material towards contract work undertaken by the assessee during the year. When the matter travelled before the Commissioner (Appeals) he observed in the impugned order that the net profit rate for assessment years 2009-10 to 2011-12 disclosed by the assessee in its regular audited books of account is 0.22 per cent, 0.17 per cent and 0.25 per cent. Even during the course of scrutiny proceeding for assessment years 2009-10 to 2011-12 net profit rate applied by the Assessing Officer was 0.16 per cent, 0.93 per cent and 0.18 per cent. Though the Commissioner (Appeals) appreciated the fact that undisputed revenue just could not have come without incurring an expenditure, but based on his observation that the purchase made by the assessee in the past were in dispute and genuineness of the same had not been proved, the Commissioner (Appeals) computed the net profit applying the rate of 8 per cent on the total revenue for the year of Rs. 87.46 crores.[Para 9]

HEADNOTE: Section 249 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Commissioner (Appeals)/Deputy Commissioner (Appeals) - Condonation of delay - Assessment years 1983- 84 and 1984-85 - Appeal was filed by assessee belatedly with application for condonation of delay of one month allegedly caused in Chartered Accountant’s office - Chartered Accountant filed affidavit explaining delay - Whether Chartered Accountant’s affidavit being categorical about entrustment of work in time and delay being caused due to staff problem in his office, delay deserved to be condoned and Commissioner (Appeals) was unjustified in not condoning it - Held, yes

Section 143 of the Income-tax, Act, 1961 - Assessment - Additions to - Assessment years 1993-84 and 1984-85 -Whether profit disclosed by assessee- contractor in succeeding year can be taken to be a sure guide for determining profit for preceding year - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, where assessee-contractor had disclosed net profit at 8.4 per cent in assessment year in question, it would be incorrect to raise it to 12 per cent merely on ground that in succeeding year net profit returned was at 12.8 per cent - Held, yes - Whether lower authorities were unjustified in not allowing separate deduction for depreciation after estimating profits on gross receipts - Held yes - Whether, on consideration of facts, it would be appropriate to estimate net profits in instant case at 11.5 per cent with separate deduction for depreciation - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, a civil contractor, showed his gross receipts less cost of material at Rs. 25 lakhs and disclosed a net profit of 8.4 per cent. The Assessing Officer estimated net profit at 12 per cent on the ground that in the succeeding year the assessee had disclosed a net profit of 12.8 per cent. While doing so, the Assessing Officer did not allow any separate deduction by way of depreciation. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessment order.

On second appeal :

HELD: In the instant case, the net profit was to be estimated at 11.5 per cent of about Rs. 25 lakhs. The reduction of 1 /2 per cent was given for the reason that the assessee’s turnover of Rs. 25 lakhs was not very high as compared to others in this line of business. The reduction was granted for the further reason that as the work progressed from year to year, the assessee would be gaining experience and expertise as a result of which economy would be affected in the later years. Therefore, the profit of 12.8 per cent disclosed by the assessee in the succeeding year could not be taken to be a sure guide for determining the profit for the preceding year. The net profit was, therefore, estimated at 11.5 per cent of the receipts of Rs. 25 lakhs (approximately). This determination of net profit was only on the working of the contract by the assessee and depreciation (the correct amount was to be quantified by the Assessing Officer after verification) which was an allowance granted under the Act, should be viewed as a separate deduction. Another reason for considering depreciation for separate deduction was that in some cases of contracts, huge machines may have to be employed; whereas in some other cases Labour intensive devices would be employed. Therefore, in order to have a uniform estimate of profit, it is desirable that profit is estimated first ignoring the depreciation and then granting depreciation separately. Then and then only true profit can be ascertained as bet been persons employing high cost machinery and persons employing Labour intensive devices. Therefore, depreciation should be separately deducted from the profit thus estimated.

HEADNOTE: Section 145(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Assessment year 1989-90 - Assessee was in business of construction of ownership flats - He got part of work done through sub-contractors and claimed deduction of payment made to them but failed to produce them for examination - Details of payment of salary, etc., to staff were also not furnished - Basis of valuing work-in-progress was also not given -Whether on facts ITO was justified in invoking provisions of section 145(1) and making an estimated addition of Rs. 30,000 to be returned net profit - Held, yes.

FACT: The assessee commenced business of construction of ownership flat on 1-9-1987 and filed income-tax returns for the transitional previous year for 19 months up to 31-3-1989. He had taken up two projects and handed over the civil works to two sub-contractors by agreements dated 29-4-1988 and 7-10-1988. In the profit and loss account, a sum of Rs. 13,70,740 was debited and was shown as having been paid to these two sub-contractors. Before the ITO the assessee filed details of sub- contract payments but was unable to produce the two sub-contractors. The ITO observed that the assessee was unable to derive his correct profit in respect of the period taking Into account the progress of the work till 31-3-1989 and payments actually to be made and payments made, and that there was no basis for work in progress estimated by the assessee at Rs. 14,116, He also noted that the profit and loss account included items like development charges, registration charges, etc., that details for salaries and staff welfare debited at Rs. 18,747 were not available on record. Considering all these defects and the ad hoc nature of payments made to sub-contractors. the Assessing Officer made a round sum addition of Rs. 30,000 to the income returned, making the assessment order under section 143(3).

On appeal, the Dy. Commissioner (Appeals) held that the Assessing Officer had not noticed any specific defect which would have amounted to a wrong statement of income and, deleted the addition of Rs. 30,000 made by the ITO.

On appeal by the revenue:

HELD: Payment in excess of the amount which an assessee is liable to pay under the terms of an agreement is not an allowable deduction under section 37(1). The accounts of the assessee had not disclosed the correct profit derived by him in respect of the accounting period in question, taking into consideration the works so far done till 31-3-1989 and the payments to be made and actually made by the assessee. The burden to prove the sub- contracts, to bring the sub-contractors and examine them with reference to the sub-contracts entered into by them with the assessee, as also to satisfied the Assessing Officer with regard to the various payments received by them under the sub-contracts, lay squarely upon the assessee and not the department. Despite several opportunities granted to the assessee, he had failed to produce them, and, therefore, the Assessing Officer had reason to doubt the payments said to have been made under the sub-contracts. Further, the details for salaries and staff welfare expenses debited at Rs. 18,747 were not available on record and they were also not produced before the ITO. For these reasons, it was a case of estimate of profit under the proviso to section 145(1).

The order of Deputy Commissioner (Appeals) was, therefore, reversed and that of the ITO was restored.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment years 1965-66 to 1967-68 - Assessee was executing constructional contract works under military authorities - He was not maintaining any account books - Military authorities had supplied certain materials to assessee - Tribunal found that there was no element of profit on cost of materials supplied by authorities - Whether having regard to Tribunal is finding, cost of materials supplied by military authorities was not liable to be included in total receipts of assessee for calculating his net profit - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was doing business of executing constructional contract works under the military authorities but he did not produce any books of account before the ITO on the ground that he was not maintaining any account books.

The assessee had received some material supplied by the M.E.S. department and the value of such materials was deducted from the contract bills. In the absence of accurate figures furnished by the assessee regarding the value of materials supplied by the M.E.S. Department, the ITO estimated 10 per cent of the net contract payments on account of the value of materials supplied by the M.E.S. department for which deductions were made from the bills and added this amount to the net contract value to arrive at the gross value of the work executed by the assessee during that year. On that gross receipt, the ITO estimated the net profit. The AAC rejected the assessee's appeals. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that there was no element of profit on the cost of materials supplied by the department and, therefore, only net receipts should be taken into consideration for all purposes.

On reference :

HELD: The Tribunal had clearly held that there was no element of profit so far as the value of the materials supplied by the M.E.S. department to the assessee in performing the construction works was concerned.

The Tribunal was justified in holding that the cost of materials supplied by the M.E.S. department was not liable to be included in the total receipts of the assessee for calculating its net profits.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

However, the profit at 8 per cent estimated for these three years was only a mere estimate and the true profit of the entire project would be arrived at when the contract was complete. The assessee was, therefore, entitled to the adjustment of profit or loss in the year of completion of the contract. Hence, the estimate of profit at 8 per cent was reasonable. Regarding the interest payments under section 40A(8) the computation of income in the case of a contractor is normally made under section 145 if the books of account are incomplete and the true profit cannot be deduced therefrom. Such an estimate of profit under the provisions of section 145 cannot include all the other statutory disallowance like section 40A(8), section 40(b) or other such disallowances. The disallowance under section 40A(8) is provided for a specific purpose and if such a disallowance is deemed to be included in the estimate of profit under section 145, this would defeat the very purpose for which the provisions of section 40A(8) are enacted. Therefore, the interest under section 40A(8) can be separately added even if the profit in the case of the assessee has been estimated under section 145. Thus, the Commissioner (Appeals) was in error in deleting the addition under section 40A(8).

The outstanding liability in the first accounting period was Rs. 72,000 but it got reduced to only Rs. 5,000 as at the end of second period of the relevant accounting year. Thus, at the end of the accounting year consisting of two separate periods, there was an outstanding liability of only Rs. 5,000. Moreover, the Commissioner (Appeals) had also observed that such liabilities were shown in the balance-sheets pertaining to the assessment years 1983-84 and 1984-85, and no additions were made in respect of such outstanding liabilities. The profit in the contract business of the assessee had been estimated by the Assessing Officer at 15 per cent which had been upheld by the Commissioner (Appeals). After rejecting the books of account and making the assessment under section 144, separate addition made in respect of such liabilities might not be justified, as the income of the assessee had been assessed on an estimate basis by the Assessing Officer after ignoring the book results. Separate addition in respect of cash credits or unexplained credits can be made in certain cases even after applying the proviso to section 145(1) or section 145(2). But, it would depend upon the facts and the circumstances of each case. However, in cases of contractors generally income is estimated by applying profit rate on contract receipts as had been done by the Assessing Officer in the instant case also. Therefore there was no justification to interfere with the view taken by the Commissioner (Appeals) so far as it related to the deletion of addition in respect of the aforesaid outstanding liabilities in the labour charges account.

HEADNOTE: I. Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting (Rejection of books of account) - Assessment year 2009-10 - Where there was non-maintenance of inventory of items purchased, some purchases not supported by bills/vouchers, payments to labourers made in cash and no supporting evidence being maintained, non-furnishing of site-wise details of expenses and non-maintenance of day-to-day stock register and quantitative details of stock consumption, books of account of assessee were defective and, therefore, were rightly rejected - Held, yes - Whether since current year was only second year of assessee in contract business and assessee declared better NP rate of 7.02 per cent than first year, addition made by Assessing Officer by applying higher NP rate of 8.5 per cent as declared by others in similar line of business was not justified - Held, yes [Para 3.6] [Partly in favour of assessee]IT : Where relevant year was second year of assessee's contract business and he had shown better results than preceding year, even if assessee's books of account were rejected for certain defects, no addition could be made on account of low NP rate  IT : In absence of any positive material to show that assessee had made undisclosed investment in plot purchased in name of partnership firm of which he was partner, no addition could be made in hands of assessee under section 69B  IT : Inquiries conducted or material gathered behind back of assessee cannot be used against assessee to make addition under section 69B without providing opportunity of confrontation to assessee

FACT: The assessee was engaged in civil construction work. He filed return declaring certain net profit which was 7.02 per cent of gross contract receipts.

The Assessing Officer observed that the books of account of the assessee consisted defects like non-maintenance of inventory of items purchased, some purchases not supported by bills/vouchers, payments to labourers made in cash and no supporting evidence being maintained, i.e., complete postal address of labourers and non-maintenance of muster-roll and wages register, non-maintenance of salary register, payments of some expenses through self-made vouchers, non-maintenance of telephone call register, non-furnishing of site-wise details of expenses and non-maintenance of day-to-day stock register and quantitative details of stock consumption. He held that due to above defect the correct profit of the assessee could not be ascertained from books of account of the assessee. Hence, he rejected the books of account of the assessee by invoking the provisions of section 145(3) and estimated profit by applying the NP rate of 8.5 per cent of total turnover of the assessee by holding that other assessees carrying out similar business activities declared this net profit rate.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld rejection of books of account but reduced addition made by the Assessing Officer by estimating net profit at 8.25 per cent.

On second appeal, the assessee contended that the defects pointed out by the Assessing Officer were of general in nature and were not serious defects on basis of which books of account could be rejected. He also contended that the rejection of books of account did not give unfettered power to the Assessing Officer to estimate the profit at his whims and fancy specially when relevant year was the second year of the assessee in contract business and the NP rate of the assessee was better than last year.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessment year 1966-67 - ITO rejected books produced by assessee, a liquor contractor and estimated sales - Thereafter, taking into consideration case of another liquor contractor of very same area for an earlier year, profit was estimated at 7½ per cent on estimated sale - Whether in absence of better material revenue was well justified in taking into consideration case relating to another liquor contractor of very area in respect of earlier year - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, rate of profit at 7½ per cent was justifiably applied on turn over of assessee - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, a liquor contractor for Mandi Dabwali, returned an income for the relevant assessment year. The ITO rejected the books produced by the assessee and estimated the sales at a higher amount as against the amount shown in the books and estimated the profit at 7½ per cent of the total estimated sales.

On appeal, the AAC arrived at the figure of 7½ per cent after taking into consideration the case of another company, which was assessed for the year 1964-65 in respect of their income as liquor contractors for Mandi Dabwali. The further appeal to the Tribunal was also dismissed.

On reference:

HELD: In the absence of better material the revenue was well justified in taking into consideration the case relating to a liquor contractor of the very area in respect of an earlier year. That was the best material available and if there was anything to be said against it, it was open to the assessee to raise the necessary ground before the Tribunal. Nothing was said against taking into consideration the case of the other liquor contractor for the assessment year 1964-65. All that was said before the Tribunal was that there was a slump in sales because of the Indo-Pakistan war in 1965. From the facts and figures as mentioned in the Tribunal's order it did not appear that there was any particular slump after September, 1965, though there appeared to be some slump in September, 1965, only. In fact it was in December, 1965, that there were peak sales of the assessee. The sales of the contractor for the year 1964-65 amounted to Rs. 4,70,000 only. Therefore, the assessee's sales, which even according to him, amounted to Rs. 10,78,898 were not in any manner hit by the Indo-Pakistan war.

Therefore, the rate of profit at 7½ per cent on the turnover was justifiably applied by the Tribunal on the turnover of the assessee.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (GP/NP Rate) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee, a joint venture, was formed for purpose to bid and execute construction work - It declared net profit at rate of 1 per cent of contractual receipts - Assessing Officer having noticed that assessee had failed to establish its claim of 1 per cent net profit by producing any evidence to that effect rejected book results and estimated net profit at rate of 4 per cent of total contractual receipts - Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed appeal on ground that assessee did not pursue its appeal before him - Whether matter required to be remanded back to Commissioner (Appeals) to decide issue on merit after affording reasonable opportunities of being heard to assessee - Held, yes [Para 11] [Matter remanded]INCOME TAX : Where assessee was engaged in construction work and Assessing Officer rejected book results and estimated net profit at rate of 4 per cent of total contractual receipts as against 1 per cent declared by assessee and Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed appeal ex parte, matter was to be remanded back to Commissioner (Appeals) to decide issue on merit

Section 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of income (GP/NP Rate) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee, a joint venture, was formed for purpose to bid and execute construction work - It declared net profit at rate of 1 per cent of contractual receipts - Assessing Officer having noticed that assessee had failed to establish its claim of 1 per cent net profit by producing any evidence to that effect rejected book results and estimated net profit at rate of 4 per cent of total contractual receipts - Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed appeal on ground that assessee did not pursue its appeal before him - Whether matter required to be remanded back to Commissioner (Appeals) to decide issue on merit after affording reasonable opportunities of being heard to assessee - Held, yes [Para 11] [Matter remanded]

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of Accounting Estimation of Profit -  Assessment year 1965-66 - Assessee carried on business of constructing buildings and doing work of maintenance of buildings, inter alia for railways - As per specific terms of contract entered into with railway authorities cement and iron had to be supplied them for execution of work and no accounting of cost of those materials was to be done while making bill in respect of contract payment - Whether value of materials supplied by railway authorities could not be included in total receipt of assessee for purpose of calculating net profit by application of rate - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee carried on business of construing buildings and doing the work of maintenance of buildings, inter alia, for railways. As per the specific terms of the contract entered into with the railway authorities, cement and iron had to be supplied by them for execution of the work and no accounting of the cost of these materials was to be done while making the bill in respect of contract payment. HEADNOTE: Section 143 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Assessment - Addition to income - Assessment year 1993-94 - Assessing Officer disallowed 1 per cent of labour payments and material purchase expenses on ground that in respect of internal vouchers genuineness could not be ascertained for want of details - Assessee contended that complete details with bills, vouchers, labour registers, etc., were produced but no comments were made by Assessing Officer and that percentage of gross profit on sales had actually gone up as compared to previous year - Assessing Officer had not made any averment that books of account were not correct or defective - Whether since additions made were not based on any cogent material nor any basis given for arriving at figure of one per cent, first appellate authority had rightly deleted addition - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a contractor. The Assessing Officer noticed that for the assessment year 1993-94, the net profit from contract came to less than 1 per cent of the net receipt which was more than rupees one crore. The Assessing Officer was of the view that in respect of materials purchased and labour payments, which were based on several internal vouchers, the genuineness could not be ascertained in the absence of complete details. He, therefore, disallowed 1 per cent of the expenses relating to the above as inflated expenses and added the same to the total income of the assessee. The assessee contended that the disallowance was arbitrary and based on assumptions, conjectures and surmises; that complete details of all purchases along with bills, vouchers, etc., and full details of labour payments with labour registers were being maintained and the same were also produced before the Assessing Officer but no comments were made by the Assessing Officer; that the percentage of the gross profit on sales in the assessment year under appeal had actually gone up as compared to the earlier year. The first appellate authority deleted the addition.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: The revenue had not brought any material on record to controvert the submission of the assessee. The additions made by the Assessing Officer were not based on cogent material. The Assessing Officer had not given any basis for arriving at the figure of 1 per cent of the expenses shown by the assessee on account of material purchases and labour payments. There was no averment by the Assessing Officer that the books of account maintained by the assessee were not correct or contained any defect. The Assessing Officer did not adopt any basis for increase made by him. As held by the Supreme Court in the case of State of Orissa v. Maharaja Sri B.P. Singh Deo [1970] 76 ITR 690 that the mere fact that the material placed by the assessee before the assessing authorities was unreliable did not empower the authorities to make an arbitrary order. In view of the above facts and for the reasons stated hereinabove, the assessee’s contention was to be upheld.

The assessee had been carrying on business of the execution of contracts. The total income of the assessee for the assessment year 1962-63 was computed at Rs. 6,380. In respect of the assessment year under consideration assessment was made on estimate by the ITO acting under section 145. After deducting from the total income of Rs. 6,380 the tax of Rs. 3,190, the distributable surplus was worked out at Rs. 3,190. Therefore, the assessee ought to have declared a dividend of Rs. 1,914, being 60 per cent of the said amount of distributable surplus of Rs. 3,190. The ITO, held that the gross profit of the year had been determined by application of section 145 and there was no other addition in determining the assessable income and as such the point of commercial profits had no relevance. On appeal, the AAC held that there was no commercial profit for distribution as dividend and, therefore, he cancelled the ITO’s order under section 104. On second appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order of the AAC holding that in determining the commercial profits of the assessee-company for the year for the purpose of section 104, no estimated profit was to be taken into account in respect of the contracts that were partly executed by the end of the year when the accounts were maintained on the basis of completed contracts.

On reference, the revenue contended that the question, as to, whether the method of maintaining of the assessee's accounts was correct or not or whether the profit of the assessment year 1962-63 was correctly and properly calculated on the basis of the estimate under section 145 or not, was a question which related to assessment proceeding and its correctness could be determined only in appeal or reference, arising out of the assessment order for the said year and not in appeal or reference arising out of an order made under section 104.

of the orders of ITO, AAC and Appellate Tribunal really furnished basis for arriving at Rs. 10,50,000 as the turnover, nor did those orders, which purported to show that the number of cases upon which the ITO was supposed to have relied in coming to the conclusion that 9 per cent was reasonable rate of profit, were ever disclosed to the assessee, nor was the assessee given an opportunity to rebut that the conclusion based on that material was not warranted. In this case, while both the AAC as well as the Tribunal stated that, in arriving at the percentage of gross profits, the ITO took into consideration similar cases, there was nothing to show that the assessee was given an opportunity to rebut that evidence. What these similar cases were whose percentage of gross profits was taken into consideration was not apparent from any of the orders attached to the statement of the case. The only observation in all the orders, viz., of the ITO, the AAC and the Tribunal was that the turnover of Rs. 10,50,000 was fair and reasonable and that the ITO was right in estimating the rate of profit at 9 per cent based on similar cases. It was not shown why the turnover was fixed at Rs. 10,50,000 and not anything less or more. In every case the rate of 9 per cent would certainly depend upon the computation of the turnover. If the turnover is Rs. 10,00,000, the gross profits would be Rs. 90,000 and if the turnover was Rs. 9,50,000, accordingly, the gross profits would be reduced. If it was more than Rs. 10,00,000, naturally the gross profits would equally swell. It would, therefore, appear that the estimate of the gross profits and the fixations of the percentage of profits in this business were two important elements which affected the assessment and, if these were fixed to the detriment of the assessee, he was entitled to know the basis and to be given an opportunity to rebut the same, both of which had not been done in this case. Consequently, the order of the income-tax authorities could be said to be capricious and without any validity.

As to the contention, of the assessee, viz., that the method of computation of the gross profits by the ITO as well as by the AAC was not in accordance with the accepted method of accounting it may be noticed that a sum of Rs. 45,748 was deducted on account of four items. Of these, one of the items, viz., Rs. 19,463, was on account of the lease of the mill. The other figures had not been given. But, it was assumed that the aggregate sum of Rs. 45,748 consisted of the four items, viz., mill samans, twine, mill contract and the factory salaries.

The profit and loss account of a trading concern is usually divided into two sections. The first section is termed the trading account which is so framed as to show the gross profit. The gross profit as shown by the trading account is transferred to the second section which is the profit and loss account proper.

The excess of the credit total over the debit is called the gross profit, i.e., the excess realised on the sales over the purchase price of the goods sold, and is transferred to the profit and loss account. These principles appear to exclude from the computation of gross profit any items which do not affect the cost of the goods sold. It was, perhaps, for this reason that the AAC deleted certain items from the items which the ITO computed for deduction from the gross profit, such as the lease amount and certain establishment charges as claimed by the assessee. But it appeared from the order of the AAC that the items which the assessee claimed had been allowed. The department contended that the assessee did not take any objection before the Appellate Tribunal that the other items ought to have also been deleted from the gross profit. But the assessee contended that his grounds of appeal covered this aspect of the matter also, and that the amounts in respect of the items which had been deleted from the gross profit returned by him were also shown in the profit and loss account, from which they had been computed. It was also contended that the computation of the gross profit must be in accordance with law and on the material on record. It was not permissible for the income-tax authorities to allow a part and disallow the rest, if, in law, he was entitled not to take any of these items into consideration in arriving at the gross profits.

For the aforesaid reason there was no basis or material for the department to compute the income.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

The Assessing Officer has rejected books of account for the reason that the assessee has failed to produce necessary bills and vouchers in respect of expenditure. The Assessing Officer has observed that most of the expenditure are supported by self-made vouchers. Although, the assessee claims that it has produced bills and vouchers in respect of major expenditure, fails to substantiate the claim with necessary evidences. The assessee failed to controvert the findings of the Assessing Officer with any positive evidence to come to the conclusion that the books of account maintained by him gave a true and correct profit from the business. The Assessing Officer was therefore right in rejecting books of account under the provisions of section 145(3) of the Act. [Para 8]

Having said, one has to examine, on facts and circumstances of the case whether the Assessing Officer was right in adopting net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts. There is no dispute with regard to the facts that the assessee is in the business of execution of works contracts. It is also an admitted fact that the assessee had disclosed 6.73 per cent to 7.44 per cent net profit, in the earlier period. For the assessment year 2007-08 in the scrutiny assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer has estimated net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts for which the assessee has not preferred any appeal. Estimation of net profit from the business is one of the accepted method of determination of income from business. But, there is no hard and fast rule for estimation of income.

The department is following estimation of net profit on various rates depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case. But, while estimating net profit from the business, there should be a basis for adopting a particular rate of net profit, either based on comparable cases of similar nature of business or assessee's own book results for earlier years. When there is no possibility of getting a comparable cases, and there is no possibility of reference to assessee's own book results for earlier periods, a reference to the provisions of section 44AD can be made, wherein the Act provides for estimation of net profit from the specified businesses subject to certain conditions. [Para 9]

The provisions of section 44AD provide for estimation of net profit of 8 per cent on gross receipts, in case where the assessees are involved in specified businesses and turnover from the business does not exceed specified limit. Although, the assessee's case does not fall within the ambit of the provisions of section 44AD of the Act, as its contract receipts exceed the specified limit, the analogy provided in the provisions of section 44AD can be adopted for estimation of net profit because of nature of business carried out by the assessee. The nature of business carried on by the assessee was squarely fit into the specified businesses referred to in the provisions of section 44AD of the Act. The presumptive rate of net profit of 8 per cent incorporated in section 44AD, reflects the legislative approved rate of net profit, which can be considered as fair and reasonable to estimate income from civil contract business, where the books of account are not found reliable by the Assessing Officer.

In this case, admittedly, the Assessing Officer had rejected books of account for the reason that the assessee has failed to produce supporting bills and vouchers in respect of expenditure. It is also an admitted fact that the assessee himself has admitted about 8 per cent net profit in the earlier period net of all deductions including depreciation. Therefore, considering the overall facts and circumstances of the case, the rate of net profit adopted by the Assessing Officer appears to be fair and reasonable. Hence, estimation of net profit of 8 per cent on total receipts net of all deductions including depreciation is upheld. [Para 10]

In so far as separate deductions towards depreciation is concerned, the assessee submitted that when estimation of net profit is made, separate deductions towards depreciation should be allowed, as depreciation is a notional deduction for normal wear and tear of the assets.

In this case, the assessee is involved in the business of execution of main works which carries more profit than sub-contract works and hence, the Assessing Officer has rightly adopted reasonable net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts and accordingly, further deductions towards depreciation is not allowed. Whether separate deductions can be allowed towards depreciation or not is a fact which is to be decided based on the facts and circumstances of each case and also based on the rate of net profit adopted for estimation of profit.

On the language of the proviso to section 13 of 1922 Act, it is plain that if no method of accounting has been regularly employed, or, if the method employed is such that, in the opinion of the ITO, income, profits and gains cannot properly be deduced therefrom, then the ITO is empowered to make the computation upon such basis, and in such manner, as he may determine.

In the instant case, the ITO had found that the assessee did not maintain any account books, as none were produced at the time of the visit of the then ITO, at least in respect of three shops which he visited, and, therefore, he was justified in concluding that the account books now produced for these shops also had been written up at a later stage. He had further given reasons, for holding that the account books produced by the assessee did not reflect the true profits of the previous years. In such circumstances, the ITO was perfectly justified in applying the proviso to section 13 of 1922 Act to the present case, and in making his own estimate of the profit upon such basis and in such manner as he thought proper.

Further fact that the Tribunal upheld the ITO’s went to show that it found no reason to differ from the decision arrived at by it in the preceding year 1945-46. This also clearly went to show that the Tribunal in the year under assessment also found the account books to be unreliable, as they were found to be so in the previous year by it, for the reasons given by it in the preceding year, and by the ITO in the present year.

There is no rule of law as to the proper way of making an estimate. The only rule of law is that the true gains are to be ascertained as nearly as it can be done. There is no way of estimating, which is right or wrong in itself. It is a question of fact and figure whether the way of making the estimate, in any case, is the best way for that case. In making the estimate, the Income-tax Officer acts under section 23(4) of the 1922 Act, and he is required under it to make an estimate to the best of his judgment against a person, who is in default as regards supplying information. He must make what he honestly believes to be a fair estimate of the proper figure of assessment, and for this purpose he must be able to take into consideration local knowledge and repute in regard to the assessee's circumstances, and his own knowledge of previous returns by, and assessments of, the assessee, and all other matters which he thinks will assist him in arriving at a fair and proper estimate: and though there must necessarily be guess-work in the matter, it must be honest guess-work. It was open to the Income-tax Officer, therefore, to maintain the same percentage in respect of the year of assessment when the assessment at a flat rate of profit at a certain percentage in the preceding year or years had been adopted, and the objection of the assessee to such an assessment taken by him had been rejected in the preceding years. The Income-tax Officer, therefore, was well warranted in maintaining the same percentage in the year of assessment, and, in taking into consideration the past records of an assessee, provided there was some evidence or material before the income-tax authorities for making the best judgment assessment, and it was not absolutely arbitrary, although in that sense too assessment must be to some extent arbitrary.

In view of aforesaid, impugned order of the Tribunal was to be affirmed.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

The Assessing Officer had estimated the gross profit at 6 per cent of the total receipts and had completed the assessment after adding the income from other sources also. The sundry creditors, as is seen from the explanation offered by the assessee before the Commissioner, came to Rs. 3.44 crores out of which the liability in the previous year was Rs. 1.92 crores. Hence the sundry credit claimed by the assessee came to Rs. 1.51 crores. Obviously this was not noticed by the Assessing Officer and presumably the same was not accounted in the total receipts as undisclosed income. If the sundry credits are not explained properly, then disclosing that in the account books would amount to a device employed to suppress the income received, as a credit taken by a third party, with whom the assessee had a transaction. [Para 9]

The assessee was a works contractor, who had executed contracts awarded by various State Government departments. There is no question of the credit being attributed to any of the awarders which even if existing, there was no difficulty in establishing the same. [Para 10]

In the assessment order the assessee has income from a firm, house property and other sources. Hence the income declared by the assessee is not solely from the contract work. When the assessment made is of income from one single source, if the total contract receipts are taken to estimate the gross profit, necessarily there cannot be any further addition made. If the gross receipts are taken, on which the net profit is assessed, the entire receipts are not reflected, then definitely there is scope for addition to the receipts. The sundry creditors if not explained will have to be added to the contract receipts before the net profit is assessed or otherwise added in the income from other sources, bringing in that quantum, as unexplained income. [Para 11]

Hence either way whether the unexplained sundry credits are added to the contract receipts or as income from other sources definitely the tax payable by the assessee would be higher than that paid by a mere estimation of net profit looking at the quantum returned on which no explanation was sought. The Commissioner in order under section 263 had also reckoned non payment of tax deducted at source. [Para 12]

Essentially the Commissioner has found the order to be erroneous for reason of non payment into the treasury of the tax deducted at source having not been verified and also the sundry creditors having not been examined. The latter of which ground results in the finding that the estimation of profit on the contract receipts alone would be an erroneous exercise and it causes prejudice to the interest of the revenue. There is absolutely no reason to interfere with the order of the Commissioner. The order of Tribunal is set aside. [Para 13]
