In the instant case, the Assessing Officer rejected the books of account on the reason that the assessee had not maintained proper books of account and also had failed to produce vouchers for verification and the expenditure claimed by the assessee was not substantiated. The assessee in the earlier years also had not maintained the proper books of account. The assessee’s past track record showed that it neglected presenting of the books of account in accordance with law. When the assessee claimed any expenditure, it was mandatory on its part to produce the books of account supported by proper bills and vouchers. Since the assessee had not produced books of account, true profits or loss could not be deduced from its books of account. The Assessing Officer having no other option rejected the books of account and estimated the income at 10 per cent of gross receipts. But the position was that the assessee was carrying on three kinds of contracts as in the earlier years, i.e., (i) own contracts, (ii ) contracts taken from the sub-contractors, (iii) contracts given to other parties on sub-contracts. The assessee had a higher rate of profit on the contracts executed by the assessee itself. In these contracts, the assessee agreed that its income was at 9 per cent of the gross receipts. Thus, the Assessing Officer was directed to estimate the income on the contracts executed by the assessee on its own at 9 per cent. In case of contracts taken by the assessee on sub-contract, the income was to be estimated at 8 per cent of the gross receipts. In case of contracts given by the assessee to the 3rd party on sub-contract, income was to be estimated at 4 per cent. This is because when the assessee gave contract to the other parties on sub-contract, it could not keep the same percentage of profit at 9 per cent. It had to forgo certain portion of the profit, i.e., around 5 per cent to the sub-contractors. Similar was the position in the case of contracts taken by the assessee on sub-contract from other parties. Further, the assessee was entitled to depreciation and remuneration, and interests to partners on the profit estimated by the Assessing Officer at applicable rates, because the income estimated as above of the assessee was before the depreciation and interest and remuneration of the partners. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer was to be directed to compute the income of the assessee afresh.

Another contention raised by the assessee was that once the books of account were rejected and income was estimated, the Assessing Officer was precluded from invoking provisions of section 40(a)( ia) to make further addition. The books of account of the assessee were not relied, these were rejected by the Assessing Officer and the same was confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as by the Tribunal. Now, placing reliance on the same books for the purpose of invoking the provisions of section 40(a)(ia ) was improper. The estimation of income took care of the irregularities committed by the assessee. Further addition by invoking section 40(a)(ia ) amounted to punishing the assessee for the same offence on double occasions, which was not permitted by law.

On cross-appeals:

After coming to the conclusion that the trading results were not prone to verification, the Assessing Officer was left with only one alternative to estimate the income of the assessee in the most appropriate and reasonable manner. In such type of cases, the net profit rate or gross profit rate could be applied or the Assessing Officer could adopt any method of estimation and work out the income from profession or business. But the method adopted must be reasonable and logical. In all civil contract cases, if accounts are not maintained or defective accounts are maintained, a net rate of 10 per cent is applied which was admitted by the Commissioner (Appeals) in his order. In those cases neither depreciation nor interest nor any other expenditure debitable to profit and loss account are separately allowed. By allowing depreciation and interest, net profit rate of approximately 3.5 per cent had been applied consequent to the order of the Commissioner (Appeals). The rate itself was absolutely abnormal. There was no evidence on record whatsoever that there were abnormal conditions prevailing with the assessee to earn such a low net profit by executing the contract. Once net rate was applied it was not open to the Assessing Officer to allow any other claim debited to profit and loss account. Depreciation and interest were definitely items which were debited in profit and loss account before the net profit was arrived at. It could have been the case of the appellant to justify the net profit rate shown as .27 per cent or to justify the net profit rate applied by the Commissioner (Appeals) at 3.5 per cent approximately. But no such discussion was available on record. The logical conclusion of the circular of the CBDT regarding claim of depreciation that in case profits were estimated, the same should be made subject to the allowance of depreciation and the assessee should file complete details of the claim of depreciation. One has again to look into the power given by the statute to the Assessing Officer when he invoked proviso to section 145(1). The first proviso to section 145(1) gives power to the Assessing Officer to decide whether or not income can properly be deduced from the accounts maintained by the assessee, even if the accounts are correct and complete.

Keeping in view the law laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. British Paints India Ltd. [1991] 188 ITR 44/ 54 Taxman 499 the Assessing Officer has to adopt rationale and reasonable method in arriving at the estimate of income, after he gives finding that the accounts maintained by the appellant are neither prone to verification nor reliable. He can use his own method but his method should be rationale and reasonable. In the case of the assessee he had used rationale and reasonable method. The application of net rate is directly dependent on the net rate shown by other cases in the line of the business. Other cases of contractors are being applied net rate of profit without giving them advantage of depreciation some contractors debit various items which relate to profit & loss or trading account expenditure and claimed 100% of depreciation. This method creates an abnormal situation in the net profit. The Assessing Officer had, therefore, taken a proper course by ignoring depreciation and the interest and applied net rate of 10%. The second positive feature in the assessment of the ITO related to the observation that the net profit rate of the person who used heavy machinery was going to be more than the net profit of a person who was not using the mechanical aid for execution of civil work.

Hence, there was no infirmity in the method adopted by the Assessing Officer. The order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was reversed and the order of the Assessing Officer maintained.

6. While making assessments the Assessing Officer compares the GP declared either with GP declared in earlier year or GP declared by other assessees and makes an addition on such comparison. In the face of ever-charging circumstances it is not possible to have uniform rate of GP without resorting to manipulation. Each year is a separate year and it is not possible to have uniform rate of profit each year. Several features of the business may affect the earning - R.V.S. & Sons Dairy Farm v. CIT [2002] 257 ITR 764 [2003] 130 Taxman 615 (Mad.). In holding so the Court referred to Karnataka High Court decision in P. Venkanna v. CIT [1969] 72 ITR 328 (Mys.) wherein it was observed that other things being equal, profits estimated during earlier period may be a guide in estimating the profits for the year on hand but only when the conditions in which the business activity of later period are similar to those of the earlier period.

n The GP rate declared by the assessee was lower than that of earlier years. The Assessing Officer applied higher GP rate without taking into consideration the fact of purchase price having increased substantially compared with sale price. n Each year is an independent unit for which liability for tax has to be determined and this would be so even when the assessee’s books are not accepted. The estimate should be done in relation to figures available for each year and one must take note of prior record as well. INCOME TAX : Where assessee was engaged in construction work and Assessing Officer rejected book results and estimated net profit at rate of 4 per cent of total contractual receipts as against 1 per cent declared by assessee and Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed appeal ex parte, matter was to be remanded back to Commissioner (Appeals) to decide issue on merit

The assessee, engaged in construction work, had started a project for construction of 30 buildings in 1980 which was to take several years for completion. Hence, it adopted ‘Project Completion Method’ as its method of accounting. According to this method the profits could be worked out only when the project was complete or at least substantially complete. Therefore, for the assessment year 1981-82, the assessee filed its return at nil income, which was accepted. However, similar returns were not accepted for the assessment years 1982-83 to 1985-86, and the Assessing Officer estimated the income by applying the profit rate at 10 per cent to 15 per cent. There was a search in the premises of the assessee on 11-5-1987 where some incriminating materials were found. The assessee declared unaccounted profit of Rs. 66 lakhs as ‘on money’ sought to be assessed in assessment years 1987-88 and 1988-89. On the basis of that, the assessment for the assessment year 1985-86 was completed where the Assessing Officer, besides making estimate of profit at the rate of 15 per cent, made a separate addition of Rs. 73,19,200 pursuant to offer of the assessee of taxing Rs. 66 lakhs as ‘on money’ receipts which were stated to have been entered in the books of account for assessment years 1987-88 and 1988-89. On appeal, the addition of estimated profit was deleted by the Commissioner (Appeals) but the addition of Rs. 73,19,200 was set aside. For the assessment year 1986-87, the assessment was completed at Rs. 55,11,859 against returned income of Rs. 7,96,450. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) set aside the assessment and directed to complete it afresh. However, in spite of repeated notices for hearing, no compliance was made and thus, the Assessing Officer completed the assessment again taking into account (i) the quantum of ‘on money’ received by the assessee, and (ii) the year in which that ‘on money’ should be taxed. For dealing with these issues, the Assessing Officer took into account the statement of ‘J’, one of the directors of the assessee-company who had stated that the assessee had been charging 15 per cent to 20 per cent ‘on money’ and no ‘on money’ was charged from institutions like BML, Dena Bank and some educational trusts. He also took into account the statements of one M, accountant, and ‘S’, supervisor, of the assessee recorded during the course of search, wherein the ‘on money’ charged was stated to be 30 per cent to 40 per cent. The above statements were taken in the presence of independent Panchas at the time of search, who had certified that no untoward incident had taken place during the course of search. Therefore, the assessee’s plea that those persons had retracted from their statements as they were stated to have been recorded under threat or duress, was rejected by the Assessing Officer. The Assessing Officer also took into account statement on oath of one ‘I’ who had deposed to the effect that he had paid 40 per cent as ‘on money’ on the shop purchased by him from the assessee in 1983. On the basis of these evidence, the Assessing Officer estimated that ‘on money’ received by the assessee could be 25 per cent of the total consideration received. The Assessing Officer, therefore, estimated ‘on money’ at Rs. 1,25,78,000 for the assessment years 1981-82 to 1988-89 against which the assessee had offered for taxation Rs. 26 lakhs in the assessment year 1987-88 and Rs. 40 lakhs in the assessment year 1988-89. The AO held that ‘on money’ was unaccounted receipt, that there was no provision in law to assess unaccounted money arbitrarily in two years only, that the contention of the assessee that it had been following project completion method of ac-counting was not correct and added Rs. 25,42,000 in the assessment year 1986-87. For the assessment year 1987-88, the assessee had filed its return of income declaring total income at Rs. 28,87,260. The assessment was completed by the Assessing Officer on a total income of Rs. 29,80,712. For the assessment year 1988-89, the assessee filed its return of income at Rs. 35,82,987 after taking into account the ‘on money’ of Rs. 40 lakhs offered to be assessed this year

The assessee was engaged in business of civil construction. He filed his return for the assessment year 1998-99 along with audited books of account. The Assessing Officer, on finding that labour payments for the month of January 1998 had actually been paid in March 1998 and for February had been paid in the month of March, held that net profit rate could not be properly deduced and, therefore, he rejected books of account of the assessee and estimated net profit at the rate of 8 per cent of declared gross receipts.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the rejection of books of account and estimation of profit at the rate of 8 per cent.

On second appeal:

The assessee, a contractor, was engaged in construction work. For the assessment year 1992-93, the Assessing Officer rejected the book result and applied net profit rate of 10 per cent on gross payment. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the action of the Assessing Officer invoking the provisions of section 145, but reduced the net profit rate to 8 per cent. On cross appeals, the Tribunal held that in the absence of proper books of account, vouchers and registers, the provisions of section 145 could not be applied when their absence itself constituted a defence in the books of account.

On reference application under section 256(1) :

The authority making a best judgment assessment must make an honest and fair estimate of the income of the assessee and though arbitrariness cannot be avoided in such estimate the same must not be capricious but should have a reasonable nexus to the available material and the circumstances of the case.

From the tender documents that were made available to the contractor and the terms and conditions of the "Lump Sum Contracts", two or three aspects emerged very clearly. In the first place, the contractor became aware that certain specified stores/materials would be supplied to him by the department at fixed rates for being used in the works to be undertaken by him for which he had not to pay from his pocket and it was on that footing that he submitted his tender quoting a particular figure for the entire work; secondly, such stores/material so supplied by the M.E.S. department had to be used, fixed or incorporated by the contractor in the works undertaken by him and the surplus, if any, that would remain after the completion of the work was to be returned to the department; thirdly, since for accounting purposes the initial supply was debited to the contractor at the specified fixed rates, credit for the balance of the stores/materials so returned was also given at the same rates, some adjustment being made in respect of the wear and tear of such stores/material but in regard to the stores/material out of such supply as was actually used, fixed or incorporated into the works, no accounting was done vis-a-vis the contract payment that is made to the contractor. In other words, in substance and in reality, such stores/material always remained the property of the department and the contractor had merely the custody of it and he fixed or incorporated the same into the works. It seemed clear that in such circumstances and having regard to the terms and conditions on which such supply of stores/materials was made there was not even a theoretical possibility of any element of profit being involved in the turnover represented by the cost of such stores/material. It was conceivable that when the contractor himself purchased materials in the open market and supplies the same to the department by using, fixing or incorporating the same in the works, as in the case of materials other than those specified in Schedule "B", some profit element would be embedded in the turnover represented by the cost of such material but when stores/material was supplied by the Government department at fixed rates for being used, fixed or incorporated in the work on terms indicated above, there would be no element of profit involved in the turnover represented by the cost of such material. It is true that, ordinarily, when a works contract is put through or completed by a contractor the income or profits derived by the contractor from such contract is determined on the value of the contract as a whole and cannot be determined by considering several items that go to form such value of the contract but in our view where certain stores/material is supplied at fixed rates by the department to the contractor solely for being used or fixed or incorporated in the works undertaken on terms and conditions mentioned above, the real total value of the entire contract would be the value minus the cost of such stores/material so supplied. Therefore, since no element of profit was involved in the turnover represented by the cost of stores/material supplied by the M.E.S. to the assessee-firm, the income or profits derived by the assessee firm from such contracts would have to be determined on the basis of the value of the contracts represented by the cash payments received by the assessee-firms from the M.E.S. department exclusive of the cost of the material/stores received for being used, fixed or incorporated in the works undertaken by them.

The appeal was, therefore, allowed.

The assessee is a contractor carrying out Government as well as private contracts. The assessee produced complete books of account before the Assessing Officer but without supporting vouchers. Even the unexplained credits/transfer entries/deposits in the bank account were inter deposits of business and these were nothing sort of cash credits or unexplained credits. Revenue could not explain how the entire addition was made and what was the basis for same. It only argued that since the books of account were not supported by vouchers, the Assessing Officer and Commissioner (Appeals) had disallowed the expenses, charges and unproved credits/transfers/deposits in the hands of the assessee. It is not the case of the revenue that these deposits /unproved credits/transfer were not related to business transaction, rather the assessee filed a complete chart stating that the entire deposits/transfers/credits were proved and these were related to business transactions only and out of contract receipts. In such circumstances, the assessment order or order of Commissioner (Appeals) cannot be upheld. [Para 6]

In the absence of supporting material of the books of account i.e., bills and vouchers, the assessing authority should have rejected books of account and should have framed assessment in terms of sections 144 and 145. For that the Assessing Officer must act honestly and not vindictively or capriciously because he must exercise judgment in the matter. However, from records it is evident otherwise. He must make what he honestly believes to be fair estimate of the proper figure of assessment, and for this purpose he must be able to take into consideration local knowledge and repute in regard to the assessee's circumstances, and his own knowledge of previous returns and assessments of the assessee and all other matters which he thinks will assist him in arriving at a fair and proper estimate; and though there must necessarily be guess-work in the matter, it must be honest guess-work. In making a best judgment assessment, the Assessing Officer does not possess absolutely arbitrary authority to assess at any figure he likes, and although he is not bound by strict judicial principles, he should be guided by rules of justice, equity and good conscience. At the same time, there is nothing in the language of section 144 or 145 for holding that an assessment made by an officer under these sections, without conducting a local enquiry and without recording the details and results of that enquiry, cannot have been made to the best of his judgment within the meaning of that section. In other words, the Assessing Officer, while making a best judgment assessment, should make an intelligent, well grounded estimate. Such estimate must be based on adequate and relevant materials. If more than one method or approach is possible, any alternative method can be restored to estimate the quantum in a best judgment assessment. The quantum to be made in a best judgment assessment should be rational and fair in all circumstances of the case. [Para 7]

The Tribunal confirmed the application of net profit at 5.35 per cent in earlier year i.e. in Assessment Year 2003-04. Keeping in view net profit of earlier years, a reasonable net profit i.e. at the rate of 8 per cent would meet the end of justice. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer is directed to recompute the assessee's income after deleting all the additions as made by him and enhanced by Commissioner (Appeals), but restrict the addition only at 8 per cent of gross contract receipts. It is also mentioned that this net profit rate at 8 per cent cannot be taken as reference to any other years, if facts are not identical or assessee claims that assessment be framed on the basis of accounts, if accounts are found correct. [Para 8]

It cannot be said that the assessee was not entitled to adopt percentage method of recognition of income for computation of income tax under accrual method of accounting. However, mere qualification in the Annual Report of the company containing the balance sheet and the profit and loss account by itself is not sufficient to conclude that the assessee has disclosed the percentage of the work completed during previous year relevant for the assessment year. [Para 33]

The assessee may have entered into several contracts with different clients with varied terms and conditions. These documents are required to be produced before the Assessing Officer at the time of assessments. The purpose of accounting under the Act, is to ascertain the taxable income and to determine the tax payable by an assessee. Therefore, these documents and other ancillary documents are required to be produced before an Assessing Officer during the assessment. [Para 34]

Further, a proper certification whether by an in-house department of the assessee or by an independent chartered engineer certifying the percentage of work completed under the contract was required to be produced by the assessee before the Assessing Officer for the purpose of assessment. [Para 35]

What was the term of the contract under which the revenue was generated on the bill raised on a client or a customer cannot be certified in the audited profit and loss account and the balance sheet. At best, they can corroborate what is there in the contract. Therefore, unless those supporting documents are produced, it cannot be said that there was full disclosure. [Para 36]

The enclosures filed before the Assessing Officer at the time of section 143(3) assessment do not indicate the same. Therefore, it cannot be said that there was true and full disclosure of all materials that were required for assessment before the Assessing Officer by the assessee. At the same time, it is to be noticed that the reasons given in the communications for reopening the respective assessment have merely questioned the method of accounting adopted by the assessee and show that it was issued in a mechanical manner. [Para 37]

As per Explanation I to section 147, production before the Assessing Officer of the account books or other evidence from which material evidence could with due diligence have been discovered by the Assessing Officer will not necessarily amount to disclosure within the meaning of section 147. [Para 38]

The conclusions arrived in the impugned communications overruling the objections of the assessee for the reopening of the assessments by the impugned notices are not conclusive. They are only prima facie views of the Assessing Officer. It is for the assessee to establish that it has correctly followed the accounting method by producing the supporting documents to substantiate the percentage of work that was completed for the purpose of proper determination of taxable turnover for payment of income tax. Mere disclosure in the profit and loss account and balance sheet is not sufficient. [Para 39]

Therefore, reassessment is directed to be completed after examining the documents to be produced by the assessee and pass reassessment orders on merits. [Para 40]

In the instant case, the assessee-company had been consistently following a particular method of accounting. Its accounts were audited both under the Companies Act, 1956, as well as under section 44AB of the Income-tax Act. Such audited accounts were being filed with the Registrar of Companies as well as with the income-tax department for more than 7 years. The revenue had scrutinized the accounts and the method of accounting regularly employed and adopted by the assessee year after year had not been found fault with. The auditors of the company both under the Companies Act and the Income-tax Act had been consistently certifying that the assessee had been regularly following the method of accounting and that the annual profits could be properly deduced from such method of accounting employed by the assessee. The auditors over the years had also been certifying that the accounts were regularly maintained and were complete in the sense that there was no significant omission therein. This finding had been accepted by different Assessing Officers over a period of seven years. For rejecting the view taken for the earlier assessment years, there must be a material change in the fact situation. No doubt, the previous view will have no application even in cases where the law itself has undergone a change but before an earlier view can be upset or digressed from, one of the two must be demonstrated, namely, a change in the fact situation or a material change in law whether enacted or declared by the Supreme Court. [Para 5.7]

In the case of a civil contractor, who undertakes major works, a contract is spread over several years. The income arising from the same contract is spread over several assessment years and part of the profit of this contract is separately arrived at assessment year-wise and brought to tax. While so, for the same contract, the books of account are accepted for certain assessment years for the purpose of arriving at the profits, and for certain other assessment years the books of account are rejected in respect of the very same contract part of which is executed in the current year and the profit is estimated on a different basis. When this is done without cogent and sufficient reasons or change in facts or law, one has to necessarily apply the principles laid down by the Apex Court in the case of Radhasoami Satsang v. CIT [1992] 193 ITR 321/ 60 Taxman 248 and it is to be held that unless the fundamental aspects permeating through different assessment years are different, a different view possibly cannot be taken as it would result in anomalous results. [Para 5.8]

In the instant case, the Assessing Officer had accepted the factum of expenditure on account of sub-contractors and, thus, the non-availability of vouchers of expenditure incurred by sub-contractors with the assessee could not be a reason for rejection. Coming to the site-wise profit and loss account which were claimed to be MIS reports, each of these works was at different stages and phases of completion. The works were of different nature and a comparison of such different works for estimating profits of such works, based on the MIS reports which were not complete, in the sense that administrative expenses and other direct expenses incurred in respect of each work or as overhead find place in the books of account of the head office and were not apportioned to these particular works, would be a wrong comparison and opinion formed. To reject the books of account on the basis of such erroneous and fallacious workings and data could not be upheld. Cash flow statements maintained at each of the sites as found in the management information system, by no stretch of imagination, could be termed as complete profit and loss account which would enable the Assessing Officer to arrive at the profit in that work so as to enable him to compare the profits of different works. It is not correct to assume that two different contract works pertaining to two different projects, at two different project sites in different States and at different stages of execution, would derive identical profit. It was found that the site-wise MIS reports which were termed as profit and loss account were not part of the financial statements drawn up as per Schedule VI of the Companies Act nor were they prescribed books of account. When these statements were not books of account, and when they were not necessary documents or records for finalizing the books of account both under the Companies Act as well as under the Income-tax Act, infirmities, if any, in these statements could not be a reason to reject the books of account. [1996] 85 TAXMAN 214 (ART) TAXATION OF PROFITS FROM CONSTRUCTION CONTRACTS EXTENDING OVER SEVERAL YEARS

R. Balasubramanian B. Sridhar

In certain types of contracts relating to construction of multi-storeyed buildings, dams, bridges, etc., the work is spread over a number of years and the question of determining profits therefrom on an annual basis bristles with difficulties. There are two basic recognised methods of accounting, viz., (i ) the 'percentage of completion' method and (ii ) the 'completed contract' method, available to an assessee-contractor to choose from, but once he has made his choice, he must stick to it for the duration of the contract. In this article, the author discusses some of the issues involved in detail and, on the basis of copious case-law cited by him, comes to the conclusion that the ITO need not wait for the completion of the contract to determine the taxable profits arising from the project and that he can determine such profits for any given assessment year on the basis of the regular method of accounting followed by the assessee - EDITOR

Introduction

1. Under section 145(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 ('the Act'), income chargeable under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession", is computed in accordance with the method of accounting regularly employed by the assessee. Even if the accounts are correct and complete, but the method employed is such that in the Assessing Officer's view the income cannot be properly be deduced therefrom, he may compute the income as he thinks best in the given circumstances. In contracts relating to construction of multi-storeyed building, bridges, dams, ships, etc., which entail operations for a number of years, a problem arises as to the allocation of revenues and related costs to various accounting periods over the duration of the contract. The determination of annual income in such cases for purposes of levy of tax under the tax statute bristles with difficulties.

Two basic types of contracts

2. According to the International Accounting Standard-(IAS-11) effective from January 1, 1980 and the Accounting Standard-7 (AS-7) of the Institute of Chartered Accountants made mandatory from April 1, 1991 in the case of companies and from April 1, 1993 in the case of non-companies, construction contracts, formulated in a variety of ways, generally fall into two basic types:

(i)fixed price contracts - the contractor agrees to a fixed contract price or rate, in some cases subject to cost escalation clauses;

(ii)cost plus contracts - the contractor is reimbursed for allowable or otherwise defined costs, and is also allowed a percentage of these costs or a fixed fee.

Two methods of accounting

3. Two methods of accounting for contracts generally followed by contractors are (i) the percentage of completion method and (ii) the completed contract method.

Under the percentage of completion method, revenue is recognised as the contract activity progresses based on the stage of completion reached. The costs incurred in reaching the stage of completion are matched with this revenue, resulting in reporting of results which can be attributed to the proportion of work completed.

Under the completed contract method, revenue is recognised only when the contract is completed or substantially completed; that is, when only minor work is expected other than warranty obligation. Costs and progress payments received are accumulated during the course of contract but revenue is not recognised until the contract activity is substantially completed.

Under both these methods, provision is made for losses for the stage of completion reached on the contract. In addition, provision is usually made for losses on the remainder of the contract. When a contractor uses a particular method of accounting for a contract, then, in respect of all other contracts that meet similar criteria, the same method is used.

Snam company case

4. In this case, which came to the notice of the Public Accounts Committee of the Parliament, a foreign company having world wide operations, entered into an agreement with Indian Refineries Ltd. for constructing pipe-line and erecting permanent stations and terminals and also supplying materials to be employed in the work. During the course of assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1964-65, the assessee-company approached the Commissioner, New Delhi for getting its assessments finalised on 'completed contract' basis. The reasons adduced for the request were the following:

(a)The assessee was receiving advance payments from its clients and incurring expenses in executing the contracts.

(b)The bills for the jobs done could not be evaluated till joint inspections by the parties as per the terms of the contracts.

(c)In the case of a contract work running over several years, it was often not possible to ascertain the profits earned during each year before the completion of the contract, because of absence of data for evaluation of the work-in-progress of the jobs actually completed during the year.

This was the case where the books of account of the assessee for the year were rejected by the Assessing Officer. In other words, by inference, the books of account did not reflect the correct profits of the year as they suffered from incompleteness and unreliability. It is settled law that the incompleteness relates to the quantity of transactions in particular books of account say ledger and also relates to the number of books of account statutorily to be maintained. In the assessee's case, the incompleteness was evidenced by the excluded entries or payments of Rs. 35,52,620. In such a situation, the best judgment assessment in the spirit of section 144 was the legal way of completing the assessment as authorized by the statute. The Assessing Officer had done exactly the same, which was approved by the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal, although they differed on applicable rate of net profit. In such a situation, it had to be decided if determination of net profit at the rate of 6 per cent of contract receipts was mere case of estimation or otherwise. It is a settled position that the levy of penalty under section 271(1)(c) is not approved in the cases of mere estimations of income. [Para 15]

In the instant case, the Assessing Officer originally estimated the income at the rate of 30 per cent relying on the figures of the assessee's own concerns. However, the Commissioner (Appeals) gave a finding that the said 30 per cent was arrived at without any basis and he proceeded to direct the Assessing Officer to adopt 15 per cent. Subsequently, in quantum appeal, the Tribunal further reduced the applicable rate to 6 per cent. [Para 16]

Thus, effectively, the Assessing Officer, the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal had adopted three different rates of profit for determining the total income of the assessee for the relevant year. However, for all the said three, the basis for arriving at the said percentages was neither any incriminating paper nor an entry on a document nor any admissible statement nor any other acceptable evidence. The facts and figures may be good enough for confirming the additions in quantum appeal. What is needed for matters of penalty proceedings is more than the said facts and figures, so far as the originally declared gross receipts are concerned. Penalty cannot be sustained in such cases where there is some possibility for the acceptance of the assessee's explanation. Further, when two views are possible on an issue, a bona fide belief for claim cannot be subjected to concealment merely because such belief is erroneous under the law. Therefore, the levy of penalty in respect of the income relatable to the said declared receipts was not proper. [Para 17]

Therefore, the instant case was the fit case for levy of penalty so far as the income relatable to suppressed labour receipts of Rs. 35,52,620 was concerned. To this extent, the assessee's argument that the increase in income was mere estimation was liable to be rejected. Therefore, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) did not call for any interference in this regard. So far as the penalty relatable to the declared gross receipts was concerned, there was no case for the revenue as the assessee had furnished the said receipts on his own while filing the return of income and relatable income, which was finally assessed at 6 per cent merely on the basis of estimations and such estimation at 6 per cent was not strengthened by any evidential support. [Para 18]

IT: Where assessee, a civil contractor, declared net profit ratio of 5.64 per cent of gross contract receipts and Assessing Officer after rejecting book results determined total income by estimating net profit ratio of 15 per cent of gross receipts, income from contracting business be estimated by applying net profit ratio of 8 per cent of gross receipts

The main case of the revenue was that the assessee should have disclosed profits on the receipts of contract on the basis of percentage completion method of accounting. As against that it was the case of the assessee that the initial price for which the contract was awarded was later on found to be unreliable as it was increased to 29 per cent, therefore, the percentage completion method was not applicable even according to the accounting standard AS-7.The assessee had never shown any profit out of the contract and the loss shown by the assessee was accepted by the lower authorities in the immediately preceding year and succeeding year. Thus, according to the accounts, the assessee had never earned profit from this contract. The accounts of the assessee were audited and it was not the case of the revenue that the assessee did not furnish details regarding accounts maintained by it. No defects whatsoever had been found in the account books maintained by the assessee. What can be assessed as income under the Act, is income. If there is an existence of income, then only it can be estimated. Therefore, not going into the controversy whether the accounting standard AS-7 was properly employed by the assessee or not, it would be considered that whether Assessing Officer was justified in assessing the net profit of the assessee from such contract at the rate of 10 per cent. There was no substance in the argument of the revenue that the assessee was under an obligation to maintain its account on the basis of the accounting standard AS-7, as the said accounting standard was not mandatory for the assessee for the year under consideration. Even if the percentage of completion method was held to be applicable to the case of the assessee, then the question would arise that what would be the basis for estimate. It is well-established law that the estimate made must be honest and fair. There must exist reasonable nexus between the available material and the estimate. Thus, the only question for determination arose whether there existed some material on the basis of which it could be said that application of net profit rate of 10 per cent was appropriate. It was the contention of the assessee that it had incurred losses while performing the contract. No material had been brought on record by the Assessing Officer that such contention of the assessee was contrary to the facts. Addition had been made without indicating any material or basis on which it could be decided that application of net profit rate of 10 per cent was appropriate. On the contrary, material was on the record to show that the assessee had incurred loss in performing such a contract. Therefore, the Assessing Officer was not justified in rejecting the books of account by invoking the provisions of section 145(3) without bringing on record any cogent reasons and infirmities in the maintenance of books of account of the assessee and further estimating the net profit. [Para 13]

Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had decided the issue correctly.

In so far as the action of the income-tax authorities in rejecting the book results by invoking section 145(3) is concerned, the same is not adjudicated on account of the submission of the assessee. The assessee has canvassed for adoption of the net profit ratio of 8 per cent on contract receipts in order to estimate the income from the business of contracting. Ostensibly there is no hard and fast rule for estimating income from the business of civil Construction. However, section 44AD prescribes estimation from contract business in cases specified there at the rate of 8 per cent of gross receipts. Section 44AD covers cases of civil construction, where the gross receipts from contract business do not exceed Rs. 40 lakhs. Of course, the assessee does not fall within the prescription of section 44AD, as its contract receipts exceed Rs. 40 lakhs. However, the presumptive rate of net profit of 8 per cent incorporated in section 44AD reflects a legislative approved rate of net profit, which can be considered as fair and reasonable to estimate income from contract business in cases like that of the instant assessee, where the books of account are not found reliable by the Assessing Officer. Moreover in the assessee's own case in the assessment year 2010-11 the determination of income from contracting business is also proximate to the rate of net profit of 8 per cent contained in section 44AD. Therefore, considering the overall facts and circumstances of the case, it would be just and proper that the income from contract business of the assessee be estimated at 8 per cent of the gross receipts and the addition be worked out accordingly. [Para 7]

It is a well-established proposition of law that when an ITO proposes to make an assessment in disregard of the assessee's account books and the evidence produced by the assessee, he must not only state the basis upon which the estimate is made but also give him an opportunity to produce evidence in rebuttal of the material; and even where during the course of the discharge of his duties under the Act he receives good deal of information, if he intends to act upon it, it is fair and just that in order to test the accuracy or otherwise of that information, he must give an opportunity to the assessee to establish that that information is incorrect or that the ITO is misinformed.

It is no doubt true that the ITO and the Tribunal while making an estimate of the income did not say on what basis they came to that conclusion, but the Tribunal unmistakably referred to the omission.

While recognising the defect in the assessment, they had themselves gone into the accounts and have determined the income from both the branches on the evidence furnished by the assessee himself. It would have, however, been better if the order was more detailed, but that was not a ground for rejecting the assessments as having no basis. A perusal of the ITO 's order would show that there were many cash credits for which no satisfactory explanation was given with respect to both the branches and the assessee had not discharged the burden of proof resting on him. If that amount was added to the amount declared by the assessee himself, the income of the assessee could be computed at Rs. 1,19,890 which was roughly that assessed by the Tribunal for both the branches. The assessment could have been made on this basis, but that was not what appeared to have been done.

From the ITO's order it was clear that the assessee's clerk had at the time of explaining the accounts to the ITO mentioned certain papers which the Officer took from him.

These papers disclosed that a profit and loss account was prepared for the 'R' branch showing a net profit of Rs. 63,768. It was thus clear that there was certainly material on record on which the Tribunal could base its computation at Rs. 70,000 and there was no doubt whatever that the assessee had clearly manipulated his accounts and attempted to conceal his income. The assessee throughout the proceedings had not denied that the profit and loss account was taken from him by the ITO, nor had he in the petitions either under section 66(1) or under section 66(2) of the 1922 Act stated anything in this behalf.

There was sufficient material on record to show that the assessee had furnished inaccurate and false statements of accounts. The very fact that he had manipulated his accounts, so as to arrive at an income of Rs. 51,774 for both the branches, while in fact he had in his possession a balance-sheet of only one branch showing income of nearly Rs. 64,000, was itself sufficient to justify the income-tax authorities in levying the penalty. The Tribunal further took into account the excessive nature of the amount of penalty and reduced it to half. It was not open for the High Court to interfere in the quantum of the levy.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

It was not the case of the department that the assessee got its cloth dyed and printed by outside professionals with the help of the dyes and chemicals, it itself supplied. From the original assessment order, it appeared as though that the ITO was proceeding on the assumption that the dyes and chemicals purchased by the assessee were only used by him for dyeing and printing the cloth in its own karkhana. If, therefore, these unaccounted dyes and chemicals were used in the assessee’s own karkhana, then the turnover in the karkhana itself would be of large proportions, while the ITO stated, evidently on the basis of the private enquiry, that the manufacture and sale of dyed and printed cloth done through professional dyers and printers constituted the major portion of its business and that the manufacture in the karkhana was of a negligible extent. If the unaccounted chemicals and dyes of the value of Rs. 4,533 were also to be taken as used in the assessee’s own karkhana, then the insignificant portion of the business (as opined by the ITO) done in the karkhana itself would be Rs. 2,35,000, the figure arrived at by the ITO on the basis of the chemicals used. If that were to be case, the turnover resulting from the manufacture done outside the karkhana which was bound to be the major portion should be much higher and the estimate of Rs. 2,35,000 would not fit into the calculations. Thus, no proper nexus or connection was made out between the unaccounted chemicals and the estimate of the total turnover. Judged from any angle, this estimate of Rs. 2,35,000 on the basis of the unaccounted chemicals and dyes appeared to be unwarranted.

Equally unwarranted in Court’s view the adoption of the rate of profit at 50 per cent of the total turnover. The assessee estimated his profit only at 18 per cent while the department put it at 50 per cent. This was done by the department on the basis of the disclosed gross-profit rate in some comparable cases. Even in that section of the business of the assessee, which deals with dyeing and printing of cloth and selling it, there were different ways of manufacture adopted by the assessee. The assessee purchased koras, mulls and handloom cloth, got them bleached, dyed and printed through professional dyers. It also purchased dyes and chemicals, dyed some cloth in its own karkhana by engaging dyeing coolies and sold the same. It also purchased the dyed cloth from other merchants and got it printed by professional printers. It also carried on purchase and sale of dyed and printed cloth. It was also quite possible that the profit in the method of manufacture of dyed and printed cloth might be different from the profit in another method of manufacture. A scrutiny of the record did not disclose any consideration by the department as to the possible rates of profit from these different methods of manufacture. No material or data had been place which could have formed the basis of the decision of the department in that behalf. It was not known whether the comparable business on the basis of which 50 per cent rate of profit was fixed by the department were doing dyeing and printing trade in all the methods which the assessee adopted during the year under assessment. There was no basis for the department to reject the assessee’s contention that the total turnover should be analysed into different types of trade and different rates with reference to different types should be adopted. In the absence of any material or data connecting the comparable businesses with the different methods of manufacture adopted by the assessee or indicating that the same rate of profit, viz., 50 per cent was uniformly derived by the assessee in all the different types of manufacture, the conclusion was irresistible that the department was not justified in importing the rule of thumb into the matter and imposing a flat and uniform rate of 50 per cent in all the classes of manufacture. Therefore, the Court was not satisfied that there was any legal and acceptable basis for fixing the rate of profit at 50 per cent of the total turnover.

In view of these conclusions, it was held that the information collected by the department was not completely disclosed to the assessee and it was not afforded an adequate opportunity of rebuttal as directed by the High Court and that there was no material which could form the basis of an order under section 13 of the Act 1922.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

The assessee had furnished the return of income declaring total income of Rs.1.93 lakhs on 30-9-2008. CIT [1980] 124 ITR 31, the Supreme Court has observed that the provisions of the Act relating to the charge on income apply in relation to a specific assessment year and the provisions of the Act providing for the computation of the chargeable income apply, in the absence of anything to the contrary, in relation to the relevant previous year. Therefore, the profits and gains have to be computed for each accounting year separately.

Completed contract method - Its acceptability 4. In the case of completed contract method, the profits of a contract are determined on the completion of the contract and not every year. It may happen that a particular contract may take several years for its completion. Therefore, if an assessee has adopted the completed contract method of accounting, he will not be in a position to compute the profits of his contract business every year. In such a situation the Assessing Officer may invoke the provisions of the proviso to section 145(1) and hold that the method of accounting employed by the assessee is such that true profits of the business cannot be deduced therefrom.

It is, no doubt, true that the completed contract method is a recognized method of accounting as per the Accounting Standard issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India. However, the main defect of this method is that it does not enable an assessee to compute his income from the contract business every year. In para 10.2 of the aforesaid Accounting Standard this defect has been highlighted in the following words:

"The principal disadvantage of the completed contract method is that periodic reported income does not reflect the level of activity on contracts during the period. For example, when a few large contracts are completed in one accounting period but no contracts have been completed in the previous period or are to be completed in the subsequent period, the level of reported income can be erratic although the level of activity on contracts may have been relatively constant throughout. Even when numerous contracts are regularly completed in each accounting period, and reported income may appear to reflect the level of activity on contracts, there is a continuous lag between the time when work is performed and the related revenue is recognized."

Since under the Act, each year is a separate self-contained year and profits and gains have to be computed each year separately, the Assessing Officer may not accept the completed contract method, even if regularly employed by the assessee, on the ground that income cannot be properly deduced therefrom. He may invoke the provisions of section 145 and compute the income either by applying a flat rate on the contract receipts or by some other method.

Relevant case law

5. Here it will be relevant to refer to a few decided cases on the subject. In the case of Tirath Ram Ahuja (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1976] 103 ITR 15 , the Delhi High Court has held that in the case of contracts, in order to ascertain the income, one need not wait till the contract is completed, and that it is open to the revenue to estimate the profits on the basis of the receipts in each year of construction, although the contract is not complete. The same view has been taken by the Patna High Court in the case of Sri Sukhdeodas Jalan v. CIT [1954] 26 ITR 617. In this case a military contract extended beyond the accounting period and the accounts were closed only after the completion of the contract. The question for determination was whether the profits should be assessed only after the completion of the contract or whether the profits accruing during the accounting period could be assessed. The Patna High Court held that it is fallacious to argue that merely because the military contract was completed after the accounting period, no profits arose or accrued to the assessee in the accounting year and that in the case of an incomplete contract there is a well-established method of calculating profits accruing in the accounting year. In the case of P.M. Mohammed Meerakhan v. CIT [1969] 73 ITR 735 , the Supreme Court also has held that the profits of an adventure can be determined even if the adventure is not completed.

Conclusion

6. Although the completed contract method is a recognized method of accounting as per the Accounting Standard issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, it is not a suitable method of accounting from income-tax point of view, as it does not enable determination of the profits of the contract business every year. Since under the Act each year is a separate self-contained year, it is necessary to determine the profit of the contract business each year separately. For this purpose, it will be advisable to adopt the percentage of completion method, which is the other method recognized by the aforesaid Accounting Standard.

The assessee's contention relying on rule 9(2) of the ITAT Rules that as the Tribunal has discretion to accept a memorandum of appeal which is not accompanied by all or any of the documents referred to in rule 9(1), non-filing of a certified copy of the order appealed from along with the memorandum of appeal was a mere irregularity and the requirement of sub rule (1) was not mandatory could not be accepted. Filing of the certified copy of the order appealed against is linked up with the period of limitation prescribed for the filing or the appeal. If a certified copy of the order appealed against can be filed at any time before the hearing of the appeal and the appeal is competent where the memorandum of appeal is unaccompanied by the certified copy of the order appealed from and the defect is merely an irregularity then section 268 providing for exclusion of the time requisite for obtaining a certified copy of the order for the purpose of computation of the period of limitation for filing of the appeal becomes meaningless. The provisions in the Act allowing exemption of time for taking a certified copy of the order appealed against in computing the period of limitation shows that the requirement, viz., the memorandum of appeal should be accompanied by a certified copy of the order appealed against, is mandatory. Rule 9(1) of the Appellate Tribunal Rules should not be construed with reference to sub rule (2) only but also with reference to or in the context of the other relevant provisions of the Act. Therefore, the requirement of rule 9(1) of the Appellate Tribunal Rules that the memorandum of appeal shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the order appealed against, is mandatory. The Tribunal was thus right to dismiss the appeal as barred by time regard being had that the appeal was filed by the assessee-firm within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of the AAC but which did not contain the certified copy of the order appealed against and such certified copy was filed on the date of hearing.

In the instant case, until 1-3-1971 when the assessee filed a certified copy of the AAC's order the appeal remained incomplete, defective and incompetent and was not admitted by the Tribunal. Such defect was removed and the appeal became complete and competent on 1-3-1971, when the certified copy of the order was filed. But on that the time for filing of the appeal had already expired. Therefore, without an order of the Tribunal under section 253(5) condoning the delay the appeal remained time barred. The assessee, though it was open to it to do so, did not apply to the Tribunal to exercise its discretion under rule 9(2) of the Appellate Tribunal Rules dispensing with the requirements of filing of the certified copy of the order appealed against along with the memorandum of appeal and to admit the appeal without a certified copy of the order. Therefore, the Tribunal was right in coming to the finding that the appeal filed by assessee was barred by limitation. No hard and fast rule could be laid down to determine the question as to whether in estimating the net profit of a contractor the percentage was to be calculated on the gross receipt inclusive of the value of the materials supplied to the contractor. It would depend on the particular facts and the circumstances of each case. Before the Tribunal the assessee did not argue the point that the finding of fact of the AAC about the rates at which "cement" and "steel materials" were supplied to the assessee by PWD or railway department and non-allowance of profit on such rates were not controverted by the revenue and, therefore, that point was not considered or decided by the Tribunal. No stock book was kept by the assessee. Further, the burden was on the assessee to prove before the authorities below that the materials supplied to the assessee were wholly used or utilized by it in the construction works or that it had returned the unused or unutilized materials to the defendants concerned or that the contracts for construction works were not on the basis of lump sum amounts or that in calculating its profits on all those contracts it has excluded the value of those materials. It did not appear from the record that any attempt was even made by the assessee to prove any one of the aforesaid facts. Therefore, the conclusion reached by the Tribunal that in estimating the net profit of the assessee in the business of contract with the Government the percentage was to be calculated on the gross receipt inclusive of the value of the materials supplied by the Government department itself, was not perverse in its accepted sense.

Note : The decision was in favour of the revenue.

The assessee's account was absolutely unbelievable because on a single day, i.e., on 31-3-1994, the assessee was stated to have given Rs. 19.2 lakhs towards tractor hiring charges, Rs. 3.71 lakhs towards water charges and Rs. 57.25 lakhs towards the labour charges for earthmoving. It was not clear how labour charges got accumulated for the whole accounting year to justify payment of cash of Rs. 57.25 lakhs on the last date of the previous year. When the cash payment of Rs. 80.16 lakhs on a single day itself gave rise to doubt in the mind of the Assessing Officer, he rightly cross checked the genuineness of the payments by issuing summons to the persons whose names were shown in the vouchers prepared by the assessee. The result was that partly vouchers were found to be bogus, and partly stood disproved. It was not clear on what ground the assessee could seek for acceptance of books of account which were found to be unworthy of credit by the three lower authorities. In the absence of credible books of account, option of the Assessing Officer under section 145(3) was to make assessment on estimation basis in terms of section 144. In the instant case, the order of the Tribunal was quite favourable to the assessee because as against the estimation of 10 per cent made by the Assessing Officer, the Tribunal had reduced the estimation to 8 per cent of the total works turnover. There was logic and reason in estimation of income from civil construction work at 8 per cent because under the presumptive scheme, section 44AD provides for assessment of income on civil construction work at 8 per cent where the contractor's turnover is below Rs. 40 lakhs. Even though the assessee contended that section 44AD had no application as the contract amount was above Rs. 40 lakhs, there was no justification to interfere with the order of the Tribunal because in the first place, the Tribunal had granted partial relief to the assessee by reducing the estimated income from 10 per cent to 8 per cent. Secondly, what the Tribunal had done, was only to follow section 44AD as a guideline for estimation of income from civil work. Therefore, there was no justification to interfere with that part of the order of the Tribunal. It was worthwhile to note that while confirming the estimation of income at reduced percentage, the Tribunal cancelled separate addition made by the Assessing Officer under the head 'Other income' which was a huge amount of Rs. 15,44,353. After getting deletion of addition of Rs. 15,44,353, the assessee could not canvass for modification of other part of the order of the Tribunal confirming estimation of income at the reduced percentage of 8 per cent which was a reason for deleting the separate addition without considering it independently on merit. [Para 6]

The provision of section 145, read with the proviso, makes it clear that the choice of method in maintaining accounts for the purposes of assessment is left with the assessee and it is open to him to adopt any method of accounting that he likes. That, however, is subject to two minimum conditions—firstly, that the method of accounting should be one which has been regularly employed by him and, secondly, that the method should be such as in the opinion of the Assessing Officer should indicate properly the income, profits and gains of the assessee. As long as these two conditions are fulfilled by the account maintained by the assessee, that account, in law, has to be the basis of computation compulsorily and the Assessing Officer has no other option to follow any other method of accounting. [Para 13.2]

The assessee had argued that the only method by which the gains or profits could be determined was to wait until the whole of the expenditure to be incurred by the assessee over this contract business had been made good. This argument was based on the assumption that unless and until the entire amount of expenditure to be incurred over the contract is known, no profit or gain can be calculated, even if the contract moneys are received by an assessee in the course of the contract. No justification was found for this assumption. It is true that "profits and gains must be ascertained of ordinary principles of commercial trading" and the word 'profits' has to be understood, "in its natural and proper sense, in a sense which no commercial man would misunderstand". But that means only this much : "that no gain or profit could be said to arise unless and until a balance had been struck between the cost of construction and the proceeds of contract." It, however, cannot be disputed that as a rule the balance between the cost of construction and the proceeds of contract for the purpose of an assessment under the Act has to be struck at an interval of every accounting year, because that is the unit of time stipulated under the Act. The exception may arise when the balance cannot be struck between the cost of acquisition and the proceeds of sale on any method known in the field of commercial trading, for in that case no profit can be said to arise in that period as in the case of a solitary adventure in the nature of trade. [Para 13.5]

The primary issue in accounting for construction contracts is the allocation of construction revenue and contract cost to the accounting periods in which construction work is performed. In the case under consideration the assessee had followed percentage of completion method. Under this method contract revenue is matched with the contract cost incurred in reaching the stage of completion of contract, resulting in the reporting of revenue, i.e., expenses and profits which can be attributed to the proportion of work completed. This method of percentage of completion is a recognized method of accounting. [Para 13.6]

In percentage of completion method contract account is to be finalised in the year of completion of contract work, when the project is to be taken as complete. [Para 13.7]

[1993] 70 TAXMAN 106 (ART) LONG-TERM CONTRACTS - WHETHER PROFITS SHOULD BE DETERMINED ANNUALLY OR ON COMPLETION OF THE CONTRACTS

K.R. Gupta

In the case of long-term contracts, the determination of profits from the contract business annually is not an easy task. For this reason, a contractor executing a long-term contract may like to determine the profit of the contract only after the contract has been completed and to file his income-tax return on that basis. In this connection, a question that arises for consideration is whether under the Income-tax Act, 1961, it is permissible to adopt such a method of accounting in respect of the contract business. The author of this article discusses various aspects of this issue concluding that although the completed contract method is a recognized method of accounting as per the Accounting Standard issued by the institute of Chartered Accountants of India, it is not a suitable method of accounting from income-tax point of view - EDITOR

Difficulty in determining profits annually

1. In the case of long-term contracts, the determination of profits from the contract business annually is not an easy task. For this reason, a contractor executing a long-term contract may like to determine the profit of the contract only after the contract has been completed and to file his income-tax return on that basis. In this connection, a question that arises for consideration is whether under the Income-tax Act. 1961 ('the Act') it is permissible to adopt such a method of accounting in respect of the contract business.

Position from accountancy point of view

2. Before examining the matter from the income-tax angle, it will be appropriate to discuss the position in this regard from the accountancy point of view. The Accounting Standard of 'Accounting for construction contracts' issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India has recognized the following two methods of accounting for contracts :

(i)the percentage of completion method;

(ii)the completed contract method.

In para 7 of the Accounting Standard (AS-7) these methods have been described as under :

"7.2 Under the percentage of completion method, revenue is recognized as the contract activity progresses based on the stage of completion reached. The costs incurred in reaching the stage of completion are matched with this revenue, resulting in the reporting of results which can be attributed to the proportion of work completed. Although (as per the principle of 'prudence') revenue is recognized only when realised, under this method, the revenue is recognized as the activity progresses even though in certain circumstances it may not be realised.

7.3 Under the completed contract method, revenue is recognized only when the contract is completed or substantially completed; that is, when only minor work is expected other than warranty obligation.

Costs and progress payments received are accumulated during the course of the contract but revenue is not recognized until the contract activity is substantially completed."

It will be seen that from the accountancy point of view, the completed contract method is a recognized method of accountancy.

Under the Act the assessee has the choice of adopting whatever method of accounting he wants to adopt, provided he follows the method regularly for his own purposes. Section 145 of the Act clearly makes the method of accounting, if regularly employed by the assessee, a compulsory basis of computation unless, as provided in the first proviso to section 145(1), in the opinion of the Assessing Officer, the income, profits and gains cannot be properly deduced therefrom. If the true income, profits and gains cannot be ascertained on the basis of the assessee's method of accounting, the Assessing Officer has the power to compute the income on such basis and in such manner as he may determine.

Each year as a self-contained unit

3. Under the Act, for the purpose of computing the profits and gains, each year is a separate self-contained period of time. In the case of Mahamudabad Properties ( P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 124 ITR 31, the Supreme Court has observed that the provisions of the Act relating to the charge on income apply in relation to a specific assessment year and the provisions of the Act providing for the computation of the chargeable income apply, in the absence of anything to the contrary, in relation to the relevant previous year. Therefore, the profits and gains have to be computed for each accounting year separately.

Completed contract method - Its acceptability

ILLUSTRATIONS

1. An assessee engaged in Transport Business acquires a truck on 1st September for, say, Rs. 5 lakhs and the purchase is financed by borrowing about Rs. 3 lacs @ 18% p.a. The truck is leased to a public sector undertaking for a rent of Rs. 18,000 per month.

The income computation may work out as follows: The assessee can claim loss (and thus, declare a lower amount than the specified amount) by filing appropriate return, complying with other requirements (like, maintenance of books, audit, adduce evidence, etc.). He may have to produce evidence relating to:

Date of acquisition and when it was put to use.

Cost of acquisition of truck.

Proof of borrowing for acquisition of truck.

Amount borrowed was actually used for acquiring truck.

Agreement for lease.

Amount of rent and that no other consideration was received; and the truck was used by lessee only and was not given to any one else and that no other income arose from the truck.

Confirmation from the lessee.

2. An assessee engaged in civil construction business has agreed to carry out certain work relating to fixing tiles of particular brand. The cost of tiles is, say Rs. 18 per sq. ft. Total area is, say 20,000 sq.ft. It has got a fixed price contract of say Rs. 5,00,000, including cost of tiles, without escalation. Labour contract given is say @ Rs. 3 per sq. ft. His estimated profit was Rs. 80,000. The deemed profits were Rs. 40,000. After completing l/4th work, the tile manufacturer increases the rate of tiles by Rs. 4 per sq.ft. Thus, his profits went down to Rs. 20,000. He can return Rs. 20,000 as his income, and submit the following as evidence:

Fixed price contract.

Fact that no escalation was allowed to him.

Purchase costs.

Fact that he did purchase the 75% requirement after price increase.

Labour contract and its costs.

The evidence requirement stated above is only illustrative. However, it may be pointed out that it will have to be proved that profits earned were lower than the specified profits.

1.11-4 At what stage evidence should be produced? - Section 44AD(5)/44AE(6) reads:

"Nothing contained in... this section shall apply, where the assessee claims and proves that the profits ... are lower... and thereupon..." [Emphasis supplied]

Considering the language of the provisions, it is felt that evidence should be produced or filed along with the return/claim.

In practical life this may be difficult inasmuch as the degree of proof and satisfaction required are difficult to determine. Accordingly, an assessee will have to take an utmost care while making such claim.

If an assessee does not substantiate his claim and/or does not file evidence to prove the claim, it could be contended by the tax department that requirement of the above provisions are not complied with and, accordingly, it may apply the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 44AD and/or sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 44AE, as the case may be.

However, considering the practical difficulties, it is felt that the CBDT may lay down instructions in this behalf and may direct at least that an opportunity may be provided to an assessee to lead the evidence.

If no evidence is produced by the assessee, it is evident that the requirements cannot be considered to have been met and accordingly, AO may then be free to make an assessment based on prescribed amount(s) as per the New Provisions.

l.11-5 Effects of 'Claim for a lower amount' - Following effects of a 'claim for the lower amount' will ensue:

Once a claim for assessment at a lower amount of profits is made, the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 44AD/44AE would not apply, as a result of which, if the claim is accepted, the taxable profits may be the lower amount, subject to any addition or disallowance.

The profits computation will have to be made in accordance with the provisions of sections 28 to 43C.

Exemption from maintenance of books of account or audit would not be available. Accordingly, the provisions of section 44AA and/or section 44AB will have to be complied with.

As discussed in details above, the necessary evidence in support of lower profits will have to be produced.

The Assessing Officer will have to proceed to make assessment under section 143(3) which implies:

(a)

Notices under section 142 and/or under section 143(2) of the Act.

(b)

Formal hearing(s) at which the evidence may be produced by the assessee as also further evidence as may be required will have to be produced.

(c)

Consideration of all evidences and material.

(d)

On that basis, a written order of assessment of the income and determination of sum payable by the assessee.

(1) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in sections 28 to 43C, in the case of an assessee engaged in the business of civil construction or supply of labour for civil construction, a sum equal to eight per cent of the gross receipts paid or payable to the assessee in the previous year on account of such business or, as the case may be, a sum higher than the aforesaid sum as declared by the assessee in his return of in come, shall be deemed to be the profits and gains of such busi ness chargeable to tax under the head Profits and gains of business or profession :

Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall apply in case the aforesaid gross receipts paid or payable exceed an amount of forty lakh rupees.

(2) Any deduction allowable under the provisions of sections 30 to 38 shall, for the purposes of sub-section (1), be deemed to have been already given full effect to and no further deduction under those sections shall be allowed.

(3) The written down value of any asset used for the purpose of the business referred to in sub-section (1) shall be deemed to have been calculated as if the assessee had claimed and had been actually allowed the deduction in respect of the depreciation for each of the relevant assessment years.

(4) The provisions of sections 44AA and 44AB shall not apply in so far as they relate to the business referred to in sub-section (1) and in computing the monetary limits under those sections, the gross receipts or, as the case may be, the income from the said business shall be excluded.

(5) Nothing contained in the foregoing provisions of this section shall apply, where the assessee claims and produces evidence to prove that the profits and gains from the aforesaid business are lower than the profits and gains specified in sub-section (1), and thereupon the Assessing Officer shall proceed to make an assessment of the total income or loss of the assessee and deter mine the sum payable by the assessee on the basis of assessment made under sub-section (3) of section 143.

Explanation. For the purposes of this section, the expression civil construction includes

(a) the construction or repair of any building, bridge, dam or other structure or of any canal or road;

(b) the execution of any works contract.
