1. An assessee engaged in Transport Business acquires a truck on 1st September for, say, Rs. 5 lakhs and the purchase is financed by borrowing about Rs. 3 lacs @ 18% p.a. The truck is leased to a public sector undertaking for a rent of Rs. 18,000 per month. The income computation may work out as follows: The assessee can claim loss (and thus, declare a lower amount than the specified amount) by filing appropriate return, complying with other requirements (like, maintenance of books, audit, adduce evidence, etc.). He may have to produce evidence relating to:

■ Date of acquisition and when it was put to use.

■ Cost of acquisition of truck.

■ Proof of borrowing for acquisition of truck.

■ Amount borrowed was actually used for acquiring truck.

■ Agreement for lease.

■ Amount of rent and that no other consideration was received; and the truck was used by lessee only and was not given to any one else and that no other income arose from the truck.

■ Confirmation from the lessee.

2. An assessee engaged in civil construction business has agreed to carry out certain work relating to fixing tiles of particular brand. The cost of tiles is, say Rs. 18 per sq. ft. Total area is, say 20,000 sq.ft. It has got a fixed price contract of say Rs. 5,00,000, including cost of tiles, without escalation. Labour contract given is say @ Rs. 3 per sq. ft. His estimated profit was Rs. 80,000. The deemed profits were Rs. 40,000. After completing l/4th work, the tile manufacturer increases the rate of tiles by Rs. 4 per sq.ft. Thus, his profits went down to Rs. 20,000. He can return Rs. 20,000 as his income, and submit the following as evidence:

■ Fixed price contract.

■ Fact that no escalation was allowed to him.

■ Purchase costs.

■ Fact that he did purchase the 75% requirement after price increase.

■ Labour contract and its costs.

The evidence requirement stated above is only illustrative. However, it may be pointed out that it will have to be proved that profits earned were lower than the specified profits.

1.11-4 At what stage evidence should be produced? - Section 44AD(5)/44AE(6) reads:

"Nothing contained in... this section shall apply, where the assessee claims and proves that the profits ... are lower... and thereupon..." [Emphasis supplied]

Considering the language of the provisions, it is felt that evidence should be produced or filed along with the return/claim.

In practical life this may be difficult inasmuch as the degree of proof and satisfaction required are difficult to determine. Accordingly, an assessee will have to take an utmost care while making such claim.

If an assessee does not substantiate his claim and/or does not file evidence to prove the claim, it could be contended by the tax department that requirement of the above provisions are not complied with and, accordingly, it may apply the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 44AD and/or sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 44AE, as the case may be.

However, considering the practical difficulties, it is felt that the CBDT may lay down instructions in this behalf and may direct at least that an opportunity may be provided to an assessee to lead the evidence.

If no evidence is produced by the assessee, it is evident that the requirements cannot be considered to have been met and accordingly, AO may then be free to make an assessment based on prescribed amount(s) as per the New Provisions.

l.11-5 Effects of 'Claim for a lower amount' - Following effects of a 'claim for the lower amount' will ensue:

■ Once a claim for assessment at a lower amount of profits is made, the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 44AD/44AE would not apply, as a result of which, if the claim is accepted, the taxable profits may be the lower amount, subject to any addition or disallowance.

■ The profits computation will have to be made in accordance with the provisions of sections 28 to 43C.

■ Exemption from maintenance of books of account or audit would not be available. Accordingly, the provisions of section 44AA and/or section 44AB will have to be complied with.

■ As discussed in details above, the necessary evidence in support of lower profits will have to be produced.

■ The Assessing Officer will have to proceed to make assessment under section 143(3) which implies:

(a) Notices under section 142 and/or under section 143(2) of the Act.

(b) Formal hearing(s) at which the evidence may be produced by the assessee as also further evidence as may be required will have to be produced.

(c) Consideration of all evidences and material.

(d) On that basis, a written order of assessment of the income and determination of sum payable by the assessee.

R. Balasubramanian B. Sridhar

In certain types of contracts relating to construction of multi-storeyed buildings, dams, bridges, etc., the work is spread over a number of years and the question of determining profits therefrom on an annual basis bristles with difficulties. There are two basic recognised methods of accounting, viz., (i ) the 'percentage of completion' method and

claims as a deduction in computation of taxable income, was a separate question which had to be resolved keeping in view the facts and circumstances of each case, [vide page 12 of Vol. VII of Compendium of Opinions].

(ii) Second illustrative case. - A public limited company, wholly owned by a State Government, undertook construction works exclusively for Government departments/undertakings, both on turnkey and non-turnkey basis and followed the mercantile system of accounting. The company followed the system of crediting the value of work done, measured by the company engineers up to 31st March every year at the rates approved by the clients and debiting all works and other expenses to the profit and loss account, irrespective of whether a certain piece of work was in the initial stage or nearing completion, since the rates for each item in the contract were quoted and accepted by the clients. The company charged the client for doing each piece of work on the basis of rate per metric cube of work done. Thus, the rate for each item of work quoted included material, labour, overheads and profit as an integral part of the rate itself.

Drawing the attention of the Committee to Accounting Standard-7(AS-7) on 'Accounting for Construction Contracts; paras 7.3 and 7.4 wherein it is mentioned that provision for losses should be made if the company anticipates that there is likelihood of losses in the remaining part of the contract, the company averred that if a contract extended for a period of three or four years, there was difficulty in quantifying the losses anticipated for the remaining portion of the contract as the reasons for possible losses like cost escalation in materials, labour, etc., and losses due to floods, fire, drought, etc., were unpredictable. Further, contracts which were not profitable in the first year might earn profit in the next year. The company felt that the system of crediting the value of work done at the rates approved by the clients and debiting all works and other expenses to the profit and loss account which it had followed from its inception and was accepted by the statutory auditors, would show a true and fair picture of the working of the company.

While reviewing a particular year's accounts, the Government auditors, however, insisted that the company should follow the procedure outlined in AS-7 and provide for anticipated losses and also should not take revenue in the contracts which were in progress.

In the circumstances, the company sought the opinion of the Expert Advisory Committee on the questions whether:

(a)the procedure followed by the company was in order and would show the true and fair picture of the working of the company, and

(b)the system outlined in AS-7 is mandatory and should be followed in the preparation of final accounts.

The Committee noted (August 1987) that the company was following the 'percentage of completion method' and not 'completed contract method' for accounting for construction contracts and that para 9 of AS-7 "Accounting for Construction Contracts", issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, has recommended the basis for recognising revenue on construction contracts where percentage of completion method is followed as under:

"9. Percentage of completion method.

9.1 Under the percentage of completion method, the amount of, revenue recognised is determined by reference to the stage of completion of the contract activity at the end of each accounting period. The advantage of this method of accounting for contract revenue is that it reflects revenue in the accounting period during which activity is undertaken to earn such revenue.

9.2 The stage of completion used to determine revenue to be recognised in the financial statements is measured in an appropriate manner. For this purpose no special weightage should be given to a single factor, instead, all relevant factors should be taken into consideration; for example, the proportion that costs incurred to date bear to the estimated total costs of the contract, by surveys which measure work performed and completion of a physical proportion of the contract work.

9.3 Progress payments and advances received from customers may not necessarily reflect the stage of completion and therefore cannot usually be treated as equivalent to revenue earned.

9.4 If the percentage of completion method is applied by calculating the proportion that costs to date bear to the latest estimated total costs of the contract, adjustments are made to include only those costs that reflect work performed. Examples of items which may need adjustment include:

(i)the costs of materials that have been purchased for the contract but have not been installed or used during contract performance; and

(ii)payments to sub-contractors to the extent that they do not reflect the amount of work performed under the sub-contract.

9.5 The application of the percentage of completion method is subject to a risk of error in making estimates. For this reason, profit is not recognised in the financial statements unless the outcome of the contract can be reliably estimated. If the outcome cannot be reliably estimated, the percentage of completion method is not used.

9.6 While recognising the profit under this method, an appropriate allowance for future unforeseeable factors which may affect the ultimate quantum of profit is generally made on either a specific or a percentage basis.

9.7 In the case of fixed price contracts, the condition which will usually provide this degree of reliability are:

(i)total contract revenues to be received can be reliably estimated,

(ii)both the costs to complete the contract and the stage of contract performance completed at the reporting date can be reasonably estimated, and

Assessee, earning income from contract business and plying trucks, did not maintain any books of account and had been assessed on estimated profit basis. In assessment year in question he purchased two vehicles allegedly out of sale proceeds of old vehicles and taking some loan. Assessing Officer, however, found that source of Rs. 13,000 invested in purchase was unexplained and further several deposits in Canara Bank was found. Assessee explained that Rs. 13,000 had come from his contract business and deposits in Canara Bank were out of withdrawals from UCO Banks. Since it was a 'no account' case Assessing Officer disbelieving oral statement of assessee made an addition of Rs. 1,50,000 as income from unexplained sources. Held - Availability of funds in hands of assessee from sale proceeds as well as from contract work, being obvious no adverse inference could be drawn simply because assessee did not maintain books of account when income from contract business had been assessed on the basis of profit rate, and as such, there was no sufficient reason to require assessee to explain entries in the bank account. Though it was a 'no account' case but keeping in view that assessment had been made in respect of contract business, treating rate of profit at 12.5 per cent on total receipts, it could not be assumed that whatever deposits were made in bank account flowed from unexplained income. Therefore, addition was unjustified. - Mohinder Pal Singh v. ITO [1995] 83 Taxman 116 (Chd.) (Mag.)

6, the assessee divided the land into 23 plots and sold away 22 of them measuring 373 acres for a sum of Rs. 5,18,500. The twenty-third plot measuring 104 acres was retained by the assessee himself. The assessee did not return any income on the plea that the transaction did not constitute an adventure in the nature of trade. The ITO, however, determined the escaped income at Rs. 1,26,500 as under:— Conceding but not granting that the transaction was an adventure in the nature of trade, the assessee, observing that the profits had not been properly computed in view of the fact that the adventure would terminate after the portion retained by him was also sold, contended that the profits in the adventure could be determined only at the time of the completion of the sale of the entire estate.

Rejecting the assessee's contention, the Supreme Court observed that the ITO had correctly estimated the profit by treating the land retained as stock-in-trade and valuing it according to the normal accountancy practice. According to the Supreme Court, the view that the profits of the adventure could be determined only at the time of the completion of the sale of the entire estate was not correct. Each year is a self-contained unit and in the case of a trading adventure, for computing the true profits of the year, the value of the stock-in-trade at the beginning and at the end of the accounting year has to be taken into account. To quote the Supreme Court:

". . . It is not a correct proposition to say that the profits of the assessee cannot be ascertained even on the assumption that the transaction of the adventure of trade was not completed. Under the Income-tax Act for the purpose of assessment each year is a self-contained unit and in the case of a trading adventure the profits have to be computed in the manner provided by the statute. It is true that the Income-tax Act makes no express provision with regard to the value of stock. It charges for payment of tax the income, profits and gains which have to be computed in the manner provided by the Income-tax Act. In the case of a trading adventure the profits have to be calculated and adjusted in the light of the provisions of the Income-tax Act permitting allowances prescribed thereby. For that purpose it was the duty of the Income-tax Officer to find out what profit the business has made according to the true accountancy practice. As a normal rule, the profit should be ascertained by valuing the stock-in-trade at the beginning and at the end of the accounting year. . . ." (p. 743)

(iii) Champion Construction Co. v. First ITO [1983] 5 ITD 495 (Bom.)

The assessee is a firm, engaged in the business of constructing multi-storeyed buildings and selling flats and other accommodation therein. The question arose whether any income arose for taxation for the assessment years 1977-78 and 1978-79 from a project undertaken during the previous year relevant to the assessment year 1976-77. The Tribunal, in this connection, delineated the legal position emerging from several judicial decisions in the following words,—

". . . it is not a correct proposition to say that profits of the assessee -from a single venture/project in the nature of trade cannot be ascertained until the venture/project has come to an end. Under the Act each year is a self-contained unit and unless it is impossible to compute the profits or losses of each year reasonably if necessary by estimating the value of the liabilities to be incurred, valuing the work-in-progress, stock- in-trade, etc., the profits should be computed year-wise and taxed...." (p. 507)

On the assessee's contention that exigibility to tax would arise only on the completion of project is accepted, the Tribunal observed—

"The acceptance of the proposition would amount to giving the assessee a licence to put off his tax liabilities for an unlimited period by seeing to it that the venture/project never comes to an end in the sense something or the other always remains to be done. That will be a very unsatisfactory state of affairs. Moreover, when the entire cost/ expenditure to the assessee is recouped and/or major portion of the venture/project is complete, there is really no justification in not taxing the income from project which quite often may represent excess of receipts over expenditure unless there is a risk/chances of the assessee's suffering heavy liabilities, subsequently, for some reasons or the other."

In the backdrop of the legal position discussed herein above, the Tribunal, in the light of the factual position obtaining in respect of each of the two assessment years 1977-78 and 1978-79, decided the chargeability to tax as under:

Assessment year 1977-78:

Neither the construction was complete, nor even half the portion of the building was sold. The net sale proceeds received were much less than the total expenditure incurred by the assessee up to that date. Therefore, profits or losses need not be estimated and assessed.

Assessment year 1978-79:

The construction was completed and 80 per cent of the area was sold. Therefore, it was possible to estimate the income of the assessee from the project and make an assessment.

The expression 'civil construction', as such, is not defined or explained but, apparently, has been used as nomenclature for grouping certain activities as part of the Civil Construction business.

Judicial decisions and decisions of Appellate Tribunal

6. The question of exigibility to tax of income from long-term contracts has been considered by the juridiciary as well as the Tribunal in a number of cases. To highlight their views on the issue, the gist of some of the decisions is set out below:

(i)( a)Sukhdeodas Jalan v. CIT [1954] 26 ITR 617 (Pat.)

(b) Tirath Ram Ahuja (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1976] 103 ITR 15 (Delhi)

A military contract entered into by the assessee Sukhdeodas Jalan extended beyond the accounting period and the accounts were closed only after the completion of the contract. The question arose for determination whether the profits should be assessed only after the completion of the contract or whether the profits accruing during the accounting period could be assessed. A Division Bench of the Patna High Court held that it was fallacious to argue that merely because the contract was completed after the accounting period, no profits arose or accrued to the assessee in the accounting year and that in the case of an incomplete contract there was a well established method of calculating profits accruing in the accounting year (vide page 971 of Batliboi's Advanced Accounting) . To quote from the High Court's decision:

"In the case of contracts, if accounts are maintained and completed on contract basis the profits or gains of the previous year cannot properly be extracted from the accounts, for a contract may take several years for being completed and payments in regard to it may also be received by the assessee in several years. It may be convenient from the point of view of the assessee that profit should be ascertained on the completion of the contract and assessment of the profit should take place after the completion of the contract. But section 3 imposes a charge of income-tax upon the profits and gains of the assessee for the accounting year and it is the duty of the income-tax authorities to ascertain the profits and gains accruing to the assessee in respect of the payment received during the accounting year.

It cannot be said that merely because a contract was completed after the accounting year, no profits arose or accrued to the assessee in the accounting year...." (p. 618)

The ratio of the decision supra was followed by the Delhi High Court in the case of Tirath Ram Ahuja (P.) Ltd. ( supra). It was held that in the case of contracts, one need not wait till the contract was completed in order to ascertain the income, and that it was open to the revenue to estimate the profit on the basis of the receipts in each year of construction, although the contract was not complete.

In the situation considered in illustration (1) above, the additions are arising because of non-application of the provisions of the Act. The return as filed by the assessee is accepted. On the same reasoning as above, it is felt that the assessment can be made on a higher amount, since a difference of opinion on particular treatment cannot be considered as a failure to prove that the profits are lower. In other words, the assessment would still be governed by normal provisions and by virtue of return under section 44AD(5)/44AE(6), the assessment cannot be reverted back to sub-section (1). In the last illustration, where the assessee's claim is not accepted, one has to consider whether non-acceptance of the claim or the failure to produce necessary evidence would take the assessee out of the provisions of sub-section (5)/(6) or the necessary consequences would follow ? It seems that having regard to the intent and purpose of the law to give an option to an assessee of rebuttal, the necesssary consequences have to follow and having exercised the option, the assessee cannot claim that the fiction should be applied.

This can also be supported on the ground that once an assessee makes the claim which is not found to be acceptable on the facts and in law the assessee cannot be given benefit of the provisions of sub-section (1).

Revision of return, whether possible, in the above circumstances ? - A further question, which may arise is that in the course of assessment, can an assessee revise the return of income and claim that he may be assessed at the specified amount, by declaring income in the revised return at the specified amount. A retrun, subject to the other provisions of section 139, can be revised under sub-section (5), if the assessee has discovered any omission or any wrong statement therein. While filing the return under section 139, read with section 44AD or section 44AE, the assessee in substance exercises the option to be assessed at an amount out of three options available to him. CHAPTER ONE

SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR COMPUTING PROFITS & GAINS OF BUSINESS OF CIVIL CONSTRUCTION AND TRANSPORT*

Introduction

1.1 The Finance Act, 1994 inserts two new sections - 44AD and 44AE - in the Income-tax Act, 1961 ('the Act") to extend the concept of 'estimated/deemed income', for determination of profits and gains of the business of Civil Construction or Transport.

The objectives of the New Provisions are:

■ simplification;

■ minimizing compliance cost; and

■ minimizing undue harassment to tax payers.

The new provisions have been justified on two grounds:

■ Such a method is prevalent in several countries; and

■ Tax Reforms Committee has recommended gradual introduction of the method.

The above provisions come into force from the assessment year 1994-95 and thus, have a retrospective effect for the previous year ended on 31-3-1994.

Provisions in brief

1.2 Following points need be noted:

■ Sections 44AD and 44AE ('the New Provisions') are applicable to all assessees engaged in the business of Civil Construction and/or Transport ('the specified business').

■ 'Civil Construction' business, as defined, will include the construction or repairs of buildings, dams, bridges, or other structures or roads or canals. It will also include the execution of any works contract.

■ ‘Transport Business' covers the business of plying, hiring or leasing of goods carriages owned by the assessee.

The value of work in progress may not form part of gross receipts. If in terms of the contract the work is approved, but, merely bill is not made, it is felt that value of such work in progress would form part of the gross receipts.

The value, if any, of stock-in-trade would not form part of gross receipts.

3.10

Percentage of Completion Method (POCM)

ICDS-III (Revised) requires a contractor to offer incomes from construction contracts to tax in accordance with the "percentage of completion method"(POCM). The recognition of contract revenue and contract costs by reference to the stage of completion of a contract is referred to as the percentage of completion method. Under this method, contract revenue is matched with the contract costs incurred in reaching the stage of completion, resulting in the reporting of revenue, expenses and profit which can be attributed to the proportion of work completed. Paras 18 and 19 of ICDS-III(Revised) explain how% of stage of completion of a contract as at reporting date is to be determined. Para 20 provides that percentage of completion method is not required to be followed during the early stages of a contract i.e. in case of a contract which has reached 25% or less stage of completion. In cases of contracts in early stage, where the outcome of the contract cannot be estimated reliably contract revenue is recognised only to the extent of costs incurred. In other words, neither profit nor loss on contracts in early stages shall be recognised.

In Dy. CIT v. Sri Jagannath Properties & Developers decided by ITAT-Cuttack on 31.08.2018 in [ITA No. 283/CTK/2017] it was held that while applying POCM as per ICDS-III, the question whether stage of completion of 25% has been reached or not is to be reckoned project-wise(contract-wise) and not by taking all projects (contracts) together on overall basis and revenue can be recognised in only those projects(contracts) where stage of completion has reached 25%.

Thus, POCM is to be applied contract-wise. There is a concept in accounts called the concept of Contract Accounts. To know the results of his operations, the contractor prepares what is called as Contract Account which is debited with various costs and which is credited with the revenue associated with a particular contract. Under the POCM, reasonable profit is calculated on the basis of the value of the work certified and the profit attributable to the work certified. For example, if the value of the work certified is one-fourth or more but less than half of the contract price, then a certain percentage of the profit accruing to the certified work is taken to the profit and loss account [CIT, Meerut v. Hyundai Heavy Industries Co. Ltd. [2007] 161 Taxman 191 (SC)]. Thus, for each construction contract, a separate contract account is to be opened and the contract costs and contract revenues related to it have to be debited and credited to it with reference to% of stage of completion reached in all individual contracts which have progressed to more than 25%. (a) Notices under section 142 and/or under section 143(2) of the Act.

(d) On that basis, a written order of assessment of the income and determination of sum payable by the assessee. ■ Where a lower amount is returned, the AO can send an intimation under section 143(1)(a); make prima facie adjustments (like correction of arithmetical inaccuracy) and levy additional tax.

■ However, AO cannot make adjustment so as to assess the income as per sub-section (1), i.e., he cannot adopt the specified amount as profit.

This is the view taken by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal in U. Shahul Hamid & Bros. v. ACIT [1990] 45 ITD 628 wherein a return, in case of a trader in tendu leaves, income as per the accounts was shown without complying with section 44AC. The Assessing Officer determined the sum payable under section 143(1)(a) by applying section 44AC. The Tribunal held that this was not permissible because the proviso does not permit adoption of a basis other than the return of income.

■ Once a return is filed under section 44AD(5) or section 44AE(6), the AO is bound to determine the income/loss and the tax payable only by an order in writing under section 143(3) as:

- the language of the provisions reflect a mandate:'... and there upon the Assessing Officer shall proceed to make an assessment of the total income ...' [Emphasis supplied],

- the provisions require an 'assessment' and determination of sum payable based on such assessment in contrast to provisions of section 143(1)(a), which require determination of sum payable after making prima facie adjustments.

In other words, only an intimation would not be sufficient.

■ Assessment at a higher amount exceeding the specified amount - The next issue is that in the computation made under sections 28 to 43C of the Act, on account of specific disallowance as well as on account of adjustment in gross profit, if an addition is required to be made, can AO make an assessment in excess of the specific profits, pursuant to the provisions of sections 143(3), 145 and other applicable provisions? For the purpose, one may consider the language of the provisions as well as certain illustrations and determine the effects of section 44AD(5), which reads as follow:

"Nothing contained in the foregoing provisions of this section shall apply where the assessee claims and produces evidence to prove ... and thereupon the Assessing Officer shall proceed to make an assessment... under sub-section (3) of section 143."

The New Provisions relating to assessment at specified amount or a higher amount would not apply, ... where the assessee claims and produces evidence to prove that the profits from the specified business are lower.

Thus, when a claim is made and evidence is produced, the provisions of normal assessment become applicable and thereafter whether the Assessing Officer accepts the same or not, as such, is of no consequence. In other words, once the claim for assessment at the lower profit is made, the New Provisions would not apply and the assessee would be governed by normal provisions and assessment at an amount higher than the specified amount is possible.

ILLUSTRATIONS

1. An assessee, while claiming the assessment at lower profit, omits to make certain disallowances under section 40A(2) or 40A(3) and in the course of assessment, an addition is required to be made under the aforesaid provisions. As a result, the profits ultimately required to be assessed exceed the amount of specified profits. Can the Assessing Officer make an assessment in excess of the specified profits ?

2. A truck operator carries out some work on a truck, to convert the same into a container carrier. He claims the expenditure as revenue expenditure and on that basis lower profits are returned.

3. A person is engaged in the business of civil construction, where the person had valued the work in progress at cost. The Assessing Officer considers that the correct method of valuation should be net realizable value and not cost and on account of the valuation difference the profits could exceed the specified profits.

4. In case of a person engaged in the business of civil construction, it is noticed that certain expenses claimed are inflated and as a result addition should be made which may exceed the specified profits.

In the situation considered in illustration (1) above, the additions are arising because of non-application of the provisions of the Act. The return as filed by the assessee is accepted. Thus, section 44AD(5)/44AE(6) apply and the profits have to be computed in accordance with sections 28 to 43C of the Act. Accordingly, AO can assess the profits at an amount higher than the specified amount.

Revenue recognition according to the Expert Committee of the Institute of Chartered Accountants

5. Some illustrative cases dealt with by the Expert Advisory Committee of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India not only throw more light on the two methods of accounting, namely, (i) the percentage of completion method and (ii) the completed contract method of accounting, recommended for adoption in executing contracts running for a number of years, but also clarify the various issues involved in accounting for and taxation of profits. Three cases are discussed below in brief.

(i) First illustrative case. - A heavy engineering equipment manufacturing company sold equipment on turnkey basis. In almost all turnkey projects, the payments for supply and erection were received separately in instalments dependent on the stage of development. According to the terms agreed to, the final balance of 5 per cent of each, i.e., 10 per cent of the total cost, was receivable on successful commissioning and acceptance by the customer or on submission of bank guarantee covering the guarantee period.

The company was recognising sales at 100 per cent contract value on despatch of equipments to the site. Due to this, sales was taken at 100 per cent though the final 10 per cent became due only after 36 months, i.e., after commissioning. This accounting procedure had necessitated payment of income-tax on the portion of 10 per cent also taken as income in the year of despatch of equipment.

Considering the disadvantages from the taxation angle, the company sought the opinion of the Expert Advisory Committee as to whether the said 10 per cent of the contract price which was not due could be recognised as revenue in the year in which it fell due, i.e., after completion of the project, thereby deferring the tax liability.

The Expert Committee observed (April 1987) that according to AS-7,

"under the percentage of completion method, the amount of revenue recognised is determined by reference to stage of completion of the contract activity at the end of each accounting period (para 9.1)... The stage of completion used to determine revenue to be recognised in the financial statements, is measured in an appropriate manner. For this purpose no special weightage should be given to a single factor; instead, all relevant factors should be taken into consideration, for example, the proportion that costs incurred to date bear to the estimated total costs of the contract, by surveys which measure work performed and completion of physical proportion of the contract work (para 9.2) . . . progress payments and advances received from customers may not necessarily reflect the stage of completion ... (para 9.3)."

Further according to AS-9, "In a transaction involving the rendering of services, performance should be measured either under the completed service contract method or under the proportionate completion method, whichever relates the revenue to the work accomplished. Such performance should be regarded as being achieved when no significant uncertainty exists regarding the amount of the consideration that will be derived from rendering the service."

As the company was following the percentage of completion method for revenue recognition, the Committee opined that the company should recognise 100 per cent contract price as revenue in the year in which the entire equipment was despatched and the contract was performed to a substantial extent. However, the estimated liability of 10 per cent must be provided in the accounts for fulfilling possible claims. According to the Committee, the question of admissibility of the provision for possible claims as a deduction in computation of taxable income, was a separate question which had to be resolved keeping in view the facts and circumstances of each case, [vide page 12 of Vol. VII of Compendium of Opinions].

(ii) Second illustrative case. - A public limited company, wholly owned by a State Government, undertook construction works exclusively for Government departments/undertakings, both on turnkey and non-turnkey basis and followed the mercantile system of accounting.

. In addition to the billed amount the closing work-in-progress representing the value of goods and service transferred during the financial year but not billed, is added. For the same reason, the opening work-in-progress representing the value of goods and services transferred during the previous financial year and billed during the current financial year is reduced. Thus, the cost of goods and services transferred during the current financial year is arrived at for the computation of taxable turnover.

Thus, income to be recognized in a works contract is: For example, in the case of a works contract continuing over a period of 3 years, the income for the 1st year is to be recognized as the aggregate amount billed during this year and the value of closing work-in-progress. In the 2nd year, the aggregate of the amount billed during the year and the value of closing work-in-progress as reduced by the value of opening work-in-progress is the income to be recognized. In the 3rd year, the amount billed during that year as reduced by the opening work-in-progress is the income to be recognized. Any subsequent escalation or reduction in the bill subsequent to the financial year shall be adjusted in the returns by filing revised return for the period for which the change has occurred. The concept of percentage of completion of the work by recognizing the volume of work completed at any stage as asset of the contractor in AS-7 needs a reconsideration.

Profit or Loss

7. The profit or loss on works contract is derived by taking the income recognized as detailed above on the income side of the profit and loss account and the cost of goods and service is taken on the expenditure side of the profit and loss account. The cost of consumables, cost of design, consultation and technology, cost of hire charges, cost of finance, establishment charges and depreciation are taken on the expenditure side. The net result is the profit/loss of the contract work.

In case of bulk purchase during the first year, such part of goods not transferred while executing the work will be in the closing stock and that part of goods used in the work but not billed is in the work-in-progress. Whatever is transfer value of goods by involving in the execution of the works contract is recognized as income. Hence, bulk purchase of goods will not create an artificial loss in the profit and loss account.

Any amount received less than the measured and billed amount is to be treated as receivables and any amount received more than the measured and bill amount is to be treated as advance. Both amounts received and receivable are taken as the contract amount. Taxable turnover is determined by deducting the value of labour components and consumables from the contract amount as per the rules. The mobilization advance is to be treated as loan repayable as deduction from every subsequent bills. Hence, such mobilization advance is not part of the contract amount.

The above method remains unchanged in the fixed price contract and cost plus contract; since the measurement and billing on fixed price contract is based on the scheduled in the agreement and the cost plus contract adopts the measurement and billing on the basis of the cost of the contractor. Therefore, the AS-7 needs amendment accordingly.

As income taxable under the Income-tax Act, 1961 from manufacturing or trading is the income generated from such activities, the income from contract is the income generated from executing the contract work. Hence, estimation of income at the rate of proportionate work completed as per technical evaluation is a notional way, unwarranted in the presence of proper records. Taxable income is a truth and not to be estimated, unless the records are insufficient or incomplete and rejected by the Assessing Officer.

Conclusion

8. Therefore, the concepts in the Accounting standard AS-7 for recognition of income and expenditure are to be modified, as being mere estimation, discarding the facts in the records and contrary to the dictum of the Supreme Court of India that the transfer of property in goods in a works contract is not as a conglomerate.

Sub-section (2) reads as follows:

"for the purpose of sub-section (1), the profits and gains from each goods carriage—

(i)

being a heavy goods vehicle, shall be... for every month or part of a month during which the heavy goods vehicle is owned by the assessee in the previous year....;

other than a heavy goods vehicle, shall be... for every month or part of a month during which the goods carriage is owned by the assessee in the previous year...." [Emphasis supplied]

A reading of the above provisions show that the profits computation has to be made in accordance with the period for which the goods carriage is owned during the previous year irrespective of the actual employment thereof in the business during the previous year. The memorandum explaining the provisions of the Finance Bill gives two illustrations, which are reproduced hereinbelow, which supports the above view, as well as explains the computation of profits for a part of the month:

"Illustration (1): An assessee owns a light commercial vehicle for 9 months 15 days, a medium goods vehicle for 9 months and a medium goods vehicle for 12 months during the previous year. As per the illustrations, if a vehicle is owned even for 7 days, profits computation should be considered for a month.

In the context of the New Provisions it is felt that ownership should be construed in the same manner as construed for the purposes of section 32 of the Act.

Accordingly, it is felt that the date on which the Motor Vehicle is registered or person obtains possession of the vehicle, whichever is earlier, would be considered as the date from which the assessee should be regarded as an owner.

2.3 Under sections 44BB and 44BBB ('the said sections'), business income of non-residents engaged in the business of :

providing services or facilities in connection with, or supplying plant and machinery on hire used, or to be used, in the prospecting for, or extraction or production of, mineral oils (section 44BB);

is deemed to be 10% of the aggregate amounts paid or payable to the non-resident (hereinafter referred to as 'presumptive basis' or 'presumptive basis of taxation').

The above sections have now been amended with effect from assessment year 2004-05 to provide that the assessees covered by these sections will have an option to compute their income on a net income basis [, i.e., income shall be computed according to the provisions of the Act] (hereinafter referred to as 'net income basis' or 'net income basis of taxation'), provided the assessee:

maintains prescribed books of account;

gets the books of account audited; and

furnishes a tax audit report under section 44AB.

It is further provided that once a claim is made by the assessee for being governed by the net income basis of taxation, the Assessing Officer shall proceed to make an assessment of the total income under section 143(3) of the Act and determine the sum payable by, or refundable to, the assessee.

Further the presumptive tax rate of 10 per cent under section 44BBB will be applicable in those turnkey power projects also which are not financed under any international aid programme.

Consequential changes have been made in sections 44AA and 44AB of the Act relating to maintenance of accounts and audit of accounts, respectively.

2.3-1 Option - The alternative to follow the net income basis as business income is optional and hence, an assessee can continue to compute the business income on presumptive basis. Even if the assessee has maintained books of account and obtained an audit report, he may still opt to be governed by taxation on presumptive basis by not making the claim of being taxed on net income basis in the return of income.

2.3-2 Delay in filing the tax audit report - One of the pre-conditions for being governed by net income basis of taxation is that the assessee should furnish a tax audit report as required under section 44AB of the Act. Now, section 44AB of the Act provides that the tax audit report should be furnished on or before 31st October of the assessment year. Hence, on a strict literal interpretation, it appears that for the purpose of sections 44BB(3) and 44BBB(2) of the Act, the tax audit report has to be furnished before the said date and any delay may disentitle the assessee from making the claim to be governed by net income basis of taxation.

2.3-3 Loss - The sections provide that the Assessing Officer can make an assessment of the total income or loss. Such loss can be set off in accordance with the provisions of section 70 of the Act and carried forward and set off in accordance with provisions of section 72 of the Act. It appears that such carry forward loss can be set off against any business income, including presumptive income of the subsequent year, if the assessee decides to be so governed in that year.

2.3-4 Computation of income - In case the assessee opts to be governed by net basis of taxation, the computation of business income would be done by applying the provisions of sections 28 to 43B, including 40(a)(i), and also 44C of the Act. Further, the provisions of transfer pricing under sections 92 to 92F of the Act will also be applicable.

Application Guide-ICDS-III (Revised) - How to apply ICDS-III (Revised) in computation of income

This ICDS may be applied as under:

(a)

Identify each construction contract for which separate contract account needs to be opened.

(b)

Identification of each separate construction based on the definition of 'construction contract' [Para 3.5.] and combining and segmenting construction contracts in accordance with their substance [Paras 3.11 to 3.13]

(c)

The exercise in (a) and (b) above will serve dual purpose-for accounting as per AS) 7 and for computation of income as per section 43CB and this ICDS.

(d)

Apply percentage of completion method [Para 3.10] for each construction contract separately as per steps (e) to (p) below

(e)

Identify contract revenues and contract costs separately for each separate construction contract identified as above for which separate contract account has been opened. [Paras 3.14 to 3.35]

(f)

Determine stage of completion of each construction contract separately [Para 3.35-1]

(g)

Recognise contract costs and contract revenues with reference to% of completion for each construction contract which has crossed the 25% completion stage. Thus contract profit/contract loss would get recognised proportionate to% of completion. Add up such proportionate profits and losses and deduct period costs and other deductions from the aggregate of proportionate profits and losses to determine taxable income [Para 3.35-1]

(h)

If stage of completion of any construction contract is 25% or less, recognise contract costs already incurred and recognise contract costs equal to contract costs incurred [Para 3.35-1]

(i)

Where, on any contract which has crossed 25% stage of completion, full anticipated loss has been provided as per (AS) 7 instead of proportionate loss as per(g) above, make adjustment for the difference in computation of income in order to comply with ICDSs.

(j)

Where proportionate profit has not been recognised in accounts as per AS 7 in respect of a contract that has crossed 25% completion stage on the grounds that outcome of contract cannot be estimated reliably, add proportionate profit as per (g) above to net profit/loss as per P&L in computation of income.

(k)

Where on any contract which has not crossed 25% stage of completion full anticipated loss has been provided as per (AS) 7, make adjustment for the loss so provided in computation of income in order to comply with ICDSs.

(l)

Where proportionate profit was offered to tax in any past FY/FYs as per (g) above though no profit was recognised in accounts as outcome of contract could not be reliably estimated and the same has been booked in accounts of current period as per AS 7 since outcome could now be reliably estimated,deduct such profit amount booked in accounts in current period.

(m)

In case of Ind AS companies, following need to be added to net profit as per Ind ASP&L in statement of computation of total income

(i)

Profits from contracts which have crossed 25% stage of completion but Contract revenues recognition postponed due to applicability of at a point in time basis.

(ii)

Proportionate profit not recognised in accounts on POCM basis in respect of construction contracts which have crossed 25% stage of completion.

(iii)

Anticipated Loss in excess of proportionate loss recognised in respect of construction contracts which have crossed 25% stage of completion.

(iv)

Finance element computed by discounting to NPV (difference between contract revenues and NPV of contract revenues).

(n)

In case of Ind AS companies, following need to be deducted from net profit:

(i)

Profit recognised in accounts in current FY on point in time basis in respect of contracts from which profit was offered to tax in past FYs on POCM basis as per ICDS III.

(ii)

Finance element computed by discounting to NPV (difference between contract revenues and NPV of contract revenues)pertaining to current year.

(o)

Adjustments for complying with this ICDS as per (i) to (k) above are not to be made in accounts but in computation of income.

(p)

The adjustments to be made to profit or loss in computation of income for complying with ICDS-III(Revised) to be disclosed against items (d) & (e) of clause 13 of Form No. 3CD.

Calculation of value of property in goods involved in works contract, transferred works contract - In Vat, the dealer can pay Vat (or sales tax) either on value of material on actual basis or under composition scheme. If Vat or sales tax has been paid or payable on actual value of material, that amount will be deductible from total value of works contract to calculate value of taxable service.

The actual words used in the rule as follows - Where value added tax (Vat) has been paid or payable on the actual value of transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of the works contract, then, such value adopted for the purposes of payment of value added tax or sales tax, shall be taken as the value of transfer of property in goods transferred in the execution of the works contract for determining the value of works contract service under this clause [Rule 2A(i)(c) of Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006].

However, if the dealer has paid under composition scheme (i.e. at flat rate without separately calculating value of material), the value of material will have to be calculated on basis of actuals. Note that 'value' includes profit relating to goods also.

Vat or sales tax paid will not form part of value for service tax - Gross amount charged for the works contract shall not include value added tax or sales tax, as the case may be, paid, if any, on transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of the said works contract.

In Sobha Developers v. CCE (2010) 24 STT 425 (CESTAT), assessee was paying Vat on 70% of value of works contract as per Karnataka Vat Act and paid service tax on 30% of value as service tax. It was held that no differential service tax is payable, even if value of material is not shown separately in invoice. - departmental appeal against the decision has been admitted by SC for hearing - CCE v. Sobha Developers (2014) 47 GST 766 = 49 taxmann.com 595 (SC).

Splitting of contract permissible - In Essar Projects v. CCE (2014) 46 GST 582 = 47 taxmann.com 152 (CESTAT), assessee had entered into two different contracts - one for supply of material/equipment and other for erection/commissioning. There were a separate defect liability clauses for different contracts. Property in goods got transferred when equipment was supplied to customer. It was held that both cannot be treated as single contract for purpose of valuation under composition scheme of works contract.

16.3-2 Composition scheme for payment of service tax

Though service tax is legally payable only on value of service and Vat/sales tax is payable on value of goods, in a composite/indivisible contract, it is difficult to find value of goods and services. Hence, both under service tax and State Vat, a provision has been made for payment of tax under composition scheme.

In a composition scheme, tax can be paid on some ad hoc basis at the option of the tax payer.

In State of Kerala v. Builders Association of India 104 STC 134 = (1997) 2 SCC 183 = AIR 1997 SC 3640 = 1997 AIR SCW 977, the position was that a convenient, hassle-free and simple method, which was 'rough and ready method' was evolved by State Government for collection of sales tax on Works Contract. This was optional to assessee. It was held that Legislature can evolve such alternate, simplified and hassle-free methods of assessment, making it optional to assessee. - . - In the field of taxation, legislation must be allowed greater 'play in joints'. Allowance must be made for 'trial and error' by the legislature. - - Contractor who has opted to the alternate method of taxation cannot complain. Having voluntarily, and with the full knowledge of the alternate method of taxation, opted to be governed by it, a contractor cannot be heard to question the validity of relevant sub-sections or the rules - followed in Karnataka State Construction Corporation v. State of Karnataka (2004) 138 STC 75 (Kar HC DB) * Indian Oil Corp v. Prasanna Welding Industries (2007) 7 VST 101 (Gau HC).

In Mycon Construction v. State of Karnataka 2002 AIR SCW 2156 = 127 STC 105 (SC), it was held that a simplified composition scheme instead of regular assessment, can be evolved, if it is on optional basis. Validity of such provision has been upheld.

Government can make a provision allowing contractors option to opt for composition by paying a sum based on total consideration of contract. - Mytcon Construction v. State of Karnataka (1998) 111 STC 322 (Karn HC).

The value, if any, of stock-in-trade would not form part of gross receipts.

Presumptive taxation in case of non-residents [Sections 44BB and 44BBB]

2.3 Under sections 44BB and 44BBB ('the said sections'), business income of non-residents engaged in the business of :

providing services or facilities in connection with, or supplying plant and machinery on hire used, or to be used, in the prospecting for, or extraction or production of, mineral oils (section 44BB);

civil construction or erection or testing or commissioning of plant or machinery in connection with a turnkey power project approved by the Government and financed under any international aid programme (section 44BBB),

is deemed to be 10% of the aggregate amounts paid or payable to the non-resident (hereinafter referred to as 'presumptive basis' or 'presumptive basis of taxation').

The above sections have now been amended with effect from assessment year 2004-05 to provide that the assessees covered by these sections will have an option to compute their income on a net income basis [, i.e., income shall be computed according to the provisions of the Act] (hereinafter referred to as 'net income basis' or 'net income basis of taxation'), provided the assessee:

maintains prescribed books of account;

gets the books of account audited; and

furnishes a tax audit report under section 44AB.

It is further provided that once a claim is made by the assessee for being governed by the net income basis of taxation, the Assessing Officer shall proceed to make an assessment of the total income under section 143(3) of the Act and determine the sum payable by, or refundable to, the assessee.

Further the presumptive tax rate of 10 per cent under section 44BBB will be applicable in those turnkey power projects also which are not financed under any international aid programme.

Consequential changes have been made in sections 44AA and 44AB of the Act relating to maintenance of accounts and audit of accounts, respectively.

2.3-1 Option - The alternative to follow the net income basis as business income is optional and hence, an assessee can continue to compute the business income on presumptive basis. Even if the assessee has maintained books of account and obtained an audit report, he may still opt to be governed by taxation on presumptive basis by not making the claim of being taxed on net income basis in the return of income.

2.3-2 Delay in filing the tax audit report - One of the pre-conditions for being governed by net income basis of taxation is that the assessee should furnish a tax audit report as required under section 44AB of the Act. Now, section 44AB of the Act provides that the tax audit report should be furnished on or before 31st October of the assessment year. Hence, on a strict literal interpretation, it appears that for the purpose of sections 44BB(3) and 44BBB(2) of the Act, the tax audit report has to be furnished before the said date and any delay may disentitle the assessee from making the claim to be governed by net income basis of taxation.

2.3-3 Loss - The sections provide that the Assessing Officer can make an assessment of the total income or loss. Such loss can be set off in accordance with the provisions of section 70 of the Act and carried forward and set off in accordance with provisions of section 72 of the Act. It appears that such carry forward loss can be set off against any business income, including presumptive income of the subsequent year, if the assessee decides to be so governed in that year.

2.3-4 Computation of income - In case the assessee opts to be governed by net basis of taxation, the computation of business income would be done by applying the provisions of sections 28 to 43B, including 40(a)(i), and also 44C of the Act. Further, the provisions of transfer pricing under sections 92 to 92F of the Act will also be applicable.

Some of the issues in computation of such income were raised in N.V. Jan De Nul v. CIT [1999] 236 ITR 489. In this case, however, the authority refused to answer the questions !

FAQ 56. Mr. A has opted for the presumptive scheme under Section 44AD in respect of one of his businesses. Is the auditor required to mention details of such business in the audit report?

Yes. He should report the nature of the presumptive business correctly in Clause 10(a) of Form No. 3CD. In case the profit and loss account of the assessee includes any profit declared under the presumptive scheme (Section 44AD, 44AE, 44AF, 44B, 44BB, 44BBA, 44BBB), then it is mandatory to mention the amount of such profit and the section under which the same is declared in Clause No. 12 of Form 3CD. FAQ 57. How to ensure that the profit has been computed correctly if the profit & loss account also includes the profit computed on a presumptive basis?

If the profit and loss account of the assessee also includes the presumptive income, the common business expenditure has to be apportioned to arrive at the correct amount of profit credited to the profit and loss account and assessable on a presumptive basis. The tax auditor, in such a situation, should arrive at a fair and reasonable estimate of such expenditure on the basis of evidence in possession of the assessee or by asking the assessee to prepare such an estimate, which should be checked by him.

It is also necessary to mention the basis of apportionment of common expenditure. However, if the tax auditor is not satisfied with the reasonableness of such apportionment, he should indicate such fact in Clause (3) of Form 3CA/Clause (5) of Form 3CB by way of a note.

In relation to liabilities on account of revenue expenditure, there is a distinction. 5. Controversies

5.1 Controversy relating to provision for foreseeable losses in construction contracts - The accounting practice of valuing unsold stocks at cost or net realisable value (market value) which is lower is widely accepted now. But when the same theory of prudence was applied to other anticipated losses in case of investments forming part of closing stock-in-trade, work-in-progress under construction contracts, fluctuations in foreign exchange transactions and other matters, litigations surfaced and persist till date.

In 1983, the Accounting Standards Board of the ICAI issued Accounting Standard (AS) 7, Accounting for Construction Contracts. Para 19 of the Standard stipulates as follows :

"19. A foreseeable loss on the entire contract should be provided for in the financial statements irrespective of the amount of work done and the method of accounting followed."

When the assessees started adopting the accounting practice envisaged in the above Accounting Standard (AS) 7, the tax authorities rejected the same. Following few cases are stated as examples.

In a case before The ITAT Mumbai Bench 'A' in Mazagon Dock Ltd. v. Jt. CIT [2009] 29 SOT 356 decided on February 18, 2009, the issue was whether as far as change in method of valuation of work-in-progress was concerned, in view of mandatory requirements of AS-7, it was a bona fide change, particularly in view of qualification made in this regard by statutory auditors as well as by the Comptroller & Auditor General of India. It was held as follows :

"The question that came up for consideration was as to whether the anticipated loss on the valuation of fixed price contract, in view of the mandatory requirements of the AS-7, was to be allowed in the year in which the contract had been entered into or it was to be spread over a period of contract, as was done by the assessee in earlier years. As far as the change in the method of valuation of work-in-progress was concerned, it could not be disputed that in view of mandatory requirements of the AS-7, it was a bona fide change in the method of valuation of work-in-progress, particularly in view of the qualification made in this regard by statutory auditors as well as by the Comptroller & Auditor General of India. Therefore, the observation of the Commissioner (Appeals) that the assessee had booked bogus loss was not correct. As far as the basis of estimation was concerned, the same was done on technical estimation basis and, therefore, merely because there were some variations in the figures furnished by the assessee at different stages, it could not be said that the estimated loss was not allowable. It was not disputed that the department in earlier years had allowed the loss on estimated basis having regard to the expenditure actually incurred in various years. Therefore, in principle, it was not disputed that the estimated loss under the present circumstances was an allowable deduction. However, merely because the change in method of accounting was bona fide, it could not lead to the inference that the income was also deducible properly under the Act. This aspect is very evident from the first proviso to section 145 as it stood prior to the amendment by the Finance Act, 1995 with effect from 1-4-1997. It could not be disputed that from the method adopted by the assessee, the assessee's income could not be deduced properly in the year in which the loss had been anticipated. As a matter of fact this aspect was not disputed by the Assessing Officer also. He had been swayed more by the revenue loss than by the correct principle to be applied. The matching principle of accounting was not of much significance in the present context because if the loss had been properly estimated in the year in which the contract had been entered into, then it had to be allowed in that very year and could not be spread over the period of contract. The matching principle is of relevance where income and expenditure, both are to be considered together. However, in the instant case, the effect of valuation of WIP would automatically affect the profits of subsequent years accordingly. Therefore, there was no reason for not accepting in principle the assessee's claim as being allowable."

(iii)Another exception is provided in section 43B of the Act whereunder certain items like sales tax, excise duty, etc., are allowable as deductions only on payment before the prescribed dates. 5.2 When assessee's method may be rejected - A question now arises whether the Assessing Officer is bound to accept the entire scheme of entries in the accounting books if the assessee has regularly followed a certain method of accounting. The expression 'method of accounting' has reference to the pattern, system and principles on the basis of which the accounts of an assessee are maintained. The accounts maintained by the assessee constitute prima facie evidence for arriving at the income chargeable to tax during the relevant previous year. A presumption can, therefore, be made that the accounts provided by the assessee represent a fair picture of his income, unless strong evidence to the contrary is adduced.

Otherwise there will be no finality to the situation and the revenue may indulge in a witch-bunt. The power to compute profits under section 145(2) arises only where no method of accounting has been regularly employed by the assessee and where the method employed is such that the income, profits and gains cannot properly be deduced therefrom. It means that the method adopted by the assessee must, prima facie, prevail where it is regularly employed, though the Assessing Officer can reject it if the same is such that true profits cannot be correctly determined therefrom. In other words, even if the assessee has regularly employed a method of accounting, it can be discarded if the method does not show correct profits of the year - S.N. Namasivayam Chettiar v. CIT [1960] 38 ITR 579 (SC). The section does not compel the Assessing Officer to accept a balance sheet of cash receipts and outgoings prepared from the books of account. It is open to him under certain circumstances to compute the income on such basis and in such manner as he may determine – CIT v. A. Krishnaswami Mudaliar [1964] 53 ITR 122 (SC).

Fundamental nature of transaction important

5.3 The courts can always go into the fundamental nature of a transaction to determine its true impact and taxability. The courts may not accept the scheme of entries adopted by the assessee to record certain transactions. In the State Bank of Travancore v. CIT [1986] 158 ITR 102 , the Supreme Court has held that where interest has accrued and the assessee has debited the account of the debtor, the difficulty of recovery would not make its accrual non-accrual. There, the assessee, a banking company, maintained its accounts on the mercantile system of accounting. It used to charge interest on sticky advances by debiting the concerned parties. Instead of carrying the interest to the profit and loss account, the assessee credited it to a separate account called 'the interest suspense account'.

The assessee claimed that having regard to the bad and deteriorating financial condition of the parties concerned as well as the history of the accounts, the recovery of even the principal amounts of the debts had become improbable and doubtful and as such the interest thereon, though debited to the respective debtors, was taken to the 'interest suspense account' to avoid showing inflated profits by including hypo-thetical and unreal income. The contention of the assessee was that such interest on sticky advances was not real income and was not taxable in its hands. The Supreme Court held that interest on sticky advances had accrued according to the mercantile system of accounting and the assessee had debited the respective parties with the interest. After the close of the accounting year, the assessee, without giving up the interest as a bad debt, did not offer it for taxation, but carried it to the interest suspense account. Even if in given circumstances the amount might be taken to the interest suspense account for accounting purposes, that would not affect its taxability as such.

In Union Co-operative Insurance Society v. CIT [1967] 66 ITR 360 (SC)an insurance company was maintaining the accounts on mercantile basis. It claimed deduction of an item of expenditure that had been debited to profit and loss appropriation account on estimate basis. It was disallowed on the ground that by adopting this method the company had itself intended to treat it not as expenditure related to business but as disbursement made out of profit after it had accrued. It was held that by adopting that method the assessee-company did not seek to alter the character of expenditure. Hence, the same was not allowable as a deduction.

If the output service is partly taxable and partly exempt, the input tax credit is restricted to only 20 per cent of the service tax liability notwithstanding the amount of service tax paid. This was 35 per cent under the earlier Service Tax Credit Rules, 2002. In case the input service is not taxable being exempt altogether or coming from a service provider who is below the threshold of Rs. 4 lakhs limit, and the output service in which the input service is incorporated, is taxable, the exemption given to the service provider or the non-taxability of the services are given a go-by and the entire service is taxed under the umbrella of another taxable service. This happens in construction contracts where the building contractor provides a variety of services under the service of cons-truction but not taxable at the input level. This also happens in many types of works contracts which are taxable at the output service tax stage but the inputs may be totally exempt from service tax. For civil construction work, the net profit is deemed to be 8 per cent of gross turnover of the contractor under section 44AD of the Income-tax Act where as the service tax levy on the same comes to now 4.04 per cent at 12 per cent tax rate with 2 per cent educational cess. For a person to bear a service tax rate of 50 per cent of his net profits is a tall order indeed. Such high rates have been frowned upon in the Tax Reforms Committee Report but a uniform tax rate is applied without looking into peculiar business conditions.

Tax credit illusory

6. It appears that cross settlement of input tax credit between the services and the goods is more on paper than real. Often the input tax credit for goods consumed in the service sector is obtained from dealers who cannot provide cenvatable invoices. The supply of goods is widespread among various dealers not all of whom provide cenvatable bills or cater to the requirements of the end-user who is a taxable service provider.

Similarly goods used in service contracts are not necessarily purchased from the first stage or second stage dealer or from the manufacturer directly. The input credit for goods consumed in service contracts is largely illusory as the output service provider purchases inputs from available sources of supply and on such terms as to credit and quantity which suit his business needs. The input credit for goods is thus not available as the cenvatable invoice essential for claiming the input credit is not there but only an ordinary purchase invoice to support the purchase of goods. Goods which are purchased under cenvatable invoices and undergoing further process not amounting to manufacture lose their cenvatable advantage when they are sold again in the processed stage; the processor is not a manufacturer of any new goods and the CENVAT chain is broken at his level and cannot be continued further into the hands of the next consumer.

Allowability of foreseeable losses in construction contracts

ABHISHEK WORAH

CA

NAVEEN WADHWA

CA

The taxability of revenues and incomes in respect of construction contracts represents a vexed issue before the revenue authorities. There are conflicting decisions by the various Benches of the ITAT on the issue of allowance for foreseeable losses in the construction contracts. In this article the authors have examined the issue in details as per the Accounting Standards and have cited various case laws where decisions have been taken in favour or against such claims.

INTRODUCTION

1. The taxability of revenues and incomes in respect of construction contracts represents a vexed issue before the revenue authorities.

The accounting for construction contracts in the financial statements is governed by the Accounting Standard (AS)-7 - Construction Contracts issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI). As per AS-7, the contract revenue and contract costs are to be recognized as revenue and expenses, respectively, by reference to the stage of completion of the contract at the reporting date. This method of recognizing contract revenue and expenses with reference to stage of completion of the contract is popularly referred to as percentage of completion method (POCM). Hence, the revenue, expenses and profit with reference to a contract are reported based on the proportion of the work completed.

Accounting Standards issued by the ICAI advocate the view that financial results should be arrived at after considering the anticipated losses and expenses on the ground of 'prudence' and 'conservatism'. Inter alia, AS – 7 requires that an expected loss on the construction contract should be recognized as an expense immediately. The relevant paras 31, 32, 35 and 36 of AS-7 dealing with the recognition of loss in contract are reproduced hereinbelow:

"Para 31….. An expected loss on the construction contract should be recognised as an expense immediately in accordance with paragraph 35.

Para 32….. However, even though the outcome of the contract cannot be estimated reliably, it may be probable that total contract costs will exceed total contract revenue. In such cases, any expected excess of total contract costs over total contract revenue for the contract is recognised as an expense immediately in accordance with paragraph 35.

Para 35. When it is probable that total contract costs will exceed total contract revenue, the expected loss should be recognised as an expense immediately.

Para 36. The amount of such a loss is determined irrespective of:

(a) whether or not work has commenced on the contract;

(b) the stage of completion of contract activity; or

(c) the amount of profits expected to arise on other contracts which are not treated as a single construction contract in accordance with paragraph 8."

As per the above paras, the expected loss in contract is to be recognized immediately irrespective of the stage of completion of the contract or commencement of the work of contract. On this basis the contractors (particularly the large companies undertaking big infrastructure projects, telecom projects and other building contracts having high values) do make provision for foreseeable losses, if they are of the opinion that the project is likely to result in a loss initially while making the estimates of contract revenue and costs.

The recognition of loss in a contract is also provided by the Ind AS-11 on Construction Contract1.

Hence, the contractors create a provision for foreseeable losses, in case they are of the opinion that the project is likely to result in a loss. The provision is created while making an estimate of the contract cost and revenue in the initial stages of a contract.

Thus, for the purpose of computing yearly profits or gains, each year is considered as a separate self-contained period of time. Any profit earned or loss incurred before its commencement is irrelevant. While ascertaining the profits and gains of one year, one may not deduct a loss/expense which had, in fact, been incurred before or may be incurred after the relevant previous year.
