The authority making a best judgment assessment must make an honest and fair estimate of the income of the assessee and though arbitrariness cannot be avoided in such estimate the same must not be capricious but should have a reasonable nexus to the available material and the circumstances of the case.

From the tender documents that were made available to the contractor and the terms and conditions of the "Lump Sum Contracts", two or three aspects emerged very clearly. In the first place, the contractor became aware that certain specified stores/materials would be supplied to him by the department at fixed rates for being used in the works to be undertaken by him for which he had not to pay from his pocket and it was on that footing that he submitted his tender quoting a particular figure for the entire work; secondly, such stores/material so supplied by the M.E.S. department had to be used, fixed or incorporated by the contractor in the works undertaken by him and the surplus, if any, that would remain after the completion of the work was to be returned to the department; thirdly, since for accounting purposes the initial supply was debited to the contractor at the specified fixed rates, credit for the balance of the stores/materials so returned was also given at the same rates, some adjustment being made in respect of the wear and tear of such stores/material but in regard to the stores/material out of such supply as was actually used, fixed or incorporated into the works, no accounting was done vis-a-vis the contract payment that is made to the contractor. In other words, in substance and in reality, such stores/material always remained the property of the department and the contractor had merely the custody of it and he fixed or incorporated the same into the works. It seemed clear that in such circumstances and having regard to the terms and conditions on which such supply of stores/materials was made there was not even a theoretical possibility of any element of profit being involved in the turnover represented by the cost of such stores/material. It was conceivable that when the contractor himself purchased materials in the open market and supplies the same to the department by using, fixing or incorporating the same in the works, as in the case of materials other than those specified in Schedule "B", some profit element would be embedded in the turnover represented by the cost of such material but when stores/material was supplied by the Government department at fixed rates for being used, fixed or incorporated in the work on terms indicated above, there would be no element of profit involved in the turnover represented by the cost of such material. It is true that, ordinarily, when a works contract is put through or completed by a contractor the income or profits derived by the contractor from such contract is determined on the value of the contract as a whole and cannot be determined by considering several items that go to form such value of the contract but in our view where certain stores/material is supplied at fixed rates by the department to the contractor solely for being used or fixed or incorporated in the works undertaken on terms and conditions mentioned above, the real total value of the entire contract would be the value minus the cost of such stores/material so supplied. Therefore, since no element of profit was involved in the turnover represented by the cost of stores/material supplied by the M.E.S. to the assessee-firm, the income or profits derived by the assessee firm from such contracts would have to be determined on the basis of the value of the contracts represented by the cash payments received by the assessee-firms from the M.E.S. department exclusive of the cost of the material/stores received for being used, fixed or incorporated in the works undertaken by them.

The appeal was, therefore, allowed.

The disallowance under section 40A(8) is provided for a specific purpose and if such a disallowance is deemed to be included in the estimate of profit under section 145, this would defeat the very purpose for which the provisions of section 40A(8) are enacted. The adoption by the ITO of the previous year, October to September, for the assessment year 1958-59, was wrongly adopted, because it did not satisfy the requirements of section 2(11)(i)(a ). It was only in cases where the assessee could adopt a different period to the financial year, 1st April to 31st March, that any other period could be adopted, which would invariably mean a period of twelve months. This was also subject to the requirement of the section.

"Previous year" ordinarily means a period from 1st April to 31st March. But if the assessee wanted to adopt any other period, then his accounts must be made up for that period. If, however, those accounts were not made up for that period, he could not ask for that period. In the instant case, admittedly the accounts had not been made up for over a period of 2 years and 8 months, so that the assessee could not adopt any other period than 1st April to 31st March. In these circumstances, the adoption by the ITO of the accounting period from October to September for year of assessment 1958-59, could not be conclusive, nor could the next ITO be barred from adopting the correct accounting period in terms of section 2(11)(i )(a).

Therefore, the ‘previous year’ for the assessment year 1959-60 in respect of the contract business was correctly taken as the year ending on 31-3-1959.

HELD: The adoption by the ITO of the previous year, October to September, for the assessment year 1958-59, was wrongly adopted, because it did not satisfy the requirements of section 2(11)(i)(a ). It was only in cases where the assessee could adopt a different period to the financial year, 1st April to 31st March, that any other period could be adopted, which would invariably mean a period of twelve months. This was also subject to the requirement of the section.

"Previous year" ordinarily means a period from 1st April to 31st March. But if the assessee wanted to adopt any other period, then his accounts must be made up for that period. If, however, those accounts were not made up for that period, he could not ask for that period. In the instant case, admittedly the accounts had not been made up for over a period of 2 years and 8 months, so that the assessee could not adopt any other period than 1st April to 31st March. In these circumstances, the adoption by the ITO of the accounting period from October to September for year of assessment 1958-59, could not be conclusive, nor could the next ITO be barred from adopting the correct accounting period in terms of section 2(11)(i )(a).

The assessee was a building contractor. It had entered into certain contracts in 1966 and also in 1970 respectively. The 1966 contracts were described as old contracts and the 1970 contracts as new contracts. It had filed a consolidated trading account and profit and loss account disclosing gross profit at 10.2 per cent. The ITO noticed that the assessee had not maintained quantity stock register and other relevant registers and a work-in-progress account which would have enabled him to verify the correctness of the book result and, therefore, decided to estimate the income by considering the profits made in earlier assessment years. He noticed that the assessee itself in the previous year had disclosed gross profits at the rate of 15.4 per cent. The ITO, therefore, after considering the explanation of the assessee that the old contracts were in the last stages of completion, assessed the gross profit in respect of the old contracts at 12 per cent, and at the rate of 15 per cent in respect of the new contracts. The assessee did not prefer any appeal. Thereafter, the ITO received an audit note wherein it was pointed out that in respect of the one of the old contract, the account books of the assessee disclosed a profit of 14.5 per cent. On the basis of the said information, the ITO reopened the assessment under section 147(b) and computed the gross profit in respect of that contract at 15 per cent. The AAC allowed the assessee’s appeal and annulled the order of assessment. But the Tribunal held that the reopening of the assessment was valid.

concealed the relatable income while filing the return of income. Therefore, this aspect of the penalty was to be confirmed. So far as the assessee's argument relating to 200 per cent of tax levied as the penalty was concerned, looking at the background of the assessee and manner of concealment of income, this was a fit case for levy of penalty under section 271(1)(c). Thus, this part of the penalty order was to be sustained. [Para 14] Regarding the concealed income relatable to the already disclosed contract receipts in the return of income, the dispute to be resolved was restricted to whether the total income of Rs. 1,82,010 derived, based on the books of account maintained by the assessee was correct total income or not. In other words, whether the assessee had concealed the particulars of income by not declaring the income equal to 6 per cent of the contract receipts. This was the case where the books of account of the assessee for the year were rejected by the Assessing Officer. In other words, by inference, the books of account did not reflect the correct profits of the year as they suffered from incompleteness and unreliability. It is settled law that the incompleteness relates to the quantity of transactions in particular books of account say ledger and also relates to the number of books of account statutorily to be maintained. In the assessee's case, the incompleteness was evidenced by the excluded entries or payments of Rs. 35,52,620. In such a situation, the best judgment assessment in the spirit of section 144 was the legal way of completing the assessment as authorized by the statute. The Assessing Officer had done exactly the same, which was approved by the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal, although they differed on applicable rate of net profit. In such a situation, it had to be decided if determination of net profit at the rate of 6 per cent of contract receipts was mere case of estimation or otherwise. It is a settled position that the levy of penalty under section 271(1)(c) is not approved in the cases of mere estimations of income. [Para 15]

In the instant case, the Assessing Officer originally estimated the income at the rate of 30 per cent relying on the figures of the assessee's own concerns. However, the Commissioner (Appeals) gave a finding that the said 30 per cent was arrived at without any basis and he proceeded to direct the Assessing Officer to adopt 15 per cent. Subsequently, in quantum appeal, the Tribunal further reduced the applicable rate to 6 per cent. [Para 16]

Thus, effectively, the Assessing Officer, the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal had adopted three different rates of profit for determining the total income of the assessee for the relevant year. However, for all the said three, the basis for arriving at the said percentages was neither any incriminating paper nor an entry on a document nor any admissible statement nor any other acceptable evidence. The facts and figures may be good enough for confirming the additions in quantum appeal. What is needed for matters of penalty proceedings is more than the said facts and figures, so far as the originally declared gross receipts are concerned. Penalty cannot be sustained in such cases where there is some possibility for the acceptance of the assessee's explanation. Further, when two views are possible on an issue, a bona fide belief for claim cannot be subjected to concealment merely because such belief is erroneous under the law. Therefore, the levy of penalty in respect of the income relatable to the said declared receipts was not proper. [Para 17]

Therefore, the instant case was the fit case for levy of penalty so far as the income relatable to suppressed labour receipts of Rs. 35,52,620 was concerned. To this extent, the assessee's argument that the increase in income was mere estimation was liable to be rejected. Therefore, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) did not call for any interference in this regard. So far as the penalty relatable to the declared gross receipts was concerned, there was no case for the revenue as the assessee had furnished the said receipts on his own while filing the return of income and relatable income, which was finally assessed at 6 per cent merely on the basis of estimations and such estimation at 6 per cent was not strengthened by any evidential support. FACT: The assessee, a civil contractor, showed his gross receipts less cost of material at Rs. 25 lakhs and disclosed a net profit of 8.4 per cent. The Assessing Officer estimated net profit at 12 per cent on the ground that in the succeeding year the assessee had disclosed a net profit of 12.8 per cent. While doing so, the Assessing Officer did not allow any separate deduction by way of depreciation. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessment order.

On second appeal :

HELD: In the instant case, the net profit was to be estimated at 11.5 per cent of about Rs. 25 lakhs. The reduction of 1 /2 per cent was given for the reason that the assessee’s turnover of Rs. 25 lakhs was not very high as compared to others in this line of business. The reduction was granted for the further reason that as the work progressed from year to year, the assessee would be gaining experience and expertise as a result of which economy would be affected in the later years. Therefore, the profit of 12.8 per cent disclosed by the assessee in the succeeding year could not be taken to be a sure guide for determining the profit for the preceding year. The net profit was, therefore, estimated at 11.5 per cent of the receipts of Rs. 25 lakhs (approximately). This determination of net profit was only on the working of the contract by the assessee and depreciation (the correct amount was to be quantified by the Assessing Officer after verification) which was an allowance granted under the Act, should be viewed as a separate deduction. Another reason for considering depreciation for separate deduction was that in some cases of contracts, huge machines may have to be employed; whereas in some other cases Labour intensive devices would be employed. Therefore, in order to have a uniform estimate of profit, it is desirable that profit is estimated first ignoring the depreciation and then granting depreciation separately. Then and then only true profit can be ascertained as bet been persons employing high cost machinery and persons employing Labour intensive devices. Therefore, depreciation should be separately deducted from the profit thus estimated.

In the assessment year 1983-84, the assessee, a civil works contractor, started construction work on behalf of Crompton Greaves Ambad and continued it up to the assessment year 1988-89.

The assessee adopted for its accounts the project completion method, by which the profit or loss was accounted for in the books of account of the year in which the project was completed.

The Assessing Officer, accepting the method of accounting of the assessee, completed the assessments for the assessment years 1983-84 and 1984-85 under section 143(3) after observing that the profit or loss would be accounted for on completion of project. However, the Commissioner, under section 263 set aside the assessments on the ground that income under construction work had not been computed correctly by taking into account the profits on the work-in-progress and that the method of accounting employed did not enable the income of the year to be properly deduced.

On appeal, before the Tribunal the following points were highlighted:

(a)Both the methods, the method adopted by the assessee and the method sought to be adopted by the Commissioner, are recognised methods.

(b)The profits of business must be computed in accordance with method of accounting regularly employed by the assessee. The choice of the method of accounting, like the choice of the previous year (Note: choice of previous year is no longer permitted) lies with the assessee.

(c)The assessee has been following the same method of accounting regularly in subsequent assessment years. Under the mandatory provisions of section 145, the department is bound by the assessee's choice of method which cannot be rejected as improper merely because it gives the assessee benefit in certain years even if this is assumed to be the case, or merely because, according to the department, another method is preferable.

(d)Independent Chartered Accountants have also found it appropriate to adopt the project completion method for the purpose of true and fair view of the financial position, including the profits earned.

(e)Merely because the profits of a project are postponed from the year of commencement of the project to the year of completion of the project, the same would not be the basis for considering the assessment made on that basis erroneous.

(f)When the rate of tax remains constant, it cannot also be said that the assessments adopting the project completion method are in any way prejudicial to the interests of revenue.

The Tribunal cancelled the orders passed by the Commissioner under section 263 and restored the assessments framed by the Assessing Officer.

Conclusion

7. From the foregoing discussion, the following guiding principles emerge:

(a)Where contracts for execution of works extend over a number of years, the Assessing Officer can estimate the profit on the basis of receipts in a year and bring the yearly profits to tax as contemplated in section 3 of the Act; the Assessing Officer need not wait for the completion of contract to charge tax on the profits.

(b)The 'completed contract basis' and the 'percentage of completion method' or the 'project completion method' are recognised methods to ascertain annual profits for purposes of levy of tax; the choice of method is that of the assessee; the choice has to be carefully made.

(c)The method adopted should be followed regularly in all years till the particular contract is over.

(d)The Accounting Standard (AS-7) having been made mandatory for corporate entities from April 1, 1991 and non-corporate assessees from 1-4-1993, the accounting for construction contracts should strictly conform to the requirements of the Standard.

In the instant case, the ITO arrived at the figure on the basis of the receipts extending over three accounting year. He took the sum total of these receipts to be the base for the net income that had accrued to the assessee during the accounting year 1943-44 as the entire contract work had been completed during that year. Mere execution of the contract work will not necessarily entitle the contractor to make a demand for payment until it is ascertained that the works are up to the standard agreed upon between the parties. Some parts of such work may be wholly rejected and like bad debts in every earning may be ignored in computing the gains or profits. It might have been open to the ITO, in exercise of his discretion, to make an enquiry into whether and when the bills for payment became due to the assessee. Much depended upon the terms in the contract, and the manner of its performance. Even as a basis of guess work, which the Income-tax Officer was entitled to do, the basis could not be said to be in consonance with honest guess work. The ITO did not seem to have taken into consideration why the payments which, according to him, were due to the assessee in the accounting year were not fully paid till three years after. Sometimes the payments to the contractors are withheld on account of unsatisfactory execution and they are held entitled to payments only if and when they replace the rejected work by acceptable and accepted ones. The bare possibility of such contingency could not be wholly eliminated in the instant case. If the ITO, in arriving at the figure for assessment, left out these considerations, he certainly could not be said to have exercised his judgment which he was none the less called upon to do in making the assessment in cases of assessee's default under sections 23(4) and 13 proviso of the 1922 Act. Any method of accounting adopted by the ITO acting under the proviso of section 13 of 1922 Act can be rejected if the method in fact does not show the true income, profits and gains. In this view of the matter, the Appellate Tribunal was right in asking the ITO to assess the assessee on receipt basis with regard to contracts carried out and completed during the year of accounting, there being every presumption that the incomes were paid as soon as they became due. At any rate, the Tribunal's decision might be upheld on the ground that when two methods of guess work are available for the purpose of assessment, the one which is more just to the assessee and which involves a much less margin of chance of uncertainty should be taken as the basis.

In the result, the Tribunal was right in asking the ITO to assess the assessee on receipts basis with regard to contracts carried on and completed during the year of account.

As regards the reduction of flat rate, the Appellate Tribunal had arrived at the lesser flat rate on the basis of their decisions in similar cases in the district. Their opinions were not receivable evidence in the instant case. The decisions in different cases must have been based upon different facts and different inferences deducible from such facts. In this connection, it might be observed that the ITO had been very fair to the assessee bearing in mind the difference between the gross value and net value of the bills. The Appellate Tribunal, therefore, did commit a mistake of law in arriving at a finding for which there was no relevant evidence to support.

Therefore, the reduction of the estimated profit rate from 40 per cent adopted by the ITO to 30 per cent by the Tribunal on the ground that 30 per cent was the general rate adopted by it in the cases of other assessees doing the same kind of contract works during the same assessment year was not legal.

Issues in British Paints case (supra)

3. The main issues that came up for consideration before the Supreme Court in the case of British Paints India Ltd. (supra) were as follows :— Is the Assessing Officer bound to accept the system of accounting regularly and consistently employed by the assessee, the correctness of which had not been questioned in the past? Is the officer bound by the method followed in earlier years? Is there any estoppel in these matters? Should the Assessing Officer consider the question as to whether or not the books disclose the true state of accounts and whether correct income could be deduced therefrom? Whether in the case of an assessee, a paint manufacturer, valuing its goods in process and finished goods consistently at cost of raw materials, totally excluding overhead expenditure, rejection of such a system by the Assessing Officer was justified?

Facts of the case

4. The assessee’s goods in process and finished products were valued at raw materials cost which worked out to be 84.49 per cent of the total cost. The company had been following this practice and it had been accepted in the past on the basis of the contention that the goods being paints had limited storage life and if not quickly disposed of, they were liable to lose their market value. The contention of the assessee was rejected by the ITO on the ground that at no time had the assessee claimed any deduction on account of deterioration/damage to goods. The ITO held that there was no justification to recognise a practice, as claimed by the assessee, of valuing its stock otherwise than in accordance with the well-recognised principle of accounting which required the stock to be valued at either cost (raw material + expenditure) or market price, whichever was lower.

The AAC and Tribunal oh successive appeals, confirmad the ITO’s view that the goods were liable to be valued at 100 per cent of the cost which included the overhead expenditure and not at 84.49 per cent as claimed by the assessee. The Calcutta High Court, however, held in favour of the assessee by accepting the method as a valid method, having regard to the consistent practice of the assessee.

Supreme Court’s ruling

5. On the case coming up finally before it the Supreme Court ruled that it is not correct to say, as contended by the assessee, that the Assessing Officer is bound to accept a system of accounting regularly employed by the assessee, the correctness of which had not been questioned in the past. According to the Court, there is no estoppel in these matters and the officer is not bound by the method followed in the earlier years. The Supreme Court observed that any system of accounting, which excludes for the valuation of the stock-in-trade all costs other than the cost of raw material for the goods in process and finished products, is likely to result in a distorted picture of the true state of the business for the purpose of computing the chargeable income. Such a system may produce a comparatively lower valuation of the opening stock and the closing stock, thus, showing a comparatively low difference between the two. In a period of rising turnover and rising prices, such a system is apt to diminish the assessment of the taxable profit of a year. The profits of one year are likely to be shifted to another year which is an incorrect method of computing profits and gains for the year of assessment.

The Supreme Court opined that as each year is a self-contained unit and the taxes of a particular year are payable with reference to the income of that year as computed in terms of the Act, income cannot properly be deduced from such a method. In this view of the matter, the Supreme Court held that it is not only the right but the duty of the Assessing Officer to act in exercise of his statutory power under section 14S and reject the accounting system adopted by the assessee, as he has done in the instant case, for determining what in his opinion is the correct taxable income. Consequently the Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the Calcutta High Court. While coming to this conclusion, the Supreme Court considered various cases, Indian as well as foreign, having relevance to the issue at hand.

This judgment of the Supreme Court can have far-reaching implications. It can help the Assessing Officers to reject methods consistently followed in earlier years. However, such a rejection can take place only if the method adopted by the assessee has been found to be such that the income cannot properly be deduced therefrom. Perhaps one cannot question such an approach as otherwise the Assessing Officer will not be in a poistion to rectify the situation at all, being helpless against the ground of consistency.

[1993] 70 TAXMAN 106 (ART) LONG-TERM CONTRACTS - WHETHER PROFITS SHOULD BE DETERMINED ANNUALLY OR ON COMPLETION OF THE CONTRACTS

K.R. Gupta

In the case of long-term contracts, the determination of profits from the contract business annually is not an easy task. For this reason, a contractor executing a long-term contract may like to determine the profit of the contract only after the contract has been completed and to file his income-tax return on that basis. In this connection, a question that arises for consideration is whether under the Income-tax Act, 1961, it is permissible to adopt such a method of accounting in respect of the contract business. The author of this article discusses various aspects of this issue concluding that although the completed contract method is a recognized method of accounting as per the Accounting Standard issued by the institute of Chartered Accountants of India, it is not a suitable method of accounting from income-tax point of view - EDITOR

Difficulty in determining profits annually

1. In the case of long-term contracts, the determination of profits from the contract business annually is not an easy task. For this reason, a contractor executing a long-term contract may like to determine the profit of the contract only after the contract has been completed and to file his income-tax return on that basis. In this connection, a question that arises for consideration is whether under the Income-tax Act. 1961 ('the Act') it is permissible to adopt such a method of accounting in respect of the contract business.

Position from accountancy point of view

2. Before examining the matter from the income-tax angle, it will be appropriate to discuss the position in this regard from the accountancy point of view. The Accounting Standard of 'Accounting for construction contracts' issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India has recognized the following two methods of accounting for contracts :

(i)the percentage of completion method;

(ii)the completed contract method.

In para 7 of the Accounting Standard (AS-7) these methods have been described as under :

"7.2 Under the percentage of completion method, revenue is recognized as the contract activity progresses based on the stage of completion reached. The costs incurred in reaching the stage of completion are matched with this revenue, resulting in the reporting of results which can be attributed to the proportion of work completed. Although (as per the principle of 'prudence') revenue is recognized only when realised, under this method, the revenue is recognized as the activity progresses even though in certain circumstances it may not be realised.

7.3 Under the completed contract method, revenue is recognized only when the contract is completed or substantially completed; that is, when only minor work is expected other than warranty obligation.

Costs and progress payments received are accumulated during the course of the contract but revenue is not recognized until the contract activity is substantially completed."

It will be seen that from the accountancy point of view, the completed contract method is a recognized method of accountancy.

Under the Act the assessee has the choice of adopting whatever method of accounting he wants to adopt, provided he follows the method regularly for his own purposes. Section 145 of the Act clearly makes the method of accounting, if regularly employed by the assessee, a compulsory basis of computation unless, as provided in the first proviso to section 145(1), in the opinion of the Assessing Officer, the income, profits and gains cannot be properly deduced therefrom. If the true income, profits and gains cannot be ascertained on the basis of the assessee's method of accounting, the Assessing Officer has the power to compute the income on such basis and in such manner as he may determine.

Each year as a self-contained unit

3. Under the Act, for the purpose of computing the profits and gains, each year is a separate self-contained period of time. In the case of Mahamudabad Properties ( P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1980] 124 ITR 31, the Supreme Court has observed that the provisions of the Act relating to the charge on income apply in relation to a specific assessment year and the provisions of the Act providing for the computation of the chargeable income apply, in the absence of anything to the contrary, in relation to the relevant previous year. Therefore, the profits and gains have to be computed for each accounting year separately.

Completed contract method - Its acceptability

Payment in excess of the amount which an assessee is liable to pay under the terms of an agreement is not an allowable deduction under section 37(1). The accounts of the assessee had not disclosed the correct profit derived by him in respect of the accounting period in question, taking into consideration the works so far done till 31-3-1989 and the payments to be made and actually made by the assessee. The burden to prove the sub- contracts, to bring the sub-contractors and examine them with reference to the sub-contracts entered into by them with the assessee, as also to satisfied the Assessing Officer with regard to the various payments received by them under the sub-contracts, lay squarely upon the assessee and not the department. Despite several opportunities granted to the assessee, he had failed to produce them, and, therefore, the Assessing Officer had reason to doubt the payments said to have been made under the sub-contracts. Further, the details for salaries and staff welfare expenses debited at Rs. 18,747 were not available on record and they were also not produced before the ITO. For these reasons, it was a case of estimate of profit under the proviso to section 145(1).

The order of Deputy Commissioner (Appeals) was, therefore, reversed and that of the ITO was restored.

For the assessment year 1962-63, the assessee's gross receipts included the cost of materials supplied by the Government for construction of a building. As no books of account were maintained by the assessee, the ITO proceeded with the computation invoking section 145 and applied a flat rate on the gross receipts. In appeal before the AAC, a certificate from the executive engineer, Public Works Department, was produced in support that no profit was allowed to the assessee on the cost of materials supplied by the Government. The Assessing Officer has rejected books of account for the reason that the assessee has failed to produce necessary bills and vouchers in respect of expenditure. The Assessing Officer has observed that most of the expenditure are supported by self-made vouchers. Although, the assessee claims that it has produced bills and vouchers in respect of major expenditure, fails to substantiate the claim with necessary evidences. The assessee failed to controvert the findings of the Assessing Officer with any positive evidence to come to the conclusion that the books of account maintained by him gave a true and correct profit from the business. The Assessing Officer was therefore right in rejecting books of account under the provisions of section 145(3) of the Act. [Para 8]

Having said, one has to examine, on facts and circumstances of the case whether the Assessing Officer was right in adopting net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts. There is no dispute with regard to the facts that the assessee is in the business of execution of works contracts. It is also an admitted fact that the assessee had disclosed 6.73 per cent to 7.44 per cent net profit, in the earlier period. For the assessment year 2007-08 in the scrutiny assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer has estimated net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts for which the assessee has not preferred any appeal. Estimation of net profit from the business is one of the accepted method of determination of income from business. But, there is no hard and fast rule for estimation of income.

The department is following estimation of net profit on various rates depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case. But, while estimating net profit from the business, there should be a basis for adopting a particular rate of net profit, either based on comparable cases of similar nature of business or assessee's own book results for earlier years. When there is no possibility of getting a comparable cases, and there is no possibility of reference to assessee's own book results for earlier periods, a reference to the provisions of section 44AD can be made, wherein the Act provides for estimation of net profit from the specified businesses subject to certain conditions. [Para 9]

The provisions of section 44AD provide for estimation of net profit of 8 per cent on gross receipts, in case where the assessees are involved in specified businesses and turnover from the business does not exceed specified limit. Although, the assessee's case does not fall within the ambit of the provisions of section 44AD of the Act, as its contract receipts exceed the specified limit, the analogy provided in the provisions of section 44AD can be adopted for estimation of net profit because of nature of business carried out by the assessee. The nature of business carried on by the assessee was squarely fit into the specified businesses referred to in the provisions of section 44AD of the Act. The presumptive rate of net profit of 8 per cent incorporated in section 44AD, reflects the legislative approved rate of net profit, which can be considered as fair and reasonable to estimate income from civil contract business, where the books of account are not found reliable by the Assessing Officer.

In this case, admittedly, the Assessing Officer had rejected books of account for the reason that the assessee has failed to produce supporting bills and vouchers in respect of expenditure. It is also an admitted fact that the assessee himself has admitted about 8 per cent net profit in the earlier period net of all deductions including depreciation. Therefore, considering the overall facts and circumstances of the case, the rate of net profit adopted by the Assessing Officer appears to be fair and reasonable. Hence, estimation of net profit of 8 per cent on total receipts net of all deductions including depreciation is upheld. [Para 10]

In so far as separate deductions towards depreciation is concerned, the assessee submitted that when estimation of net profit is made, separate deductions towards depreciation should be allowed, as depreciation is a notional deduction for normal wear and tear of the assets.

In this case, the assessee is involved in the business of execution of main works which carries more profit than sub-contract works and hence, the Assessing Officer has rightly adopted reasonable net profit of 8 per cent on gross contract receipts and accordingly, further deductions towards depreciation is not allowed. Whether separate deductions can be allowed towards depreciation or not is a fact which is to be decided based on the facts and circumstances of each case and also based on the rate of net profit adopted for estimation of profit.

The assessee's account was absolutely unbelievable because on a single day, i.e., on 31-3-1994, the assessee was stated to have given Rs. 19.2 lakhs towards tractor hiring charges, Rs. 3.71 lakhs towards water charges and Rs. 57.25 lakhs towards the labour charges for earthmoving. It was not clear how labour charges got accumulated for the whole accounting year to justify payment of cash of Rs. 57.25 lakhs on the last date of the previous year. When the cash payment of Rs. 80.16 lakhs on a single day itself gave rise to doubt in the mind of the Assessing Officer, he rightly cross checked the genuineness of the payments by issuing summons to the persons whose names were shown in the vouchers prepared by the assessee. The result was that partly vouchers were found to be bogus, and partly stood disproved. It was not clear on what ground the assessee could seek for acceptance of books of account which were found to be unworthy of credit by the three lower authorities. In the absence of credible books of account, option of the Assessing Officer under section 145(3) was to make assessment on estimation basis in terms of section 144. In the instant case, the order of the Tribunal was quite favourable to the assessee because as against the estimation of 10 per cent made by the Assessing Officer, the Tribunal had reduced the estimation to 8 per cent of the total works turnover. There was logic and reason in estimation of income from civil construction work at 8 per cent because under the presumptive scheme, section 44AD provides for assessment of income on civil construction work at 8 per cent where the contractor's turnover is below Rs. 40 lakhs. Even though the assessee contended that section 44AD had no application as the contract amount was above Rs. 40 lakhs, there was no justification to interfere with the order of the Tribunal because in the first place, the Tribunal had granted partial relief to the assessee by reducing the estimated income from 10 per cent to 8 per cent. Secondly, what the Tribunal had done, was only to follow section 44AD as a guideline for estimation of income from civil work. Therefore, there was no justification to interfere with that part of the order of the Tribunal. It was worthwhile to note that while confirming the estimation of income at reduced percentage, the Tribunal cancelled separate addition made by the Assessing Officer under the head 'Other income' which was a huge amount of Rs. 15,44,353. After getting deletion of addition of Rs. 15,44,353, the assessee could not canvass for modification of other part of the order of the Tribunal confirming estimation of income at the reduced percentage of 8 per cent which was a reason for deleting the separate addition without considering it independently on merit. The accounts may be rejected as unreliable if important entries and transactions are omitted therefrom or if proper particulars and vouchers, bills, etc., are not forthcoming or if they do not include entries relating to particular class of business transaction. Reasons for rejecting wages record as commented by the Assessing Officer related to full address of the labour, which was not given on the muster roll register. The wages record had been kept by the assessee as per regulation known as 'Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970. The addresses of the labourers to whom wages had been paid were not mentioned, since the labourers stayed in the Jhugi Jhoperies at a work site itself and to that effect the assessee had already replied to the Assessing Officer vide its letter dated 23-3-2001, through which site of construction where labourers resided was given which was, however, not taken notice of by the Assessing Officer and the same was sent to him by courier and was found to be duly received by the Assessing Officer. The Assessing Officer had also alleged that the actual date of payment was not mentioned by the payee receiving the wages. The date on which the entry had been made in the wages register was the actual date of payment. As per the nature of the contract work executed by the assessee, he had got a contract to carry out a particular job or a contract for which the material was supplied by the CPWD/DOT and the labour was provided by the assessee-contractor. The assessee used to make payments to the labourers on the basis of mandays put in by the labourers and not on the basis of work performed by them on each day. Therefore, there was no merit in the allegations of the Assessing Officer that work performed by the labour was not mentioned on the payment vouchers and in making them as basis for rejection of books of account. The payment to the assessee-contractor was also made on the basis of work completed which was measured by the department itself and not on the basis of what the labourer had done. The bills for such a contract were prepared, which were not verified by the engineers of contractee before making payments. On the basis of those bills which were finally approved by the Government engineers/contractee, the payment was given to the assessee-contractor after deducting TDS. Thus, it was humanly not possible to provide the details as to what work a particular labourer had done at the site. Further, the Assessing Officer had also not indicated any defect in the system of accounting regularly followed by the assessee, or its correctness, nor was there any change in the method of accounting during the year under consideration as compared to the earlier years to indicate any intention of the assessee to show low profit.

While examining the books of the assessee, the Assessing Officer has to consider the following aspects : (i) whether the assessee has regularly employed a method of accounting; (ii) even if regular adoption of a method of accounting is there, whether the annual profits can properly be deduced from the method employed; (iii ) whether the accounts have been correctly maintained; (iv) whether the accounts maintained are complete in the sense that there is no significant omission therein. If the answers to above four questions would be in the affirmative, then the assessee's profits would be computed on the basis of his accounts. In such cases, proviso to section 145(1) or section 145(2) cannot be invoked. On the perusal of the materials placed on record in the instant case, it was found that the answers to all the above four questions were in the affirmative. No finding had been recorded by either of the lower authorities as to the unacceptability of the method and to the irregularity of the accounts kept by the assessee. It is well-settled that in the absence of such a finding recorded by the authorities, the book results cannot be ignored or brushed aside.

In the instant case the assessee as sub-contractor to execute the civil construction works awarded by the principals, which was a small part of the projects executed by the principals. On the contract receipts, the principals had also deducted the tax under section 194C. Besides, the assessee was also engaged in the business of trading of sarees. It was also a fact that the assessee filed duly audited profit and loss account and balance sheet along with its annexure. It also produced the audited books of account, bills/vouchers and bank statements before the Assessing Officer as admitted by him in the assessment order. Besides, it further produced all the details and explanations called for by the Assessing Officer from time to time. It also produced labour registers before the Assessing Officer. However, he was of the opinion that the said registers had not been maintained in a conventional manner and according to him, there were no signatures or thumb impressions of all the recipients. Because of the aforesaid observations, the Assessing Officer rejected the audited books of account of the assessee and estimated the net profit. The Assessing Officer gave the examples of net profit earned by three companies and, thereafter, he relied on the provisions of section 11AD and estimated the net profit at the rate of 8 per cent of gross receipts. Now the assessee argued that the estimation of net profit at the rate of 8 per cent by relying on provisions of section 44AD was totally incorrect and without any basis for the reason that the assessee was sub-contractor and its profit margin was low in comparison to the contractors. Further, the Assessing officer had compared the profit of the assessee with the companies whose turnover and business paraphernalia was huge in comparison to the assessee. Further, the assessee had executed the part of work of civil construction for these companies and, therefore, it was not correct to compare the profit of those companies with the profit margin of the assessee. In fact the profit margin of those companies was also less than the margin which had been estimated by the Assessing Officer in the case of assessee. In the case of assessee as per audited books of account, the net profit margin for assessment years 2007-08, 2008-09, 2009-10 and 2010-11 was 1.94 per cent, 0.67 per cent, 0.20 per cent and 0.09 per cent respectively. Now, the assessee argued that the Assessing Officer had failed to appreciate that the profit margins of contractors and sub-contractors could not be same. In the assessment order he had worked out the average profit margins in the case of those three companies at 5.93 per cent, 6.15 per cent and 5.19 per cent respectively and in the case of assessee he had estimated the profit at the rate of 8 per cent, whereas, in the case of assessee the profit margin would be much less than in these companies being a sub-contractor of these companies. [Para 5]

In view of the above factual position and comparative figures given by assessee of its principal, wherein the net profit was ranging from 5.19 per cent to 6.15 per cent, it was held that definitely there would be lower profit in the case of sub-contractor, i.e., the assessee and, hence, the Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly estimated the net profit rate at 4 per cent. Accordingly, the order of Commissioner (Appeals) and this issue of revenue's appeal was dismissed. [Para 6]

The transfer value of goods involved in the execution of works contract is taxable under the sales tax law/VAT law and the value of taxable service is taxable under the service tax law and the income generated out of such deemed sale is taxable under the Income-tax Law; at the time of fixing any goods on the awarder’s asset.

Revenue recognization 3. In a works contract, the amount received or receivable from the awarder in consideration of executing the work includes consideration for transfer of goods and providing of service. The amount receivable as consideration is the billed amount less the amount received as advance. But the revenue recognition is to be based on the consideration for transfer of property in goods fixed by the contractor. Hence, the consideration receivable for the unbilled part of transfer of property in goods fixed by the contractor during the year is also to be included as revenue to be recognized for the year. The work-in-progress is to be taken as the unbilled part of transfer of property in goods fixed by the contractor during the year, valued on the end of the year; as being the part of work executed, but not charged by the contractor and unrecognized by the awarder. Thus, the aggregate of the billed amount and unbilled part of transfer of property in goods fixed by the contractor during the year as valued at the end of the year (work-in-progress) constitute the revenue to be recognized on the credit side of the profit and loss account for the relevant year. Any subsequent change in the contract amount recognized based on litigation or escalation results may be adjusted on accrual basis. Thus, the revenue to be recognized is to be based on the transfer of goods and providing of service during the year. Therefore, the contradiction in AS-7 is to be removed.

3.1 Indivisible Contract - A works contract is either a divisible contract or an indivisible contract. In the case of a divisible contract, the cost of materials and cost of service are separable and, hence, the levy of tax on sale of goods and services provided can be fixed easily. But in the case of indivisible and composite works contract, the computation of taxable turnover of goods is governed by rules in the VAT Law and value of taxable service is governed by Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006. The transfer value of goods and value of taxable services are to be divided for the levy of sales tax /VAT as per the direction of the Supreme Court of India in 88 STC 204 and the Rules framed by the States based on this judgment and for levy of service tax as per the Service tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006. The taxable turnover and taxable service are determined under this principle by deducting the value of labour component and consumables from the contract amount and, hence, it is not based on the percentage of completion of the work as stipulated by AS-7.

Method of stock valuation

4. Sub-section (1) of section 145 stipulates the need for a method of stock valuation and its being regularly employed by the assessee. It has been repeatedly pointed out by the Courts, that it is the assessee and not the department, that has the choice of the method of stock valuation.

An assessee's choice of the method, is influenced by various economic and commercial factors. Accounting and trade customs play a major role in the choice of method. Inventories are held in the expectation of deriving revenue directly or indirectly, from their sale or use. In order to determine the results of a business for a given period, it is necessary to carry forward the cost related to inventories, until the inventories are sold or consumed. However, if there is no reasonable expectation that the net realisable value would cover the cost incurred (as a result, for example, of deterioration, obsolescence or a change in demand), it is necessary that cost which cannot be recovered should be charged against the revenue of the current period. The inventories are, therefore, normally stated at the lower of historical cost and the net realisable value - Accounting Standard 2, Valuation of Inventories, Institute of Chartered Accountants of India. A system of accounting must, therefore, include an acceptable basis for valuing stock in trade too - Indo Commercial Bank Ltd. v. CIT [1962] 44 ITR 22 (Mad.). The method of accounting adopted by the assessee, should ordinarily be accepted by the department, unless it is either improper or patently false. It was aptly remarked by the Madras High Court in Chari and Ram's case (supra), that an assessee is entitled to compute the income, profits and gains, in accordance with the method of accounting regularly employed by the assessee and ordinarily this method must be accepted by the department, in the absence of anything to suggest that it is improper or patently false. This proposition has been later reiterated in a catena of decisions. The Act also imposes a statutory duty on the ITO to examine in every case, the method of accounting employed and to see, whether or not it has been regularly employed - CIT v. A. Krishna Swami Mudaliar [1964] 53 ITR 122 (SC).

The most common method of stock valuation, viz., cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower, has found universal acceptance with the Courts- Ramswarup Bengalimal v. CIT [1954] 25 ITR 17 (All.) and Chhaoni Lal Pragdas v. CIT [1957] 31 ITR 597 (All.). While anticipated loss is taken into account, anticipated profit in the shape of appreciated value of the closing stock, is not brought into account, as no prudent trader would care to show increased profits before actual realisation - Chainrup Sampatram's case (supra). The value of opening and closing stocks are essential factors in determining the profits of the year and wrong and arbitrary valuation cannot, therefore, be accepted as a system or method of accounting that may be adopted by an assessee. The Allahabad High Court in the case of Chhaoni Lal Pragdas ( supra) while recognising that stock must be valued at cost price or market value, rejected the assessee's stand of valuing stock arbitrarily and neither at cost nor market value. This does not in any way bar an assessee from adopting a mixed system of stock valuation, where some items are valued at market price and some at cost, so long as such method is regularly followed.

Change in the method of stock valuation

In the instant case, the Assessing Officer rejected the books of account on the reason that the assessee had not maintained proper books of account and also had failed to produce vouchers for verification and the expenditure claimed by the assessee was not substantiated. The assessee in the earlier years also had not maintained the proper books of account. The assessee’s past track record showed that it neglected presenting of the books of account in accordance with law. When the assessee claimed any expenditure, it was mandatory on its part to produce the books of account supported by proper bills and vouchers. Since the assessee had not produced books of account, true profits or loss could not be deduced from its books of account. The Assessing Officer having no other option rejected the books of account and estimated the income at 10 per cent of gross receipts. But the position was that the assessee was carrying on three kinds of contracts as in the earlier years, i.e., (i) own contracts, (ii ) contracts taken from the sub-contractors, (iii) contracts given to other parties on sub-contracts. The assessee had a higher rate of profit on the contracts executed by the assessee itself. In these contracts, the assessee agreed that its income was at 9 per cent of the gross receipts. Thus, the Assessing Officer was directed to estimate the income on the contracts executed by the assessee on its own at 9 per cent. In case of contracts taken by the assessee on sub-contract, the income was to be estimated at 8 per cent of the gross receipts. In case of contracts given by the assessee to the 3rd party on sub-contract, income was to be estimated at 4 per cent. This is because when the assessee gave contract to the other parties on sub-contract, it could not keep the same percentage of profit at 9 per cent. It had to forgo certain portion of the profit, i.e., around 5 per cent to the sub-contractors. Similar was the position in the case of contracts taken by the assessee on sub-contract from other parties. Further, the assessee was entitled to depreciation and remuneration, and interests to partners on the profit estimated by the Assessing Officer at applicable rates, because the income estimated as above of the assessee was before the depreciation and interest and remuneration of the partners. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer was to be directed to compute the income of the assessee afresh.

Now, placing reliance on the same books for the purpose of invoking the provisions of section 40(a)(ia ) was improper. The estimation of income took care of the irregularities committed by the assessee. Revenue recognition according to the Expert Committee of the Institute of Chartered Accountants

5. Some illustrative cases dealt with by the Expert Advisory Committee of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India not only throw more light on the two methods of accounting, namely, (i) the percentage of completion method and (ii) the completed contract method of accounting, recommended for adoption in executing contracts running for a number of years, but also clarify the various issues involved in accounting for and taxation of profits. Three cases are discussed below in brief.

(i) First illustrative case. - A heavy engineering equipment manufacturing company sold equipment on turnkey basis. In almost all turnkey projects, the payments for supply and erection were received separately in instalments dependent on the stage of development. According to the terms agreed to, the final balance of 5 per cent of each, i.e., 10 per cent of the total cost, was receivable on successful commissioning and acceptance by the customer or on submission of bank guarantee covering the guarantee period.

The company was recognising sales at 100 per cent contract value on despatch of equipments to the site. Due to this, sales was taken at 100 per cent though the final 10 per cent became due only after 36 months, i.e., after commissioning. This accounting procedure had necessitated payment of income-tax on the portion of 10 per cent also taken as income in the year of despatch of equipment.

Considering the disadvantages from the taxation angle, the company sought the opinion of the Expert Advisory Committee as to whether the said 10 per cent of the contract price which was not due could be recognised as revenue in the year in which it fell due, i.e., after completion of the project, thereby deferring the tax liability.

The Expert Committee observed (April 1987) that according to AS-7,

"under the percentage of completion method, the amount of revenue recognised is determined by reference to stage of completion of the contract activity at the end of each accounting period (para 9.1)... The stage of completion used to determine revenue to be recognised in the financial statements, is measured in an appropriate manner. For this purpose no special weightage should be given to a single factor; instead, all relevant factors should be taken into consideration, for example, the proportion that costs incurred to date bear to the estimated total costs of the contract, by surveys which measure work performed and completion of physical proportion of the contract work (para 9.2) . . . progress payments and advances received from customers may not necessarily reflect the stage of completion ... (para 9.3)."

Further according to AS-9, "In a transaction involving the rendering of services, performance should be measured either under the completed service contract method or under the proportionate completion method, whichever relates the revenue to the work accomplished. Such performance should be regarded as being achieved when no significant uncertainty exists regarding the amount of the consideration that will be derived from rendering the service."

As the company was following the percentage of completion method for revenue recognition, the Committee opined that the company should recognise 100 per cent contract price as revenue in the year in which the entire equipment was despatched and the contract was performed to a substantial extent. However, the estimated liability of 10 per cent must be provided in the accounts for fulfilling possible claims. According to the Committee, the question of admissibility of the provision for possible claims as a deduction in computation of taxable income, was a separate question which had to be resolved keeping in view the facts and circumstances of each case, [vide page 12 of Vol. VII of Compendium of Opinions].

(ii) Second illustrative case. - A public limited company, wholly owned by a State Government, undertook construction works exclusively for Government departments/undertakings, both on turnkey and non-turnkey basis and followed the mercantile system of accounting.

In the facts and circumstances of the instant case, it appeared that it was not possible to answer the questions referred without further findings on fact. It was not clear whether the lower authorities had seen or considered the terms and conditions of the contracts under which the assessee had carried on the work of construction. The terms and conditions as to supply of materials by the contractee were also not known.

Such terms were of some importance. It would be necessary to determine whether the materials to be supplied would be free of cost or price on the basis of market value or otherwise would be charged. On such facts it may be found that an element of profit was there on such supply (sic ). Whether the assessee submitted its tenders for the said contracts anticipating on being assured of supply of such materials were also not known. In this view, the matter was remanded back to the Tribunal. The Tribunal was directed to ascertain the terms and conditions of the contracts in question, if any, in respect of supply of materials and determine whether the assessee bid for such contracts taking into account such materials which were in fact supplied. If it was found on such facts that there was an element of profit involved in the materials supplied then the profits of the assessee will be estimated on the gross receipts of the assessee computed by including the value of the materials supplied to the net receipts. The Tribunal will be at liberty to take further evidence in the matter and will afford opportunity to the parties to adduce further evidence and to make further representations in the matter.

Jaganmohan Reddy, CJ.—These two references arise from the same transactions entered into by the assessee, namely, renovation and repairs to what is known as "Rashtrapathi Nilayam" at Bolarum, and the period of assessment is in respect of the "previous year" 1959-60. Two questions are before us, the one referred by the Tribunal under section 66(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, viz.,

"Whether, on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the 'previous year' for the assessment year 1959-60 in respect of the contract business was correctly taken as the year ending on the 31st day of March, 1959?"

and the second question referred by the Tribunal as required by us, under section 66(2) in R.C. No. 36 of 1966, namely :

"Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, estimation of profit on the gross amount instead of estimating on the net amount received by the assessee after deduction of costs of material supplied by the Government is justified in law."

The assessee is an individual contractor and has several sources of income, such as interest on securities, income from house property and income from business. In the previous year, relating to the assessment year 1959-60, he had undertaken to complete the building contract work. In fact, this building contract was undertaken by him even earlier to the previous year. But the question that has been referred is only confined to the previous year relating to the assessment year 1959-60. It is, however, stated in the statement of the case that the contract actually started on 1st January, 1957, and was completed on 30th August, 1959. Accounts maintained for this business were, however, closed only once, i.e., when the contracts were completed ; so much so, the profit from the contracts was ascertained for the entire period from 1st January, 1957, to 30th August, 1959, when the accounts were so closed and not periodically with reference to any previous year. For the assessment year 1st January, 1957, to 30th August, 1959, the Income-tax Officer had adopted the previous year as the year ending with 30th September, because the assessee was maintaining accounts from October to September in respect of his other businesses, such as film exhibition business, medical stores, etc., and this was also the accounting period which he preferred for the earlier assessment year in respect of the contract business. But when it came to 1959-60, it was found by the next Income-tax Officer that the assessee could not so adopt and, therefore, he apportioned the entire profits as between the two assessment years 1958-59, and 1959-60 for which the previous years are 1957-58 and 1958-59 in the proportion of 3:1. The basis for doing so as appears from the Income-tax Officer's report is the receipts in each of the above assessment years, which according to him justify the fixing of that proportion.

Mr. Ramachandra Rao contends that once a year of assessment has been adopted by the Income-tax Officer, he cannot give a go-by to that period and adopt another. As a proposition of law it is unexceptionable. But in this case the adoption by the Income-tax Officer of the previous year, October to September, for the assessment year 1958-59, was wrongly adopted, because it does not satisfy the requirements of section 2(11)(i)( a) of the Income-tax Act. It is only in cases where the assessee could adopt a different period to the financial year, 1st April to 31st March, that any other period could be adopted, which would invariably mean a period of twelve months. This is also subject to the requirement of the section. Section 2(11)(i)(a ) is as follows :

"2. (11) 'previous year' means—

(i)in respect of any separate source of income, protits and gains—

(a)the twelve months ending on the 31st day of March next preceding the year for which the assessment is to be made, or, if the accounts of the assessee have been made up to a date within the said twelve months in respect of a year ending on any date other than the said 31st day of March, then, at the option of the assessee, the year ending on the date to which his accounts have been so made up."

1.5-2 In case of transport business - Computation provisions are discussed below :

1.5-2a Profit computation linked with ownership period during the year -Section 44AE(1) provides:

"... in the case of an assessee who owns... and is engaged in the business... the income of such business... shall be deemed to be the aggregate of the profits and gains from all the goods carriage owned by him in the previous year, computed in accordance with the provisions of sub-section (2)." [Emphasis supplied]

Sub-section (2) reads as follows:

"for the purpose of sub-section (1), the profits and gains from each goods carriage—

(i)

being a heavy goods vehicle, shall be... for every month or part of a month during which the heavy goods vehicle is owned by the assessee in the previous year....;

(ii)

other than a heavy goods vehicle, shall be... for every month or part of a month during which the goods carriage is owned by the assessee in the previous year...." [Emphasis supplied]

A reading of the above provisions show that the profits computation has to be made in accordance with the period for which the goods carriage is owned during the previous year irrespective of the actual employment thereof in the business during the previous year. The memorandum explaining the provisions of the Finance Bill gives two illustrations, which are reproduced hereinbelow, which supports the above view, as well as explains the computation of profits for a part of the month:

"Illustration (1): An assessee owns a light commercial vehicle for 9 months 15 days, a medium goods vehicle for 9 months and a medium goods vehicle for 12 months during the previous year. His profits and gains from the three trucks shall be deemed to be (Rs. 1,800 × 10) + (Rs. 1,800 × 9) + (Rs. 1,800 × 12), i.e., Rs. 55,800.

Illustration (2) : An assessee owns a heavy goods vehicle for 9 months 7 days, a medium goods vehicle for 9 months and a light commercial vehicle for 12 months during the previous year. His profits and gains from the three trucks shall be deemed to be (Rs. 2,000 × 10) + (Rs. 1,800 × 9) + (Rs. 1,800 × "12), i.e., Rs. 57,800."

As per the illustrations, if a vehicle is owned even for 7 days, profits computation should be considered for a month.

As per section 2(30)of the Motor Vehicle Act, 1988 'owner' is defined as follows:

' "Owner" means a person in whose name a motor vehicle stands registered, and where such person is a minor, the guardian of such minor, and in relation to a motor vehicle which is the subject of a hire-purchase, agreement, or an agreement of lease or an agreement of hypothecation, the person in possession of the vehicle under that agreement';

In the context of the New Provisions it is felt that ownership should be construed in the same manner as construed for the purposes of section 32 of the Act.

Accordingly, it is felt that the date on which the Motor Vehicle is registered or person obtains possession of the vehicle, whichever is earlier, would be considered as the date from which the assessee should be regarded as an owner.

In the instant case, the assessee-company had been consistently following a particular method of accounting. Its accounts were audited both under the Companies Act, 1956, as well as under section 44AB of the Income-tax Act. Such audited accounts were being filed with the Registrar of Companies as well as with the income-tax department for more than 7 years. The revenue had scrutinized the accounts and the method of accounting regularly employed and adopted by the assessee year after year had not been found fault with. The auditors of the company both under the Companies Act and the Income-tax Act had been consistently certifying that the assessee had been regularly following the method of accounting and that the annual profits could be properly deduced from such method of accounting employed by the assessee. The auditors over the years had also been certifying that the accounts were regularly maintained and were complete in the sense that there was no significant omission therein. This finding had been accepted by different Assessing Officers over a period of seven years. For rejecting the view taken for the earlier assessment years, there must be a material change in the fact situation. No doubt, the previous view will have no application even in cases where the law itself has undergone a change but before an earlier view can be upset or digressed from, one of the two must be demonstrated, namely, a change in the fact situation or a material change in law whether enacted or declared by the Supreme Court. [Para 5.7]

In the case of a civil contractor, who undertakes major works, a contract is spread over several years. The income arising from the same contract is spread over several assessment years and part of the profit of this contract is separately arrived at assessment year-wise and brought to tax. While so, for the same contract, the books of account are accepted for certain assessment years for the purpose of arriving at the profits, and for certain other assessment years the books of account are rejected in respect of the very same contract part of which is executed in the current year and the profit is estimated on a different basis. When this is done without cogent and sufficient reasons or change in facts or law, one has to necessarily apply the principles laid down by the Apex Court in the case of Radhasoami Satsang v. CIT [1992] 193 ITR 321/ 60 Taxman 248 and it is to be held that unless the fundamental aspects permeating through different assessment years are different, a different view possibly cannot be taken as it would result in anomalous results. [Para 5.8]

In the instant case, the Assessing Officer had accepted the factum of expenditure on account of sub-contractors and, thus, the non-availability of vouchers of expenditure incurred by sub-contractors with the assessee could not be a reason for rejection. Coming to the site-wise profit and loss account which were claimed to be MIS reports, each of these works was at different stages and phases of completion. The works were of different nature and a comparison of such different works for estimating profits of such works, based on the MIS reports which were not complete, in the sense that administrative expenses and other direct expenses incurred in respect of each work or as overhead find place in the books of account of the head office and were not apportioned to these particular works, would be a wrong comparison and opinion formed. To reject the books of account on the basis of such erroneous and fallacious workings and data could not be upheld. Cash flow statements maintained at each of the sites as found in the management information system, by no stretch of imagination, could be termed as complete profit and loss account which would enable the Assessing Officer to arrive at the profit in that work so as to enable him to compare the profits of different works. It is not correct to assume that two different contract works pertaining to two different projects, at two different project sites in different States and at different stages of execution, would derive identical profit. It was found that the site-wise MIS reports which were termed as profit and loss account were not part of the financial statements drawn up as per Schedule VI of the Companies Act nor were they prescribed books of account. When these statements were not books of account, and when they were not necessary documents or records for finalizing the books of account both under the Companies Act as well as under the Income-tax Act, infirmities, if any, in these statements could not be a reason to reject the books of account. There was no finding by the lower authorities that the books of account produced before them were incomplete. [Para 5.9]

CHAPTER ONE

SPECIAL PROVISIONS FOR COMPUTING PROFITS & GAINS OF BUSINESS OF CIVIL CONSTRUCTION AND TRANSPORT*

Introduction

1.1 The Finance Act, 1994 inserts two new sections - 44AD and 44AE - in the Income-tax Act, 1961 ('the Act") to extend the concept of 'estimated/deemed income', for determination of profits and gains of the business of Civil Construction or Transport.

The objectives of the New Provisions are:

■ simplification;

■ minimizing compliance cost; and

■ minimizing undue harassment to tax payers.

The new provisions have been justified on two grounds:

■ Such a method is prevalent in several countries; and

■ Tax Reforms Committee has recommended gradual introduction of the method.

The above provisions come into force from the assessment year 1994-95 and thus, have a retrospective effect for the previous year ended on 31-3-1994.

Provisions in brief

1.2 Following points need be noted:

■ Sections 44AD and 44AE ('the New Provisions') are applicable to all assessees engaged in the business of Civil Construction and/or Transport ('the specified business').

■ 'Civil Construction' business, as defined, will include the construction or repairs of buildings, dams, bridges, or other structures or roads or canals. It will also include the execution of any works contract.

■ ‘Transport Business' covers the business of plying, hiring or leasing of goods carriages owned by the assessee.

The assessee carried on contract business of construction of roads by obtaining contracts from the Government departments. For the assessment year 1992-93, the assessee filed the return of income along with the tax audit report under section 44AB. It was accepted that the books maintained by the assessee were not verifiable. During the course of the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer asked the assessee to furnish the names and addresses of the parties and sundry creditors from whom raw material for construction of the roads had been purchased. The assessee furnished the addresses and the Assessing Officer issued letters of enquiry under section 133(6). However, the letters sent to 17 parties returned unserved to the Assessing Officer. The assessee was directed to prove the genuineness of the transactions made with the parties. The assessee filed copies of the accounts and copies of the confirmation letters stated to have been obtained from the parties before the Assessing Officer. However, the Assessing Officer did not agree with the confirmation letters as the letters sent to the parties had returned unserved. The assessee was asked to prove the genuineness of those parties but could not prove except filing confirmation letters from those parties. The Assessing Officer further pointed out that there might be standard specification but it was difficult to arrive at a definite conclusion in the absence of specific formula for construction of roads of various thickness and it was further observed that in the absence of details, general statement would not support any measurement and it was not possible to arrive at the exact consumption of raw material. He therefore, made certain additions to income of the assessee on that account.

As regards the payments made to the labourers, the assessee had submitted samples and muster rolls before the Assessing Officer. They were examined by the handwriting expert, which indicated that the thumbs’ impressions were not of different parties and the Assessing Officer observed that it could be easily deduced that the labour payments were excessive and inflated and, accordingly, made certain disallowance. However, the Assessing Officer allowed depreciation to the assessee as per profit and loss account. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee had not maintained verifiable accounts and as such, net profit rate should be applied. The consumption of the raw material claimed was within the parameters laid down by the laboratories for particular type of road construction. He also held that the Assessing Officer had not made out a fool-proof case for addition on account of bogus purchases and the road constructed by the assessee during the year was found up to the specification by the principals while making payment to the contractor and it could not be held that the assessee had not utilized grit and had not paid the wages for construction of roads. Accordingly, the Commissioner (Appeals) applied net profit rate of 10 per cent on the receipts as against 8 per cent applied in the immediately preceding year, keeping in view the discrepancy pointed out in the maintenance of the books of account. However, the Commissioner (Appeals) granted the depreciation after applying net profit rate as allowed by the Assessing Officer also.
