The provision of section 145, read with the proviso, makes it clear that the choice of method in maintaining accounts for the purposes of assessment is left with the assessee and it is open to him to adopt any method of accounting that he likes. That, however, is subject to two minimum conditions—firstly, that the method of accounting should be one which has been regularly employed by him and, secondly, that the method should be such as in the opinion of the Assessing Officer should indicate properly the income, profits and gains of the assessee. As long as these two conditions are fulfilled by the account maintained by the assessee, that account, in law, has to be the basis of computation compulsorily and the Assessing Officer has no other option to follow any other method of accounting. [Para 13.2]

The assessee had argued that the only method by which the gains or profits could be determined was to wait until the whole of the expenditure to be incurred by the assessee over this contract business had been made good. This argument was based on the assumption that unless and until the entire amount of expenditure to be incurred over the contract is known, no profit or gain can be calculated, even if the contract moneys are received by an assessee in the course of the contract. No justification was found for this assumption. It is true that "profits and gains must be ascertained of ordinary principles of commercial trading" and the word 'profits' has to be understood, "in its natural and proper sense, in a sense which no commercial man would misunderstand". But that means only this much : "that no gain or profit could be said to arise unless and until a balance had been struck between the cost of construction and the proceeds of contract." It, however, cannot be disputed that as a rule the balance between the cost of construction and the proceeds of contract for the purpose of an assessment under the Act has to be struck at an interval of every accounting year, because that is the unit of time stipulated under the Act. The exception may arise when the balance cannot be struck between the cost of acquisition and the proceeds of sale on any method known in the field of commercial trading, for in that case no profit can be said to arise in that period as in the case of a solitary adventure in the nature of trade. [Para 13.5]

The primary issue in accounting for construction contracts is the allocation of construction revenue and contract cost to the accounting periods in which construction work is performed. In the case under consideration the assessee had followed percentage of completion method. Under this method contract revenue is matched with the contract cost incurred in reaching the stage of completion of contract, resulting in the reporting of revenue, i.e., expenses and profits which can be attributed to the proportion of work completed. This method of percentage of completion is a recognized method of accounting. [Para 13.6]

In percentage of completion method contract account is to be finalised in the year of completion of contract work, when the project is to be taken as complete. [Para 13.7]

In view of the above background of discussion, it was to be seen as to whether Jogeshwari and Nalasopara Projects of the assessee were completed in the assessment year 2002-03 or not. The Commissioner (Appeals) had given a categorical finding that originally the assessee had applied for construction of Jogeshwari Project only up to third floor by utilizing full FSI. The fourth floor was not proposed to be constructed originally. As regards Nalasopara Project, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that originally the assessee had applied for approval of construction of 40 flats in Wing-A up to second floor; Wing-B up to third floor and Wing-C up to third floor. The competent authority, CIDCO had approved the project. The construction as approved was completed and, therefore, CIDCO issued occupancy certificate on 4-5-2001. The possession of all the flats were handed over to the respective buyers before 31-3-2002. Subsequently, the assessee applied for construction of third and fourth floors of Wing-A(Flats). CIDCO issued commencement certificate for construction on 14-5-2003, almost three years after the first phase of the project was fully constructed. [Para 13.9]

From the accounting standard AS-7 issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, it is found that in case where separate proposals have been submitted, such contracts should be taken as separate contract works. Even additional contract works are also to be taken separately. [Para 13.11]

3.10

Percentage of Completion Method (POCM)

ICDS-III (Revised) requires a contractor to offer incomes from construction contracts to tax in accordance with the "percentage of completion method"(POCM). The recognition of contract revenue and contract costs by reference to the stage of completion of a contract is referred to as the percentage of completion method. Under this method, contract revenue is matched with the contract costs incurred in reaching the stage of completion, resulting in the reporting of revenue, expenses and profit which can be attributed to the proportion of work completed. Paras 18 and 19 of ICDS-III(Revised) explain how% of stage of completion of a contract as at reporting date is to be determined. Para 20 provides that percentage of completion method is not required to be followed during the early stages of a contract i.e. in case of a contract which has reached 25% or less stage of completion. In cases of contracts in early stage, where the outcome of the contract cannot be estimated reliably contract revenue is recognised only to the extent of costs incurred. In other words, neither profit nor loss on contracts in early stages shall be recognised.

In Dy. CIT v. Sri Jagannath Properties & Developers decided by ITAT-Cuttack on 31.08.2018 in [ITA No. 283/CTK/2017] it was held that while applying POCM as per ICDS-III, the question whether stage of completion of 25% has been reached or not is to be reckoned project-wise(contract-wise) and not by taking all projects (contracts) together on overall basis and revenue can be recognised in only those projects(contracts) where stage of completion has reached 25%.

Thus, POCM is to be applied contract-wise. There is a concept in accounts called the concept of Contract Accounts. To know the results of his operations, the contractor prepares what is called as Contract Account which is debited with various costs and which is credited with the revenue associated with a particular contract. Under the POCM, reasonable profit is calculated on the basis of the value of the work certified and the profit attributable to the work certified. For example, if the value of the work certified is one-fourth or more but less than half of the contract price, then a certain percentage of the profit accruing to the certified work is taken to the profit and loss account [CIT, Meerut v. Hyundai Heavy Industries Co. Ltd. [2007] 161 Taxman 191 (SC)]. Thus, for each construction contract, a separate contract account is to be opened and the contract costs and contract revenues related to it have to be debited and credited to it with reference to% of stage of completion reached in all individual contracts which have progressed to more than 25%. Where progress is 25% or less, contract account will be debited only with contract costs incurred and credited with contract revenue equal to contract costs incurred and contract account will neither reflect a profit nor a loss.

HEADNOTE: Section 145(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Assessment year 1989-90 - Assessee was in business of construction of ownership flats - He got part of work done through sub-contractors and claimed deduction of payment made to them but failed to produce them for examination - Details of payment of salary, etc., to staff were also not furnished - Basis of valuing work-in-progress was also not given -Whether on facts ITO was justified in invoking provisions of section 145(1) and making an estimated addition of Rs. 30,000 to be returned net profit - Held, yes.

FACT: The assessee commenced business of construction of ownership flat on 1-9-1987 and filed income-tax returns for the transitional previous year for 19 months up to 31-3-1989. He had taken up two projects and handed over the civil works to two sub-contractors by agreements dated 29-4-1988 and 7-10-1988. In the profit and loss account, a sum of Rs. 13,70,740 was debited and was shown as having been paid to these two sub-contractors. Before the ITO the assessee filed details of sub- contract payments but was unable to produce the two sub-contractors. The ITO observed that the assessee was unable to derive his correct profit in respect of the period taking Into account the progress of the work till 31-3-1989 and payments actually to be made and payments made, and that there was no basis for work in progress estimated by the assessee at Rs. 14,116, He also noted that the profit and loss account included items like development charges, registration charges, etc., that details for salaries and staff welfare debited at Rs. 18,747 were not available on record. Considering all these defects and the ad hoc nature of payments made to sub-contractors. the Assessing Officer made a round sum addition of Rs. 30,000 to the income returned, making the assessment order under section 143(3).

On appeal, the Dy. Commissioner (Appeals) held that the Assessing Officer had not noticed any specific defect which would have amounted to a wrong statement of income and, deleted the addition of Rs. 30,000 made by the ITO.

On appeal by the revenue:

HELD: Payment in excess of the amount which an assessee is liable to pay under the terms of an agreement is not an allowable deduction under section 37(1). The accounts of the assessee had not disclosed the correct profit derived by him in respect of the accounting period in question, taking into consideration the works so far done till 31-3-1989 and the payments to be made and actually made by the assessee. The burden to prove the sub- contracts, to bring the sub-contractors and examine them with reference to the sub-contracts entered into by them with the assessee, as also to satisfied the Assessing Officer with regard to the various payments received by them under the sub-contracts, lay squarely upon the assessee and not the department. Despite several opportunities granted to the assessee, he had failed to produce them, and, therefore, the Assessing Officer had reason to doubt the payments said to have been made under the sub-contracts. Further, the details for salaries and staff welfare expenses debited at Rs. 18,747 were not available on record and they were also not produced before the ITO. For these reasons, it was a case of estimate of profit under the proviso to section 145(1).

The order of Deputy Commissioner (Appeals) was, therefore, reversed and that of the ITO was restored.

Judicial decisions and decisions of Appellate Tribunal

6. The question of exigibility to tax of income from long-term contracts has been considered by the juridiciary as well as the Tribunal in a number of cases. To highlight their views on the issue, the gist of some of the decisions is set out below:

(i)( a)Sukhdeodas Jalan v. CIT [1954] 26 ITR 617 (Pat.)

(b) Tirath Ram Ahuja (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1976] 103 ITR 15 (Delhi)

A military contract entered into by the assessee Sukhdeodas Jalan extended beyond the accounting period and the accounts were closed only after the completion of the contract. The question arose for determination whether the profits should be assessed only after the completion of the contract or whether the profits accruing during the accounting period could be assessed. A Division Bench of the Patna High Court held that it was fallacious to argue that merely because the contract was completed after the accounting period, no profits arose or accrued to the assessee in the accounting year and that in the case of an incomplete contract there was a well established method of calculating profits accruing in the accounting year (vide page 971 of Batliboi's Advanced Accounting) . To quote from the High Court's decision:

"In the case of contracts, if accounts are maintained and completed on contract basis the profits or gains of the previous year cannot properly be extracted from the accounts, for a contract may take several years for being completed and payments in regard to it may also be received by the assessee in several years. It may be convenient from the point of view of the assessee that profit should be ascertained on the completion of the contract and assessment of the profit should take place after the completion of the contract. But section 3 imposes a charge of income-tax upon the profits and gains of the assessee for the accounting year and it is the duty of the income-tax authorities to ascertain the profits and gains accruing to the assessee in respect of the payment received during the accounting year.

It cannot be said that merely because a contract was completed after the accounting year, no profits arose or accrued to the assessee in the accounting year...." (p. 618)

The ratio of the decision supra was followed by the Delhi High Court in the case of Tirath Ram Ahuja (P.) Ltd. ( supra). It was held that in the case of contracts, one need not wait till the contract was completed in order to ascertain the income, and that it was open to the revenue to estimate the profit on the basis of the receipts in each year of construction, although the contract was not complete.

The ITO, however, determined the escaped income at Rs. 1,26,500 as under:— Conceding but not granting that the transaction was an adventure in the nature of trade, the assessee, observing that the profits had not been properly computed in view of the fact that the adventure would terminate after the portion retained by him was also sold, contended that the profits in the adventure could be determined only at the time of the completion of the sale of the entire estate.

Rejecting the assessee's contention, the Supreme Court observed that the ITO had correctly estimated the profit by treating the land retained as stock-in-trade and valuing it according to the normal accountancy practice. According to the Supreme Court, the view that the profits of the adventure could be determined only at the time of the completion of the sale of the entire estate was not correct. Each year is a self-contained unit and in the case of a trading adventure, for computing the true profits of the year, the value of the stock-in-trade at the beginning and at the end of the accounting year has to be taken into account. To quote the Supreme Court:

". . . It is not a correct proposition to say that the profits of the assessee cannot be ascertained even on the assumption that the transaction of the adventure of trade was not completed. Under the Income-tax Act for the purpose of assessment each year is a self-contained unit and in the case of a trading adventure the profits have to be computed in the manner provided by the statute. It is true that the Income-tax Act makes no express provision with regard to the value of stock. It charges for payment of tax the income, profits and gains which have to be computed in the manner provided by the Income-tax Act. In the case of a trading adventure the profits have to be calculated and adjusted in the light of the provisions of the Income-tax Act permitting allowances prescribed thereby. For that purpose it was the duty of the Income-tax Officer to find out what profit the business has made according to the true accountancy practice. As a normal rule, the profit should be ascertained by valuing the stock-in-trade at the beginning and at the end of the accounting year. . . ." (p. 743)

The question arose whether any income arose for taxation for the assessment years 1977-78 and 1978-79 from a project undertaken during the previous year relevant to the assessment year 1976-77. ". . . it is not a correct proposition to say that profits of the assessee -from a single venture/project in the nature of trade cannot be ascertained until the venture/project has come to an end. Under the Act each year is a self-contained unit and unless it is impossible to compute the profits or losses of each year reasonably if necessary by estimating the value of the liabilities to be incurred, valuing the work-in-progress, stock- in-trade, etc., the profits should be computed year-wise and taxed...." On the assessee's contention that exigibility to tax would arise only on the completion of project is accepted, the Tribunal observed—

"The acceptance of the proposition would amount to giving the assessee a licence to put off his tax liabilities for an unlimited period by seeing to it that the venture/project never comes to an end in the sense something or the other always remains to be done. That will be a very unsatisfactory state of affairs. Moreover, when the entire cost/ expenditure to the assessee is recouped and/or major portion of the venture/project is complete, there is really no justification in not taxing the income from project which quite often may represent excess of receipts over expenditure unless there is a risk/chances of the assessee's suffering heavy liabilities, subsequently, for some reasons or the other."

HEADNOTE: Section 147 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income escaping assessment - In formation - Position prior to 1-4-1989 - Assessment year 1970-71 - Whether an audit note can be a source of information - Held, yes - ITO having noted that assessee had not maintained quantity stock register and other relevant registers, estimated income by considering profits made in earlier assessment years - subsequently, ITO received an audit note which pointed out that account books of assessee disclosed more profit than estimated by ITO - On basis of said information ITO reopened assessment and estimated gross profit at higher rate - Whether on facts, reopening of assessment on basis of audit note was valid - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a building contractor. It had entered into certain contracts in 1966 and also in 1970 respectively. The 1966 contracts were described as old contracts and the 1970 contracts as new contracts. It had filed a consolidated trading account and profit and loss account disclosing gross profit at 10.2 per cent. The ITO noticed that the assessee had not maintained quantity stock register and other relevant registers and a work-in-progress account which would have enabled him to verify the correctness of the book result and, therefore, decided to estimate the income by considering the profits made in earlier assessment years. He noticed that the assessee itself in the previous year had disclosed gross profits at the rate of 15.4 per cent. The ITO, therefore, after considering the explanation of the assessee that the old contracts were in the last stages of completion, assessed the gross profit in respect of the old contracts at 12 per cent, and at the rate of 15 per cent in respect of the new contracts. The assessee did not prefer any appeal. Thereafter, the ITO received an audit note wherein it was pointed out that in respect of the one of the old contract, the account books of the assessee disclosed a profit of 14.5 per cent. On the basis of the said information, the ITO reopened the assessment under section 147(b) and computed the gross profit in respect of that contract at 15 per cent. The AAC allowed the assessee’s appeal and annulled the order of assessment. But the Tribunal held that the reopening of the assessment was valid.

On reference :

HELD: It was no doubt true that the account books of the assessee were before the ITO when he made the original assessment. But, the ITO doubted the correctness of the accounts maintained by the assessee and, therefore, without adopting the account books as the basis, he estimated the profit on the basis of the margin of profits normally earned by persons in such types of business and the rate of profit earned by the assessee in the previous year. Thus, the ITO had not considered this material while estimating the profit of the old contracts at 12 per cent. Since the ITO had not considered the said material, it had not come to his notice that the account books of the assessee showed that in respect of the one of the old contract, the assessee had earned profit at the rate of 14.5 per cent. That an audit note can be a source of information is no longer in dispute now.

The relevant material in the shape of book result was not considered by the ITO on the ground that the books of account were not properly maintained by the assessee. Thus, this was not a case where it could be said that the ITO had considered the material while making the original assessment. This was a case where the ITO had not considered the said material and only subsequently he came to know about that material when his attention in that behalf was drawn by the audit note. Thus, this case would squarely fall within the scope of section 147(b).

The reopening of the assessment under section 147(b ) was thus valid.

The new provisions incorporate a provision permitting a rebuttal of the presumption. Accordingly, it is felt that the new provisions may stand the test, in case of a challenge of its vires.

Applicability of the new provisions

1.4 The new provisions are applicable to all assessees, irrespective of the residential status or the status as a person or whether old or new assessee.

Thus, the new provisions would apply to:

■ resident as well as non-resident assessees;

■ all categories of persons, corporate or non-corporate (including a firm or a trust or an AOP or a BOI); and

■ whether new or old assessees, (that is, an assessee already engaged in the specified business or proposing to engage in the specified business as also a person who is presently liable to tax or not).

1.4-1 Applicability of New Provisions in case of Civil Construction business - Explanation to section 44AD, for the purpose of the New Provisions, explains 'Civil Construction' inclusively as:

■ Construction or repair of any building, bridge, dam or other structure or of any canal or road ('specified structure'); and

The expression 'civil construction', as such, is not defined or explained but, apparently, has been used as nomenclature for grouping certain activities as part of the Civil Construction business.

The expression 'civil construction', as such, does not have any technical meaning. This case raises a very short point. Messrs. K.S. Rashid & Sons were military contractors, who used to supply to the military messes various commodities of various kinds. The assessee was one of the favourite contractors and had a very large number of contracts. For the assessment year 1941-42 and the previous year 1940-41 the assessee produced his books. As regards four of the contracts, the assessee claimed that he had given sub-contracts to others and had, therefore, to pay the sub-contractors some rebate. The Income-tax department had been accepting in previous years the claim of the assessee that he had been privately sub-letting some of the contracts as it was not possible for him to look after all the contracts and this had continued ever since 1921-22 to the assessment year 1940-41 and even subsequent to the assessment year in question 1941-42. In the years previous to the assessment year 1941-42 and in the years subsequent to the year 1941-42, the Income-tax department had always accepted the assessee's claim that some of the contracts had been sub-let.

In the assessment year in question 1941-42 the Income-tax Officer required the assessee to disclose the names of the sub-contractors to enable the Income-tax Officer to verify the claim of the assessee that some of the contracts had been sub-let. The assessee refused to disclose the names of the sub-contractors on the ground that under the rules of the military department it was not permissible to sub-let military contracts, and the sub-contractors, if their names were disclosed, might find themselves in trouble. The assessee relied on an order of the then Commissioner of Income-tax, dated the 28th of November, 1934, in a previous assessment where a similar question had been asked and the assessee had refused to answer the question. The Commissioner had observed as follows:—"The Income-tax Officer must seek other avenues for the discovery of the names of subcontractors than the assistance of the assessee".

The Income-tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was bound to disclose the names of the subcontractors, and inasmuch as he had refused to disclose the names of the sub-contractors, they had no means .of verifying the claim of the assessee that he had sub-let some of the contracts. The Income-tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissiner rejected the claim of the assessee that he had sub-let any of the four contracts and decided to assess him on all the contracts at the same flat rate.

When the matter came up before the Tribunal, the Tribunal was of the opinion that the assessee's claim, that he had sub-let some of the contracts to others, must be accepted. The Tribunal was also of the opinion that the assessee was a very respectable person and in regard to other entries, which were perhaps bigger entries, no mistake was found by the Income-tax authorities. The Tribunal was of the opinion, however, that the assessee was bound to disclose the names of the sub-contractors, and as he had not disclosed their names, the Income-tax Officer was not able to verify the correctness of the return as regards the contracts, which were said to have been sub-let.

After having come to this conclusion, the Tribunal adopted a very curious attitude. They held that the Income-tax Officer had, on the footing that the assessee had done all the business himself, estimated his profits at Rs. 52,000. On the basis of the finding of the Tribunal that some of the contracts had been sub-let this estimate should be reduced. The assessee had made a return of Rs. 38,118, and the Tribunal said that they would add a token figure of Rs. 1,882 to make the estimated income into a round figure of Rs. 40,000. The Tribunal could not add a token figure to round up the figure of Rs. 38,118. On what principle this amount of Rs. 1,882 was estimated it is difficult to find. The assessment was under Section 23(3) of the Income-tax Act, and if there were no materials on which the Tribunal could come to a definite finding as regards those four contracts which were said to have been sub-let, the Tribunal could not just add a sum of Rs. 1,882 to have a nice round figure of Rs. 40,000 instead of Rs. 38,118.

The questions referred to us under Section 66 (1) are as follows:— (1) Whether on the findings arrived at by the Tribunal, there was any justification for making a token addition of Rs. 1,882 to the accounted version? In view of what we have already said, the answer to this question must be in the negative.

. In addition to the billed amount the closing work-in-progress representing the value of goods and service transferred during the financial year but not billed, is added. For the same reason, the opening work-in-progress representing the value of goods and services transferred during the previous financial year and billed during the current financial year is reduced. Thus, the cost of goods and services transferred during the current financial year is arrived at for the computation of taxable turnover.

Thus, income to be recognized in a works contract is: For example, in the case of a works contract continuing over a period of 3 years, the income for the 1st year is to be recognized as the aggregate amount billed during this year and the value of closing work-in-progress. In the 2nd year, the aggregate of the amount billed during the year and the value of closing work-in-progress as reduced by the value of opening work-in-progress is the income to be recognized. In the 3rd year, the amount billed during that year as reduced by the opening work-in-progress is the income to be recognized. Any subsequent escalation or reduction in the bill subsequent to the financial year shall be adjusted in the returns by filing revised return for the period for which the change has occurred. The concept of percentage of completion of the work by recognizing the volume of work completed at any stage as asset of the contractor in AS-7 needs a reconsideration.

Profit or Loss

7. The profit or loss on works contract is derived by taking the income recognized as detailed above on the income side of the profit and loss account and the cost of goods and service is taken on the expenditure side of the profit and loss account. The cost of consumables, cost of design, consultation and technology, cost of hire charges, cost of finance, establishment charges and depreciation are taken on the expenditure side. The net result is the profit/loss of the contract work.

In case of bulk purchase during the first year, such part of goods not transferred while executing the work will be in the closing stock and that part of goods used in the work but not billed is in the work-in-progress. Whatever is transfer value of goods by involving in the execution of the works contract is recognized as income. Hence, bulk purchase of goods will not create an artificial loss in the profit and loss account.

Any amount received less than the measured and billed amount is to be treated as receivables and any amount received more than the measured and bill amount is to be treated as advance. Both amounts received and receivable are taken as the contract amount. Taxable turnover is determined by deducting the value of labour components and consumables from the contract amount as per the rules. The mobilization advance is to be treated as loan repayable as deduction from every subsequent bills. Hence, such mobilization advance is not part of the contract amount.

The above method remains unchanged in the fixed price contract and cost plus contract; since the measurement and billing on fixed price contract is based on the scheduled in the agreement and the cost plus contract adopts the measurement and billing on the basis of the cost of the contractor. Therefore, the AS-7 needs amendment accordingly.

As income taxable under the Income-tax Act, 1961 from manufacturing or trading is the income generated from such activities, the income from contract is the income generated from executing the contract work. Hence, estimation of income at the rate of proportionate work completed as per technical evaluation is a notional way, unwarranted in the presence of proper records. Taxable income is a truth and not to be estimated, unless the records are insufficient or incomplete and rejected by the Assessing Officer.

Conclusion

8. Therefore, the concepts in the Accounting standard AS-7 for recognition of income and expenditure are to be modified, as being mere estimation, discarding the facts in the records and contrary to the dictum of the Supreme Court of India that the transfer of property in goods in a works contract is not as a conglomerate.

Tribunal in Shapoorji Pallonji & Co. (Rajkot) (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [1994] 49 ITD 479 . Recently, this method was upheld in the case of CIT v. V.S. Dempo (Income-tax Review July, 1995, page 15) by the Bombay High Court as mentioned in the summary of a Study Circle Meeting of Bombay Chartered Accountant Journal (Nov. 95-585). In the following cases, it was held that profit from construction contracts should be ascertained each year, when the contract is beyond the preliminary stage and a reasonable stage of execution has been achieved – CIT v. Nanduri Suryanaryana [1962] 46 ITR 894 (AP), if profits can be arrived, i.e., a case were profits were realised in the first year itself; P.M. Mohammed Meerakhan v. CIT [1969] 73 ITR 735 (SC) it was held that the unsold land forms part of stock-in-trade which should be valued for ascertaining profit for each year, as it was not correct to say that profits should be determined only on completion of the sale of the entire estate; Tirath Ram Ahuja (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1976] 103 ITR 15 (Delhi) [affirmed by the Supreme Court as in Tirath Ram Ahuja (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1990] 186 ITR 428 on a different issue], Sri Sukhdeodas Man v. CIT [1954] 26 ITR 617 (Pat.); Champion Construction Co. v. First ITO [1983] 5 ITD 495 (Bom.); Bhagyanagar Construction (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [1993] 46 ITD 236 (Hyd.) in all these cases it was held that in the case of a building contractor, revenue need not wait till the completion of contract and that reasonable profit can be estimated from year to year.

Much can be said for and against the completed contract method but the chances of its acceptance by the assessing authorities are bleak in view of several judicial pronouncements against it. It is important to note that in most of the above-mentioned cases, profit has been estimated due to difficulty in estimation of work-in-progress. The other significant feature in building contracts is the point of time of revenue recognition, i.e., whether it is to be considered at the time of registration or handing over of physical possession or on payment of installments pursuant to agreement on estimated completion of construction. The answer to this question again depends on the method of accounting adopted and recognition of revenue on handing over of units of construction combined with a reasonable estimate of work-in-progress may be acceptable in income-tax assessments. The advantage of this procedure is that it combines both the methods in determining the income.

As per AS 7, provision has to be made for contingent loss in the incomplete portion of contract and for future foreseeable costs. However, such provisions would not be deductible under the Act. Those entities engaged in the business of construction should be careful to adjust accounts prepared in accordance with AS 7 suitably, disallowing such provisions for tax purposes and considering the acceptability of the method of accounting. Such contingent losses can, however, be indirectly covered by adopting the method of valuing work-in-progress at cost or realisable value, whichever is lower.

7. With regard to changes in foreign currency liabilities relating to fixed assets on account of difference in exchange rates, there is not much variance between the standard (AS 11) and the provisions of the Act. However, in the case of assets acquired in India utilized borrowings made in foreign currency, provisions of section 43 A of the Act do not provide for adjustment, as in the case of liabilities incurred for acquiring assets abroad, while under AS 11, such difference has to be adjusted even in case of money borrowed directly or indirectly in foreign currency specifically for the purpose of acquiring such assets. This distinction between the standard and provisions of the Act on the one hand and between the liability incurred in foreign currency for acquisition of assets abroad and the borrowings made in foreign currency utilized for acquiring assets in India on the other, is not warranted and there is a need for amending the provisions of section 43A for bringing about uniformity. The omission might have been unintended, as when the provisions of section 43A were introduced way back in 1967 primarily to compensate for devaluation of the Indian rupee on June 6, 1966, it might not have been estimated that there would be occasion for Indian business community to borrow in foreign currency for acquisition of fixed assets within India, as is presently being resorted to in the liberalised economy. In relation to liabilities on account of revenue expenditure, there is a distinction. As per AS 11, increase in such liability on the balance sheet date has to be accounted for, ignoring the decrease, if any, while under the Act such increase in liability is not considered ascertained and is, therefore, allowable as a deduction only in the year of actual settlement.

1.3 Section 44AC (as existed prior to assessment year 1993-94), which deemed a certain amount of profits related to purchase price, as assessable profits from the business of trading in certain goods, was challenged, inter alia, on a ground that the provisions raised a conclusive presumption of law that the assessee will make a net taxable income of the specified amount and this presumption was not allowed to be rebutted. The Kerala High Court upheld the vires of the provisions in T.K Aboobacker v. Union of India [1989] 177 ITR 358. The Andhra Pradesh High Court in A. Sanyasi Rao v. Government of Andhra Pradesh [1989] 178 ITR 31 held the provisions to be constitutional by reading it down and observing that it would be upon assessee to prove in the assessment proceedings his real assessable income.

The new provisions incorporate a provision permitting a rebuttal of the presumption. Accordingly, it is felt that the new provisions may stand the test, in case of a challenge of its vires.

whether new or old assessees, (that is, an assessee already engaged in the specified business or proposing to engage in the specified business as also a person who is presently liable to tax or not).

ACIT [1990] 45 ITD 628 wherein a return, in case of a trader in tendu leaves, income as per the accounts was shown without complying with section 44AC. The Assessing Officer determined the sum payable under section 143(1)(a) by applying section 44AC. The Tribunal held that this was not permissible because the proviso does not permit adoption of a basis other than the return of income.

Once a return is filed under section 44AD(5) or section 44AE(6), the AO is bound to determine the income/loss and the tax payable only by an order in writing under section 143(3) as:

-

the language of the provisions reflect a mandate:'... and there upon the Assessing Officer shall proceed to make an assessment of the total income ...' [Emphasis supplied],

-

the provisions require an 'assessment' and determination of sum payable based on such assessment in contrast to provisions of section 143(1)(a), which require determination of sum payable after making prima facie adjustments.

In other words, only an intimation would not be sufficient.

Assessment at a higher amount exceeding the specified amount - The next issue is that in the computation made under sections 28 to 43C of the Act, on account of specific disallowance as well as on account of adjustment in gross profit, if an addition is required to be made, can AO make an assessment in excess of the specific profits, pursuant to the provisions of sections 143(3), 145 and other applicable provisions? For the purpose, one may consider the language of the provisions as well as certain illustrations and determine the effects of section 44AD(5), which reads as follow:

"Nothing contained in the foregoing provisions of this section shall apply where the assessee claims and produces evidence to prove ... and thereupon the Assessing Officer shall proceed to make an assessment... under sub-section (3) of section 143."

The New Provisions relating to assessment at specified amount or a higher amount would not apply, ... where the assessee claims and produces evidence to prove that the profits from the specified business are lower.

Thus, when a claim is made and evidence is produced, the provisions of normal assessment become applicable and thereafter whether the Assessing Officer accepts the same or not, as such, is of no consequence. In other words, once the claim for assessment at the lower profit is made, the New Provisions would not apply and the assessee would be governed by normal provisions and assessment at an amount higher than the specified amount is possible.

ILLUSTRATIONS

1. An assessee, while claiming the assessment at lower profit, omits to make certain disallowances under section 40A(2) or 40A(3) and in the course of assessment, an addition is required to be made under the aforesaid provisions. As a result, the profits ultimately required to be assessed exceed the amount of specified profits. Can the Assessing Officer make an assessment in excess of the specified profits ?

2. A truck operator carries out some work on a truck, to convert the same into a container carrier. He claims the expenditure as revenue expenditure and on that basis lower profits are returned.

3. A person is engaged in the business of civil construction, where the person had valued the work in progress at cost. The Assessing Officer considers that the correct method of valuation should be net realizable value and not cost and on account of the valuation difference the profits could exceed the specified profits.

4. In case of a person engaged in the business of civil construction, it is noticed that certain expenses claimed are inflated and as a result addition should be made which may exceed the specified profits.

In the situation considered in illustration (1) above, the additions are arising because of non-application of the provisions of the Act. The return as filed by the assessee is accepted. Thus, section 44AD(5)/44AE(6) apply and the profits have to be computed in accordance with sections 28 to 43C of the Act. Accordingly, AO can assess the profits at an amount higher than the specified amount.

Notification of Accounting Standards by the Central Government 4. The Bill proposes to amend the Income-tax Act to empower the Central Government to prescribe by a Notification in the Official Gazette the accounting standard which an assessee will have to follow in computing the income under the head 'Profits and gains of business or profession' or 'Income from other sources'. The new section 145(2) provides for notification of accounting standards from time to time. Section 145(3) as brought in by the Finance Act, 1995 lays down that if the Assessing Officer is not satisfied about the correctness or completeness of the accounts of the assessee or where the method of accounting provided or the accounting standards notified have not been regularly followed by the assessee, the Assessing Officer may make an assessment in the manner provided in section 144 of the Act. This is the law applicable to the current assessment year 1997-98 and subsequent years. The amendment re moved the proviso to section 145 which enabled the Assessing Officer to compute the income on such basis and in such manner as he may determine wherever the method of accounting is such that income cannot be properly deduced therefrom. The removal of the proviso is no doubt a handicap to the Assessing Officers. As long as the accounting standards are followed, the Assessing Officer is bound to accept the results shown in the books of account.

Accounting Standards notified by the CBDT

5. The CBDT followed up the amendment in the law and notified certain accounting standards under section 145(2) to be followed by all assessees following the mercantile system of accounting - [1996] 218 ITR (St.) 1. These standards related to disclosure of accounting policies, prudential norms, presentation of accounts showing how substance prevailed over form, the materiality of the financial statement, etc. Expressions like 'Accounting Policies', 'accrual', 'consistency', etc., were all defined. Standard-II related to the disclosure of prior period and external items and changes in accounting policies. The notification came into effect from April 1, 1996 and applied to the assessment year 1997-98 and subsequent years.

Schedule IV to the Companies Act, 1956 also refers to disclosure practices. The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India issued accounting standards making them mandatory. In its notification issued in July 1990, the ICAI required that wherever the disclosure norms set by the accounting standards were not followed, the Chartered Accountants should qualify such audited reports with regard to non-disclosure. Fifteen Standards running from AS-1 to AS-15 were issued by the ICAI.

Old law proposed to be revived

6. Now comes the rub. With such great fanfare, section 145 was amended and the new law is in place in the current assessment year. At this stage of the development of the law, the Working Draft proposes a complete somersault. Section 106 of the Draft Bill brings back the legal position as it was before the amendment of the present section 145 by the Finance Act of 1995 and even the proviso is back in the Bill. This reversion to the old law is explained by the Expert Group in the following words : "Section 145 of the Act is sought to be brought under the head 'Profits and gains of business or profession'. Apart from this change, an important departure from the present law is to allow assessees to compute the profits in accordance with the method of accounting regularly employed. Even if an assessee is employing the hybrid method of accounting in respect of business or profession, he would be permitted to employ such method and the requirement that only mercantile or cash system should be followed is proposed to be done away with".

Section 106(4) of the Bill proposes that the Central Government may, in consultation with the ICAI, prescribe the basis of accounting to be followed by any class of assessees or in respect of any class of income or any category of transactions.

1.11-4 At what stage evidence should be produced? - Section 44AD(5)/44AE(6) reads:

"Nothing contained in... this section shall apply, where the assessee claims and proves that the profits ... are lower... and thereupon..." [Emphasis supplied]

Considering the language of the provisions, it is felt that evidence should be produced or filed along with the return/claim.

In practical life this may be difficult inasmuch as the degree of proof and satisfaction required are difficult to determine. Accordingly, an assessee will have to take an utmost care while making such claim.

If an assessee does not substantiate his claim and/or does not file evidence to prove the claim, it could be contended by the tax department that requirement of the above provisions are not complied with and, accordingly, it may apply the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 44AD and/or sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 44AE, as the case may be.

However, considering the practical difficulties, it is felt that the CBDT may lay down instructions in this behalf and may direct at least that an opportunity may be provided to an assessee to lead the evidence.

If no evidence is produced by the assessee, it is evident that the requirements cannot be considered to have been met and accordingly, AO may then be free to make an assessment based on prescribed amount(s) as per the New Provisions.

l.11-5 Effects of 'Claim for a lower amount' - Following effects of a 'claim for the lower amount' will ensue:

The profits computation will have to be made in accordance with the provisions of sections 28 to 43C.

Exemption from maintenance of books of account or audit would not be available. Accordingly, the provisions of section 44AA and/or section 44AB will have to be complied with.

Consideration of all evidences and material.

(d)

This is the view taken by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal in U. Shahul Hamid & Bros. v. ACIT [1990] 45 ITD 628 wherein a return, in case of a trader in tendu leaves, income as per the accounts was shown without complying with section 44AC. The Assessing Officer determined the sum payable under section 143(1)(a) by applying section 44AC. The Tribunal held that this was not permissible because the proviso does not permit adoption of a basis other than the return of income.

■ Once a return is filed under section 44AD(5) or section 44AE(6), the AO is bound to determine the income/loss and the tax payable only by an order in writing under section 143(3) as:

- the language of the provisions reflect a mandate:'... and there upon the Assessing Officer shall proceed to make an assessment of the total income ...' [Emphasis supplied],

- the provisions require an 'assessment' and determination of sum payable based on such assessment in contrast to provisions of section 143(1)(a), which require determination of sum payable after making prima facie adjustments.

In other words, only an intimation would not be sufficient.

■ Assessment at a higher amount exceeding the specified amount - The next issue is that in the computation made under sections 28 to 43C of the Act, on account of specific disallowance as well as on account of adjustment in gross profit, if an addition is required to be made, can AO make an assessment in excess of the specific profits, pursuant to the provisions of sections 143(3), 145 and other applicable provisions? For the purpose, one may consider the language of the provisions as well as certain illustrations and determine the effects of section 44AD(5), which reads as follow:

"Nothing contained in the foregoing provisions of this section shall apply where the assessee claims and produces evidence to prove ... and thereupon the Assessing Officer shall proceed to make an assessment... under sub-section (3) of section 143."

The New Provisions relating to assessment at specified amount or a higher amount would not apply, ... where the assessee claims and produces evidence to prove that the profits from the specified business are lower.

Thus, when a claim is made and evidence is produced, the provisions of normal assessment become applicable and thereafter whether the Assessing Officer accepts the same or not, as such, is of no consequence. In other words, once the claim for assessment at the lower profit is made, the New Provisions would not apply and the assessee would be governed by normal provisions and assessment at an amount higher than the specified amount is possible.

3. A person is engaged in the business of civil construction, where the person had valued the work in progress at cost. Thus, section 44AD(5)/44AE(6) apply and the profits have to be computed in accordance with sections 28 to 43C of the Act. Accordingly, AO can assess the profits at an amount higher than the specified amount.

Finance Act, 2003

Presumptive taxation in case of non-residents [Sections 44BB and 44BBB]

2.3 Under sections 44BB and 44BBB ('the said sections'), business income of non-residents engaged in the business of :

providing services or facilities in connection with, or supplying plant and machinery on hire used, or to be used, in the prospecting for, or extraction or production of, mineral oils (section 44BB);

civil construction or erection or testing or commissioning of plant or machinery in connection with a turnkey power project approved by the Government and financed under any international aid programme (section 44BBB),

is deemed to be 10% of the aggregate amounts paid or payable to the non-resident (hereinafter referred to as 'presumptive basis' or 'presumptive basis of taxation').

The above sections have now been amended with effect from assessment year 2004-05 to provide that the assessees covered by these sections will have an option to compute their income on a net income basis [, i.e., income shall be computed according to the provisions of the Act] (hereinafter referred to as 'net income basis' or 'net income basis of taxation'), provided the assessee:

maintains prescribed books of account;

gets the books of account audited; and

furnishes a tax audit report under section 44AB.

It is further provided that once a claim is made by the assessee for being governed by the net income basis of taxation, the Assessing Officer shall proceed to make an assessment of the total income under section 143(3) of the Act and determine the sum payable by, or refundable to, the assessee.

Further the presumptive tax rate of 10 per cent under section 44BBB will be applicable in those turnkey power projects also which are not financed under any international aid programme.

Consequential changes have been made in sections 44AA and 44AB of the Act relating to maintenance of accounts and audit of accounts, respectively.

2.3-1 Option - The alternative to follow the net income basis as business income is optional and hence, an assessee can continue to compute the business income on presumptive basis. Even if the assessee has maintained books of account and obtained an audit report, he may still opt to be governed by taxation on presumptive basis by not making the claim of being taxed on net income basis in the return of income.

2.3-2 Delay in filing the tax audit report - One of the pre-conditions for being governed by net income basis of taxation is that the assessee should furnish a tax audit report as required under section 44AB of the Act. Now, section 44AB of the Act provides that the tax audit report should be furnished on or before 31st October of the assessment year. Hence, on a strict literal interpretation, it appears that for the purpose of sections 44BB(3) and 44BBB(2) of the Act, the tax audit report has to be furnished before the said date and any delay may disentitle the assessee from making the claim to be governed by net income basis of taxation.

2.3-3 Loss - The sections provide that the Assessing Officer can make an assessment of the total income or loss. Such loss can be set off in accordance with the provisions of section 70 of the Act and carried forward and set off in accordance with provisions of section 72 of the Act. It appears that such carry forward loss can be set off against any business income, including presumptive income of the subsequent year, if the assessee decides to be so governed in that year.

2.3-4 Computation of income - In case the assessee opts to be governed by net basis of taxation, the computation of business income would be done by applying the provisions of sections 28 to 43B, including 40(a)(i), and also 44C of the Act. Further, the provisions of transfer pricing under sections 92 to 92F of the Act will also be applicable.

The assessee in view thereof, prepared profit and loss account and balance sheet in respect of said work being carried out from its Pune office. The assessee, however, claims that only profit element out of the said receipts was taxable in his hands and not the entire receipts.

The plea of the assessee that in order to execute any work contract, the assessee has to incur certain expenditure in order to earn the said remuneration was acceptable. In respect of the said contract with FIPL, the gross receipts for the year under consideration were Rs.1.55 crores and the entire receipts cannot be income of the assessee. There is no merit in the plea of the authorities below that the total expenditure has been booked by the assessee, in the absence of any details being brought on record to the effect. Accordingly, the expenditure relatable to such receipts is duly allowable in the hands of the assessee and the entire receipts cannot be brought to the tax in the hands of the assessee. In the entirety of the above facts and circumstances, the estimation of income has to be made on account of such receipts by applying net profit rate of 20 per cent as against the plea of the assessee that net profit rate of 10 per cent be applied. 1. An assessee engaged in Transport Business acquires a truck on 1st September for, say, Rs. 5 lakhs and the purchase is financed by borrowing about Rs. 3 lacs @ 18% p.a. The truck is leased to a public sector undertaking for a rent of Rs. 18,000 per month. The income computation may work out as follows: The assessee can claim loss (and thus, declare a lower amount than the specified amount) by filing appropriate return, complying with other requirements (like, maintenance of books, audit, adduce evidence, etc.).

He may have to produce evidence relating to:

Date of acquisition and when it was put to use.

Cost of acquisition of truck.

Proof of borrowing for acquisition of truck.

Amount borrowed was actually used for acquiring truck.

Agreement for lease.

Amount of rent and that no other consideration was received; and the truck was used by lessee only and was not given to any one else and that no other income arose from the truck.

Confirmation from the lessee.

2. An assessee engaged in civil construction business has agreed to carry out certain work relating to fixing tiles of particular brand. The cost of tiles is, say Rs. 18 per sq. ft. Total area is, say 20,000 sq.ft. It has got a fixed price contract of say Rs. 5,00,000, including cost of tiles, without escalation. Labour contract given is say @ Rs. 3 per sq. ft. His estimated profit was Rs. 80,000. The deemed profits were Rs. 40,000. After completing l/4th work, the tile manufacturer increases the rate of tiles by Rs. 4 per sq.ft. Thus, his profits went down to Rs. 20,000. He can return Rs. 20,000 as his income, and submit the following as evidence:

Fixed price contract.

Fact that no escalation was allowed to him.

Purchase costs.

Fact that he did purchase the 75% requirement after price increase.

Labour contract and its costs.

The evidence requirement stated above is only illustrative. However, it may be pointed out that it will have to be proved that profits earned were lower than the specified profits.

1.11-4 At what stage evidence should be produced? - Section 44AD(5)/44AE(6) reads:

"Nothing contained in... this section shall apply, where the assessee claims and proves that the profits ... are lower... and thereupon..." [Emphasis supplied]

Considering the language of the provisions, it is felt that evidence should be produced or filed along with the return/claim.

In practical life this may be difficult inasmuch as the degree of proof and satisfaction required are difficult to determine. Accordingly, an assessee will have to take an utmost care while making such claim.

If an assessee does not substantiate his claim and/or does not file evidence to prove the claim, it could be contended by the tax department that requirement of the above provisions are not complied with and, accordingly, it may apply the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 44AD and/or sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 44AE, as the case may be.

However, considering the practical difficulties, it is felt that the CBDT may lay down instructions in this behalf and may direct at least that an opportunity may be provided to an assessee to lead the evidence.

If no evidence is produced by the assessee, it is evident that the requirements cannot be considered to have been met and accordingly, AO may then be free to make an assessment based on prescribed amount(s) as per the New Provisions.

l.11-5 Effects of 'Claim for a lower amount' - Following effects of a 'claim for the lower amount' will ensue:

Once a claim for assessment at a lower amount of profits is made, the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 44AD/44AE would not apply, as a result of which, if the claim is accepted, the taxable profits may be the lower amount, subject to any addition or disallowance.

The profits computation will have to be made in accordance with the provisions of sections 28 to 43C.

Exemption from maintenance of books of account or audit would not be available. Accordingly, the provisions of section 44AA and/or section 44AB will have to be complied with.

As discussed in details above, the necessary evidence in support of lower profits will have to be produced.

The Assessing Officer will have to proceed to make assessment under section 143(3) which implies:

(a)

Notices under section 142 and/or under section 143(2) of the Act.

(b)

Formal hearing(s) at which the evidence may be produced by the assessee as also further evidence as may be required will have to be produced.

(c)

Consideration of all evidences and material.

(d)

On that basis, a written order of assessment of the income and determination of sum payable by the assessee.

FAQ 56. Mr. A has opted for the presumptive scheme under Section 44AD in respect of one of his businesses. Is the auditor required to mention details of such business in the audit report?

Yes. He should report the nature of the presumptive business correctly in Clause 10(a) of Form No. 3CD. In case the profit and loss account of the assessee includes any profit declared under the presumptive scheme (Section 44AD, 44AE, 44AF, 44B, 44BB, 44BBA, 44BBB), then it is mandatory to mention the amount of such profit and the section under which the same is declared in Clause No. 12 of Form 3CD. The tax auditor is not required to indicate if the amount of presumptive income has been correctly computed under the relevant section relating to presumptive taxation. The reporting requirement is satisfied if the amount as per profit and loss account is reported.

FAQ 57. How to ensure that the profit has been computed correctly if the profit & loss account also includes the profit computed on a presumptive basis?

If the profit and loss account of the assessee also includes the presumptive income, the common business expenditure has to be apportioned to arrive at the correct amount of profit credited to the profit and loss account and assessable on a presumptive basis. The tax auditor, in such a situation, should arrive at a fair and reasonable estimate of such expenditure on the basis of evidence in possession of the assessee or by asking the assessee to prepare such an estimate, which should be checked by him.

ILLUSTRATIONS

1. An assessee engaged in Transport Business acquires a truck on 1st September for, say, Rs. 5 lakhs and the purchase is financed by borrowing about Rs. 3 lacs @ 18% p.a. The truck is leased to a public sector undertaking for a rent of Rs. 18,000 per month. The income computation may work out as follows: The assessee can claim loss (and thus, declare a lower amount than the specified amount) by filing appropriate return, complying with other requirements (like, maintenance of books, audit, adduce evidence, etc.). He may have to produce evidence relating to:

■ Date of acquisition and when it was put to use.

■ Cost of acquisition of truck.

■ Proof of borrowing for acquisition of truck.

■ Amount borrowed was actually used for acquiring truck.

■ Agreement for lease.

■ Amount of rent and that no other consideration was received; and the truck was used by lessee only and was not given to any one else and that no other income arose from the truck.

■ Confirmation from the lessee.

2. An assessee engaged in civil construction business has agreed to carry out certain work relating to fixing tiles of particular brand. The cost of tiles is, say Rs. 18 per sq. ft. Total area is, say 20,000 sq.ft. It has got a fixed price contract of say Rs. 5,00,000, including cost of tiles, without escalation. Labour contract given is say @ Rs. 3 per sq. ft. His estimated profit was Rs. 80,000. The deemed profits were Rs. 40,000. After completing l/4th work, the tile manufacturer increases the rate of tiles by Rs. 4 per sq.ft. Thus, his profits went down to Rs. 20,000. He can return Rs. 20,000 as his income, and submit the following as evidence:

■ Fixed price contract.

■ Fact that no escalation was allowed to him.

■ Purchase costs.

■ Fact that he did purchase the 75% requirement after price increase.

■ Labour contract and its costs.

The evidence requirement stated above is only illustrative. However, it may be pointed out that it will have to be proved that profits earned were lower than the specified profits.

1.11-4 At what stage evidence should be produced? - Section 44AD(5)/44AE(6) reads:

"Nothing contained in... this section shall apply, where the assessee claims and proves that the profits ... are lower... and thereupon..." [Emphasis supplied]

Considering the language of the provisions, it is felt that evidence should be produced or filed along with the return/claim.

In practical life this may be difficult inasmuch as the degree of proof and satisfaction required are difficult to determine. Accordingly, an assessee will have to take an utmost care while making such claim.

If an assessee does not substantiate his claim and/or does not file evidence to prove the claim, it could be contended by the tax department that requirement of the above provisions are not complied with and, accordingly, it may apply the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 44AD and/or sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 44AE, as the case may be.

However, considering the practical difficulties, it is felt that the CBDT may lay down instructions in this behalf and may direct at least that an opportunity may be provided to an assessee to lead the evidence.

If no evidence is produced by the assessee, it is evident that the requirements cannot be considered to have been met and accordingly, AO may then be free to make an assessment based on prescribed amount(s) as per the New Provisions.

l.11-5 Effects of 'Claim for a lower amount' - Following effects of a 'claim for the lower amount' will ensue:

■ Once a claim for assessment at a lower amount of profits is made, the provisions of sub-section (1) of section 44AD/44AE would not apply, as a result of which, if the claim is accepted, the taxable profits may be the lower amount, subject to any addition or disallowance.

■ The profits computation will have to be made in accordance with the provisions of sections 28 to 43C.

■ Exemption from maintenance of books of account or audit would not be available. Accordingly, the provisions of section 44AA and/or section 44AB will have to be complied with.

■ As discussed in details above, the necessary evidence in support of lower profits will have to be produced.

■ The Assessing Officer will have to proceed to make assessment under section 143(3) which implies:

(a) Notices under section 142 and/or under section 143(2) of the Act.

(b) Formal hearing(s) at which the evidence may be produced by the assessee as also further evidence as may be required will have to be produced.

(c) Consideration of all evidences and material.

(d) On that basis, a written order of assessment of the income and determination of sum payable by the assessee.

Charging for works contract

20. There is a wide difference between the invoicing process of WC, on the one hand, and sale of goods and other services on the other. In the case of WC for construction services, bills submitted are subject to certification by architect/engineers and other agencies. Deductions are made therefrom for various reasons. Clients make the payment thereafter and, that too, in instalments. Moreover, as per the terms of the contract, certain percentage of the amount billed is held as security deposit for performance guarantee. Secondly, in the case of VAT, liability is computed on mercantile basis, i.e., the amount billed. However, in the case of ST, liability for payment of tax arises on receipt of contract money only. As can be seen, there is a wide gap between methodology to be adopted for computation of tax liability under VAT and ST.

Since Explanation (a) to clause (i ) provides for the computation under VAT as the base for computation under ST, it can function only if the basic foundation in both the cases is the same. To the extent of divergence between the two, conflicts are bound to arise. To that extent operation of clause (a) to Explanation will raise a number of issues.

Advance received

21. In the case of WC, at times, advance payment is being made by the contractee. This may not raise any issue under the VAT. However, in terms of provisions of section 65(105), and Explanation 3 to section 67 of the Act, ST is required to be paid thereon. At the time of receipt of advance, there is no certainty as to in which month billing for the work done will take place. Apart from that, in the case of large contracts, billing takes place periodically, resulting in more than one bill depending upon progress of the work done. In such cases, the assessee will have no option but to keep track of ST paid in advance and make adjustments of it against the liability arising in future. This will be a complex process and there are bound to be mistakes. Apart from that, problems will arise at the time of filing of half-yearly returns, i.e., ST-3.

Tax credit illusory

6. It appears that cross settlement of input tax credit between the services and the goods is more on paper than real. Often the input tax credit for goods consumed in the service sector is obtained from dealers who cannot provide cenvatable invoices. The supply of goods is widespread among various dealers not all of whom provide cenvatable bills or cater to the requirements of the end-user who is a taxable service provider.

Similarly goods used in service contracts are not necessarily purchased from the first stage or second stage dealer or from the manufacturer directly. The input credit for goods consumed in service contracts is largely illusory as the output service provider purchases inputs from available sources of supply and on such terms as to credit and quantity which suit his business needs. The input credit for goods is thus not available as the cenvatable invoice essential for claiming the input credit is not there but only an ordinary purchase invoice to support the purchase of goods. Goods which are purchased under cenvatable invoices and undergoing further process not amounting to manufacture lose their cenvatable advantage when they are sold again in the processed stage; the processor is not a manufacturer of any new goods and the CENVAT chain is broken at his level and cannot be continued further into the hands of the next consumer.

Drawing the attention of the Committee to Accounting Standard-7(AS-7) on 'Accounting for Construction Contracts; paras 7.3 and 7.4 wherein it is mentioned that provision for losses should be made if the company anticipates that there is likelihood of losses in the remaining part of the contract, the company averred that if a contract extended for a period of three or four years, there was difficulty in quantifying the losses anticipated for the remaining portion of the contract as the reasons for possible losses like cost escalation in materials, labour, etc., and losses due to floods, fire, drought, etc., were unpredictable. "9. Percentage of completion method.

9.1 Under the percentage of completion method, the amount of, revenue recognised is determined by reference to the stage of completion of the contract activity at the end of each accounting period. The advantage of this method of accounting for contract revenue is that it reflects revenue in the accounting period during which activity is undertaken to earn such revenue.

9.2 The stage of completion used to determine revenue to be recognised in the financial statements is measured in an appropriate manner. For this purpose no special weightage should be given to a single factor, instead, all relevant factors should be taken into consideration; for example, the proportion that costs incurred to date bear to the estimated total costs of the contract, by surveys which measure work performed and completion of a physical proportion of the contract work.

9.3 Progress payments and advances received from customers may not necessarily reflect the stage of completion and therefore cannot usually be treated as equivalent to revenue earned.

(ii)payments to sub-contractors to the extent that they do not reflect the amount of work performed under the sub-contract.

9.5 The application of the percentage of completion method is subject to a risk of error in making estimates. For this reason, profit is not recognised in the financial statements unless the outcome of the contract can be reliably estimated. If the outcome cannot be reliably estimated, the percentage of completion method is not used.

9.6 While recognising the profit under this method, an appropriate allowance for future unforeseeable factors which may affect the ultimate quantum of profit is generally made on either a specific or a percentage basis.

9.7 In the case of fixed price contracts, the condition which will usually provide this degree of reliability are:

(i)total contract revenues to be received can be reliably estimated,

Though there are a few judgments upholding the liberal concept that prior period items should be allowed in the year in which they are accounted, with due respect, it is submitted that such a proposition may not find favour with the majority view. To error is human and common and one should not be penalised for an error irrevocably.

In this connection, the difference between expenditure of an earlier year debited to the profit and loss account and the expenditure relating to an earlier year which crystallised during the year on account of the claim being preferred for the first time by the party concerned during the year, as stressed by the Taxation Committee of ICAI in its 'Guidance Note on Tax Audit under section 44AB of the Act', is very relevant for practitioners while considering presentation of prior period items. In the latter case, the Committee emphasises, that even though the expenditure relates to an earlier year it can be considered as arising during the year on the basis that the liability materalised or crystallised during the year and, therefore, would not constitute a prior period item. Such items are also allowable as deduction under the Act. But if they are shown as prior period items in the tax audit report, there is likelihood of their being disallowed as prima facie adjustments under section 143(1)(a) of the Act although such action is unwarranted.

Accounting for construction contracts - AS 7

6. This standard deals with construction contracts generally and recognises two methods of accounting, viz., percentage of completion method and completed contract method. At the outset, it has to be mentioned that this standard does not throw much light on contracts for construction of commercial and residential complexes which are gaining momentum in many cities due to scarcity of land. Considering that such contracts involve peculiar complications arising because of sharing of land and in identifying accrual of revenue, it would be appropriate for the ICAI to consider issuing a separate standard to cover such situations. The business of construction merits separate consideration, in view of recent developments and the multitude of complexities involved. Hence, only board issues are discussed herein. Regarding the method, there is conflict in judicial pronouncements. While the completed contract method is shunned on the ground that under the Act, income for each year should be determined separately, there are some decisions in favour of this method and they relate mostly to adventure in the nature of trade involving development of land. In the following cases, this method was upheld: K.H. Mody, In re [1940] 8 ITR 179 (Bom.), Asstt. CIT v. Madan Lal Ahuja [1982] 136 ITR 640 (All.) and CIT v. A.K.A.R. Family [1941] 9 ITR 347 (Rang.). All these cases are of a single adventure in the nature of trade involving purchase of plots for sale and hence, it was held that profit can be ascertained only on sale of all plots. In the case of D.K. Enterprises v. ITO [1991] 39 ITD 394 , the attempt of the Assessing Officer to assess estimated income on work-in-progress was rejected by the Bombay Bench of the Tribunal because the completed contract method was consistently followed in the earlier years in which it was accepted and also as no construction activity had actually commenced. A similar view was expressed by the Bombay Bench of the Tribunal in Shapoorji Pallonji & Co. (Rajkot) (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [1994] 49 ITD 479 . Recently, this method was upheld in the case of CIT v. V.S. Dempo (Income-tax Review July, 1995, page 15) by the Bombay High Court as mentioned in the summary of a Study Circle Meeting of Bombay Chartered Accountant Journal (Nov. 95-585).
