Deviations from the standards prescribed by the ICAI warrant qualificatory remarks from the auditor and the Assessing Officer will be well within his rights to probe into such issues and quantify the proper income while framing the assessment even under the existing provisions. By its very nature income from business or profession defies precision in computation. A mathematically correct income from a running business is not generally feasible to arrive at due to various factors affecting the business and such factors are not amenable to precise computation. Risks in business both in relation to completed transactions and those lying in the womb of future compel the businessman to estimate his income and not measure it mathematically. Conservatism is built into business computations and lurking fear of the unknown future influences business sentiment.

Any system of accounting will have to come to terms with the business realities and be acceptable from the business point of view for wide acceptance and implementation. A pedantic approach, however, scholarly it may seem, is unlikely to be widely followed unless it is realistic from the point of view of the businessman.

Certainly the ICAI has not come in for praise in the memorandum accompanying the Finance Bill for setting Accounting Standards after much research and debate. The standards are described as lacking requisite rigidity with too many alternatives, butter-fingered and so resulting in tax avoidance.

But the standards are mandatory and disclosed in published accounts compulsorily and when contravened, reported upon by the auditor. The user of such accounts now knows the effects of non-compliance with the standards of accounting prescribed by the ICAI, though such reporting may be in fine print. But the Assessing Officer is posted with this information and equipped with the Tax Audit Report under section 44AB of the Act, he can unravel the mystery in the accounts to assess the proper income.

In prescribing accounting standards for the entire field of business and industry and profession, a certain amplitude necessarily comes in. This is because of the different requirements of accounting for various types of business, but the underlying requirement in any business accounting is the true and fair view of the final results.

The accounting standards prescribed by the ICAI after due deliberation cannot, thus, be termed as ‘flexible’ with a connotation that they help avoid payment of tax. Nor can they be truncated in the name of standardisation as that would result in inadequate coverage.

Instead of venturing to set fresh standards under section 145, the Government would do well to adopt the standards set by the ICAI under the Income-tax Act as it has done for the companies under the recently promulgated Companies (Amendment) Ordinance, 1998. It would be wiser to align the measurement of income under section 145 with the scope of total income under section 5 to avoid potential litigation.

Conclusion

7. An attempt has been made above to look at the amended section 145 from the standpoint of section 5 and the inherent nature of income as it comes in for measurement is also seen. Income is often found to present itself rather than accrue continuously on a time-bound linear scale and any system of measurement has to face this fact.

And income is such a concept that it is not confined to the two domains of accounting methods exclusively. The observation of Lord Tankerton in CIT v. Sarangpur Cotton Mfg. Co. Ltd. [1938] 6 ITR 36, 40 (PC) on section 145 that "their Lordships are clearly of the opinion that the section relates to a method of accounting regularly employed by the assessee for his own purposes - in this case for the purpose of the company’s business - and does not relate to a method of making up a statutory return for assessment of income-tax" appears to be valid even after the amendment of section 145 by the Finance Act, 1995 [Emphasis supplied].

4.14-11 An assessee would be obliged to file the return of income before the due date applicable in his case and in the return declare income, based on his option, as said above.

4.14-11a Assessment provision - Note the following:

If an assessee chooses to return the specified amount as his income in the return of income, unless he has some other income, the assessment may be completed by sending an intimation under section 143(1)(a) of the Act and there would be no cause for scrutiny as the amount of income is determined by the section itself.

Further, as said above, the department would be bound to assess the assessee on the specified amount for assessing the tax liability.

There cannot be any question of prima facie adjustment insofar as intimation is concerned except any arithmetical error.

In a case where higher amount of income is returned, the same position would prevail, as the higher amount declared has to be adopted as the taxable income, in terms, of sub-section (1) of section 44AD. There would be no scope for any adjustment.

As said above, where income returned is specified amount or a higher amount, possibly, there may not be any scrutiny assessment, unless the Assessing Officer wants to examine certain other information, like gross receipts, cash credits, sources of investment, claims for deductions under Chapter VI-A, etc.

4.14-11b Advance tax - Sub-section (4) provides that an eligible assessee is not obliged to pay advance tax in respect of income relating to eligible business.

It implies that the exemption from payment of advance tax is restricted to profits and gains of eligible business. In respect of the other income of an eligible assessee, he would be liable to pay advance tax thereon, in terms of the provisions of Chapter XVII-C of the Act.

Consideration received on sale of fixed assets employed in the business cannot form part of the gross receipts on account of business, i.e., civil construction business. It arises on account of sale of assets employed in the business.

Any security or other deposits obtained from employees or sub contractors cannot form part of gross receipts. Works contract tax or sales tax collected would form part of the gross receipts.

Retention money may not be considered as part of gross receipts.

Receipts arising on account of sale of scrap, etc., would form part of gross receipts on account of business.

Any refund of sales tax or works contract tax, etc., may constitute a part of gross receipts on account of business. However, any income-tax refund or interest thereon would not constitute part of the gross receipts of business. Interest on refund would, however, be separately taxable.

In case of contract with material, where a part or the whole of it is supplied by the contractee, and is included in the value of contract, the value of materials supplied by the contractee would not form part of gross receipts of the assessee. In this connection, a reference may be made to the decision of the Supreme Court in Brij Bhushan Lal Parduman Kumar v. CIT [1978] 115 ITR 524.

The value of work in progress may not form part of gross receipts. However, if in respect of such work in progress, a bill/claim has been made and approved by the contractee, then to the extent of value billed, having regard to terms of contract, such value would form part of the gross receipts, as the accrued value. If in terms of the contract the work is approved, but, merely bill is not made, it is felt that value of such work in progress would form part of the gross receipts.

The value, if any, of stock-in-trade would not form part of gross receipts.

Application Guide-ICDS-III (Revised) - How to apply ICDS-III (Revised) in computation of income

This ICDS may be applied as under:

(a)

Identify each construction contract for which separate contract account needs to be opened.

(b)

Identification of each separate construction based on the definition of 'construction contract' [Para 3.5.] and combining and segmenting construction contracts in accordance with their substance [Paras 3.11 to 3.13]

(c)

The exercise in (a) and (b) above will serve dual purpose-for accounting as per AS) 7 and for computation of income as per section 43CB and this ICDS.

(d)

Apply percentage of completion method [Para 3.10] for each construction contract separately as per steps (e) to (p) below

(e)

Identify contract revenues and contract costs separately for each separate construction contract identified as above for which separate contract account has been opened. [Paras 3.14 to 3.35]

(f)

Determine stage of completion of each construction contract separately [Para 3.35-1]

(g)

Recognise contract costs and contract revenues with reference to% of completion for each construction contract which has crossed the 25% completion stage. Thus contract profit/contract loss would get recognised proportionate to% of completion. Add up such proportionate profits and losses and deduct period costs and other deductions from the aggregate of proportionate profits and losses to determine taxable income [Para 3.35-1]

(h)

If stage of completion of any construction contract is 25% or less, recognise contract costs already incurred and recognise contract costs equal to contract costs incurred [Para 3.35-1]

(i)

Where, on any contract which has crossed 25% stage of completion, full anticipated loss has been provided as per (AS) 7 instead of proportionate loss as per(g) above, make adjustment for the difference in computation of income in order to comply with ICDSs.

(j)

Where proportionate profit has not been recognised in accounts as per AS 7 in respect of a contract that has crossed 25% completion stage on the grounds that outcome of contract cannot be estimated reliably, add proportionate profit as per (g) above to net profit/loss as per P&L in computation of income.

(k)

Where on any contract which has not crossed 25% stage of completion full anticipated loss has been provided as per (AS) 7, make adjustment for the loss so provided in computation of income in order to comply with ICDSs.

(l)

Where proportionate profit was offered to tax in any past FY/FYs as per (g) above though no profit was recognised in accounts as outcome of contract could not be reliably estimated and the same has been booked in accounts of current period as per AS 7 since outcome could now be reliably estimated,deduct such profit amount booked in accounts in current period.

(m)

In case of Ind AS companies, following need to be added to net profit as per Ind ASP&L in statement of computation of total income

(i)

Profits from contracts which have crossed 25% stage of completion but Contract revenues recognition postponed due to applicability of at a point in time basis.

(ii)

Proportionate profit not recognised in accounts on POCM basis in respect of construction contracts which have crossed 25% stage of completion.

(iii)

Anticipated Loss in excess of proportionate loss recognised in respect of construction contracts which have crossed 25% stage of completion.

(iv)

Finance element computed by discounting to NPV (difference between contract revenues and NPV of contract revenues).

(n)

In case of Ind AS companies, following need to be deducted from net profit:

(i)

Profit recognised in accounts in current FY on point in time basis in respect of contracts from which profit was offered to tax in past FYs on POCM basis as per ICDS III.

(ii)

Finance element computed by discounting to NPV (difference between contract revenues and NPV of contract revenues)pertaining to current year.

(o)

Adjustments for complying with this ICDS as per (i) to (k) above are not to be made in accounts but in computation of income.

[2011] 15 taxmann.com 330 (Article)

Allowability of foreseeable losses in construction contracts

ABHISHEK WORAH

CA

NAVEEN WADHWA

CA

The taxability of revenues and incomes in respect of construction contracts represents a vexed issue before the revenue authorities. There are conflicting decisions by the various Benches of the ITAT on the issue of allowance for foreseeable losses in the construction contracts. In this article the authors have examined the issue in details as per the Accounting Standards and have cited various case laws where decisions have been taken in favour or against such claims.

INTRODUCTION

1. The taxability of revenues and incomes in respect of construction contracts represents a vexed issue before the revenue authorities.

The accounting for construction contracts in the financial statements is governed by the Accounting Standard (AS)-7 - Construction Contracts issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI). As per AS-7, the contract revenue and contract costs are to be recognized as revenue and expenses, respectively, by reference to the stage of completion of the contract at the reporting date. This method of recognizing contract revenue and expenses with reference to stage of completion of the contract is popularly referred to as percentage of completion method (POCM). Hence, the revenue, expenses and profit with reference to a contract are reported based on the proportion of the work completed.

Accounting Standards issued by the ICAI advocate the view that financial results should be arrived at after considering the anticipated losses and expenses on the ground of 'prudence' and 'conservatism'. Inter alia, AS – 7 requires that an expected loss on the construction contract should be recognized as an expense immediately. The relevant paras 31, 32, 35 and 36 of AS-7 dealing with the recognition of loss in contract are reproduced hereinbelow:

"Para 31….. An expected loss on the construction contract should be recognised as an expense immediately in accordance with paragraph 35.

Para 32….. However, even though the outcome of the contract cannot be estimated reliably, it may be probable that total contract costs will exceed total contract revenue. In such cases, any expected excess of total contract costs over total contract revenue for the contract is recognised as an expense immediately in accordance with paragraph 35.

Para 35. When it is probable that total contract costs will exceed total contract revenue, the expected loss should be recognised as an expense immediately.

Para 36. The amount of such a loss is determined irrespective of:

(a) whether or not work has commenced on the contract;

(b) the stage of completion of contract activity; or

(c) the amount of profits expected to arise on other contracts which are not treated as a single construction contract in accordance with paragraph 8."

As per the above paras, the expected loss in contract is to be recognized immediately irrespective of the stage of completion of the contract or commencement of the work of contract. On this basis the contractors (particularly the large companies undertaking big infrastructure projects, telecom projects and other building contracts having high values) do make provision for foreseeable losses, if they are of the opinion that the project is likely to result in a loss initially while making the estimates of contract revenue and costs.

The recognition of loss in a contract is also provided by the Ind AS-11 on Construction Contract1.

Hence, the contractors create a provision for foreseeable losses, in case they are of the opinion that the project is likely to result in a loss. The provision is created while making an estimate of the contract cost and revenue in the initial stages of a contract.

ALLOWABILITY OF PROVISION FOR FORESEEABLE LOSSES UNDER THE NORMAL COMPUTATION PROVISIONS OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961 ('THE ACT')

2. As per section 4 of the Act, income-tax shall be charged in respect of the total income of the previous year of every person. Thus, for the purpose of computing yearly profits or gains, each year is considered as a separate self-contained period of time. Any profit earned or loss incurred before its commencement is irrelevant. While ascertaining the profits and gains of one year, one may not deduct a loss/expense which had, in fact, been incurred before or may be incurred after the relevant previous year. If one does so he would not arrive at the true profits and gains of the year 2..

This is also in consonance with the judicial view that cash and mercantile systems of accounting do not encompass every conceivable business activity to bring out the true profits for the purpose of tax and that other methods exist in the ‘hybrid or heterogeneous’ zone and that it would be more proper to characterise the recognition of income under the ‘arisal basis’ in a given situation than under the ‘accrual basis’ on the basis of the accounting employed. Lulla, Seventh ITO [1989] 176 ITR 253/[1988] 40 Taxman 329 (Bom.) dealing with an advocate’s accounts and the point of time when income ‘arises’ in such cases is an example where mercantile and cash systems were held inapplicable in the facts and circumstances of the case. Though the fees of an advocate is included in the advances received from the clients, the time of taxation of the same is determined by his method of accounting whereby ‘income arises’ for tax.

Thus, the amendment confining the systems of accounting to only accrual or cash for the purpose of computation of taxable income conflicts with the concept of taxability of total income on its ‘arising in previous year’ as provided in section 5. Besides, the limitation and inadequacy of the two systems to compute the true profit income on arisal basis make them unsuitable for such applications.

Neither white nor black but grey

5. Secondly, the amendment to section 145 presumes that all computations of business income are possible within the range of the cash or mercantile systems of accounting in prescribing computation according to them only. It is a fact that not every business activity takes place in the form of receipt or accrual for these accounting systems to record and measure. A casual perusal of balance sheets of non-banking financial companies engaged in hire purchase and leasing would show that myriad methods of accounting for such transactions are adopted by them and change of methods midway is not uncommon.

The above-mentioned transactions are usually spread over three to five years and the income is shown to ‘arise’ over the period of the contracts according to certain methods of accounting. The accounting methods employed to compute the income are neither cash nor mercantile but only determine the arisal of income embedded in such contracts in each year. So also in construction contracts and real estate development, the profits are ‘spreadover’ the period of the contract in relation to the job done. The spreadover is neither under the mercantile nor under the cash system of accounting but estimated. Under the mercantile system, the right to receive the income is essential whereas under the cash system, the receipt of income would make it taxable and none would operate during the period of execution of the contract when profits are indeterminate. It is relevant here to look into monographs on accounting issued by the ICAI for certain types of business.

In the monograph on accounting for poultry farming, 1980 edition, the issue of capital costs of chicken and the amortisation of their cost over a period is dealt with. Chicken are classified according to their age in batches and accounting starts with each batch as basis.

This measure deals with the profitability of the business from year to year and valid in normal business years when no natural calamity or disease strikes the poultry farm. The capital cost of a chicken is spread over its estimated egg lying period and the charge to each year is that proportion of the capital cost as the actual yield bears to the estimated total yield. The yielding period is not an accounting year but extends over 18 months. This accounting of cost of chicken depleted or used in the process of the business also directly affects the valuation of chicken on hand as at the end of the year. Added to the above is the valuation of natural accretion of new born chicken to the existing stock.

It is evident that income does not accrue in the form of a legal claim (due and receivable or payable) in this business, but it ‘arises’ or presents itself in each year if measured in the manner suggested in the monograph. The basic features, viz., the coming of age of chicks and their yielding period thereafter do not lend themselves to any precise annual measurement needed for accounting of the same and some estimated basis is used instead and this results in some kind of ‘spread over’ of profit or income over the effective life of a batch of chicken.

The monograph dealing with accounting in Rubber Plantations, 1983 edition offers another perspective. Rubber trees take six to eight years to develop from planting and their rubber yielding period spreads over many years. While the monograph recommends writing off of the capital cost of the trees over their productive life, it notes that business practice is different. While the write-off is not done, in lieu thereof, a rehabilitation reserve is built over 25 to 30 years sufficient to replant the area exploited and on that basis, the profits of the business are measured. For the practical businessman, what it takes to build or create a new asset after the existing asset exhausts itself is more important and, accordingly, he allocates so much out of each year’s revenue for such build-up and only the balance available is considered surplus.

While the write-off is not done, in lieu thereof, a rehabilitation reserve is built over 25 to 30 years sufficient to replant the area exploited and on that basis, the profits of the business are measured. For the practical businessman, what it takes to build or create a new asset after the existing asset exhausts itself is more important and, accordingly, he allocates so much out of each year’s revenue for such build-up and only the balance available is considered surplus. The accounts of a forest contractor taking forest lands on lease or other acquisition for timber presents a similar problem. The forest wealth increases or decreases due to natural causes apart from human efforts. While some timber-yielding trees multiply on their own, others require systematic replanting over the period of lease. The wealth of timber, so crucial to determine the profits of the business, is reckoned on yearly survey basis for accounting.

The monograph on Accounting for Livestock, 1983 edition, presents yet another dimension to measurement and recognition of income. While the livestock multiply as a natural consequence over a period of time, they also gain or lose their value according to their status as a ‘producer’ or ‘worker’. The accretion in physical numbers, and more important, the qualitative development in livestock by way of their capacity to yield or work determine their value and so the profit of the unit. The valuation of the livestock based on the qualitative and quantitative aspects is a key factor in recognition of income in this business. Sheep kept for wool shearing is a fine example cited in the monograph regarding accretion in their value.

If the profit is to be recognised this way on an annual basis, it is neither accrual nor cash system of accounting in their pure form but only recognition of income ‘as it presents itself’.

It is clear from the examples dealt with above, that income seldom accrues or is received in all cases and it would be an oversimplification to think that either the accrual system of accounting or the cash system of accounting would measure all business transactions and compute the income there from. On the contrary, almost in all cases, it is recognition of income at a stage or ‘arisal’ thereof and methods of recognition vary.

Even in pure accrual or cash system of accounting of basic transactions, factors as noted earlier intervene and the result is mostly ‘arisal of income’ in the broad and proper sense. Natural factors do not adhere to any uniformity and predictability and the results of such factors have to be recognised when they appear or present themselves.

It is by limiting the computation of taxable income to the two systems of accounting that the newly recast section 145 is posing trouble to the assessee having income from business or other sources. To invoke section 144 in such a situation when the recommended methods are inadequate (as seen above) would result in gross injustice to the assessee and the result is litigation.

Apart from the above, it is the true and fair view that is more important to achieve through any method of accounting, whether pure bred or hybrid. Where hybrid or heterogeneous is considered advisable in consonance with basic accounting concepts, it should be adopted.

Thus, it would be wrong to shut out other methods of accounting and confine only to cash or mercantile systems of accounting to determine the profits of every type of business or profession. The cash and mercantile systems are not bereft or blemish and both are stated to be ‘somewhat rough’ and ‘in some cases may not give a clear picture of the true profits earned and certainly not of taxable profits’ as per the Supreme Court in A. Krishnaswami Mudaliar’s case (supra).

It sounds odd to note that suitable hybrid and heterogeneous systems bringing out the true income are shunned in favour of Cash/Mercantile systems and that too in the name of attempting to arrive at the ‘correct tax payable’. While the cash system of accounting is given recognition in the amendment to section 145 as an acceptable basis of computation of income, the hybrid which is conceptually superior and heterogeneous which is more apt to adopt in many situations are discarded as giving rise of avoidance of tax. And the standards of accounting prescribed by the Central Government are partial in coverage as they deal with Mercantile System only.

Assessment and Accounting Standards

6. Flexibility in accounting standards prescribed by the ICAI is also cited as a reason for tax avoidance in the memorandum explaining the amendment to section 145. As pointed out supra, business transactions are not uniform to fall in line between the two systems of accounting and even within the two systems, different standards are set for different types of transactions. A blanket approach will not bring out the fair estimate of the profit of the year. So long as a recognised standard followed consistently from year to year, the results are to be accepted and even this does not prevent the Assessing Officer from questioning the correctness or completeness of the accounts. Deviations from the standards prescribed by the ICAI warrant qualificatory remarks from the auditor and the Assessing Officer will be well within his rights to probe into such issues and quantify the proper income while framing the assessment even under the existing provisions.

As the company was recognising revenue in respect of even those contracts which were at their inception stage, i.e., they might not have progressed to a reasonable extent, the Committee was of the view that the procedure to that extent was apparently not in accordance with para 9.8 of AS-7 reproduced above.

Regarding provision for losses, the Committee noted that para 7.4 of AS-7 stated that "under both methods, provision is made for losses for the stage of completion reached on the contract. In addition, provision is usually made for losses on the remainder of the contract". Holding that the company's contention that para 7.4 was relevant only where 'completed contract method' was followed, was not correct, the Committee referred to para 13 of AS-7, dealing with "Provision for Foreseeable Losses", which recommends as below:

"13. Provision for Foreseeable Losses

13.1 When current estimates of total contract costs and revenues indicate a loss, provision is made for the entire loss on the contract irrespective of the amount of work done and the method of accounting followed. In some circumstances, the foreseeable losses may exceed the costs of work done to date. Provision is, nevertheless, made for the entire loss on the contract.

13.2 When a contract is of such magnitude that it can be expected to absorb a considerable part of the capacity of the enterprise for a substantial period, indirect costs to be incurred during the period of the completion of the contract are sometimes considered to be directly attributable to the contract and included in the calculation of the provisions for loss on the contract.

13.3 If a provision for loss is required, the amount of such provision is usually determined irrespective of:

(i)whether or not work has commenced on the contract;

(ii)the stage of completion of contract activity; and

(iii)the amount of profits expected to arise on other unrelated contracts.

13.4 The determination of a future loss on a contract may be subject to a high degree of uncertainty. In some of those cases, it is possible to provide for the future loss and in other cases only the existence of a contingent loss is disclosed."

Observing that the difficulty in quantifying the 'anticipated' losses was not the ground for not making a provision, the Committee felt that an estimate could be made on the basis of the given factors in the normal course of business. However, where determination of a future loss on a contract is subject to a high degree of uncertainty and it is not possible to provide for the future loss the Committee held that the existence of a contingent loss should at least be disclosed as recommended in AS-4 on "Contingencies and Events occurring After the Balance Sheet Date", issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India.

FAQ 32. How can tax auditor report payments referred to in section 43B if the same is unpaid as on the date of submission of tax audit report but paid before the due date of filing of return of income? Clause 26 of Form 3CD seek details of liability incurred in respect of any sum referred to in clause (a), (b), (c), (d), (e) or (f) of section 43B in the previous year and was paid or not paid on or before the due date for furnishing the Return of Income of the previous year.

Since the due date of filing of the tax audit report is one month before the due date of filing of return of income, it is practically not possible for the auditor to report if any payment is made after the filing of the tax audit report but before the due date of return of income.

To address this difficulty, the CBDT has inserted sub-rule (3) in Rule 6G. It provides that a person may get a revised audit report from an accountant and furnish it before the end of the relevant assessment year for which the report pertains. Thus, if there is payment after furnishing of the report, which necessitates a recalculation of disallowance under section 40 or section 43B, a revised report may be filed.

FAQ 33. If shares of members of AOP are unknown during the previous year, whether it is required to be reported in Form 3CD?

If shares of members are unknown during the previous year, the auditor needs to disclose this fact in Clause 9(a) of Form 3CD.

FAQ 34. How does the auditor need to report the interest inadmissible under section 23 MSMED Act, 2006?

Clause 22 of Form 3CD seeks the disclosure of the amount of interest inadmissible under section 23 of the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006.The tax auditor needs to report the amount of interest inadmissible under section 23 of the MSMED Act, 2006 irrespective of whether the amount of such interest has been debited to profit and loss account or not.

The auditor should verify that the auditee has disclosed the information as required under section 22 of the MSMED Act, 2006 in the financial statements under audit. If the auditee makes no disclosure in the financial statements, the tax auditor should appropriately qualify his report in Form No. 3CB and also report the fact of non-disclosure in clause 22 of Form No. 3CD.

FAQ 35. Whether it is mandatory to disclose the nature of all the businesses carried on by the assessee and any change therein?

Clause 10 of Form 3CD mandates disclosure of the nature of every business or profession carried on by an assessee during the previous year.

Any material change in the nature of business should be precisely disclosed. The change will include a change from manufacturer to the trader as well as a change in the principal line of business. Any addition to or permanent discontinuance of a particular line of business may also amount to change requiring reporting. However, temporary suspension of the business may not amount to change and therefore need not be reported.

FAQ 36. Mr A has opted for the presumptive scheme under section 44AD in respect of one of his businesses. Whether auditor is required to mention details of such business in the audit report?

In case the profit and loss account of the assessee includes any profit declared under the presumptive scheme (section 44AD, 44AE, 44AF, 44B, 44BB, 44BBA, 44BBB), then it is mandatory to mention the amount of such profit and the section under which the same is declared in Clause No. 12 of Form 3CD.The tax auditor is not required to indicate whether the amount of presumptive income has been correctly computed under the relevant section relating to presumptive taxation. The reporting requirement is satisfied if the amount per profit and loss account is reported.

(Read more : Presumptive Taxation Schemes on Taxmann.com/Practice)

FAQ 37. How to ensure that the profit has been computed correctly if the profit & loss account includes the profit computed on a presumptive basis?

If the profit and loss account of the assessee also includes the presumptive income, the common business expenditure has to be apportioned to arrive at the correct amount of profit. Clause 22 of Form 3CD seeks the disclosure of the amount of interest inadmissible under section 23 of the Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006. 4.1 For a Service provider rendering services under the category of construction services, opting for Notification No. 26/2012, dated 20-6-2012 whether it is mandatory or not?

After carefully reading the Notification No. 26/2012, dated 20-6-2012 one reaches the conclusion that there is nowhere mention of in this notification that it is a mandatory notification. Besides, this notification is a conditional notification and benefit of the same is available only when some conditions are fulfilled. Conditional notification can never be mandatory and we can choose not to fulfil those conditions.

4.2 If answer to Q.1 above is in the negative, then can service provider claim that value of land or value of some materials is not included in the gross price charged from flat owners, then whether service provider can opt for the normal scheme specified under section 67?

Notification No. 26/2012, dated 20-6-2012 is a conditional notification. No where it stipulated that this is a mandatory notification. Thereby in a case such notification is not applicable then service provider would fall under the normal provisions of service tax and would be required to pay tax as per such provisions. The author would like to draw your attention towards the word 'service' defined in section 65B(44). "Service" means any activity carried out by a person for another for consideration, and includes a declared service, but shall not include an activity which constitutes merely a transfer of title in goods or immovable property, by way of sale, gift or in any other manner; or such transfer, delivery or supply of any goods which can be deemed to be a sale within the meaning of clause (29A) of article 366 of the Constitution.

Tax in this case would be payable on the value of services only and no tax is to be imposed on transfer of title in goods or immovable property, as given in the definition of service explained above. In fact, this has always case that the scope of service tax law cannot extend above the powers given to them under the constitution which is only to tax service portion in any activity. Notification No. 26/2012-ST, dated 20-6-2012 works within ambit of the constitutional power and gives a pre-defined proportion to compute the value of land and goods included in total consideration received by a builder.

Service provider can always opt for the basic schemes and pay tax only on the service portion, if he can correctly and without any bias compute the same.

4.3 How can a service provider compute and create documentary evidence to prove that ratio of materials to total cost is 70% in light of the facts that every project is separate one and exact calculation would be available only after completion of entire project, whereas payment of service tax is to be made on monthly basis from the receipt of first instalment?

It is the toughest part in the entire scheme. Herein first of all we have to understand that each project is a separate project for assessment of service tax of the same. After the completion of project he shall be required to pay tax on the final assessment of this project and the actual ratio that this project has seen, based upon the audited profit and loss account for the period under which it was under construction.

Besides, service provider may also analyze the option of provisional assessment which has already been provided for under the law.

For the benefit of readers the author would like to say that at times construction contract takes a decade to complete, however, in such period cost of construction does not escalate as fast as the prices of land. 5.1 Controversy relating to provision for foreseeable losses in construction contracts - The accounting practice of valuing unsold stocks at cost or net realisable value (market value) which is lower is widely accepted now. But when the same theory of prudence was applied to other anticipated losses in case of investments forming part of closing stock-in-trade, work-in-progress under construction contracts, fluctuations in foreign exchange transactions and other matters, litigations surfaced and persist till date.

In 1983, the Accounting Standards Board of the ICAI issued Accounting Standard (AS) 7, Accounting for Construction Contracts. Para 19 of the Standard stipulates as follows :

"19. A foreseeable loss on the entire contract should be provided for in the financial statements irrespective of the amount of work done and the method of accounting followed."

When the assessees started adopting the accounting practice envisaged in the above Accounting Standard (AS) 7, the tax authorities rejected the same. Following few cases are stated as examples.

In a case before The ITAT Mumbai Bench 'A' in Mazagon Dock Ltd. v. Jt. CIT [2009] 29 SOT 356 decided on February 18, 2009, the issue was whether as far as change in method of valuation of work-in-progress was concerned, in view of mandatory requirements of AS-7, it was a bona fide change, particularly in view of qualification made in this regard by statutory auditors as well as by the Comptroller & Auditor General of India. It was held as follows :

"The question that came up for consideration was as to whether the anticipated loss on the valuation of fixed price contract, in view of the mandatory requirements of the AS-7, was to be allowed in the year in which the contract had been entered into or it was to be spread over a period of contract, as was done by the assessee in earlier years. As far as the change in the method of valuation of work-in-progress was concerned, it could not be disputed that in view of mandatory requirements of the AS-7, it was a bona fide change in the method of valuation of work-in-progress, particularly in view of the qualification made in this regard by statutory auditors as well as by the Comptroller & Auditor General of India. Therefore, the observation of the Commissioner (Appeals) that the assessee had booked bogus loss was not correct. As far as the basis of estimation was concerned, the same was done on technical estimation basis and, therefore, merely because there were some variations in the figures furnished by the assessee at different stages, it could not be said that the estimated loss was not allowable. It was not disputed that the department in earlier years had allowed the loss on estimated basis having regard to the expenditure actually incurred in various years. Therefore, in principle, it was not disputed that the estimated loss under the present circumstances was an allowable deduction. However, merely because the change in method of accounting was bona fide, it could not lead to the inference that the income was also deducible properly under the Act. This aspect is very evident from the first proviso to section 145 as it stood prior to the amendment by the Finance Act, 1995 with effect from 1-4-1997. It could not be disputed that from the method adopted by the assessee, the assessee's income could not be deduced properly in the year in which the loss had been anticipated. As a matter of fact this aspect was not disputed by the Assessing Officer also. He had been swayed more by the revenue loss than by the correct principle to be applied. The matching principle of accounting was not of much significance in the present context because if the loss had been properly estimated in the year in which the contract had been entered into, then it had to be allowed in that very year and could not be spread over the period of contract. The matching principle is of relevance where income and expenditure, both are to be considered together. However, in the instant case, the effect of valuation of WIP would automatically affect the profits of subsequent years accordingly. Therefore, there was no reason for not accepting in principle the assessee's claim as being allowable."

FAQ 43. Which address should be reported in Clause 11 if the books of accounts are maintained in a computerised system?

Clause 11(b) requires reporting the address at which the books so maintained are kept. As per the "Guidance Note on Tax Audit" issued by the ICAI, when the books of account are maintained and generated through a computer system, the auditor should obtain from the assessee the details of the address of the place where the server is located or the principal place of business/Head office or registered office by whatever name called and mention the same accordingly in clause 11(b). If the books of account are stored on the cloud or online, a unique IP address of the same may be reported. The auditor should also specify which books of account have been maintained in the computer system and which records have been maintained in hard copy form.

The Guidance does not provide any direction on reporting in Clause 11 if the IP Address is not unique but a dynamic IP address. In that situation, the name of the cloud should be mentioned.

FAQ 46. An assessee has changed the method of accounting from mercantile to cash basis. What disclosure is required in Form 3CD?
